records.name: Mutation concurrency and the source-tree build lock
records.summary: Serializes resource mutations two ways: one coarse mutex inside the daemon covering every lifecycle verb, and a fail-fast kernel flock on the git toplevel covering the build phase across processes.
records.confidence_label: Both locks read in full and every caller enumerated; the contention error reproduced through redact.Text; no two-process race was actually staged, which would have needed a live mutation

relationships.note: opMu lives on the supervision lane's runtime service
the lock is held through build, install and activation of the artifact join
the pipeline build and deploy actions take the same lock
an in-process fallback runs outside opMu entirely
the monitor takes opMu before acting on a restart decision
nothing serializes apply, sync, reload, stop or remove across processes
the config file with no backup also has no writer lock
installing to a fresh inode and renaming is the other half of concurrent-safety

records.body:
Two operators, or two agents, or an agent and the daemon's own monitor, can all
reach the same resource at the same time. Cerberus has two locks for that and
they cover different things.

**Inside the daemon: one coarse mutex.** `ResourceRuntimeService` holds
`opMu sync.Mutex` for the entire duration of `ReloadResource`, `StopResource`,
`DeployResource`, `ApplyResource`, `SyncResource` and `RemoveResource`, and
`resource_monitor.go` takes the same mutex before acting on a restart decision.
It is not per-resource and it is not a read-write lock: every mutation served
by one daemon process queues behind every other. Two agents calling
`cerberus_resource_deploy` concurrently therefore serialize rather than race,
and the monitor cannot restart a resource in the middle of somebody's deploy.
The cost is that a slow deploy blocks an unrelated reload, which is a
throughput choice, not a correctness one.

**Across processes: an flock on the source tree.** `internal/buildlock` is 70
lines and every line is load-bearing. `Acquire` opens
`<root>/.cerberus-build.lock`, takes `LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB`, and on contention
decodes the holder record to produce

    build in progress for source tree <root> (resource "<id>", PID <n>,
    age <d>); retry when it finishes

It fails fast rather than waiting, so a second caller gets an answer instead of
a hang. It never unlinks the lock file, because removing it would let another
caller lock a different inode while a holder is still active. The kernel
releases the flock when the process exits, crashes included, so there is no
stale-lock recovery path to get wrong. The holder metadata is explicitly
diagnostic only — the comment notes it can be briefly incomplete while the
holder writes it, and the kernel lock is authoritative either way.

`WithBuildLock` in the local connector decides the lock's scope. It resolves
the build root from the strategy's `source.root`, then asks
`git rev-parse --show-toplevel` and locks *that*, so two resources built from
different subdirectories of one monorepo share a single lock. It is re-entrant
through a context key, so a deploy that internally calls the standalone build
path does not deadlock against itself. And it is taken by exactly three
callers: `DeployResource`, the pipeline's `build` and `deploy` actions, and
`BuildProcessResultContext`. Held, per its own doc comment, through build,
install and activation.

The gap between those two locks is the whole of the concurrency story that is
not covered. `WithBuildLock` returns a no-op when the spec has no build
strategy, and `apply`, `sync`, `reload`, `stop` and `remove` never ask for it
at all — so cross-process serialization exists only for the build phase of a
resource that has a build (CERB-GAP-731). `~/.cerberus/config.yaml` and the
registry index have no writer lock of any kind: a grep for `Flock`, `O_EXCL` or
a mutex across `internal/registry` and `internal/configops` returns nothing.

One control that used to exist no longer does. `internal/pausectl` still
exports `PauseAll` and `ResumeAll`, writing and removing `~/.cerberus/paused`,
and nothing calls either — `cmd_pause.go` was deleted in the v2 runtime
cut-over. What remains reachable is per-service pause, which `StopResource`
sets and `apply`/`deploy`/`reload` clear, surfaced as `OperatorStopped`. So
there is no way to quiesce the monitor across the estate for a maintenance
window; you stop resources one at a time.

## What it owns

- `opMu`: full serialization of every resource mutation within one daemon process
- the monitor taking the same mutex, so auto-restart cannot interleave with an operator action
- `buildlock`: a fail-fast, crash-safe, kernel-enforced flock on the git toplevel
- an error that names the holding resource, PID and lock age rather than just refusing
- re-entrancy, so nested build calls reuse one lock
- monorepo scoping: one lock per repository, not per build directory

## What it does not own

- any lock on apply, sync, reload, stop or remove (CERB-GAP-731)
- any lock for a resource with no build strategy
- writer locking for `config.yaml` or the registry index
- a global pause: `PauseAll` has no caller
- per-resource granularity — `opMu` is one lock for the whole service

records.confidence_label: The whole package read end to end and every surface traced; zero pipelines are defined here so nothing in the lane has been executed

records.body:
`AGENTS.md` opens its architecture section with "Two lanes, and they are not
interchangeable." There are three. `internal/pipeline` is a complete execution
lane with its own DAG, its own executor, its own action set and its own
surfaces on the CLI, the socket, the console and MCP — and it is named in that
document only in passing, as a thing the config can contain.

A pipeline is declared under `pipelines:` in the v2 config: an id, a name, and
ordered `stages`, each with `depends_on` and one or more `actions`. `Resolve`
turns that declaration into executable actions, `buildDAG` turns the stage
dependencies into levels with DFS cycle detection, and `Executor.Run` walks the
levels, running the stages within a level in parallel.

Six action types resolve:

- `build` / `build_app` — the local connector's build strategy for a resource
- `deploy` / `deploy_app` — build then install then activate
- `start`, `stop` — the local connector's `Apply` and `Stop`
- `health_wait` — HTTP GET the resource's `health_check.url` (or `health`)
  until 2xx, 2-second interval, 5-second per-attempt timeout, 30-second default
  budget overridable per action
- `shell` — `sh -c <command>` in an optional `dir`, via `CombinedOutput`

`health_wait` deserves the emphasis. It is the only code in Cerberus that
actually fetches a declared `health:` URL. The supervision lane never does
(CERB-GAP-143) and `internal/service/healthcheck.go`, which implements the
richer version with command checks and intervals, has no caller outside its own
tests (CERB-GAP-631). So the one live prober in the binary lives in the lane
nobody has a pipeline in.

The lane reaches the local connector directly rather than through
`ResourceRuntimeService`. That has two consequences and they pull in opposite
directions. It does take the source-tree build lock, so a pipeline build cannot
race a CLI deploy's build. It does not take `opMu`, so a pipeline's install and
activation can interleave with a daemon-side apply of the same resource. The
serving-daemon self-mutation guard does reach it: `actions.Deploy` calls
`ValidateMutation` through an interface assertion, and the guard is installed on
the connector itself, so a pipeline cannot deploy the daemon over itself.

What it has that the admin lane has is the destructive-operation vocabulary —
and that was the sharp edge. Until PR #63 a pipeline run took no `--ack`, offered no
`--dry-run`, and was not flagged destructive on any surface, while `shell` runs
arbitrary commands and `stop` stops production resources. `cerberus_pipeline_run`
put that behind one MCP tool call whose only required argument was a pipeline id
(CERB-GAP-733). Since PR #63 a run is `exec` and needs acknowledgment on every
surface; it still offers no dry-run.

Rollback is advertised and largely absent. On failure the executor calls
`Rollback` on completed stages in reverse order, logging rather than
propagating rollback errors. `Start` and `Stop` are genuine inverses of each
other. `Build`, `Deploy`, `Shell` and `HealthWait` all return `nil` — `Build`
says why in a comment, "builds are not rollbackable", and `Deploy` says nothing
at all. A three-stage pipeline that deploys in stage one and fails in stage
three reports `failed`, runs its rollback, and leaves the new artifact
installed and running (CERB-GAP-734).

Verified live on 2026-09-17: `cerberus pipeline list` returns "No pipelines
defined." The live config declares none, so nothing in this lane has ever run
on this machine. Author-time validation would not catch much if one were added
— registry validation checks neither action types nor stage dependencies
(CERB-GAP-536); the checks that exist are in `Resolve` and `Builder.Build` and
fire at run time.

Marked `partial`: the implementation is complete and coherent, and it is
entirely unexercised here, undocumented as a lane, and has no dry-run.

## What it owns

- the `pipelines:` config shape: stages, `depends_on`, actions
- stage DAG construction, level ordering and cycle detection
- level-parallel execution with a first-error result
- six action types, including the only live health prober in the binary
- reverse-order rollback of completed stages, best-effort
- MCP progress notifications and socket NDJSON progress for a run
- surfaces: `pipeline list|show|run`, `GET|POST /pipelines…`, `/api/pipelines…`,
  `cerberus_pipeline_list`, `cerberus_pipeline_run`

## What it does not own

- acknowledgment or dry-run for anything it executes (CERB-GAP-733)
- rollback of a build or a deploy (CERB-GAP-734)
- `opMu`, so it does not serialize against daemon-side resource mutations
- author-time validation of action types or stage dependencies (CERB-GAP-536)
- any non-local resource: `build`, `deploy` and `health_wait` all require
  `type: process` / `connector: local`
- an MCP tool or console view for `pipeline show`

## Since PR #63

`pipeline.Definition()` declares `run` as `exec` — a stage can be `sh -c`, and a
static contract cannot see which stages a pipeline declares (CERB-DEC-820) — and
`list` as a read. `RunPipeline` passes the runtime gate before it takes the
pipeline lock: `cerberus pipeline run <id> --ack`, `acknowledged` on
`cerberus_pipeline_run`, and a confirm step in the console. The stages call the
local connector directly, so the run's one acknowledgment covers them. The
acknowledgment travels as an explicit option, never in a context, so it cannot
leak into what the stages call (CERB-DEC-819). The P1-3 branch stopped the CLI
printing `Running pipeline:` before a refusal. The console's pipelines page now
decodes the run result, which arrives as base64 JSON.

Since P1-4b a run is recorded in the audit log (CERB-CAP-604): one intent
before the gate and one outcome after, with a run that reports failure
recorded as `operation_failed`. An unwritable log refuses the run before the
pipeline lock.

records.body:
Cerberus's connector lane and its supervision lane have opposite surface
profiles, and pass 1 measured only the first. Where 48 connector operations
reach the socket API, the console HTTP API and the console UI mechanically —
the socket has one generic route, `POST /connectors/{id}/operations/{op}`, and
`web/src/pages/connectors.tsx` iterates `connector.operations` from discovery
metadata — the supervision lane has no generic route anywhere. Every one of its
thirteen verbs is a hand-written entry in a hand-maintained list, and there are
five such lists:

- `cmd/cerberus/cmd_resource.go` — one cobra subcommand per verb.
- `internal/cerbapi/socket_server.go`, `handleResourcesID` — a `switch action`.
- `internal/webui/server.go`, `handleResourceByID` — a second, independently
  written `switch action`.
- `cmd/cerberus/cmd_mcp.go` and again `cmd/cerberus/cmd_daemon.go` — one
  `NewCerberusResourceXxxTool` per verb, registered twice.
- `web/src/pages/resources.tsx` — an `ACTIONS` array of six buttons.

Five hand-maintained lists have drifted to four different lengths.

## The matrix

Legend: **Y** exposed · **n** not exposed · **~** partial or composed.
"HTTP API" is the `cerberus web` JSON API on 127.0.0.1:4783; "Console UI" is
what the React app actually calls, which is not the same set.

| Verb | CLI | Socket API | HTTP API | MCP | Console UI |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `list` | Y | Y | Y | Y | Y |
| `status` | Y | Y | ~ bare `{id}` | Y | Y |
| `logs` | Y | Y | Y | Y | Y |
| `inspect` | Y | Y | Y | Y | **n** |
| `doctor` | Y | Y | Y | Y | **n** |
| `deploy` | Y | Y | Y | Y | Y |
| `apply` | Y | Y | Y | Y | Y |
| `reload` | Y | Y | Y | Y | Y |
| `sync` | Y | Y | Y | Y | Y |
| `stop` | Y | Y | Y | Y | Y |
| `remove` | Y | Y | Y | Y | Y |
| `ensure-fresh` | Y | **n** | **n** | Y | **n** |
| `show` | ~ resolved locally | **n** | **n** | **n** | **n** |
| **total** | **13** | **11** | **11** | **12** | **10** |

The direction of the asymmetry inverts. On connector operations the CLI (44 of
48) and MCP (33 of 48) are the weak surfaces and the console is complete; on
supervision verbs the CLI is complete at 13 of 13, MCP is nearly complete at 12
of 13, and **the console UI is the weakest surface at 10 of 13**. Anyone
planning from the connector-operation matrix alone would conclude that the
console never misses a verb — and for the lane an operator is most likely to
open a browser for, the opposite holds.

Three holes are worth naming, because each has a different cause.

**`inspect` and `doctor` are served and never called.** `handleResourceByID`
answers `GET /api/resources/{id}/inspect` and `GET /api/resources/{id}/doctor`,
and `web/src/api/client.ts` defines no method for either; a search of `web/src`
for `doctor` returns one unrelated `recommended_action` comparison and nothing
else. The console is the surface an operator reaches for when something looks
wrong, and it offers no diagnostic view at all. This is the cheapest gap on the
board — the routes, the DTOs and the token plumbing already exist — and it is
the one pass 1 recorded as present on every surface.

**`ensure-fresh` has no route**, because it is composed in the client from
status plus one of deploy/apply/sync. It therefore exists on exactly the two Go
consumers of `cerbapi` — the CLI and the MCP adapter — and on nothing else.

**`show` has no route either**, and resolves the config in the calling process,
so it reports the caller's registry view rather than the daemon's.

Two smaller observations belong here rather than in the connector matrix. The
HTTP API serves status at the bare `/api/resources/{id}` via
`GetResourceRuntime` rather than at a `status` sub-path, so a reader diffing
route tables between the socket and the console will see a verb that looks
missing and is not. And MCP's four SSH tools are registered inside an `else`
branch: if `loadUnifiedForTools` fails, `cerberus mcp` logs a warning and serves
49 tools instead of 53, with no indication to the agent that four are gone.
That is a client-side config resolution in a surface whose whole point is to be
a thin shell over the daemon.

what the verbs do — that is CERB-CAP-100

records.name: Do not widen the supervision lane to remote kinds
records.summary: Remote containers and remote hosts are administered imperatively through the connector lane rather than being let through resource_runtime_service.go, because widening it buys supervision nobody asked for.
records.confidence_label: reasoning taken from docs/plans/infra-admin-control-plane.md; the unsupervised reporting path it depends on is verified live

relationships.note: defines the lane's outer boundary
the reporting path that makes the deferral liveable
where remote kinds live instead

records.body:
The two lanes are not two implementations of one idea. Supervision is stateful and continuous: `auto_restart`, launchd, artifact staleness, a resource you watch. Administration is imperative and stateless: run a verb against a system, get a result, resolved per call. `docs/plans/infra-admin-control-plane.md` is blunt that the distinction decides the architecture, and that the infra-admin work is therefore **breadth of verbs, not new architecture**.

The specific option closed off was letting `type: container` through `resource_runtime_service.go`. The plan's reasoning, which is worth carrying rather than summarising: that service is hardcoded to local/process in roughly ten places, and changing it buys supervision we do not want. Cerberus is not trying to watch remote containers — a container on a remote host is not a long-lived local workload, and giving it a supervision loop would mean owning restart policy, health interpretation and drift detection across a network boundary and someone else's Docker daemon.

Auditing the count makes the argument stronger than the plan states. The local/process pair is hardcoded at 17 non-test sites, not ten: 8 in `resource_runtime_service.go`, 12 across `internal/cerbapi` once `unsupervised.go`, `resource_dependencies.go`, `drift_cache.go` and `resource_monitor.go` are counted, and 5 more in `internal/pipeline/resolve.go`, `internal/config/paths.go`, `internal/registry/ports.go`, `internal/registry/schema.go` and `cmd/cerberus/cmd_resource.go`. The assumption has leaked into port validation and pipeline resolution, so widening the lane is not a contained refactor of one file.

What was chosen instead is cheap and has shipped: a non-local/process resource is a **named handle for connector operations**. `type: container` + `connector: docker` + a `compose_file` is supported, and `cerberus docker up <id>` resolves it through the registry exactly the way `cerberus ssh` resolves `muctlvaig`. The resource declaration buys id resolution and registry membership without buying a supervision loop.

Reversible in principle — nothing has been deleted — but the 17 call sites are the real cost of reversing it, and the alternative that was rejected (a second, remote-aware supervision lane) would be a new subsystem rather than a widening.

data.decision: Remote containers and remote hosts are handled by the imperative admin lane; resource_runtime_service.go stays hardcoded to local/process and reports everything else as unsupervised.
alternatives_considered: Let type: container through resource_runtime_service.go — rejected: buys supervision of remote workloads that nobody wants, across a network and someone else's Docker daemon
Build a second, remote-aware supervision lane — rejected implicitly: a new subsystem for a capability that is not wanted
Refuse non-local/process resources outright — rejected: muctlvaig is server/ssh and has always worked as a named handle
data.rationale: Supervision is stateful and continuous; administration is imperative and per-call. Conflating them would mean owning restart and health semantics across a network boundary. The admin lane already carries the furniture an admin tool needs (ack, dry-run, progress, redaction, per-call resolution), so the work is breadth of verbs rather than new architecture. A resource declaration still buys id resolution for those kinds without buying a supervision loop.

records.name: resources: is the only local workload model; services: and the TUI are frozen
records.summary: ADR 0002 made the v2 resource model the single local workload abstraction and froze the v1 services: lane and TUI as deletion debt rather than maintaining two first-class models.
records.confidence_label: ADR read in full; freeze confirmed in code — the daemon never constructs ServiceRegistry and the health DTO's services block is always null

relationships.note: the model this decision selected
auto_start's only implementation was left behind in the frozen lane

records.body:
Cerberus once had two first-class local workload models: `services:` backed by `ManagedService`, PID files, daemon restart heuristics and the original TUI, and `resources:` backed by the v2 domain model, connectors, runtime backends, the daemon socket and MCP. ADR 0002's reasoning for collapsing them is worth keeping verbatim in spirit: local APIs, daemons, schedulers, frontends and external tools all fit naturally as `process` resources; runtime policy is better expressed as `dev_session` vs `os_service`; the resource model already powers the modern operator surfaces; and Cerberus has no external customers, very low migration risk, and no need to spend product energy preserving two abstractions for the same thing.

So `resources:` became the only future model — `resource` the managed unit, `type: process` the local workload kind, `mode: dev_session | os_service` the runtime policy — and `services:` was frozen immediately as compatibility and deletion debt. The TUI was frozen with it, on the grounds that future UI work should target the resource-native model rather than extend a v1 surface. `internal/service/*` was explicitly allowed to survive as implementation plumbing for `dev_session`, which is exactly what it still is: `AcquireLock`, `WritePIDFile`, `ReadMetaFile`, `ConfigHash`, `CheckPortConflict`.

The freeze is real in the shipped binary. `cmd_daemon.go` never constructs a `ServiceRegistry` or the v1 `daemon.Monitor`; it starts exactly one `cerbapi.ResourceMonitor` plus the drift cache. `cerberus_health` returns `"services": null`. The ADR's own "negative consequences" list predicted that v1-oriented code would need consolidation or deletion and that temporary layering would remain — both are still true, and the cost has a name: the only implementation of `auto_start` was left behind in the frozen lane, so the field is silently inert in the lane that replaced it (CERB-GAP-142).

Not reversible in practice. The ADR is Accepted, the v2 model carries every surface, and the four-step follow-up direction (freeze, migrate, build the shared service layer, retire the legacy paths) is three quarters done.

data.decision: resources: is the only future local workload model; services: and the v1 TUI are frozen as compatibility/deletion debt and gain no new capability.
alternatives_considered: Maintain both models as first-class — rejected: two abstractions for the same thing, operator confusion, and no customer demanding the old one
Delete services: outright — rejected at the time: it remains as transitional affordance, though internal/service/* is still needed as dev_session plumbing
Extend the existing TUI to cover resources — rejected: future UI work targets the resource-native model
data.rationale: Every local workload shape fits a process resource; runtime policy is better expressed as dev_session vs os_service; the v2 model already powers CLI, daemon, API and MCP. No external customers and negligible migration risk meant the cost of collapsing was low and the cost of maintaining two lanes was ongoing.

records.name: unsupervised is a word, not a blank cell
records.summary: A resource kind the lane does not own reports the literal status `unsupervised` with the connector commands that do operate it, because a blank status reads as a defect and a refusal that names nothing leaves the operator guessing.
records.confidence_label: reasoning recorded in unsupervised.go's own comments (WP-6, 2026-09-17); behaviour verified live on muctlvaig

relationships.note: the capability implementing it
the deferral this makes liveable

records.body:
Two prior behaviours were judged worse than the problem they described. A blank STATUS cell for a `server`/`ssh` resource is indistinguishable from a probe that failed, so the one honest answer — this resource is administered, not watched — read as a bug. And the error `status currently supports local process resources only` told an operator what did not work while leaving them to guess what did.

The decision has three parts, each recorded in `unsupervised.go`'s comments. First, the status is a literal word (`UnsupervisedStatus = "unsupervised"`), chosen over an empty string specifically so it cannot be misread as a failure. Second, every refusal and every report names the commands that do operate the resource, switching on the connector: docker resources get `docker up|down|logs`, ssh resources get `ssh status` and `ssh exec`, anything else gets `connectors describe <connector>`. Third, the read verbs answer instead of refusing — `resource status` on a server resource is a reasonable question with a real answer (the kind, the connector, the commands), so it returns that rather than an error, while the mutation verbs refuse with the same guidance attached.

This is a small decision with outsized leverage, because it is what makes CERB-DEC-160 liveable. Declining to supervise remote kinds is only tolerable if a resource of that kind does not look broken in every listing. It also sets a house style worth generalising: an error that names its own recovery, which the redaction rules in AGENTS.md then protect (a safety net that eats the instruction is worse than no instruction).

Trivially reversible — it is one file and a status literal — but there is no reason to.

data.decision: Report non-local/process resources as status `unsupervised` with a reason and connector-specific next-step commands; read verbs answer, mutation verbs refuse with the same guidance.
alternatives_considered: Empty status — rejected: indistinguishable from a failed probe, so the honest answer read as a defect
Error on every verb including status — rejected: `resource status` on a server resource is a reasonable question with a real answer
Generic 'unsupported resource type' error — rejected: names what does not work and nothing that does
data.rationale: An operator-facing answer should say what is true and what to run next. A blank cell and a dead-end refusal both fail that test, and the second actively trained operators to think the resource was misconfigured.

records.name: Never deploy the daemon through its own socket
records.summary: The serving runtime refuses any resource mutation targeting itself and prints the out-of-band upgrade procedure, because a self-deploy dies on EOF mid-sync and can leave the launchd job booted out.
records.confidence_label: failure mode recorded in AGENTS.md; guard read in source and unit-tested; deliberately not triggered live

relationships.note: the capability implementing it
the resource it protects is not registered on this machine

records.body:
`deploy` or `ensure-fresh` on the daemon resource restarts the daemon in the middle of its own operation. The call dies on EOF, the artifact is left half-synced, and the launchd job can end up booted out where `KeepAlive` will not bring it back — which is to say the recovery requires a terminal and `launchctl`, from a tool whose whole point is that you do not need one.

The decision was to make it structurally impossible rather than documented. Three things follow from that choice and each is deliberate. The refusal lives in the *serving* runtime, gated on `servingDaemon`, so the same code path used in-process by a CLI with no daemon running is unaffected — the guard is about who is executing, not about which resource is named. It is installed as a connector-level `SetMutationGuard` as well as being called from each service method, so a pipeline driving the local connector directly is covered too. And identity is tested three ways — resource id, launchd label, and executable sameness via `os.SameFile` — because any single test can be sidestepped by a symlink, a renamed resource or a custom `service_name`.

The refusal text is the recovery, which is the other half of the decision: build to a temporary path, atomically move the binary over the daemon artifact, then `launchctl kickstart -k gui/<uid>/com.fragments-engine.cerberus` from an external terminal. An operator who hits the guard gets the procedure, not a policy.

The same reasoning produced a sibling decision worth noting: `selfexec.WatchAndExit` must not return to `cerberus mcp`, because deploying the daemon replaces the binary on disk and every running `cerberus mcp` child would notice and exit, wiping MCP access fleet-wide under hosts that do not respawn children. Both are cases of "the tool replacing its own binary" and both were resolved by removing the self-referential behaviour rather than by timing it more carefully.

Not reversible: it prevents an outage with a manual recovery path and costs nothing that anyone wants.

data.decision: The serving runtime refuses resource mutations that target itself, identified by resource id, launchd label or executable identity, and the refusal carries the build-to-temp / mv / launchctl kickstart procedure.
alternatives_considered: Document the hazard and rely on operator care — rejected: it had already happened, and the recovery needs an external terminal
Special-case only the canonical resource id — rejected: a custom service_name or a symlinked artifact would slip past
Detach the deploy so the daemon survives its own replacement — rejected: the half-synced artifact and the booted-out launchd job are the real damage, not the dropped connection
data.rationale: A self-mutation through the socket fails in the worst possible way: partially applied, with the control plane that would fix it gone. Making it unreachable and handing over the known-good manual procedure is strictly better than making it reliable. The principle predates the guard by three weeks and by five months: docs/control-plane-direction.md (2026-08-22) already required that "Cerberus installation and self-upgrade should execute through a standalone installer/CLI control path. A live daemon should not be the sole authority responsible for replacing its own executable or service registration", and listed "self-deployment through the running daemon creates a circular lifecycle" among the current-model tensions; earlier still, e2908da (2026-03-14) removed auto_restart from the daemon's own resource because "a daemon must not restart itself" after it produced a recursive fork loop. The guard in 350a700 is the structural form of a rule that had already been stated twice.

records.name: Artifact staleness is source-binary content hash, not git state
records.summary: Git HEAD and dirtiness are recorded in the install manifest for operator inspection but excluded from the staleness computation, because any commit in a shared repo would mark every artifact in it stale.
records.confidence_label: reasoning recorded verbatim in artifact.go's own comments; no artifact resource here to observe it

relationships.note: the capability implementing it
what artifact_stale means on a status report

records.body:
`install-manifest.json` carries an `artifactRepoState` — repo root, git HEAD, a dirty flag and a hash of `git status --porcelain`. The comment above the type states the rule and the reason in one breath: it is recorded for operator inspection ("what HEAD was this artifact built from?") but is **not** used to compute staleness, because the content-hash check on the source binary is authoritative, and any commit or untracked-file change in the source repo would otherwise mark every artifact in that repo stale even when the resource's own binary is byte-identical.

That is a false-positive argument, and it is the right one for a monorepo-ish layout where several resources build out of one checkout. Editing a README would have turned every artifact in the tree red.

The replacement signal is narrow and honest: hash the source binary, compare against the manifest, and classify the difference — `source_changed`, `source_missing`, `source_unreadable`, `source_path_changed`, `source_unresolvable`, or `installed_artifact_changed` when the installed copy itself no longer matches what was recorded. Every verb that reports staleness says what it does not cover: `apply` appends "no build ran and source freshness was not checked", and `ensure-fresh`'s clean result says "no built-binary drift detected; source freshness is not checked; use deploy or ensure-fresh --force after source changes".

The accepted cost is that unbuilt source edits are invisible to the staleness system. That gap is filled partially and separately for `dev_session` by `RecommendedDevSessionAction`, which compares the run binary's mtime against the recorded launch time and deliberately stays silent for resources without a build strategy (an `npm run dev` or `go run` has no built binary to compare, and flagging those would be noise). A second design decision in the same file, `InspectArtifactInstallBasic`, is now an alias of the full inspect precisely because dropping the git probe removed the reason to have a cheap variant — no per-poll git invocation either way.

Reversible, but reverting would reintroduce the false positives that motivated it.

data.decision: Compute artifact staleness from the source binary's SHA-256 against the install manifest; record git repo state for inspection only.
alternatives_considered: Use git HEAD / dirtiness as the staleness signal — rejected: one commit marks every artifact in a shared repo stale while the binaries are byte-identical
Use mtime comparison — rejected for artifacts as too noisy, though it is the chosen cheap signal for dev_session drift
Probe git per status poll — rejected on cost, which is also why the 'basic' inspect variant collapsed into an alias
data.rationale: Staleness must answer 'is the installed binary the one the build produced', which is a content question. Repo state answers a different, coarser question and produces false positives proportional to how many resources share a checkout. The trade is that unbuilt source edits are out of scope, and every verb says so rather than implying coverage it does not have.

records.name: Install an artifact to a fresh inode and rename
records.summary: copyFile writes to a temp file in the destination directory, chmods, syncs and renames over the artifact, so macOS cannot serve a cached code-signing identity and readers keep the previous complete binary until the swap.
records.confidence_label: reasoning recorded in the code comment; the platform behaviour it defends against is not something I re-verified

relationships.note: the capability implementing it
the same build-to-temp-then-mv shape the daemon self-upgrade procedure prescribes

records.body:
`copyFile` in `internal/connector/local/artifact.go` does not open the destination and overwrite it. It creates `.artifact-*` in the destination's own directory, copies, applies the source's permission bits, `Sync()`s, closes, and then `os.Rename`s over the artifact path. The comment gives two reasons and both are load-bearing on macOS: a fresh inode avoids the cached code-signing identity the kernel associates with a binary's inode, and rename keeps readers on the previous complete binary until the new one is fully written.

The first is the subtle one. Writing new bytes into an existing executable's inode can leave macOS validating the old signature against the new contents, which surfaces as a killed process rather than as an install error — a failure that looks like the service crashing for its own reasons. The second is ordinary atomicity: a partially written artifact is never observable, and a concurrent `launchctl kickstart` either gets the whole old binary or the whole new one.

Worth noting that the same shape is prescribed to humans for the one artifact Cerberus will not touch: CERB-DEC-163's recovery procedure is build to a temp path, `mv` it over the daemon artifact, then `launchctl kickstart -k`. The installer and the manual self-upgrade path agree, which is a good sign that the reasoning is about the platform rather than about convenience.

The defensive check above it belongs to the same decision: the source must be a regular file (`artifact source must be a regular file`), so a directory or device path fails with an explanation rather than producing a nonsense artifact.

Reversible and cheap to revert, which is exactly why it is worth recording — a future simplification to "just write the file" would reintroduce a failure mode that presents as an unrelated crash.

data.decision: Install artifacts by copying to a temp file in the destination directory and renaming over the target, never by overwriting the existing inode.
alternatives_considered: Open and overwrite the artifact in place — rejected: macOS can validate the cached code-signing identity of that inode against the new bytes, killing the process for reasons that look unrelated
Write to a temp path elsewhere and move — rejected implicitly: a cross-filesystem rename is not atomic, so the temp file is created in the destination directory
Stop the service, copy, restart — rejected: a longer outage window for a problem rename already solves
data.rationale: A new inode sidesteps signature caching and rename gives atomic visibility, so an install is never half-applied and never resurrects a stale signature. The cost is one temp file in the bin directory, cleaned up on every failure path.

records.name: Deploy refuses an ambiguous build-to-artifact join
records.summary: An artifact-mode resource with a build strategy must declare rules.output naming the binary the build produces; command[0] is explicitly not accepted as a build-output contract.
records.confidence_label: reasoning in ValidateDeployOutput's comment and the post-build guard's; enforcement gap on apply and sync recorded separately as GAP-145

relationships.note: the capability implementing it
the same contract is not enforced on apply or sync
deploy is the verb that enforces it

records.body:
The installer needs to know which file to copy. Historically it used `command[0]`, on the theory that the thing the service runs is the thing the build produced. `resolveArtifactSource` now prefers the build strategy's declared `output` for exactly the reason the comment gives: the build writes to that path, so installing from it guarantees the artifact is exactly what the build produced, closing the gap where a build wrote to its declared output while the installer blindly copied a divergent — and possibly stale — `command[0]`.

Preferring `output` is not enough on its own, because a strategy can decline to declare one. So `ValidateDeployOutput` refuses the ambiguous case up front: a resource with `run_from: artifact` and a build strategy with no `rules.output` gets `artifact deployment requires build_strategy.rules.output naming the binary the build produces; command[0] is not a build-output contract`. `go_standard` already cannot build without an `output`; the rule exists for `make_standard` and `legacy_command`, where a `make build` target's real output is not discoverable from the config. And after a successful build, deploy stats the resolved source and fails with a message naming the fix if nothing is there, because a "successful" build that wrote elsewhere would otherwise silently sync a stale or absent artifact — described in the code as the exact failure mode behind recurring stale-after-deploy incidents.

The interesting part of this decision is what it declined to do. It did not make `output` mandatory for every artifact resource: a resource with `run_from: artifact` and *no* build strategy at all is legitimate — it installs a pre-built `command[0]`, which is what `nanite-local`'s config comment describes for the workspace case — so the refusal is scoped to "you have a build, therefore you must tell me what it produces".

Recorded here with its unfinished half: the contract is enforced on `deploy` and bypassed on `apply` and `sync`, both of which reach the installer directly. See CERB-GAP-145. A guard on the verb rather than on the installation is the part of this decision that has not landed.

data.decision: On deploy, an artifact-mode resource that declares a build strategy must also declare build_strategy.rules.output; command[0] is not accepted as evidence of what the build produced.
alternatives_considered: Keep installing command[0] — rejected: the installer could copy a divergent or stale binary the build never wrote
Make rules.output mandatory for all artifact resources — rejected: a resource with no build strategy legitimately installs a pre-built command[0]
Infer the output by scanning for recently modified files — rejected implicitly: guessing is what the contract exists to eliminate
data.rationale: The build-to-install join is the one place where 'changed source is not deployed source' becomes silent. Requiring the build to name its output makes the join explicit and lets deploy verify it afterwards, turning a silent stale install into a loud failure with the fix in the message.

records.name: A new provider integration is a plugin, not a built-in
records.summary: Anything that talks to a provider and carries a vendor SDK ships as a runtime-loaded plugin; adding one to go.mod for a connector is the signal you are in the wrong lane.
records.confidence_label: Two plugins ship and load today; the table and reasoning are recorded in the plan

relationships.note: The migration half of the same decision
Azure is the worked example
ContextForge was built first to learn plugin authoring

records.body:
Cerberus ships as a single installed binary, so what goes into it is a real
budget rather than a preference. The split was decided 2026-09-16 on two axes at
once: does anything else depend on this, and does it carry a third-party SDK.

**Core** is the primitives the control plane is built on. `local` *is* the
supervision lane. `ssh` is a primitive because remote docker rides it and
deploys and file transfer are built on it. `docker` shells out to a CLI and
carries no SDK. `github` is the deliberate exception: it carries `go-github` and
still earns a built-in slot because Cerberus's own release and pipeline story
leans on it.

**Plugin** is everything else that talks to a provider — optional per user,
carrying a vendor SDK, shipping on its own schedule, loaded at runtime with no
rebuild of the host.

The operational form of the rule is the useful part: **if you are about to add a
vendor SDK to `go.mod` for a connector, that is the signal you are in the wrong
lane.** It is checkable in review without an architecture argument.

Two supporting choices came with it. Our plugins live together in
`hollis-labs/cerberus-plugins`, one directory per plugin with shared CI and
release, because separate repositories buy independent tagging nobody needs yet
and three repositories for two plugins is overhead. And ContextForge was built
before any migration, deliberately: a v0.x SDK against an evolving gateway is
where rebuild-independence pays most, and building it first meant learning what
authoring a plugin actually feels like before moving anything onto that lane.

Reversible in principle — a plugin can be compiled in. The reason it will not be
is the binary, currently around 81MB.

data.decision: New provider integrations ship as plugins in hollis-labs/cerberus-plugins; core keeps only the primitives the control plane is built on.
alternatives_considered: Compile every connector in, as the first four were
One repository per plugin for independent tagging
A vendored-SDK build tag per provider
data.rationale: Core is for primitives other connectors depend on and that carry no vendor SDK: local, ssh and docker. github is the one exception, earned because Cerberus's own release and pipeline story leans on it. Everything else is optional per user, ships on someone else's schedule, and should be loadable without rebuilding the host.

records.name: The four compiled-in provider connectors moved to plugins
records.summary: cloudflare, digitalocean, namecheap and forge are plugins in hollis-labs/cerberus-plugins; the host compiles in only local, ssh, docker and github, and a stripped build went from 62.8MB to 21.7MB.
records.confidence_label: Recorded in the plan with the dependency sizes; all four still compiled in and reported by connectors list

relationships.note: The rule this is the deferral under
First to migrate
Last, having no SDK to shed

records.body:
The rule is that a provider integration is a plugin. Four provider connectors
are compiled in anyway, and that is a decision rather than an inconsistency —
with a sequence attached.

**Do not migrate them yet.** They work, and moving them is cost with no feature
benefit. The stronger reason is sequencing: migrating them first would have
meant moving working code onto a lane that had never carried a plugin authored
as one from day one. ContextForge was built first precisely to learn what
authoring feels like, and it found real gaps in the lane — the host secret
channel among them — that a migration would have hit while also carrying the
risk of regressing something that already worked.

**The order follows the payoff.** `cloudflare-go/v4` is 33MB, the largest
dependency win available in the binary, so cloudflare goes first. `godo` is
2.7MB, so digitalocean follows. Forge and Namecheap have no vendor SDK at all —
both are hand-written HTTP clients — so they are last, and their migration buys
modularity rather than size.

**And no fifth is added.** This is the part with teeth, because the natural
reading of "four are compiled in" is that compiling one in is an available
option. It is not. The four are legacy with a migration plan; the rule for
anything new is the plugin lane.

There is a mechanism backing the decision rather than only a note.
`Registry.BuiltInIDs` is derived from what is actually registered rather than
hardcoded, and it is the set a plugin may not claim — so when cloudflare moves
out it stops being reserved on its own, and a cloudflare plugin becomes
installable the same day. The reservation shrinks by itself as the migration
happens.

**Under way since 2026-09-25.** The deferral ended with `docs/plans/provider-plugin-extraction.md`. `cloudflare` moved first, as ordered here, and a stripped build fell from 62.8MB to 23.6MB, far more than the SDK's symbol sizes predicted. The reserved-id set shrank by itself, as designed. `digitalocean`, `namecheap` and `forge` follow in that order; their plugins are built, and each built-in is removed once the one before it is live.

**digitalocean followed on 2026-09-25**, taking `godo` and two hashicorp HTTP modules out of the binary (23.7MB → 21.8MB stripped). `namecheap` and `forge` remain.

**namecheap followed on 2026-09-25.** It had no SDK to shed, so the binary barely changed. The move gave its record-set operations a CLI verb and fixed the console's `client_ip`. `forge` remains.

**forge moved last, on 2026-09-25**, and with it no provider connector remains compiled in. The core set is what the decision names: `local`, `ssh`, `docker` and `github`.

**Closed 2026-09-25.** The sequence ran as ordered: cloudflare, digitalocean, namecheap, forge. Each moved as a plugin with the same id and secret names, so no credential had to migrate, and each built-in was removed once its plugin was proven and the host could generate its MCP tools. Final state: the core is `local`, `ssh`, `docker` and `github`, and a stripped build went from 62.8MB to 21.7MB (default build 88.1MB to 31.6MB), with no provider SDK left in the host. The record of how is `docs/plans/provider-plugin-extraction.md`.

data.decision: Do not migrate the four existing provider connectors yet; migrate cloudflare first when the time comes, forge and namecheap last.
alternatives_considered: Migrate all four immediately, before building any new plugin
Leave them compiled in permanently
Migrate namecheap first as the smallest
data.rationale: They work today and moving them is cost with no feature benefit. More decisively, migrating them first would mean migrating onto a plugin lane that had never carried a plugin authored as a plugin from day one. Order follows payoff: cloudflare-go is 33MB and the largest dependency win available; forge and namecheap have no SDK to shed and go last.

records.name: Work infrastructure is not ours to change on our own say-so
records.summary: Connectors may implement write operations, behind --ack with a real preview; whether a write runs against an Adtran resource is the owning team's decision, not something the connector's existence grants.
records.confidence_label: Amended 2026-09-25: the kubernetes plugin ships writes, and the rule now governs using them against work resources rather than building them

relationships.note: Azure ships read and probe only
ContextForge ships read only
Azure's locked paths are the worked example
The first connector to ship writes under the amendment

records.body:
This is a scope decision and is worth keeping distinct from a permissions
workaround, because the two look identical in the code and lead to opposite
follow-ups.

An infrastructure team administers the Adtran estate. Cerberus is a tool that
helps operate it, not a control plane that owns it. So connectors targeting work
resources implement read and probe operations, and lifecycle and write
operations are **documented as locked, with what would unlock them**, rather
than built speculatively.

The difference matters in two directions. A permissions workaround implies the
capability should exist and the access is the obstacle, so the next step is to
find a way around it. A scope decision says the capability is not Cerberus's to
have yet, so the next step — if the write is genuinely wanted — is an ask to the
team that owns the resource. And writing the unlock conditions down instead of
leaving a gap means the next person finds the reason rather than an absence they
will read as an oversight.

The exceptions already in place are deliberate and narrow, which is what keeps
the rule meaningful: the local dev services in `~/.cerberus/config.yaml`, and
`muctlvaig` reached over SSH **as the operator's own account** — not as a
service identity with standing privilege. That second qualifier is the whole
distinction. `ssh exec` against the work host is the operator doing by hand,
faster, what they were already entitled to do; it is not Cerberus holding
credentials of its own.

Two observable consequences. Azure ships six read operations and documents its
VM lifecycle as locked with the exact roles and provider registrations that
would unlock it. ContextForge ships four reads and nothing that registers,
edits or removes an upstream. And the SSH tunnel resources carry `auto_start`
and `auto_restart` both false, because an auto-restarting tunnel against a
corporate auth endpoint is a good way to get an account locked out — the same
restraint applied to supervision rather than to verbs.

**Amended 2026-09-25.** The rule above said what connectors *build*. It now says what we *do*. Cerberus is built in public, so a connector may implement writes whether or not any work target will accept them. It builds them the usual way: `Destructive`, `SupportsDry`, behind `--ack`, with a real preview. What stays is the part that was always the point: a write against a work resource is the owning team's decision, and a connector that can write is not that decision. Until per-target policy exists, the credential is the policy. Point a connector at a work target with an identity that cannot write. The kubernetes plugin is the first connector built under the amendment.

## Since P2-3

Decision 18 gives this rule a target to key off. A resource declares `owner` (who provisions it) and `admin` (who administers it day to day, per sub-target kind), and every operation's audit record names both. "Not ours to change on our own say-so" becomes the policy default for `admin: owner`, not a blanket rule for every work target: a box another team provisions but we administer (`admin: { default: owner, docker: self }`) is ours for its containers. The labels are recorded now; the default is evaluated in shadow in P2-4 and enforced with approvals in P3. Until then the credential is still the policy.

**Since P2-4.** The policy default exists: `builtin.admin-owner` denies write, lifecycle, destructive and exec on a target whose admin for that sub-target kind is `owner`, and `builtin.admin-unknown` does the same for an unlabeled one (Decisions 17 and 18, `internal/policy/evaluate.go`). It is recorded in shadow mode; P3 enforces it.

data.decision: Cerberus helps operate the Adtran estate; it does not own it. Connectors may build write operations, since Cerberus is built in public for estates unlike ours, but a write against a work resource needs the owning team's agreement.
alternatives_considered: Build write operations and gate them behind stronger acknowledgment
Request the access first, then build
Build them and leave them untested against the real estate
As first decided: build no write operation for any connector that could target work resources
data.rationale: An infrastructure team administers the Adtran estate, so a write against it is that team's call. But Cerberus is built in public and most of its users do not share our estate. Withholding a capability because our own targets may not accept it made the tool less useful to everyone else, and that bought nothing for us that the target's RBAC and --ack do not already give. The control belongs at use, not at build: a read-only identity for a work target today, and per-target write policy with a human in the loop next.

records.name: A connector operation returns a Cerberus DTO, never a vendor SDK type
records.summary: Response types are Cerberus-defined allow-lists, so a vendor adding a credential field in a minor release cannot silently widen what Cerberus emits.
records.confidence_label: ADR accepted 2026-09-16 and implemented for ContextForge; the three SDK connectors still return vendor types by the ADR's own sequencing

relationships.note: The connector whose vendor type forced the decision
The unimplemented remainder

records.body:
The shortcut this closes off is attractive and was already in use: return the
SDK's own struct. It is typed, it has JSON tags, and it needs no mapping code.
`digitalocean` returns `godo.Droplet`; `github` returns `go-github` types.

What broke it was a concrete type. `go-contextforge`'s `Gateway` — the upstream
MCP server registration — declares `AuthToken`, `AuthPassword`,
`AuthHeaderValue`, `AuthValue`, `AuthUsername`, `AuthHeaders` and `OAuthConfig`,
with 32 secret-bearing field references across the package. A `list_gateways`
that marshalled it would have emitted live upstream credentials into four places
at once: CLI stdout and from there shell history and scrollback; the daemon
socket response and `~/.cerberus/` logs; MCP tool results, which land directly
in an agent's context window and are then sent to a model provider; and any run
log downstream that captures those.

Three properties of that failure are what generalise, and they are the actual
argument:

The severity belongs to the vendor type, not to our code. Nobody wrote anything
wrong. The exposure is invisible at the call site — `return gateways, nil` reads
identically whether the struct holds a name or a bearer token — and neither the
compiler, the tests nor the linter objects. And the existing house rule, "never
log or return a secret value", is easy to satisfy in spirit while breaking in
practice, because the author never sees a secret in the code they wrote.

So the DTO is an allow-list: it names the fields we intend to expose, and a
field not named is not emitted. For credentials specifically, expose the *shape*
of the configuration and never the value — `auth_type`, that some bearer auth is
configured, never `auth_token`. This mirrors the `probe-*` convention already in
use in `~/Projects/tools`: environment variable names, never values, so output
is safe to paste into a document.

The cost is honest and was accepted: mapping code per operation, which will feel
redundant where the vendor type is benign, and a field the vendor adds that we
*do* want is not picked up for free. That second cost is the point — opting in
is the behaviour wanted at this boundary.

Not retroactive. The five connectors returning vendor types today are to be
audited in the order they are touched and migrated alongside the plugin
migration they are already scheduled for. The audit question for each is narrow:
does any type this connector returns carry a token, password, key, header value
or OAuth blob? If yes, it is a DTO now, not later.

data.decision: Define response DTOs in the connector package and map explicitly; the mapping function is the security boundary.
alternatives_considered: Return the SDK struct and rely on the house rule against returning secrets
Strip known credential fields post-hoc before marshalling
Redact the marshalled output
data.rationale: The severity is a property of the vendor type, not of our code, and it is invisible at the call site: `return gateways, nil` looks identical whether the struct holds a name or a bearer token. An allow-list makes the exposure decision explicit and reviewable in one place per connector, and opts out of fields added later by default.

records.name: Remote systems belong in the admin lane; the supervision lane is not widened
records.summary: A remote container or host is administered by imperative verbs, not supervised — and a non-local resource is a named handle for those verbs rather than a broken workload.
records.confidence_label: muctlvaig is registered as server/ssh and reports unsupervised with connector commands named; verified in the briefing's ground truth

relationships.note: The lane remote work lives in
The lane that is deliberately not widened

records.body:
Two lanes, and the decision is that they stay separate.

The supervision lane is for long-lived local workloads: `auto_restart`, health
probes, launchd, artifact staleness. It is hardcoded to local/process in roughly
ten places, and that is deliberate rather than incidental. The admin lane is
imperative and stateless: run a verb against a remote system, get a result.

Remote containers and remote hosts go in the admin lane. The reasoning is short
and worth quoting rather than paraphrasing: **the work is breadth of verbs, not
new architecture.** Letting `type: container` through
`resource_runtime_service.go` would buy supervision of remote containers, and
Cerberus is not trying to watch remote containers. Nothing about a container on
someone else's host wants `auto_restart` decided here.

The consequence that needed working out was what a non-local resource then *is*.
It is a **named handle for connector operations** — not a degraded workload and
not a configuration error. `muctlvaig` is `server`/`ssh` and has always worked
that way. Declaring `type: container` / `connector: docker` with a
`compose_file` is a supported pattern: `cerberus docker up <id>` resolves it
through the registry the way `cerberus ssh` does.

That distinction only holds if the supervision lane reports it honestly, which
is the part that had to be built rather than merely decided. Supervision-lane
verbs report such a resource as `unsupervised` and name the connector commands
that do operate it, instead of erroring or leaving a blank status. A container
resource is a legitimate declaration; a lane that cannot supervise it should say
which lane can.

Reversible, but expensive in the wrong direction: widening supervision is ten
call sites and a behavioural commitment to watching things on other people's
machines.

data.decision: Keep remote work in external_connector_service.go; do not let type: container through resource_runtime_service.go.
alternatives_considered: Widen the supervision lane to accept container and server resources
A second supervision service for remote workloads
Treat non-local resources as configuration errors
data.rationale: The supervision lane is hardcoded to local/process in roughly ten places, deliberately. Changing that buys supervision of remote containers, which is not wanted: the work here is breadth of verbs, not new architecture.

records.name: Namecheap per-record DNS writes are disabled
records.summary: Per-record create and delete are refused before credential resolution, because the underlying API makes them capable of silently deleting records nobody named.
records.confidence_label: Verified live: cerberus dns create returns the refusal and its recovery on a machine with no Namecheap credential

relationships.note: The connector this shapes
The safe replacement is MCP-only

records.body:
The Namecheap API composes badly with itself. `getHosts` can omit existing
records, and `setHosts` replaces the entire zone. A per-record "create"
implemented the obvious way — read the set, append, write it back — therefore
deletes everything `getHosts` chose not to return, silently, with no error and
nothing to roll back to.

So the per-record operations are disabled rather than implemented carefully. The
refusal is placed at the very top of `Execute`, before credential resolution,
before the dry-run branch and before plugin dispatch, and the ordering is the
point: an operator on a machine with no Namecheap token learns *why the
operation is wrong* rather than that their credential is missing. Verified live
— `cerberus dns create` returns the refusal and its recovery, not
`credential_missing`.

What replaces them makes the destructiveness impossible to miss, which is the
better property. `set_dns_record_set` requires the caller to supply the complete
authoritative record array **and** an explicit `email_type`. Both are required;
neither is inferred. The email mode has to be explicit because Namecheap
entangles MX handling with it, so MX records under `EmailType=FWD` are refused
before the write rather than written into a zone that half-works. The dry-run
preview states plainly that all omitted records will be deleted.

That is the design principle worth carrying: where an API's destructive
behaviour cannot be narrowed, make the caller construct an argument that shows
it. A caller assembling a complete record set knows they are replacing a zone. A
caller passing one record does not.

The CLI commands remain, labelled `Disabled: unsafe per-record Namecheap writes`
in `--help`, so someone reaching for the obvious command finds the reason rather
than a missing subcommand. Reversible only by solving the underlying API
problem, which would need a reliable complete read — and `getHosts` is exactly
what cannot provide one.

data.decision: Disable namecheap create_dns_record and delete_dns_record; support whole-zone replacement with an explicit email mode instead.
alternatives_considered: Implement per-record writes by read-modify-write on getHosts
Warn but allow
Expose per-record writes only over the CLI with an extra confirmation
data.rationale: getHosts can omit existing records and setHosts replaces the entire zone. A read-modify-write per-record path therefore deletes whatever getHosts left out, silently and irreversibly. Whole-zone replacement with a caller-supplied authoritative set makes the destructiveness visible in the argument the caller has to construct.

records.name: Docker resolves per call, and liveness comes from the daemon
records.summary: The connector is registered as a factory rather than an instance, and connectors list asks the daemon which connectors are live rather than answering from the CLI's own environment.
records.confidence_label: Verified live: with the daemon serving, connectors list reports docker live=yes and docker ps and docker logs both return real output

relationships.note: The connector
What liveness still does not distinguish

records.body:
This is the decision the whole audit is built on, because it is the one where
reading the code would have recorded a working connector and the system was
broken for weeks.

Two independent causes. The Docker connector resolved the `docker` binary once
at registration and cached the result for the daemon's lifetime. And the daemon
is started by launchd, which hands it `PATH=/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`, so
Docker Desktop's CLI at `/usr/local/bin/docker` was invisible to it even though
it resolved fine in an interactive shell. The first cause made the second
permanent: starting Docker Desktop could not recover it, correcting the PATH
could not recover it, and `cerberus connectors list` reported the connector
healthy throughout.

Two decisions came out of it, and taking only one would not have been enough.

**Resolution is per call.** Docker is registered with `RegisterFactory`, beside
the credentialed connectors, with the reason written next to it. The factory
runs `DetectDocker()` on every operation and every probe: a
`CERBERUS_DOCKER_PATH` override, then `PATH`, then five compiled-in fallback
locations — with a test asserting it finds the binary with `PATH` emptied.
`AGENTS.md` generalises it correctly: prefer explicit paths, fallback search
locations, and per-call resolution over boot-time resolution.

**Liveness comes from the daemon.** `cerberus connectors list` asks the daemon
for the live set and falls back to its own view only if the daemon cannot answer.
The comment states the failure it prevents: "This process has the user's shell
PATH and credentials; the daemon has launchd's. Reporting the CLI's view here is
how a connector could read LIVE=yes while every call against it failed."

The second is the more transferable insight. The first cause was a caching bug.
The second was a *reporting* bug — a health signal computed in a different
environment from the one that does the work. Fixing only the caching would have
left a connector that recovered on its own and still lied about its state in the
window where it mattered.

Verified live, both halves together: daemon serving on its socket, `connectors
list` reporting `docker live=yes` under launchd's PATH (which only the fallback
list can explain), and `cerberus docker ps` and `cerberus docker logs
mtbf-monitor-app-1 --lines 3` both returning real output.

data.decision: Register docker with RegisterFactory so DetectDocker runs per operation, and source liveness from the daemon that will run the operation.
alternatives_considered: Resolve docker at boot and cache it
Retry the boot-time resolution on a timer
Require CERBERUS_DOCKER_PATH to be set explicitly
data.rationale: Boot-time resolution cached a failure for the daemon's lifetime, and the daemon's launchd PATH cannot see Docker Desktop's CLI. Reporting the CLI's own liveness view is how a connector reads LIVE=yes while every call against it fails, because the CLI has the user's shell PATH and the daemon has launchd's.

records.name: Dry-run extraction was skipped, not done
records.summary: WP-1 would turn the single dry-run switch into a per-connector dispatch table; it was never blocking, so it was passed over and remains open.
records.confidence_label: the switch and the dry-run refusal re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54)

relationships.note: The gap this deferral leaves
The hazard the structure hides

records.body:
WP-1 is recorded in the sequencing with an unusual annotation: "WP-1 was
skipped, never blocking; still open." It is worth recording as a decision rather
than leaving as an absence, because the reasoning is sound and the consequence
is live.

The plan was explicit that WP-1 "rewrites the 600-line `dryRunPreview` switch,
so nothing else that touches that file should run beside it." Every other
connector work package touches that file — a new verb needs a `case` in
`execute<X>` and a `case` in `dryRunPreview`. So WP-1 was a serialisation point
in a plan being worked in parallel, and the thing it buys is maintainability
rather than capability. Skipping it was the right call under the constraint.

Two things about that trade are worth being straight about now.

It was never blocking in the sense of "nothing could not be built". It *was*
paying its cost the whole time: WP-3, WP-5 and WP-6 each edited inside the
switch, which is exactly the merge-conflict surface WP-1 exists to remove. The
cost was paid in the currency the refactor was meant to save.

And the structure hides a hazard the plan documented only half of. Because a
connector's `SupportsDry: true` declaration and the preview that implements it
live in different files with nothing tying them together, a declared dry-run
with no case is possible — and the plan records the destructive-operation
symptom ("`--dry-run` demands `--ack`") without the non-destructive one, where
the request is silently ignored and the operation runs for real. There was a live
instance of the second over MCP until PR #49 made a dry run with no preview a
`preview_unsupported` refusal (CERB-GAP-270). The previews are still all in
the one switch.

Marked not reversible in the sense that matters: the deferral has already been
taken and the debt accrued. The refactor itself is entirely available, and the
right moment for it is immediately before the next connector is added, not as a
standalone piece of work.

data.decision: Leave all 13 dry-run previews in one switch in external_connector_service.go for now.
alternatives_considered: Do WP-1 first, before the connectors that depend on that file
Do it incrementally, moving one connector's previews at a time
Generate previews from the input schema instead
data.rationale: WP-1 is a pure refactor with no feature benefit, and it rewrites the file every other connector work package touches — so running it alongside them would have been the collision it exists to prevent. Nothing downstream was blocked on it.

records.name: Azure's VM lifecycle is documented as locked, not implemented
records.summary: list_vms, start_vm, create_vm and their siblings are blocked on subscription-level provider registration and role assignments, and the unlock conditions are written into the plugin README.
records.confidence_label: WP-5 records the failing authorization check dated 2026-09-17; not re-probed in this audit

relationships.note: The connector
The read-only scope this sits under

records.body:
The original brief for the Azure connector asked for VM lifecycle. It shipped
with six read operations and none of it, and the shape of that non-delivery is
the decision.

The block is not a code problem. `Microsoft.Compute` is `NotRegistered` on the
subscription, so no VM can exist for `list_vms` to return or `start_vm` to act
on. Registering it requires subscription Contributor or Owner — there is no
narrower built-in role that grants only registration, and the check was verified
failing: `AuthorizationFailed … does not have authorization to perform action
'Microsoft.Compute/register/action'`.

The unlock conditions are written down with the same specificity, which is what
makes them useful to whoever picks this up. An admin must register
`Microsoft.Compute` and `Microsoft.Network` at subscription scope. VM management
additionally needs **Contributor scoped to one resource group** — and the
sharpest detail is that `Virtual Machine Contributor` alone is *not* sufficient
to create a VM, because it does not cover the VNet, NIC and public IP a new VM
attaches to. Scoping to a single resource group is what makes it
least-privilege, not picking a narrower-sounding role name. That is precisely
the kind of finding that costs an afternoon to rediscover.

And the governance question was named rather than assumed away: this is a shared
quality-management subscription, so putting a persistent billable VM in it is a
decision for whoever owns it, and a sandbox subscription would be the better
home. That is not a technical blocker and it is the one most likely to be the
real one.

The instruction that makes this a decision rather than a gap: write them in the
plugin's README as "not implemented, here is why", so the next person finds the
reason instead of the absence. An absence reads as an oversight; a documented
lock reads as a scoped decision with a named next step. It is also the concrete
form of the wider read-only stance on work infrastructure — where a write is
genuinely wanted, the ask goes to the team that owns the resource.

data.decision: Ship Azure read and probe operations; record the VM lifecycle operations as not implemented, with the exact conditions that would unlock them.
alternatives_considered: Implement the operations and let them fail at runtime
Wait for access before shipping anything
Register the providers and request the roles as part of the work package
data.rationale: Microsoft.Compute is NotRegistered on the subscription, so no VM can exist to act on. Registration needs subscription Contributor or Owner, verified failing. And this is a shared quality-management subscription, so a persistent billable VM in it is a governance decision for its owner rather than a technical one.

records.name: Recursive transfer will use SFTP, not rsync
records.summary: rsync is absent on the primary target and the local machine has only openrsync, and shelling out would introduce a second SSH transport beside the in-process one.
records.confidence_label: WP-9 records the probe dated 2026-09-17 and the library survey; not re-probed in this audit

relationships.note: The gap this decides the approach for
The connector

records.body:
Decided by probing, which is why it is worth recording rather than
re-litigating.

**rsync is not an option for the primary target.** `command -v rsync` on
muctlvaig returns absent; GNU tar 1.35 is present. Locally the machine has
`openrsync`, macOS's BSD replacement speaking protocol 29, not GNU rsync. So an
rsync-based design depends on a binary that is missing at one end and old at the
other.

It would also break an architectural property worth keeping: **Cerberus shells
out to nothing for SSH.** The connector is entirely in-process over
`golang.org/x/crypto/ssh`. Shelling out to rsync would introduce a second SSH
transport with different auth, different config resolution — `~/.ssh/config`,
which the in-process path deliberately does not read — and different failure
modes from the one the connector already uses. One transport is worth more than
delta transfer here.

**The library survey found nothing to build on, and that is the finding rather
than a lookup failure.** `pkg/sftp`'s `Walk` is the ecosystem's standard answer
and recursion is still yours to write. `bramvdbogaerde/go-scp` is tagged but
speaks SCP, which OpenSSH has deprecated and now implements over SFTP anyway.
`povsister/scp` supports recursion and has no tagged release. `melbahja/goph`
wraps what is already a dependency. The existing packages are prior art, not a
base: read what they got right and where they stopped. The opinions worth having
are the ones they tend not to have — preserve mode, refuse symlink escapes out
of the tree, temp-and-rename per file, honour cancellation between files as well
as within one — and those are exactly what makes it safe to point at a real
host. Which also makes the sync logic a candidate to extract as an OSS library
once it has earned its keep here.

**The tradeoff, stated honestly:** SFTP has no delta transfer and no
compression. It copies every byte every time. That is fine for what this is for
— compose files, env files, config directories, agent definitions — and wrong
for shipping a 600MB image, which is why the shell predecessor tars and ships a
single blob for that case. If a large tree shows up, add a tar-over-exec path
(GNU tar is confirmed present on the target) as a second strategy rather than
replacing this one.

data.decision: Build recursive directory transfer on pkg/sftp, writing the recursion ourselves, with tar-over-exec reserved as a second strategy for large trees.
alternatives_considered: rsync over ssh
SCP via bramvdbogaerde/go-scp
povsister/scp as a base
tar-over-exec as the primary path
data.rationale: Probed rather than assumed: rsync is absent on muctlvaig and the local machine has openrsync, so an rsync design depends on a binary missing at one end and old at the other. It would also break the property that Cerberus shells out to nothing for SSH — a second transport means different auth, different config resolution and different failure modes.

records.name: Core or plugin: what earns a place in the binary
records.summary: Only the primitives the control plane is built on are compiled in, plus github; everything else that talks to a provider is a plugin.
records.confidence_label: Carried from AGENTS.md, docs/plans/connector-work-packages.md and the cerberus-plugins README; the two real plugins are the worked examples
records.body:
The rule: `local`, `ssh` and `docker` are compiled in because the control plane is built on them and none carries a vendor SDK. `github` is compiled in as a named exception, because Cerberus's own release and pipeline story depends on it. Everything else that talks to a provider is a plugin.

The test is mechanical and that is the point of it. If you are about to add a vendor SDK to `go.mod` for a connector, you are in the wrong lane. Azure is the case that proves it works: the Azure Resource Manager SDK lives in `~/Projects-apps/cerberus-plugins/azure/go.mod`, not in this repo, and the Cerberus binary carries none of it while `cerberus connectors list` still shows `azure` with six operations.

Ours live in `hollis-labs/cerberus-plugins`, one directory per plugin, each its own Go module. Third-party plugins are standalone repos importing `pkg/plugin`, `pkg/connector` and `pkg/resource`. `cloudflare`, `digitalocean`, `forge` and `namecheap` are compiled in today and are slated to migrate out; the instruction is not to add a fifth.

Reversible in the sense that a plugin could be absorbed into the binary — but the direction of travel is the other way, and the reserved-id guard is deliberately derived from what is registered so that a connector leaving the binary frees its id for a plugin the same day.

relationships.note: the lane this decision creates
the reserved set shrinks as connectors migrate out

data.decision: Compile in local, ssh and docker (the primitives, none carrying a vendor SDK) plus github; make every other provider integration a runtime-loaded plugin in its own repo with its own release schedule.
alternatives_considered: Compile every connector in, as the four legacy ones are today
Make everything including the primitives a plugin
Vendor SDKs behind build tags in the single binary
data.rationale: Cerberus ships as one installed binary, so anything compiled in is something every operator carries and every release must build. The primitives are different in kind: the control plane is built on them, and none of them drags in a vendor SDK. github does carry one and is compiled in anyway, because Cerberus's own release and pipeline story leans on it — a stated exception, not a precedent. Everything else is optional per user, moves on someone else's schedule, and should be installable without rebuilding the host. The operational tell is concrete: adding a vendor SDK to go.mod for a connector means you are in the wrong lane.

records.name: Plugin credentials travel in the Init config channel, never the environment
records.summary: A resolved credential is passed in the plugin/init config map keyed by secret name; the launch environment is a fixed allow-list carrying none.
records.confidence_label: pluginLaunchEnv() read directly: fourteen names, no credential, used by both hosts. The property has no regression test
records.body:
A plugin declares its credentials in its manifest; the host resolves them and hands them over `plugin/init`. It does not put them in the environment, and that is a decision with a reason rather than a style preference.

Environment is ambient.
