A subprocess inherits it wholesale, so `CERBERUS_CONTEXTFORGE_TOKEN` placed in the plugin launch environment would be handed to the Azure plugin too, and to every plugin installed later — including one installed by someone else next month. `pluginLaunchEnv()` is therefore an allow-list, not a deny-list: `PATH`, `HOME`, `TMPDIR`, `TMP`, `TEMP`, `USER`, `LOGNAME`, `LANG`, `LC_ALL`, `DOCKER_HOST`, `DOCKER_CONTEXT`, `DOCKER_CONFIG`, `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, plus a `GO_WANT_` prefix for test re-exec. The subprocess's `cmd.Env` is built from that list alone. Both the one-shot and the managed host use the same function, so there is one place to get this wrong and it is guarded by a comment saying not to.

The `plugin/init` config map is the opposite shape: it is constructed per plugin by walking that plugin's own `config.secrets`, so a plugin structurally cannot receive a credential it did not declare, and never receives the store.

Marked not reversible because reversing it means handing every plugin every credential — there is no partial version of putting a secret in the environment. The one thing on the allow-list worth a second look is `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`: not a credential, but a handle that lets a plugin authenticate as the operator over SSH. It is there because a plugin may legitimately need to reach a host the operator can already reach, and it is worth knowing it is there.

relationships.note: the channel this decision defines
the property is unenforced by any test

data.decision: Resolve a plugin's declared secrets host-side and pass them in SDKInitParams.Config; build the subprocess environment from pluginLaunchEnv(), an allow-list with no credential entries, and never widen it with one.
alternatives_considered: Export credentials into the plugin subprocess environment
Give the plugin a handle to the credential store and let it fetch its own
Pass credentials as command-line arguments to the entrypoint
data.rationale: Environment is ambient: a subprocess inherits it wholesale, so a credential placed there would reach every plugin rather than the one that declared it, and would show up in any process listing or crash dump that captures env. The config map is addressed — it is built per plugin from that plugin's own manifest, so the blast radius of a credential is exactly the plugin that asked for it. Handing the plugin the store instead would move the trust decision into the plugin, which is precisely what the internal/pluginhost boundary exists to prevent; SecretResolver is deliberately Get-only so nothing in the plugin lane can write or delete.

records.name: A missing credential fails an operation, not a load
records.summary: A plugin whose declared credential does not resolve still loads; the operation that needed it fails as credential_missing with the recovery named.
records.confidence_label: Verified live: contextforge loaded true with missing_secrets [token], get_health returns ok, the three authenticated operations 401 with the guidance
records.body:
The alternative is tempting and wrong. Refusing to load a plugin whose required credential is absent would be tidier, and it would have cost this machine its most useful diagnostic.

ContextForge decided it. `/health` on the gateway is open, so `get_health` needs no token; the other three operations need an admin JWT and there is none here. If the missing token failed the load, `get_health` would be unavailable too — and `get_health` is precisely how you distinguish "the tunnel to `muctlvaig` is down" from "the tunnel is up and the gateway is unhealthy" from "everything is up and I have no credential". Three different problems with three different fixes, told apart by an operation that works without authentication.

So the host resolves what it can, records the names of required secrets it could not, warns on stderr naming `credential_missing`, and loads. `managed list` reports `missing_secrets` so the state is visible before anything fails. And the failure, when it comes, is a real failure wrapped rather than a guess: the host cannot tell which operation needs which secret, because the manifest maps secrets to the connector and not to an operation, so `MissingSecretsError` wraps the actual error and appends the recovery.

Verified live in all four positions: `loaded: true, missing_secrets: ["token"]`; `get_health` → `{"ok": true, "status": "healthy"}`; `list_gateways` → 401 plus the guidance; and over the socket the same failure classified as `credential_missing` with a 503.

The same reasoning produced the non-fatal restore path, and one gap: the recovery instruction the error prints does not work (GAP-331).

relationships.note: the behaviour this decision specifies
the printed recovery is a no-op

data.decision: Resolve what is available, record the names of required secrets that were not, warn, and load anyway. Report missing_secrets on managed list and wrap the first real failure as credential_missing rather than pre-empting the call.
alternatives_considered: Refuse to load a plugin whose required secrets are absent
Pre-empt any operation on a plugin with missing secrets
Map secrets to operations in the manifest so only affected operations fail
data.rationale: A plugin is optional by definition and must not be able to take the host down or disable itself wholesale — the managed-plugin restore bug already taught that lesson by crash-looping the daemon over a deleted plugin directory. More specifically, the host cannot tell which operation needs which secret, because the manifest maps secrets to the connector rather than to an operation; pre-empting would therefore break operations that work. ContextForge is the case that decided it: get_health is open and must keep working as the way to tell a down tunnel from a down gateway, while list_gateways 401s and deserves to say why.

records.name: Built-in connector ids are reserved, and the set is derived not hardcoded
records.summary: A plugin claiming an id this binary serves itself is refused at install, from a set the daemon fills from Registry.BuiltInIDs().
records.confidence_label: Wiring read end to end from cmd_daemon.go through BuiltInIDs(); three tests cover refusal, non-refusal and restore
records.body:
Refusing the collision at install is cheap; recovering from it was not. WP-0 added a fallback so that an installed-but-unloaded plugin does not disable the built-in it shadows, because unloading one had left `cerberus docker ps` permanently broken with no uninstall command and hand-editing the state file as the only way out. That fallback is recovery for a state that should not be reachable. `ReservedIDs` makes it unreachable.

The check runs first — before trust is evaluated, before the entrypoint is hashed, before any subprocess exists — on the principle that a plugin which may not be installed at all should not have its signature considered.

Two reasons to refuse, and the second is the one that makes this a security decision. A shadowing plugin takes over a connector the host serves itself. And the secret channel namespaces by connector id: a plugin called `github` declaring a secret named `token` would be handed `CERBERUS_GITHUB_TOKEN`.

The set is supplied by the caller, not hardcoded, because `pluginhost` has no opinion about what a host compiled in. The daemon fills it from `Registry.BuiltInIDs()` — the union of instances, factories and definitions — which on this machine is eight ids, not the four `AGENTS.md` names: `local`, `ssh`, `docker`, `github`, `cloudflare`, `digitalocean`, `forge`, `namecheap`. That breadth is the feature. The four legacy connectors are slated to migrate out to plugins, and when one does it stops being registered and its id frees itself. A hardcoded list would have had to be edited on the same day, by someone who remembered.

An inventory registered before the guard can still hold a shadowing plugin. Restore skips it with a warning and keeps the registration, rather than dropping the operator's record or taking the daemon down — and WP-0's fallback stays as the net for exactly that case.

relationships.note: the capability this decision defines
derived so the set shrinks as connectors migrate out

data.decision: Check ReservedIDs first in DirectoryInstaller.Install — before trust, hashing or any subprocess — and have the daemon supply the set from Registry.BuiltInIDs(), the union of registered instances, factories and definitions.
alternatives_considered: Hardcode the reserved list in pluginhost
Allow the shadow and rely on WP-0's installed-but-unloaded fallback
Namespace plugin connector ids to make collision impossible
data.rationale: A shadowing plugin would take over a connector Cerberus serves itself, and because the secret channel namespaces by connector id it would also be handed that connector's credentials by declaring a secret of the same name — so the guard is a credential boundary, not only a naming one. WP-0's fallback was recovery for a state that should not be reachable: unloading a shadowing plugin once left `cerberus docker ps` permanently broken with no uninstall command. Deriving the set rather than hardcoding it means it shrinks on its own: when cloudflare migrates out of the binary it stops being registered, and a cloudflare plugin becomes installable the same day with no guard to edit.

records.name: Unsigned local install is the supported path, and sits with the trusted tiers
records.summary: Superseded by CERB-DEC-815. TrustTierUnsigned could run destructive operations subject to --ack, rather than being grouped with the dev tiers that were refused them; PR #51 removed the tiers.
records.confidence_label: historical: the tiers this argued over were removed in PR #51
records.body:
The tier table has an asymmetry that looks like a mistake and is not. `unsigned` is listed with `builtin` and `signed` as tiers that may run anything; `local_dev` and `unsigned_dev` are refused every destructive operation. An unsigned plugin is therefore *more* privileged than a developer-mode one.

The distinction is what the two mechanisms attest to. A signature attests to **provenance** — this artefact came from who it claims to. `--ack` attests to **intent** — the operator means to do this destructive thing. An operator installing an unsigned plugin from a local path has established provenance out of band: they built it, or they read it. What a signature would add, in that case, is already present in another form. The dev tiers are for a different situation — a build-tagged binary, an allow-listed root, code in motion — where refusing destruction is a reasonable blanket.

The consequence of the alternative is the argument. Group `unsigned` with the dev tiers and every destructive plugin operation is refused, which makes the plugin lane read-only, which means it cannot carry the provider integrations DEC-350 exists to push into it. A lane that can only read is not a lane.

Two caveats worth carrying. First, `--ack` still applies: `OperationAllowed` requires acknowledgment for any operation the manifest marks `destructive` with `requires_ack`, at every tier. Second, this decision is currently load-bearing for nothing, because the tier that gates is unreachable and neither shipped plugin declares a destructive operation (GAP-335). The reasoning is sound; it is just not being tested by anything that runs.

## Superseded by CERB-DEC-815 (PR #51)

The tiers are gone. What survives of this argument is its conclusion: a plugin
installed from a directory, now origin `installed`, may run destructive
operations subject to `--ack`, and only the `dev` origin refuses them. The
provenance half of the reasoning no longer applies, because Cerberus makes no
provenance claim about a plugin at all. And since PR #49, `--ack` is demanded
for any `destructive` operation whatever `requires_ack` says.

relationships.note: the gate this decision shapes
the tiers this decision reasons about are largely unreachable
the install origin that replaced the tiers

data.decision: Make TrustModeLocal a first-class mode requiring no devmode build, record TrustTierUnsigned honestly, and let that tier run anything the manifest's requires_ack allows.
alternatives_considered: Group unsigned with local_dev/unsigned_dev and refuse destructive operations
Require a devmode build for any unsigned install
Require signatures for every install
data.rationale: A signature attests to provenance; the --ack flag attests to intent. An operator installing an unsigned plugin from a local path has established provenance out of band by building or vetting it themselves, so the thing a signature would add is already present in a different form. Grouping unsigned with the dev tiers would refuse every destructive operation and make the plugin lane read-only — and a read-only plugin lane cannot carry the provider integrations it exists for, which is the whole point of DEC-350. Destructive operations still require explicit acknowledgment, so the intent gate remains.

records.name: The host computes the entrypoint hash rather than asking the operator
records.summary: The installer always hashes the entrypoint binary itself and records the result as entrypoint_sha256, change detection rather than a trust signal.
records.confidence_label: installer and managed list DTO re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54)
records.body:
`LocalTrustPolicy` keeps `RequireArchiveHash: true` while dropping both signature requirements, which raises an obvious question: what is the hash *for*, if the operator supplies it themselves about a file they just built?

The answer is that they should not have to. `DirectoryInstaller.Install` computes it when the caller passes none, and the comment says why: requiring an operator to paste a digest of a binary they control is friction that buys nothing, because the value carries no information the operator did not already assert by choosing the directory. Computing it converts a ceremonial requirement into a useful one — a fingerprint of the entrypoint as installed, which would make a binary replaced underneath us detectable even for an unsigned plugin with no provenance at all.

The hashing step also turns out to be the first real integrity check in the install path: on a prototype directory with no built binary, install fails at `hash plugin entrypoint …: no such file or directory` rather than at launch. Verified live.

The decision is sound and the follow-through is not: the computed value lives only on the in-memory `InstalledPlugin`. It is not written to `plugin-connectors.json`, not compared on restore or reload, and not in the `managed list` payload — so the detection this reasoning was aimed at does not happen (GAP-336). Recorded as a decision anyway, because the reasoning is right and the gap is a small piece of missing wiring rather than a change of mind.

## Since PR #51

The caller override is gone: `--archive-sha256` is an unknown flag, and the host
computes the hash on every install. The field is `entrypoint_sha256`.
`ValidateInstall` refuses an install whose entrypoint cannot be fingerprinted.
`managed list` now reports it. It is still not persisted to
`plugin-connectors.json` and nothing compares it (CERB-GAP-336). Decision 12 of
`docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md` states the purpose this record
argued for: change detection, "not the binary you reviewed", never a trust
signal.

## Since P1-5

The follow-through landed, in a broader form. What load compares is the digest of the whole bundle, accepted in the install review and persisted as `bundle_digest`, so a changed `plugin.yaml` is caught along with a changed binary (CERB-GAP-336, closed). The entrypoint hash is still computed on every install and recorded in the audit log as `plugin_entrypoint_sha256`.

relationships.note: closed in P1-5 by the bundle digest
satisfies the policy's archive-hash requirement

data.decision: Compute the SHA-256 of the validated entrypoint in DirectoryInstaller.Install on every install (entrypoint_sha256), with no caller override, and refuse an install whose entrypoint cannot be fingerprinted.
alternatives_considered: Require the operator to pass --archive-sha256 for every install
Drop the archive-hash requirement for local installs entirely
data.rationale: Requiring an operator to paste a sha256 of a binary they just built is friction that buys nothing: they are attesting to a file they control, so the value carries no independent information. Computing it turns a requirement that was pure ceremony into something with a purpose — a recorded fingerprint that would make a binary changing underneath us detectable even for an unsigned plugin. The alternative, dropping the requirement, would leave nothing to build that on later.

records.name: A plugin that cannot be restored is skipped, never fatal
records.summary: Restore-at-startup warns and keeps an unrestorable registration instead of returning an error, because an optional component must not take the daemon down.
records.confidence_label: Rationale is in-code and in the commit history; three restore tests cover missing directory, unrestorable entries and a now-reserved id
records.body:
This one was learned the expensive way. `restoreManagedPlugins` used to return its error, the constructor propagated it, the daemon failed to start, and launchd's `KeepAlive` crash-looped. The trigger was mundane: `make clean` in a plugin repo, or a fresh clone where `dist/` is gitignored. An absent plugin directory bricked Cerberus entirely.

The rule that came out of it generalises past this function: **a plugin is optional by definition and must not be able to take the host with it.** Restore now installs what it can, warns for what it cannot with the recovery named ("the registration is kept; reinstall or run `… managed uninstall <id>` to drop it"), and carries on.

The second half is less obvious and equally deliberate. A skipped entry is kept in `unrestored` and re-appended by `persist()`, so the registration survives. Silently dropping it would mean an operator loses the record that they ever installed the plugin, and a rebuilt plugin would need reinstalling rather than simply reappearing on the next restart. The same path handles a plugin whose id has since become reserved: skipped, warned, kept.

The same instinct — non-fatal for optional things — produced DEC-352. It is the strongest single piece of reasoning in the plugin lane, and it is worth noticing that it argues in the opposite direction from GAP-333: nothing is allowed to fail the daemon, and as a result nothing notices when a plugin quietly stops working.

relationships.note: the restore path this decision governs
non-fatal everywhere is why a dead plugin is never noticed

data.decision: In restoreManagedPlugins, skip an entry that fails to install, warn with the recovery named, and keep it in `unrestored` so persist() does not drop the registration.
alternatives_considered: Return an error from the constructor when a persisted plugin cannot be restored
Drop the registration silently and carry on
data.rationale: Returning the error took the whole daemon down: the launchd job failed to start and KeepAlive crash-looped, so deleting a plugin directory — `make clean` in a plugin repo, or a fresh clone with a gitignored dist/ — bricked Cerberus entirely. A plugin is optional by definition and must not be able to take the host with it. Dropping the registration silently is the other failure: the operator loses their record of an install, and a rebuilt plugin would have to be reinstalled rather than simply coming back on the next restart.

records.name: The one-shot plugin exec lane does not reserve connector ids
records.summary: Only the daemon-managed lane refuses a reserved id; `connectors plugin exec` and `plugin health` accept any id.
records.confidence_label: PluginConnectorService and socket routes re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54)
records.body:
Consistency would be wrong here, which is worth saying because the asymmetry looks like an oversight.

The managed lane keeps an inventory, and a plugin in that inventory is dispatched ahead of the built-in registry in `ExternalConnectorService.Execute`. That is the shadow the reserved-id guard exists to prevent. The one-shot lane behind `connectors plugin exec` and `connectors plugin health` builds a `Manager` for one call, installs into it, runs, unloads and throws it away. It registers nothing and persists nothing, so there is no state in which it could shadow a built-in — the risk is structurally absent rather than merely unlikely.

The second reason is concrete. `cerberus connectors write-plugin-prototype docker <dir>` generates its manifest from the compiled-in Docker connector's own `Definition()`, so the prototype's id is `docker` — reserved. Applying the guard uniformly would make the reference example for plugin authoring impossible to run, which is a poor trade for a guard against a state the lane cannot reach.

A consequence worth knowing: the prototype is the only plugin artefact anywhere that declares a destructive operation (`destroy`, `requires_ack: true`), and the only lane that can run it is the one with no inventory, no persistence and no record of the call. That is not a reason to change the decision, but it is a reason to know it.

## Since PR #50

The one-shot lane now exists only in the operator's shell. The socket routes
that reached it (`/plugins/connectors/health` and
`/plugins/connectors/operations/`) answer 410 on the socket and on the web, and
the daemon no longer builds a `PluginConnectorService`. So the lane with no
inventory and no record is reachable only from a CLI process. The argument above
holds, and the exposure it accepted is now in-process only (CERB-GAP-846). Its
dry run is also no longer forwarded to a plugin that does not declare
`supports_dry` (CERB-DEC-814).

relationships.note: the scope of the reservation guard
the prototype this exception exists for

data.decision: Pass ReservedIDs only from the managed service, leaving DirectoryInstaller's set empty for the throwaway host behind `connectors plugin exec` and `connectors plugin health`.
alternatives_considered: Reserve ids in both lanes for consistency
Drop the Docker prototype so both lanes can reserve
data.rationale: The one-shot host installs into a throwaway manager for a single call and registers nothing, so it cannot shadow anything — the risk the guard exists to prevent is structurally absent. And refusing there would break the Docker plugin prototype, whose entire purpose is to demonstrate plugin authoring against a built-in connector's shape: its generated id is `docker`, which is reserved, so a consistent guard would make the reference example unrunnable.

records.name: The authoring half of the plugin contract is public; the host half stays internal
records.summary: plugin.yaml, entrypoint and MCP tool naming live in pkg/plugin; the manager, installer, trust policy and launcher stay in internal/pluginhost.
records.confidence_label: Stated in the package doc comment for pkg/plugin and realised by the alias file; both real plugins import only the public packages
records.body:
The boundary is drawn by a single question: can a plugin be allowed to influence this?

What a plugin must be able to build is public. `PluginYAML`, `Entrypoint` and the `cerberus.connector` block, because a plugin has to write a valid descriptor. `ToolNameForOperation`, because it is the rendezvous — the host routes `cerberus_<id>_<op>` and the plugin must serve exactly that name, so one of them owning the format privately would be a bug waiting to happen. `SecretFromConfig`, because reading a credential out of the init map should not require guessing the key.

What decides whether to trust a plugin is internal. `Manager`, `DirectoryInstaller`, `TrustPolicy` (now `InstallPolicy`), `SubprocessLauncher`, the SDK protocol types. The package doc says it plainly: "Those are host decisions and must not be something a plugin can influence." A plugin that could import and construct a `TrustDecision` could present itself as signed.

The seam is `internal/pluginhost/plugin_yaml.go`, which is nothing but type aliases back onto `pkg/plugin` so the host side reads as it always did. That matters more than it looks: the alternative — a separate SDK repo duplicating the descriptor types — lets the host's idea of a manifest and the author's idea of a manifest drift, and a manifest is exactly the artefact where drift shows up as a validation error nobody can explain.

Both real plugins import only `pkg/plugin`, `pkg/connector` and `pkg/resource`, which is the check that the boundary holds. What is not settled is what the public half *promises* across versions (GAP-340).

## Since PR #51

`TrustPolicy` and `TrustDecision` are gone. The host-side types are `InstallPolicy` and `InstallDecision`, which record an install origin (`installed` or `dev`) rather than a tier (CERB-DEC-815). The argument is unchanged: a plugin that could construct one could choose its own origin, and so escape the `dev` restriction.

relationships.note: the contract this decision scopes
no stability promise attached to the public half

data.decision: Move the descriptor types, entrypoint validation, tool naming and the secret reader into pkg/plugin, alias them back into internal/pluginhost, and keep every host decision internal.
alternatives_considered: Publish the whole plugin host so a plugin can reuse it
Keep everything internal and have plugin authors copy the schema
Publish a separate SDK repo duplicating the descriptor types
data.rationale: A plugin module outside this repository must be able to construct a valid plugin.yaml and serve the right MCP tool names without importing internal/, so those things are part of the public contract by necessity. The host's manager, installer, trust policy and launcher are the opposite: they are decisions about whether and how to trust a plugin, and they must not be something a plugin can influence or reuse to present itself differently. Copying the schema into a separate SDK would let the two drift, which is the failure the aliases in internal/pluginhost/plugin_yaml.go exist to avoid.

records.name: Plugin secrets resolve at load, not per call
records.summary: Unlike a built-in connector, which resolves a credential on every call, a plugin receives its credentials once in plugin/init and does not see a later change until it is reloaded.
records.confidence_label: Stated in pkg/plugin's doc comment and docs/secrets.md, and demonstrated live: managed load on a loaded plugin does not re-resolve
records.body:
A built-in connector resolves its credential when it is constructed, per call. A plugin gets its credentials once, in `plugin/init`, and holds them for the life of the subprocess. That difference is deliberate and it has a cost that is worth being explicit about.

The reasons for resolving once are good ones. The subprocess is long-lived, so a credential handed at init lets the plugin build its client once rather than per call. The alternative — shipping credentials with every `mcp/call_tool` — would put them in the arguments of every operation, which is exactly where they end up in logs, error echoes and crash dumps. And letting the plugin *pull* a credential from the host on demand would invert the trust direction that keeping the manager internal exists to protect.

The cost is rotation. An operator who adds, changes or revokes a credential under a loaded plugin changes nothing until the plugin is reloaded — and "reloaded" here means `unload` then `load`, because `Manager.Load` short-circuits on an already-running plugin. Verified live: `managed load contextforge` against the loaded plugin returned `missing_secrets: ["token"]` unchanged. Nothing invalidates a plugin's held credential, and nothing notices that the store has moved on. For a rotated-under-you credential the observable symptom is a plugin that authenticated fine an hour ago returning 401s with no local explanation.

This is a decision rather than a gap because the alternatives are worse, but it needs the operational note attached: **rotating a secret for a plugin means unloading and loading it.** The error text that tells operators otherwise is GAP-331.

relationships.note: the channel's timing model
the reload instruction does not reload

data.decision: Resolve declared secrets in Manager.Load and pass them in SDKInitParams.Config; do not re-resolve per operation.
alternatives_considered: Resolve per operation and pass credentials with each mcp/call_tool
Have the plugin request a credential from the host over the protocol when it needs one
data.rationale: The plugin subprocess is long-lived and the protocol is request/response over stdio, so a credential handed at init is held by the plugin for its lifetime — which is what lets a plugin build a client once instead of per call. Passing credentials with every tool call would put them on the wire repeatedly and in every call's arguments, where they would reach logs and error echoes. Letting the plugin pull from the host would invert the trust direction the internal/pluginhost boundary exists to protect.

relationships.note: the subprocess this governs
the statelessness that makes it safe

records.name: selfexec.WatchAndExit stays out of cerberus mcp
records.summary: A binary-swap watcher was removed from the MCP subprocess because deploying the daemon would make every running cerberus mcp child exit at once, wiping MCP access on any host that does not respawn children.
records.confidence_label: Comment read in full and the absence of any selfexec call in cmd_mcp.go confirmed by search
records.body:
Verified: `internal/selfexec` exists, and `cmd/cerberus/cmd_mcp.go` contains no
call to it — only the comment recording why, tagged `CW-20260519-0053`.

`CERB-4` originally added `selfexec.WatchAndExit` so that swapping the binary on
disk caused the MCP subprocess to exit and be respawned on the next tool call,
picking up the new build. That reasoning depends on the MCP host respawning dead
children. Claude Code does. `mux mcp --proxy` does not — it leaves dead children
dead.

`cerberus resource deploy cerberus-daemon-service` rewrites the binary on disk.
Every `selfexec` watcher in every running `cerberus mcp` process across every
host notices within 30 seconds and exits. Under a host that does not respawn,
that is fleet-wide loss of MCP access triggered by a routine daemon deploy — and
triggered simultaneously, so there is no partial signal to notice it by.

What makes the removal cheap is that the problem it solved does not exist. The
subprocess holds no config state: it dials the socket and re-dials on every tool
call. So a daemon restart is already survivable without the watcher, and the
in-memory subprocess picking up new *daemon* behaviour needs nothing. The only
thing it cannot pick up is a change to its own tool definitions, and the parent
host can recycle children at its own cadence for that.

The general shape is worth carrying beyond this case: a self-updating mechanism
whose correctness depends on the *parent's* restart policy is only as reliable as
the least capable parent, and a mechanism that fires everywhere at once has no
safe failure mode.

data.decision: Remove selfexec.WatchAndExit from the cerberus mcp subprocess and rely on per-call socket re-dialing
alternatives_considered: Keep the watcher and accept that non-respawning hosts lose MCP access on every daemon deploy
Make the watcher conditional on a host capability flag the subprocess cannot actually observe
Have the subprocess re-exec itself rather than exit, which risks a restart loop against a half-written binary
data.rationale: The watcher's benefit assumed a respawning parent; its cost under a non-respawning parent is simultaneous fleet-wide loss of MCP access, and per-call re-dialing already delivers the resilience the watcher was added for

relationships.note: the adapter's architecture
the socket is the single source of truth
the same PATH argument applied to liveness

records.name: cerberus mcp holds no state and re-dials per call
records.summary: The MCP subprocess was made a stateless RPC client to the daemon socket rather than a second consumer of the config, so the daemon is the single source of truth for execution.
records.confidence_label: Contract read from the command's own help text and confirmed against the call path; the SSH exception verified in source
records.body:
`cerberus mcp`'s long help states the contract: "The standalone subprocess holds
NO config state of its own: it dials the running 'cerberus daemon' over
~/.cerberus/cerberus.sock and forwards every tool call to the daemon, which owns
the single source of truth for runtime execution."

The alternative — the subprocess loading and caching config itself — is what
`CERB-2` replaced, and the failure mode it removed is the same one the connector
liveness code warns about in `connectorDefinitions`: a second process with a
different `PATH`, a different environment and a different view of the registry
reports state that does not match what actually runs. The daemon has launchd's
minimal `PATH`; a subprocess spawned by an MCP host has the host's. Two
processes answering "is this connector live?" from different environments is how
you get a healthy-looking connector that fails every call.

Two consequences follow, both deliberate:

- The boot ping is non-fatal. An MCP host may spawn the subprocess before the
  daemon exists, so an unreachable daemon logs
  `client.mcp.daemon_unreachable_on_boot` and warns on stderr; tool calls then
  return `DaemonUnreachableError` until the daemon is up.
- Re-dialing per call is what makes CERB-DEC-470 safe, and it means a daemon
  restart is invisible to a running subprocess.

One exception survives, and it is a real leak in the contract: the four SSH
tools take a `*config.ConfigV2` resolved locally by `loadUnifiedForTools`, and
if that resolution fails the tools are simply not registered — the subprocess
logs "SSH tools will be unavailable; daemon-routed tools still work" and serves
49 tools instead of 53. So the tool surface an agent sees depends on whether the
subprocess could read the config, which is exactly the coupling the decision set
out to remove.

data.decision: Make cerberus mcp a stateless forwarder over the daemon socket, re-dialing on every tool call
alternatives_considered: Have the subprocess load and cache config itself, as CERB-2 replaced
Serve MCP only from inside the daemon over stdio, which the daemon still does but which no MCP host can spawn per-client
data.rationale: One process owning execution means one answer to what is running and what is live; a second process with a different PATH and environment is how a connector reads healthy while every call fails

relationships.note: the 410 tombstone lives in the console

the pattern internal/infra should follow if retired

records.name: Retired surface entries are tombstoned, not deleted
records.summary: Two retired capabilities — per-record Namecheap DNS writes and centralized config migration — remain visible on their surfaces, returning a refusal that names the replacement, rather than disappearing.
records.confidence_label: Both tombstones read in source; the DNS refusal observed live on the CLI and in the MCP tool description
records.body:
Two instances, handled the same way for the same reason.

**Per-record Namecheap DNS writes.** `cerberus dns create` and `cerberus dns
delete` still exist, still accept all their flags, and return
`ncconn.ErrUnsafePerRecordWrite`. Their short help is literally "Disabled:
unsafe per-record Namecheap writes". The MCP tools `cerberus_dns_create` and
`cerberus_dns_delete` are registered with full input schemas and a description
that says "Disabled: per-record Namecheap writes can silently delete hidden
records. Use cerberus_set_dns_record_set with an authoritative whole-zone set."
The underlying hazard is that Namecheap's `getHosts` can omit records, so a
per-record write computed from it deletes what it could not see.

**Centralized config migration.** `POST /api/config/migrate` and
`GET /api/config/migrate/preview` return `410 Gone` with "centralized config
migration is retired", and `TestCentralizedMigrationEndpointsAreGone` asserts
both the status and the message.

The alternative is deletion, and deletion is worse on both surfaces for
different reasons. An operator who knows `cerberus dns create` gets "unknown
command" and no idea what to do instead; a tombstone tells them. An agent is
more affected still: a tool that vanishes from `tools/list` leaves a model
working from stale knowledge with nothing to correct it, while a tool that
remains and returns "disabled, use X" is self-correcting on first call. Keeping
the input schema matters too — a model that constructs a call from remembered
parameters gets a schema-valid call and a useful refusal rather than a
validation error.

The cost is honest: dead entries accumulate, and a tombstone with an input
schema is a tool an agent may spend a call on. The 410-plus-test form is the
stronger version, because the test stops the endpoint being quietly resurrected.
Worth noting that the DNS tombstone created CERB-GAP-436 — it names a
replacement that has an MCP tool and no CLI command, so on one surface the
tombstone points nowhere.

**Superseded for the provider migration (2026-09-25).** The operator chose to drop the pseudo-neutral `dns`, `domain` and `server` verbs and every retired hand-written MCP tool with no tombstones, because two dozen dead tools would cost every agent context on every session. The replacements share a discoverable prefix (`cerberus connectors exec <id>` and `cerberus_<id>_<op>`). The decision stands for other surfaces, such as the config-migration endpoints.

data.decision: Keep a retired surface entry in place, returning a refusal that names its replacement, and pin it with a test
alternatives_considered: Delete the command, route or tool outright
Leave the operation enabled with a warning, which keeps the data-loss hazard reachable
data.rationale: A refusal that names the replacement is self-correcting for both operators and models, where a vanished entry leaves both working from stale knowledge; a test stops the retired path being resurrected

relationships.note: this decision is the cause
the console package that no longer builds

records.name: Removing internal/webui/dist/.gitkeep, and what it cost
records.summary: The dist placeholder was deleted in a54daa8 on the reasoning that make all populates the directory before go build — which is true of make all and of nothing else, so a fresh checkout stopped compiling.
records.confidence_label: Commit message quoted in full; the consequence reproduced live in a clean worktree
records.body:
Commit `a54daa8`, 20 May 2026, "chore: remove obsolete
internal/webui/dist/.gitkeep":

> The placeholder is no longer needed — `make all` rebuilds the web bundle
> into internal/webui/dist before `go build`, and the daemon's cerberus-web
> service depends on that path being populated at build time, not present
> empty.

Every clause is correct. The conclusion does not follow, because `make all` is
not the only thing that compiles the package:

- `make test` is `go test ./cmd/cerberus ./internal/... ./pkg/...` and does not
  depend on `ui-build`.
- `make lint` runs `go vet` over the same set.
- Lefthook's pre-push hook is the full `go test`, and there is no CI behind it.
- `make clean` deletes the contents of `internal/webui/dist` while explicitly
  preserving `! -name .gitkeep` — a guard for a file that no longer exists.
- `.gitignore` still carries `!/internal/webui/dist/.gitkeep`, the negation
  written to keep the placeholder tracked.

So the repository still contains two artefacts that assume the file is there,
and the quality gate is now passable only in a working copy where somebody has
run the web build at least once. Reproduced live in a clean worktree:
`go vet ./internal/webui/` and `go test ./cmd/cerberus` both fail with
`pattern all:dist: no matching files found` (CERB-GAP-441).

Recorded as a decision rather than only a gap because the reasoning is sound and
the failure is a scope error — it evaluated the change against the build path the
author was using and not against the ones the tooling actually invokes. The
tell was available at the time: two other files in the repo were written to
protect the thing being removed.

data.decision: Delete internal/webui/dist/.gitkeep on the grounds that make all populates the directory
alternatives_considered: Keep the placeholder, which is what .gitignore and make clean still assume
Make test and lint depend on ui-build, which puts npm install on the path of every test run
Guard the embed so an empty or absent directory is tolerated
data.rationale: make all does populate dist before go build; the error was not checking the other entry points — make test, make lint, plain go build and the lefthook pre-push gate — none of which run ui-build

relationships.note: the decision this gap is about
the console
the socket's contrasting uid-based model
the Host and Origin rules the design needed

records.name: The console guards mutation with a per-process token, not authentication
records.summary: cerberus web generates a random token per process, hands it out at GET /api/session, and requires it on mutating routes — a CSRF defence chosen on the premise that a loopback listener needs no authentication.
records.confidence_label: internal/webui/server.go and internal/loopback re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54)
records.body:
`webui.New` generates 32 random bytes at construction.
`allowStateChangingRequest` requires a JSON content type, that token in
`X-Cerberus-Web-Token`, and — only when an `Origin` header is present — a
same-origin `Origin`. `GET /api/session` returns the token to anyone who asks.
A comment marks the choice explicitly: "This authenticated UI bootstrap
intentionally delivers a credential, unlike diagnostic responses. Keep it out of
the redaction path."

Against a browser the design is coherent and the pieces each earn their place.
Same-origin policy stops a hostile page reading `/api/session`, so the token is
unforgeable from another origin. The `Origin` check catches a cross-origin POST
that guessed. The JSON content-type requirement blocks form-based CSRF, which
cannot set that header. Per-process generation means a token does not outlive
the console. The listener is `127.0.0.1` by default. For the threat this was
built for — a random page the operator visits while the console is open — it is
the right construction.

What it is not is authentication, and the code reads as though it were. Any
local process gets the token from an open endpoint, sends no `Origin`, and is
indistinguishable from the console; behind that sit resource deploy and remove,
pipeline run, registry mutation, the plugin lifecycle, and the generic connector
route that accepts `acknowledged: true` and therefore reaches every destructive
connector operation (CERB-GAP-442).

The comparison that clarifies it: the socket API's model is mode `0600` and the
same uid, with no token at all — an honest statement that local uid is the trust
boundary. The console is a TCP listener and so inherits none of that, but it
adopted a token that implies a stronger boundary than it has. Either barrier
would be defensible; the problem is that the weaker one is dressed as the
stronger.

## Since PR #48

"Same-origin policy stops a hostile page reading `/api/session`" was not true
under DNS rebinding. A page that re-points its own name at `127.0.0.1` is
same-origin with the console, so it could read the token. It could then pass the
Origin check, which compared against `r.Host`, also attacker-controlled. The
browser-CSRF design this record defends is now true: a loopback Host allow-list
runs before every handler, and Origin is matched exactly against loopback
origins on the listen port (CERB-DEC-810). The local-process half is unchanged
(CERB-GAP-442).

data.decision: Guard console mutation with a per-process random token served at /api/session, plus a conditional same-origin check
alternatives_considered: No guard at all, matching the socket API's uid-is-the-boundary model
A token written to a 0600 file or printed at startup, which a browser cannot read but a local process must be granted
Requiring Origin unconditionally, which blocks every non-browser client by design
data.rationale: Correctly scoped to the browser CSRF threat a local console actually faces; the gap is that it reads as authentication against local processes, which it was never designed to resist

relationships.note: the CLI behaviour
the same single-owner argument
the outage this decision corrects

records.name: Connector liveness is reported by the daemon, not the calling CLI
records.summary: cerberus connectors takes its LIVE column from the daemon and falls back to the local view only when the daemon cannot answer, because the CLI process has the operator's PATH and credentials while the daemon has launchd's.
records.confidence_label: Reasoning quoted from source; the live liveness map verified against the running daemon on CLI, socket and MCP
records.body:
The comment in `connectorDefinitions` states the whole argument:

> Liveness has to come from the daemon, because the daemon is what runs the
> operation. This process has the user's shell PATH and credentials; the daemon
> has launchd's. Reporting the CLI's view here is how a connector could read
> LIVE=yes while every call against it failed.

So the CLI calls `client.ListLiveConnectors(ctx)`, builds the map from the
daemon's answer, overlays managed-plugin loaded state, and only on error falls
back to `connectorLive(local, id)`. Verified live: 9 connectors, with `azure`,
`contextforge`, `docker` and `ssh` live and the rest not — liveness meaning
"constructible right now", not "installed".

This is the correction for a real outage `AGENTS.md` records: the Docker
connector resolved `docker` once at boot under launchd's minimal `PATH`
(`/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`), failed, cached the failure for the daemon's
lifetime, and `cerberus connectors list` reported it healthy the whole time
because the CLI could see `docker` on the operator's `PATH`.

Two things generalise from it. First, whoever executes must be the one who
reports on their ability to execute — any other arrangement is a
time-of-check/time-of-use bug across a process boundary. Second, the same
reasoning drove CERB-DEC-471: one process owning execution means one answer, and
a second process with a different environment answering the same question is
the bug.

The fallback is the remaining soft spot. When the daemon is unreachable the CLI
silently reports its own view, which is the view the comment says is wrong, with
no marker on the output saying which source answered. That is arguably the right
trade — some answer beats none — but it should say so.

data.decision: Take the connector LIVE column from the daemon, falling back to the local view only when the daemon cannot answer
alternatives_considered: Report the calling process's own view, which is what caused the cached-Docker-failure outage
Report nothing when the daemon is unreachable rather than falling back to a view known to be misleading
data.rationale: The daemon executes the operation, so only the daemon's environment can answer whether a connector is constructible; the CLI's shell PATH and credentials made a dead connector read as healthy for weeks

relationships.note: the duplicated tool list is its cost
the adapter
the socket server it sits alongside

records.name: The daemon keeps its own stdio MCP server alongside the socket
records.summary: cerberus daemon runs a stdio MCP server against its in-process client as well as the socket server, preserved for consumers that pipe stdio to the daemon directly — at the cost of a second hand-maintained tool list.
records.confidence_label: Comments and both registration blocks read in full; lists extracted and diffed as identical
records.body:
The comment records the intent: "Preserved for consumers that invoke `cerberus
daemon` directly with stdio piping. Runs against the same InProcessClient so it
sees identical state to the socket-routed subprocess." And for the socket server
alongside it: "Sits alongside (not instead of) the stdio MCP server below so
direct-MCP-over-stdio consumers still work."

Backward compatibility for stdio consumers is a reasonable thing to keep, and
running both against the same `InProcessClient` does guarantee identical state.
Two costs came with it that are worth recording.

The tool list is registered a second time, inline, in a 60-line block — a
separate hand-maintained copy of the list in `buildCerberusMCPServer`. Extracted
and diffed, the two agree exactly at HEAD (52 constructors each), so this is a
latent divergence rather than a live bug (CERB-GAP-431). `cmd_mcp_http.go` shows
the fix: it reuses `buildCerberusMCPServer` and cannot drift. The daemon's copy
does not, and the only reason it cannot trivially do the same is that it passes
`a.Config` to the SSH tool constructors where `cerberus mcp` resolves its own.

And under launchd — which is how the daemon runs on this machine, from a
hand-written plist — stdin is not a pipe from any MCP client. The goroutine
serves a stdio session nobody is on the other end of, for the daemon's lifetime.
Harmless, but it means the compatibility path is dead weight in the
configuration that is actually deployed, and the cost of carrying it is a
duplicated list that will eventually drift.

data.decision: Run a stdio MCP server inside the daemon in addition to the socket server, for direct-stdio consumers
alternatives_considered: Socket only, requiring direct-stdio consumers to move to cerberus mcp
Have the daemon reuse buildCerberusMCPServer, which would keep the compatibility path without duplicating the list
data.rationale: Backward compatibility for consumers that pipe stdio to cerberus daemon, with identical state guaranteed by sharing the InProcessClient; the duplicated registration was accepted as the cost

records.name: port: 0 is banned by the schema
records.summary: A resource declaring port: 0 is a validation error, because lsof -ti :0 returns arbitrary system PIDs that the monitor reads as a false-positive 'running'.
records.confidence_label: both guards read in source and both verified: TestValidateProjectConfigPortZeroIsError passes and the installed binary rejects port: 0 with the omit-the-field recovery text

data.decision: Reject port: 0 at validation time and refuse it again at the lookup, rather than treating 0 as 'no port'.
alternatives_considered: treat 0 as equivalent to omitted
filter it in findPIDByPort only
document it as a convention
data.rationale: The failure is silent and inverted: a process that is not running reports as running, and the daemon monitor acts on that. A convention had already failed to hold it. Two independent guards were chosen over one because either alone leaves a path in: a config written before the check still reaches findPIDByPort, and a caller that bypasses validation still needs the lookup to refuse.

relationships.note: the defining property of the registry
the footgun this decision knowingly accepts

records.name: the registry index stores a path handle, never config content
records.summary: A registry entry is an absolute path plus metadata; the config body is re-read from the owning app's file on every resolution and never cached.
records.confidence_label: read from internal/registry package docs, index.go and location.go; the retirement is enforced in code and carries its own error text
records.body:
The property is stated three times in the code and enforced twice.

`index.go`: "IndexEntry is one registered project config — a pointer, never the config body. The body is always re-read fresh from Path, keeping the index a local-first resolver handle (Tether D2)." `Registry` itself "owns no in-memory state beyond the index path: every operation reads the index fresh".

The enforcement is the interesting part. A central directory was built and then retired, and the retirement is not passive — `ValidateConfigLocation` refuses any path under `~/.cerberus/projects` (or `<state-dir>/projects` for a `--config` override), checking the symlink target as well as the path, with the reasoning in the error: a pointer in Cerberus state is not repo-owned merely because its content lives elsewhere. `configops.ErrCentralizedMigrationRetired` names the replacement flow, and the two web routes that used to migrate return 410 Gone.

What the decision costs is recorded honestly in CERB-GAP-539: because the index holds only a handle, a config that disappears takes its resources with it. Detection was built rather than caching — the skip/warn diagnostics and the `resource list` notice — which is the consistent choice, not a compromise: caching would have made the list *right* at the cost of making it a lie about what is on disk.

Reversible in the sense that a cache could be added later, but the retirement of the central directory has been enforced in code with an operator-facing error, so reversing it means undoing that too.

data.decision: Keep only a pointer index, local-first (Tether D2).
alternatives_considered: copy the config body into the index at register time
cache a parsed copy with an invalidation scheme
a central config directory Cerberus owns (built, then retired)
data.rationale: Ownership. The app is the author of its own definitions, and a copy in Cerberus state is a second source of truth that drifts silently and makes 'which one is live' unanswerable. The centralized alternative was actually built and then retired — ValidateConfigLocation now refuses configs under ~/.cerberus/projects, symlink targets included, because a pointer in Cerberus state is not repo-owned merely because its content lives elsewhere.

relationships.note: the author-time half is validate's strictness
the runtime half is the resolver's leniency

records.name: runtime config parsing is lenient; author-time parsing is strict
records.summary: An unrecognised field is a warning to the resolver and a refusal to register and to single-file validate — forward compatibility at runtime, typo detection at author time.
records.confidence_label: the reasoning and the incident date are carried in the LoadProjectConfig and unknownFields doc comments; the strict/lenient split verified by reading both call paths
records.body:
The mechanism is a second parse whose only job is to produce data instead of a failure. `LoadProjectConfig` decodes leniently, then `unknownFields` re-decodes with `KnownFields(true)` and keeps only the yaml.v3 complaints containing "not found in type". It never returns an error — anything that would break a real parse was already surfaced by the lenient decode, and a strict-only complaint is information.

`ValidateProjectConfig` files each one as a *warning* under the field name `unknown-field`. The resolver skips a config only on error-severity issues, so the project survives. Author-time callers then select on exactly those warnings via `UnknownFieldIssues()` and refuse:

    %s has %d unrecognised field(s), first: %s — fix the typo, or upgrade
    cerberus if the field is newer than this binary

That message names both causes because the reader genuinely cannot tell them apart from the file alone. Note it is also an error message carrying a recovery instruction, which is the class `redact.Text` has eaten four times — worth a survives-redaction test if one does not exist.

One asymmetry this creates is worth knowing and is not documented: `cerberus validate <path>` refuses unrecognised fields, and `cerberus validate` with no argument does not. `checkEntry` fails an entry only on error severity, so a registered config with a typo'd field reports `ok` with a warning detail and the command exits 0. Author-time strictness is attached to the file form, not to the registered form — defensible, since the registered form is a runtime health check, but it means "validate passes" means two different things depending on the arguments.

data.decision: Parse leniently everywhere, then re-parse strictly only to name the ignored fields, and let author-time callers select on those warnings and reject.
alternatives_considered: strict parsing everywhere (the prior behaviour)
lenient everywhere
a config schema version gate per field
data.rationale: Strict parsing at runtime is a silent-outage generator: the resolver drops any config that fails to load, so on 2026-05-25 a single field written by a newer writer — registry_urn — took 17 of 18 projects offline with no error anywhere. A field from a newer Cerberus must never cost a project. Nothing is lost by leniency, because a typo is introduced at author time and register and validate still refuse it there.

relationships.note: defines the two-place layout
install.md documents this split incorrectly

records.name: only the main database moved onto go-apppaths; the dotdir stays
records.summary: The XDG layout resolves the main DB and nothing else — config.yaml, registry.yaml, install roots, sockets, pids and locks stay in the hand-made ~/.cerberus/ dotdir.
records.confidence_label: the scope note and the WithLegacyNames rejection are in layout.go's doc comment; the split confirmed live from cerberus path output
records.body:
One of the better-documented decisions in the repo, and it carries its own change id (CW-20260517-0065).

`config.ResolveLayout` resolves via `paths.Resolve("cerberus", …)` in default XDG mode. Project mode is "deliberately not used". The scope note enumerates what stays behind rather than gesturing at it: "config.yaml, registry.yaml, projects/*.cerberus.yaml, the apps/<project>/ install roots, sockets, pids, locks — STAYS where it is by design … Do not route those through go-apppaths."

The `WithLegacyNames` paragraph is the part worth carrying forward, because it records a considered-and-rejected option and the reason is a capability limit rather than a preference: the option adopts XDG-root to XDG-root by app name and structurally cannot reach a hand-made dotdir. And the migration would have been a no-op regardless — the old `cerberus.db` was 0 bytes, lazily opened and never populated.

Verified live 2026-09-17, and the irony is worth recording: the *new* database is also never populated. `~/.local/share/cerberus/workspaces/default/` exists and is empty. The store is still lazily opened and nothing on this machine has opened it, so the decision moved a path that no data has yet travelled.

Reversible, but reversing it means coordinating with every other Hollis Labs app whose plists point into the dotdir. `docs/install.md` describes this split wrongly in two places; see CERB-GAP-543.

data.decision: Adopt go-apppaths for the database path only, with an explicit scope note, and leave the dotdir alone (CW-20260517-0065).
alternatives_considered: move the whole dotdir onto the XDG layout
use go-apppaths project mode
use WithLegacyNames to adopt the old location
data.rationale: The dotdir is the deploy substrate other Hollis Labs apps' plists and migration runbooks point into, and it is referenced by absolute path across the Cerberus codebase; moving it would break things outside this repo. WithLegacyNames was considered and rejected on capability grounds — it only adopts XDG-root to XDG-root by app name and cannot reach a hand-made dotdir. There was nothing to adopt anyway: the old cerberus.db was 0 bytes, lazily opened and never populated.

relationships.note: normalization is where this is realised
the residue that is a genuine gap
the descriptors only stay wrong because nobody registers them

records.name: dir: is a literal path, with no interpolation and no override layer
records.summary: A resource's dir: is taken literally — ~ is expanded for local/process resources and nothing else is — which is a deliberate limitation, not an unfinished feature.
records.confidence_label: argued from the code (ExpandHomePath is the only expansion; no interpolation exists anywhere) and from AGENTS.md's framing of the descriptors as templates; no ADR or commit states the reasoning explicitly, so the rationale is reconstructed
records.body:
The audit was asked directly: is config portability a gap, or a deliberate limitation? **Deliberate limitation** — and the argument has to be made from the code, because no ADR states it.

The evidence that it is deliberate rather than unfinished:

1. **An expansion mechanism exists and was scoped, not forgotten.** `ExpandHomePath` handles `~` and `~/` and is applied to a specific, enumerated list of keys: `dir`, `env_file`, `log_file`, `artifact_path`, `install_root`, `install_work_dir`, `command`, `env` values, `health_check.command`, and the `build_strategy` `source`/`rules` maps. Somebody wrote that list out. An unfinished feature does not have a hand-curated key list.
2. **No interpolation machinery exists anywhere in the config lane.** Not a disabled flag, not a TODO, not a partial implementation. `${VERSION}` and `${BUILD_DATE}` do appear in this repo's own `build_strategy.rules.ldflags`, so the codebase knows what interpolation looks like — it is just confined to the build strategy, where the values are build metadata rather than filesystem locations.
3. **`AGENTS.md` frames the consequence as a property, not a bug**: "`dir:` is a literal path with no interpolation or override, so those descriptors are not registered and editing them changes nothing that runs here. Treat them as templates, not as live configuration." That is a limitation being *used* to draw a boundary.

The rationale, reconstructed: `dir` is where a build runs and where a process's working directory points. `resolveArtifactSource` installs the build strategy's declared output from it, and `AGENTS.md` already records that a strategy missing an `output` rule can install a binary the build never wrote. Adding a layer that can make `dir` resolve to an unintended directory puts a silent wrong-target build behind an environment variable — and it would fail at deploy time, on the machine, not at author time. One line you can read literally is worth more than a template that is correct on the author's machine.

The defensible priority for the portability question is therefore **not must-have**. Two things support that. First, `~` expansion already makes a portable config writable today: `dir: ~/Projects-apps/cerberus` would resolve correctly on both this machine and the author's, and this repo's own descriptors simply do not use it. Second — and this is the real reason the descriptors stay wrong — nothing registers them, so nothing forces them to be correct. Fix CERB-GAP-544 and the descriptors have to resolve or the project does not start; the portability question stops being theoretical either way.

What *is* a gap is narrow and is recorded separately as CERB-GAP-538: expansion is gated to `local`/`process` resources, so a container or server resource cannot use `~` at all, and that asymmetry is invisible from the file.

Reversible — nothing prevents adding interpolation later — but doing so should come with an answer to "what happens when this resolves to the wrong directory during a deploy".

data.decision: Keep paths literal. Expand ~ during normalization for local/process resources; add no $VAR interpolation, no machine-profile layer and no override file.
alternatives_considered: $VAR / ${HOME} interpolation
a per-machine override or profile layer
relative paths resolved against the config file's directory
data.rationale: A resource's dir is a real directory a real build and a real process run in, and every interpolation layer adds a way for that path to resolve to something the author did not mean — silently, at deploy time, in a build that then writes to the wrong place. Literalness makes 'where does this run' answerable by reading one line. ~ expansion was accepted because it has exactly one meaning per machine and no ambiguity.

relationships.note: the rotation property of the credential chain
the load-time half of the same split

records.name: built-in connectors resolve credentials per call; plugins resolve at load
records.summary: A built-in connector constructs its credential provider per operation, so adding or rotating a credential needs no daemon restart; a plugin is handed its secrets once at load and needs an explicit reload.
records.confidence_label: read from the RegisterFactory wiring in app.go and ReferenceProvider.Get, which re-reads the mapping file per call; not demonstrated by rotating a real credential

data.decision: Resolve credentials inside the per-call connector factory, reading the reference mapping file fresh on every lookup.
alternatives_considered: resolve once at daemon boot and cache
cache with a TTL
resolve at load for connectors too, matching plugins
data.rationale: Boot-time resolution caches a failure for the daemon's whole lifetime. The Docker connector proved it: eager registration cached 'docker CLI not found' and starting Docker Desktop or correcting the daemon's PATH could not recover without a restart, while connectors list reported it healthy. The same shape applies to a credential — a secret added after boot would be invisible until restart, and a restart is the most expensive recovery Cerberus has.

relationships.note: one of the checks validate actually performs

records.name: project.id is validated against a stricter pattern than owner
records.summary: owner and namespace allow any lowercase kebab-case; project.id additionally forbids trailing and doubled hyphens, because other systems join on it.
records.confidence_label: both patterns and the reasoning are in schema.go's comments; the cross-system consumers are asserted there rather than verified from those repos
records.body:
A small decision with a disproportionate comment, and the comment is the valuable part.

    identPattern = ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$          // owner, namespace
    slugPattern  = ^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$      // project.id

`identPattern` admits `app-` and `a--b`; `slugPattern` does not. The stated reason: "those are harmless as a local registry key but this value is also a Tesseract namespace segment and an agent-setup template basename, and a slug that round-trips differently through those is a join that silently misses."

Two related calls ride along. `owner` and `project.id` must be equal, with the reasoning given as "two names for one project is a join waiting to pick the wrong one. They have never diverged in practice; this keeps it that way rather than deciding later which one other systems meant." And `owner` may be omitted entirely, defaulting from `project.id` at load — previously a hard error, relaxed to remove the duplication without changing anything that worked.

Worth recording because it is the clearest case in this area of Cerberus validating something on another system's behalf. It also sets up an expectation the rest of the validator does not meet: an identifier other systems join on is checked against a regex, while a `dir:` the local build depends on is not checked at all (CERB-GAP-530).

By contrast, `Link.Kind` is deliberately left free-form, following Tether ADR 0041 D16: a closed vocabulary means every new relation needs a coordinated schema change in every reader. So the decision is not "validate identifiers strictly" but "validate exactly what other systems join on, and nothing else".

data.decision: Two patterns: identPattern for registry-local identifiers, slugPattern for the portfolio-wide project slug.
alternatives_considered: one pattern for all identifiers
validate the slug only in the systems that consume it
no validation, convention only
data.rationale: project.id is not merely a local label: Cerberus keys the registry on it, Tesseract uses it as a memory namespace segment, and agent-setup names project templates after it. A slug that round-trips differently through those is a join that silently misses — and Cerberus's validator is the only place the invariant can be enforced before those systems join on it.

records.name: no writer remains for project configs; the central directory was retired
records.summary: Cerberus has no code path that writes a project config; configs are authored in their owning repos, committed on main, then registered.
records.confidence_label: the sentinel error, the two 410 Gone routes and the location refusal all read in source; grep confirms no config writer exists

data.decision: Retire the centralized migration entirely and refuse configs living under Cerberus state, rather than keeping a write path with a warning.
alternatives_considered: keep config migrate with a deprecation warning
keep a write path for the monolith only
a Cerberus-owned central directory (built, then retired)
data.rationale: A writer is a second author, and a second author means the question 'which copy is live' has no answer. Retiring the write path rather than deprecating it makes the model enforceable: ValidateConfigLocation can refuse a config under Cerberus state because there is no supported way to have put one there.

the decision is not enforced against a literal in env:

records.name: credentials are named in config, never carried in it
records.summary: A resource or connector references a credential by scheme and name; the value is resolved in the consuming process at the moment it is needed.
records.confidence_label: the reasoning is carried in the secretref package doc and docs/secrets.md; the shim path is not exercised on this machine
records.body:
Stated in `internal/secretref`'s package doc, and the reasoning is a specific mechanism rather than a principle: "Cerberus writes a managed service's environment into a launchd plist, so any literal credential in `*.cerberus.yaml` is copied verbatim into `~/Library/LaunchAgents/*.plist` — two plaintext copies of the same secret in files that operators and agents routinely read."

Three sub-decisions carry their own reasoning and are worth keeping distinct.

**Resolve in the consuming process, not in the daemon.** `run-secrets` resolves and then `syscall.Exec`s, so launchd supervises the real process and the credential exists only in that process's memory. The daemon never holds it. A daemon-side resolution would have needed to write the value somewhere launchd could read, which is the problem restated.

**Delegate rather than copy.** The `helper://` scheme runs another app's resolver — `helper://mux-apikey-helper/openai/work` reaches the same single keychain entry Tether's own resolver reads. The rejected alternative, a Cerberus credential store, would have made every shared secret exist twice, with the rotation problem that implies. `docs/secrets.md` is explicit that the 1Password adapter "does not copy credentials into a second store".

**Absence is an error, not a fallback.** `KeychainProvider.Get` reports a missing entry as `("", nil)`, and `Resolver.Resolve` converts that to `ErrEmptySecret`, because "handing an empty credential to a service produces failures far from their cause". An unresolved reference fails the operation without falling back to a different credential and without reporting success.

The decision is not fully enforced, and that is CERB-GAP-533: `connector-secrets.yaml` refuses a literal by name, while a resource's `env:` accepts one silently and `writePlist` copies it into the plist — the exact outcome this decision exists to prevent.

data.decision: Support keychain:// and helper:// references, front reference-carrying services with the run-secrets exec shim, and keep the reference mapping file reference-only.
alternatives_considered: literal credentials in config with tighter file permissions
a Cerberus-owned encrypted credential store
environment-variable injection into the plist
data.rationale: Cerberus renders a managed service's environment into a launchd plist, so a literal credential in a project file becomes a second plaintext copy in ~/Library/LaunchAgents — a file operators and agents read routinely. A reference keeps both files free of credential material. A second store was rejected because a secret shared with another Hollis Labs app would then need a second copy in a second namespace, which the helper:// scheme exists to avoid.

records.name: Resources are defined in the global config, not registered descriptors
records.summary: Every resource on this machine is declared inline in ~/.cerberus/config.yaml because dir: is a literal path with no interpolation, and all nine app-owned descriptors carry another user's layout.
records.confidence_label: reasoning taken verbatim from the live config's own header and verified against all nine descriptors

relationships.note: the check that would have surfaced this

records.body:
The live config states the reasoning in its own header, and it is worth carrying
rather than restating: "all seven app-owned <app>.cerberus.yaml descriptors carry
`dir: /Users/<other-user>/dev/hollis-labs/apps/<app>` — a different user and a
different directory layout. `dir:` is a literal path with no interpolation or
override in v0.4, so none of them resolve on this machine. Defining the
resources in the global config keeps the app repos untouched."

Two corrections from re-verification. There are nine descriptors across
`~/Projects-apps/*`, not seven — `tachyon` and `tangent` also carry one, both
unregistered and both pointing at `/Users/<other-user>`. And
`infrastructure.cerberus.yaml` is not wholly foreign: it uses the portable
`dir: /opt/homebrew/var` for PostgreSQL and Jaeger, and only its third resource
points at `/Users/<other-user>/.cerberus/bin`. It is the nearest of the nine to
being registerable.

The decision is explicitly reversible and the header says on what condition:
"Once the descriptors grow machine-portable paths, these can be replaced with
`cerberus register <path>` per app." That names the unlock — interpolation or an
override for `dir:` — without pre-committing to a design.

The cost of the decision is the one that matters for this catalog: the entire
descriptor lane is unexercised here (CERB-TOOL-515), and validation does not
report the mismatch that caused it (CERB-GAP-638). Anyone who reads the repo's
descriptors as live configuration will change nothing that runs, which is why
AGENTS.md says to treat them as templates.

data.decision: Declare resources inline in the global config rather than registering per-repo descriptors
alternatives_considered: cerberus register per app
editing each app's descriptor to this machine's paths
adding interpolation or an override to dir:
data.rationale: dir: is a literal path with no interpolation or override, so a descriptor written against one machine's layout cannot resolve on another; editing nine app repos to suit one workstation would put local paths into shared repos

records.name: The work tunnel is on/off, never auto-started
records.summary: auto_start and auto_restart are both false on tunnel-muctlvaig because a Cerberus-started ssh has no TTY and an auto-restarting tunnel against a corporate auth endpoint is a way to get an account locked out.
records.confidence_label: reasoning taken from the live config and corroborated by the connector's single-publickey-attempt auth path

relationships.note: the monitor therefore never touches it

records.body:
The config carries both reasons in full and they are worth preserving. First:
"A Cerberus-started ssh has NO TTY, so it can never answer a password or MFA
prompt. The moment key auth stops working — key rotated, account locked, policy
change, VPN down — an auto-restarting tunnel becomes a silent fail-loop against
a corporate auth endpoint. That is a good way to get an account locked out."
Second: "A work tunnel should be a deliberate act. Off by default is correct."

Reading the ssh connector confirms the first reason is structural rather than
cautious. `APIBackend.Connect` offers exactly one auth method,
`ssh.PublicKeys(signer)`, built from the single `key_file` in the resource
config. There is no password method, no keyboard-interactive, no agent, and it
does not read `~/.ssh/config`. One publickey attempt per call. That is also why
`cerberus ssh status muctlvaig` is safe to run repeatedly, and why the
supervised tunnel — which uses the real `ssh` binary via `ssh -N
tun-muctlvaig`, not the connector — is the risky one.

Two related choices sit alongside it and are also deliberate. The forwards live
in `~/.ssh/config` under `Host tun-muctlvaig` rather than in the Cerberus
resource, so the ports are editable in one place, and that block sets
`ExitOnForwardFailure yes` — "without it ssh stays up with a dead forward and
the supervisor sees a healthy process tunnelling nothing." And liveness is a TCP
dial on 18095, which the config notes "proves the local end is bound; it does
not prove the far end is reachable."

The consequence for the supervision lane is that `ResourceMonitor` skips this
resource entirely, since it only considers resources with `auto_restart: true`.
The tunnel is running now and was up throughout this audit, by the operator's
hand rather than the monitor's.

data.decision: Keep tunnel-muctlvaig deliberately manual: auto_start false, auto_restart false
alternatives_considered: auto-restarting the tunnel like any other supervised process
a health probe that proves the far end rather than the local bind
data.rationale: a Cerberus-started ssh has no TTY and can never answer a password or MFA prompt, so the moment key auth stops working the supervisor turns into a silent fail-loop against a corporate auth endpoint; and a work tunnel should be a deliberate act

records.name: The daemon is not Cerberus-managed on this machine
records.summary: The daemon runs from a launch agent that no Cerberus resource owns, so the self-mutation guard, the canonical cerberus-daemon-service resource and the whole daemon-as-resource story are unexercised here.
records.confidence_label: plist, launchctl state and the absent resource all verified; the intent behind the choice is inferred
records.body:
`launchctl print gui/501/com.fragments-engine.cerberus` reports `state =
running`, `pid = 8188`, `program = ~/go/bin/cerberus`, `runs = 31`,
`last exit code = 0`. `cerberus resource list` contains no
`cerberus-daemon-service`. The daemon supervises ten resources and is not one of
them.

The top-level help and both `install` and `uninstall` describe
`cerberus-daemon-service` as "the canonical ongoing management path", with
`install` reduced to "a low-level bootstrap and recovery helper when the daemon
is not yet available over the socket". On this machine that is the other way
round: the low-level helper is the only path in use.

Recorded as a decision rather than a gap because the reasoning holds up.
Managing the daemon as a resource means every lifecycle verb aimed at it goes
through its own socket, and AGENTS.md is emphatic about what that does: the call
dies on EOF, the artifact is left half-synced, and the launchd job can end up
booted out where `KeepAlive` will not bring it back. The runtime now refuses
such mutations outright (`internal/cerbapi/daemon_self_guard.go`), which is the
right guard — but not registering the resource removes the failure mode instead
of guarding it, and costs only the convenience of `resource status` on the
daemon.

The costs are worth naming. The self-guard, the best-engineered part of
CERB-CAP-603, never fires here. The upgrade procedure exists only as that
guard's error string and a paragraph in AGENTS.md (CERB-GAP-636). And the
daemon's own supervision is launchd's `KeepAlive`, which restarts on exit and
