knows nothing about health. Confidence is 0.95 rather than 1.0 because the
observable facts are certain but the intent is inferred from AGENTS.md rather
than recorded as a decision anywhere in the repo.

data.decision: Run the daemon from a standalone launch agent rather than as the canonical cerberus-daemon-service v2 resource
alternatives_considered: registering cerberus-daemon-service and managing the daemon through the resource lane
data.rationale: managing the daemon as a resource means mutating it through its own socket, which the runtime now refuses outright; keeping it outside the resource lane removes the failure mode rather than guarding against it

records.name: Work infrastructure is read and probe only
records.summary: Connectors targeting the Adtran estate implement reads and probes; lifecycle and write operations are documented as locked with what would unlock them, because an infrastructure team owns those resources.
records.confidence_label: the scope rule is stated in AGENTS.md and holds in every operation list checked live
records.body:
AGENTS.md states it as a scope decision and is explicit that it is not a
permissions workaround: "An infrastructure team administers the Adtran estate.
Cerberus is a tool that helps operate it, **not a control plane that owns it.**"

The live operation lists bear it out. `cerberus connectors describe azure`
reports `can_create: false`, `can_destroy: false`, `can_build: false`,
`can_health: true`, and six operations that are all reads —
`list_subscriptions`, `get_subscription`, `list_resource_groups`,
`list_resources`, `list_ai_accounts`, `list_model_deployments`. `contextforge`
reports the same capability shape with four operations. Both were run live
during this audit and returned real data.

The decision has a second-order consequence this audit ran into, and it is worth
recording next to the decision rather than only as a gap. `ssh exec` is the one
work-host verb that is not read-shaped, and it is classified destructive
unconditionally — so the read-only probes the prior art is full of cannot be run
through it without `--ack` (CERB-GAP-639). A read-only scope decision that
forces `--ack` on reads undercuts itself, because it makes the acknowledgment
routine.

The exceptions AGENTS.md carves out are narrow and were both observed holding:
the local dev services in `~/.cerberus/config.yaml`, and `muctlvaig` reached
over SSH as the operator's own account.

## Since P2-3

Decision 18 refines this rule: it becomes a policy default for targets whose `admin` is `owner`, keyed off the labels a resource now declares, rather than a rule that holds by connector (CERB-DEC-292). A work resource declares `env: work`, its `owner` and its `admin`. Nothing is enforced on the labels until the P2-4 policy engine (shadow) and P3 (enforcement).

**Since P2-4.** The policy default exists: `builtin.admin-owner` denies write, lifecycle, destructive and exec on a target whose admin for that sub-target kind is `owner`, and `builtin.admin-unknown` does the same for an unlabeled one (Decisions 17 and 18, `internal/policy/evaluate.go`). It is recorded in shadow mode; P3 enforces it.

data.decision: Implement read and probe operations against work resources; document writes as locked rather than building them speculatively
alternatives_considered: building write operations behind --ack and relying on the acknowledgment gate
requesting broader access first and designing later
data.rationale: an infrastructure team administers the Adtran estate and Cerberus is a tool that helps operate it, not a control plane that owns it; where a write is genuinely wanted the ask goes to the team that owns the resource

records.name: ~/Projects/tools is the capability spec, and it is a staging post
records.summary: Seventy-nine shell scripts already administer the work host with their failure modes documented in-line; AGENTS.md says to promote that proven behaviour into connectors rather than redesign it, and the scripts' own README agrees it should not live there forever.
records.confidence_label: directory surveyed and counted; the intent quoted from both AGENTS.md and the tools README
records.body:
First, the path, because getting it wrong would put a fabricated location in the
catalog: **both** `~/Projects/tools` and `~/Projects-apps/tools` exist and they
are different things. The shell scripts are at `~/Projects/tools`, which is what
AGENTS.md names. `~/Projects-apps/tools` holds `folio` and
`leaderboard-explorer` and contains no shell scripts at all. Neither reference
is a typo for the other.

The survey. 79 `.sh` files: 53 under `nanite/`, 22 under `workday-ess/`, 3
under `host/`, 1 shared library. 36 of them are `_remote-*.sh` payloads, 32 are
numbered stage scripts from `00-` to `82-` chained by `release.sh`, and 8 are
`probe-*` drivers. 167 captured run logs sit under `out/`. The conventions are
stated in the README: numbered scripts run in order, `probe-*` never changes
anything and never prints a secret ("environment variable *names* only, never
values, so output is safe to paste into a doc"), every script carries a
`# Version:` header, anything destructive asks first via `confirm()`, and every
run tees to `out/<date>/<script>-<time>.log` and prints the path.

Five themes, each of which maps to a gap in this catalog rather than to a
connector that exists. **Stage-and-run** — `run_remote` ships a script and runs
it as root, and 36 scripts depend on it (CERB-GAP-641). **Elevation** — `rsudo`
allocates a TTY because this host's sudo refuses without one, and the Cerberus
ssh connector never requests one (CERB-GAP-640). **Read-only probing** — 8
probe drivers whose whole value is that they are safe, versus an `ssh exec` that
demands `--ack` for `id -nG` (CERB-GAP-639). **Remote logs** — `logs.sh`,
`71-log-window.sh` and their payloads, versus `can_logs: false`
(CERB-GAP-642). **Run provenance** — every invocation recorded to a dated log
with the path printed, versus a control plane that records method and path and
nothing else (CERB-GAP-630).

That last parallel is the one worth dwelling on. `70-audit-gate.sh` exists
because "the smoke test's own verdict is a report *about* the gate, not the gate
itself" — so it reads the remote log to find out whether the approval gate
actually fired, or whether a write reached Workday. A shell script directory has
a better answer to "did the guard hold, and what happened" than the control
plane meant to replace it does.

The README is honest about its own status — "Deliberately outside the product
repos ... This is a staging post, not the final home — the long-term answer is a
proper internal tool" — and about why it is not inside one: "these commands span
`workday-mcp`, `ess-agent-workday`, ContextForge and the host itself, and
pinning them inside any one repo would mean three copies drifting apart." That
is the same drift argument that puts this catalog in-repo.

One caveat on promotion: the scripts are not uniformly current. The README
states "SSH is password auth as `cburks`", and key auth with `~/.ssh/id_rsa` is
in fact configured and working — `cerberus ssh status muctlvaig` succeeds. Read
the scripts for the failure modes they encode, not as a current description of
the estate.

data.decision: Treat ~/Projects/tools as the capability specification for connector growth and promote proven behaviour from it
alternatives_considered: designing connector verbs from first principles
pinning the scripts inside one of the product repos
leaving them as the permanent answer
data.rationale: the scripts encode failure modes learned in production against this specific estate, and their README is explicit that a staging post outside the product repos beats three drifting copies inside them

records.name: The Azure dev box is pending, and the subscription has no compute
records.summary: Azure is read and probe only by decision, and the current state of the estate is that the subscription holds two Cognitive Services resources and nothing to administer.
records.confidence_label: three read-only operations run live against the real subscription
records.body:
Verified live on 2026-09-17 through the managed Azure plugin, which loads with
no missing secrets. `list_subscriptions` returns exactly one:
`MCA-subscription-qualitymgmt`, Enabled. `list_resource_groups` returns five,
all `Succeeded`, in `eastus` and `eastus2`. `list_resources` — described as
listing "the whole resource inventory of a subscription" — returns two, both
`Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts` under `Azure-rg-qualitymgmt-ai`: the
`PCB-Drawings-Extraction` AI Services account and its project.

So the subscription contains no compute of any kind. Three of the five resource
groups are empty. The Azure dev box that development, testing and Docker
experiments are meant to move to does not exist yet, and nothing in this
subscription is a host Cerberus could administer.

That makes the read-and-probe scope a straightforwardly correct call rather than
a cautious one: there is nothing to start, stop or destroy. The connector's
capability block reports `can_create: false`, `can_destroy: false`,
`can_build: false`, `can_health: true`, and all six operations are reads. Cost,
Key Vault and Resource Graph are deferred with recorded unlock conditions, which
is the right shape for a deferral.

Recorded here so the catalog states the estate's current state rather than the
plan. When the dev box is provisioned, `list_resources` will say so, and that is
the trigger to revisit — not a date.

data.decision: Keep the Azure connector read and probe only, and record the estate's current state rather than the provisioning plan
alternatives_considered: building VM lifecycle operations ahead of the dev box existing
deferring the connector entirely until there is compute to manage
data.rationale: reads and probes are useful against what exists today and carry no risk; lifecycle operations against compute that has not been provisioned would be speculative code with no way to verify it

records.name: Shell completion and help are cobra-generated and deliberately not catalogued as tools
records.summary: cerberus completion bash|zsh|fish|powershell and cerberus help are the five CLI leaves with no tool record, because cobra generates them and Cerberus writes no behaviour for them.
records.confidence_label: Both commands enumerated from the installed binary; neither appears in any Cerberus source file

relationships.note: the CLI surface these leaves belong to
the README's command count and this exclusion use the same denominator

records.body:
The inverse sweep over the installed binary finds 91 invocable CLI leaves. Eighty-six now carry a `tool` record. The remaining five are `cerberus completion bash`, `completion zsh`, `completion fish`, `completion powershell` and `cerberus help`, and they are excluded on purpose.

The reason is ownership, not size. Both commands are supplied entirely by `github.com/spf13/cobra`: `AddCompletionCommand` and the default help command. No Cerberus source file registers, wraps, overrides or tests either one, so there is nothing to record that would not simply be cobra's documentation. A `tool` record exists to say what a verb does, on which surfaces, how destructive it is and whether anyone has verified it — and for these five every one of those answers is "ask cobra".

This is written down rather than left as a hole because a gap in an inverse sweep is indistinguishable from an oversight. A future sweep that finds 91 leaves and 86 records should find this record, not re-derive the same five.

The boundary it sets is narrow and worth stating: a cobra-generated leaf with no Cerberus behaviour gets no record. A cobra-generated leaf that Cerberus *does* customise — a flag added, output changed, a subcommand hidden — gets one. `cerberus config migrate` is the nearby contrast: also nearly empty, but Cerberus wrote its refusal, so it has CERB-TOOL-521.

Reversible at no cost. If completion ever grows Cerberus-specific behaviour — dynamic resource-id completion, for instance, which would need the daemon and would therefore have a degraded mode — that is a tool and gets a record.

data.decision: Do not write tool records for cobra-generated leaves that carry no Cerberus behaviour; record the exclusion instead.
alternatives_considered: Write five thin tool records for completeness — rejected: they would document cobra, not Cerberus, and would need re-verifying on every cobra upgrade
Leave the five leaves uncatalogued and unexplained — rejected: an absence in an inverse sweep cannot be told apart from a miss
Suppress the completion command entirely — rejected: shell completion is useful and costs nothing
data.rationale: A catalog's value is that a hole means something. Five silent holes in a 91-leaf sweep cost more than one record explaining them, and the rule generalises to any future vendored subcommand.

records.name: Reads prefer the daemon and fall back in-process; the mutation verbs inherited the pattern without a second decision
records.summary: Resource, project and pipeline read commands try the socket and re-run locally on DaemonUnreachableError so introspection still works with the daemon down — a choice with a stated rationale, which the six lifecycle verbs then copied.
records.confidence_label: The policy is stated in code comments at two call sites; the extension to mutations has no comment, no test and no document, which is the basis for calling it inherited rather than decided

relationships.note: the capability this decision shapes
the unexamined half of the pattern
resource show went further and dropped the daemon-first half
connector liveness is the one thing the fallback deliberately degrades
the guard the in-process path does not carry

records.body:
The decision is recorded in the codebase, in comments rather than in a document, and it is a good one.

`projectClient` says it outright: *"projectClient prefers the daemon and falls back in-process, matching the resource commands. The returned surface is also the diagnostics source, so a trailing skip notice describes the same view the rows came from."* `resourceListCmd` carries the same reasoning about diagnostics: *"Diagnostics come from whichever surface served the list, so the notice describes the same view of the config tree the rows came from."*

The rationale holds. A daemon-down machine is when an operator most wants to read what is declared, and a read has no side effect, so re-running it locally costs only accuracy — and the accuracy loss is itself surfaced, because the resolve-diagnostics notice comes from the same surface that served the rows. `connectors` takes the same route and degrades knowingly: liveness reverts to the CLI's own view, which the code comment names as the way a connector can read `LIVE=yes` while every call against it fails.

The connector lane then made the stricter version of the same decision, and wrote the invariant down: *"Choose a transport before executing anything. Once an operation is sent, an error must never trigger an in-process retry of a possible mutation."* `commandSocket` pings first and routes in-process only on an unreachable probe. Two decisions, compatible, each documented where it lives.

What has no decision behind it is the third case. `deploy`, `apply`, `reload`, `stop`, `sync` and `remove` in `cmd_resource.go` use the read pattern — send, then fall back on `DaemonUnreachableError` — not the connector pattern. There is no comment, no test and no document arguing that a mutation should be retried in-process, and the invariant eight files away says it should not. That is why this record is `partial` rather than `shipped`: the read half is a decision, the mutation half is a copied shape, and CERB-GAP-730 is the cost.

Reversible, and the reversal is narrow: keep the read fallback exactly as it is, and move the six lifecycle verbs onto `commandSocket`.

data.decision: Read commands try the daemon socket first and re-run in-process when it is unreachable, reporting diagnostics from whichever surface answered; the connector lane instead selects its transport before executing.
alternatives_considered: Fail every command when the daemon is down — rejected: introspection is most valuable precisely then, and the CLI already holds everything a read needs
Always resolve locally and never ask the daemon — rejected: the daemon's view is the authoritative one for liveness and runtime state, and `resource show` shows what divergence costs (CERB-GAP-448)
Ping before every command, as the connector lane does — not taken for reads: it adds a round trip to the common path for an operation that is safe to retry
data.rationale: A read has no side effect, so the only cost of a local retry is accuracy, and that cost is surfaced through the resolve-diagnostics notice. A mutation does have a side effect, which is why the connector lane chose the stricter rule — and why extending the read rule to the lifecycle verbs was a mistake rather than a trade.

records.name: Config hot-reload was built three converging ways, then thrown away for re-read-per-call
records.summary: The daemon once reloaded config on SIGHUP, on an fsnotify event and on a `cerberus daemon reload` subcommand, all through one ServiceRegistry.Reload(); the v2 cut-over replaced all three with re-reading config inside each operation, and the only trace left is a SIGHUP handler that exists to log that it is ignored.
records.confidence_label: SIGHUP-ignored goroutine, absent fsnotify wiring and the declaration-less daemonReloadCmd comment all read in cmd_daemon.go; `cerberus daemon --help` on the installed binary lists no reload subcommand

relationships.note: the orphaned v1 config machinery this decision stranded
auto_start is inert because nothing detects a newly added resource
the v2-only cut-over that carried this out
the per-call resolution that replaced it
the daemon whose signal handling this describes

records.body:
This is the largest reversal in the repository's history and there is no
document anywhere that says it happened.

`1396b85` (2026-04-18, CERB-1) closed a live incident: the daemon loaded
`~/.cerberus/config.yaml` once at boot and cached the struct for its lifetime, so
editing config required a daemon bounce. The fix was deliberately three doors
onto one room — a SIGHUP handler installed *before* the pidfile write (the
default disposition for SIGHUP is terminate, so a reload fired immediately after
startup would otherwise have killed the daemon), an fsnotify watcher that
watches the parent directory so editor rename-into-place saves still fire, and a
`cerberus daemon reload` subcommand that signals the daemon's PID. All three
called `ServiceRegistry.Reload()`, which diffed the snapshot, registered added
services, stopped removed ones, marked changed ones `Stale`, and kept the
last-good snapshot on a parse failure so a bad edit could not crash the daemon.

Four months later none of it runs. `runDaemonBody` in `cmd/cerberus/cmd_daemon.go`
still installs the SIGHUP handler, with the original race comment intact, and
the goroutine that reads it does exactly one thing:

    logger.Info("daemon.sighup.ignored",
        "message", "config is re-read on demand in the v2 runtime")

There is no fsnotify watcher in the daemon — `config.NewWatcher` is called only
from its own tests. There is no `daemon reload` subcommand: the installed binary
offers `daemon restart|start|status|stop` and nothing else. And
`daemonReloadCmd` survives as a **doc comment with no declaration**, stranded
directly above `runDaemonStart`, still asserting that "the daemon routes SIGHUP,
fsnotify events, and this subcommand through the same `ServiceRegistry.Reload()`
call, so any of the three entry points produces identical behavior." Every
clause of that sentence is now false, and it is the first thing a reader of the
daemon command file meets.

The replacement is genuinely better and that is why this is a decision rather
than rot. `registry.ResolveConfig` and `LoadUnified` are called inside each
runtime operation, so freshness is a property of the call rather than of a
notification arriving — which removes the whole class of bug where the event was
missed, debounced away, or delivered to a daemon that had already answered. The
cost is equally real: there is no longer any event at which Cerberus notices a
config change, so nothing can log `config.reloaded`, nothing diffs added against
removed resources, and `auto_start` on a newly appearing resource has nobody to
honour it — which is exactly the inert field `CERB-GAP-142` records. The v1 path
had a spec-review fix for that case (`b99fb13`); the v2 path never needed one
because it never learns that a resource is new.

What makes this worth a record is that the reversal was never argued anywhere.
`CERB-GAP-541` correctly reports the orphaned machinery as dead weight, but a
reader still cannot find out that re-read-per-call was *chosen* over
notification, or what was given up. Three artefacts are left behind and each
lies in a different way: a signal handler that catches only to ignore, a
justifying comment for a race against a command that does not exist, and a doc
comment for a symbol that does not exist.

data.decision: Reload config inside every runtime operation instead of on a reload event; retire SIGHUP, the fsnotify watcher and `cerberus daemon reload`, keeping the signal handler only to log that the signal is ignored.
alternatives_considered: Keep the three converging reload paths and rewire them onto the v2 runtime service — not taken; the commit history shows no discussion, and the v2 monitor already re-resolved config on each tick, making the event redundant for the only consumer left

Delete the SIGHUP handler outright — not taken, and the reason is visible in the code: the handler is still installed and now serves only to keep the default terminate disposition from killing the daemon if anything ever sends it a HUP

Keep only `cerberus daemon reload` as an explicit operator verb — not taken; the subcommand was removed with the rest, so an operator has no way to ask the daemon to re-read anything and does not need one
No record of a fourth option: the reversal is not discussed in any commit message, ADR, plan or handoff — the rationale exists only as a one-line comment at the point of the change
data.rationale: Per-call resolution makes freshness a property of the read rather than of a delivered notification, which removes missed, debounced and out-of-order reload events entirely. The price is that no code path ever learns that config changed, so add/remove diffing, reload logging and auto_start on newly declared resources all lose their trigger — and the abandoned notification machinery stays in the binary telling readers the opposite.

records.name: The v2 cut-over's cleanup pass was deferred on purpose and has never been scheduled
records.summary: The 2026-04-28 handoff declared the operational cut-over complete and the remaining debt to be repo cleanup, to be done in one pass after the v2 surface settled; five months on, that pass has not run and three whole packages are orphaned in the shipped binary.
records.confidence_label: Handoff read in full; orphan status of each package proven by import-graph grep over the whole tree

relationships.note: the v2-only decision this deferral is the tail of
the orphaned v1 config and registry machinery
the orphaned alerting path
the two orphaned packages pass 1 did not reach
the change that orphaned internal/selfexec

records.body:
The decision here is a deferral, and it is recorded — once, in a handoff nobody
has cited since.

`docs/handoffs/2026-04-28-v2-runtime-handoff.md` closes with a section called
*Remaining Architectural Debt* that is unusually precise about what it is
choosing not to do: "The operational cut-over is complete. Remaining debt is
repo cleanup rather than runtime behavior: unused legacy packages still exist
in-tree (`internal/service`, `internal/tui`, related docs/tests/comments)."
The *Recommended Next Slice* is equally explicit: "Let the v2-only surface
settle under real use, then delete dead legacy packages and stale docs in one
cleanup pass."

Exactly one item on that list was ever done. `internal/tui` was deleted in
`6f6681c` (2026-05-25) with its own reasoning — already orphaned, imported by
nothing, wired to no cobra subcommand, and only able to describe the v1 model.
The rest is still here, and it has since grown:

- `internal/service` stays because `dev_session` genuinely needs its plumbing —
  a defensible outcome, and the one `CERB-DEC-161` already names.
- `internal/daemon/monitor.go` carries the entire three-layer alerting path and
  `daemon.NewMonitor` has zero callers, not even a test (`CERB-GAP-632`).
- `internal/config`'s `Source`, `FileSource`, `Watcher` and `DiffConfigs`, plus
  `service.NewServiceRegistry`, have no production caller (`CERB-GAP-541`).
- `internal/procscan` — fourteen files, a raw darwin `SYS_PROC_INFO` syscall
  written specifically to stay cgo-free, and a darwin integration test — has no
  importer at all. Nor does `internal/selfexec` (`CERB-GAP-820`).

So the state today is not "someone forgot". It is that a deferral whose
condition was *let the surface settle* was never converted into a scheduled
action, and the deferral now covers strictly more code than when it was made.
The two most recent additions arrived by different routes and neither was
noticed: `selfexec` lost its only caller in `9e5a7dd` when the watcher was
pulled out of `cerberus mcp` (`CERB-DEC-470`), and `procscan` lost both of its
call sites when the v2 cut-over deleted `cerberus rebuild` and the v1
`RebuildService` RPC that wired it in.

The open question this leaves is real and unowned: for each orphan, delete or
revive. `procscan` and the `daemon.Monitor` alert path are not equivalent cases.
Cascade-killing stale subprocesses solved a symptom — a Nanite-spawned
`clockwork mcp` child executing a pre-build inode — that the v2 lane has no
replacement for, so deleting `procscan` closes a capability rather than removing
dead weight. Alerting has no live equivalent either, but its only remote
destination was a hardcoded localhost port for an app nobody installs, so
reviving it verbatim is not on the table. Recording this as one decision rather
than four gaps is the point: the choice is a single cleanup pass with a per-file
verdict, and the reason it has not happened is that the verdict was deferred to
a condition rather than to a date.

data.decision: Defer deletion of the legacy packages until the v2-only surface has settled under real use, then do it in one pass — a condition that was never converted into a scheduled action, so the deferral still stands and now covers more code than when it was made.
alternatives_considered: Delete the legacy packages with the cut-over — rejected at the time in favour of letting the new surface settle first, which was reasonable while the v2 lane was days old
Keep them permanently as reference implementations — never argued for, but it is the de facto outcome and nothing in the repo distinguishes it from the deferral

Revive the orphans onto the v2 lane — never argued for as a whole; only the alerting path has a pass-1 gap asking for it, and its compiled-in localhost destination means a revival would need a config surface first
data.rationale: The condition attached to the deferral — 'once the v2 surface has settled under real use' — was satisfied months ago and nothing fires on it, so a decision recorded as temporary has become permanent by default. Each orphan needs its own verdict: internal/service is load-bearing, the config watcher is pure dead weight, and procscan and the alert path each represent a capability the v2 lane never replaced.

records.name: The socket protocol is pinned to v1 and a mismatch is a hard 400 with no shim
records.summary: Every request carries an X-Cerberus-Api header pinned to v1 and a mismatch is refused outright, because the daemon and the CLI are always installed as one binary — a premise that has since been broken three separate times on this machine.
records.confidence_label: dto.go comment and the CERB-2 commit read; route-level degradation verified in the #19 and #20 commit records rather than re-run here

relationships.note: the socket API this governs
the stateless MCP client that speaks it
the version header's practical reach

records.body:
`6c416f4` (CERB-2) introduced the socket and chose the version contract in one
sentence: "Protocol version is pinned to 'v1' via an X-Cerberus-Api header;
mismatch is a hard 400, no migration shim." `internal/cerbapi/dto.go:38` still
says so — "intentionally no migration logic (see CERB-2 non-goals)".

The premise is that the CLI, the MCP subprocess and the daemon are the same
binary at the same version, so a mismatch is an operator error rather than a
compatibility case. Under that premise a shim is pure cost: two behaviours to
test, and a silent wrong answer instead of a loud refusal.

The premise has failed repeatedly, and interestingly the failures have all been
*route* skew rather than *protocol* skew, which is why the decision has survived
them. `9b22c6c` (#19) added `GET /registry/diagnostics` and explicitly verified
that "a new CLI against a daemon that predates the route degrades to no notice
rather than an error". `630cee5` (#20) recorded the sharper version of the same
thing — a May-26 daemon artifact parsing a config written for a newer schema
dropped a whole project, 33 resources down to 30, with no error on any surface.
And `AGENTS.md`'s "changed source is not deployed source" boundary exists
precisely because the installed daemon artifact routinely lags the binary in
`~/go/bin`.

So the version header has never fired in anger, and route-level graceful
degradation — a 404 read as "this daemon is older than this route" — is the
mechanism that actually carries skew. That is worth recording because the two
sit awkwardly together: the header promises a loud refusal on any version
difference, while the surfaces are individually built to be quiet about one. An
operator debugging a stale daemon gets nothing from the header and everything
from a missing route.

data.decision: Pin the unix-socket HTTP protocol to v1 via an X-Cerberus-Api header, refuse a mismatch with a hard 400, and write no migration shim — while letting individual routes degrade gracefully when a daemon predates them.
alternatives_considered: Version each route independently — not chosen, but it is what the code does in practice: new routes are added and callers tolerate a 404 from an older daemon
Negotiate a version and shim the difference — rejected explicitly as a CERB-2 non-goal, on the premise that CLI and daemon ship as one binary
No version header at all — rejected: a silently mismatched wire shape is worse than a refusal, and the header costs one constant
data.rationale: When the client and server are the same binary, a version mismatch is an installation fault and the right response is a loud refusal rather than a compatibility layer. The premise is imperfect — the installed daemon artifact lags the shell's binary routinely on this machine — but the skew that actually occurs is route-level, and per-route graceful degradation covers it without a shim.

records.name: The socket is stdlib net/http over a unix path, and hand-rolled JSON-RPC is forbidden
records.summary: The daemon transport is vanilla net/http on net.Listen("unix"), with no dependencies and no second RPC dialect, because a portfolio-wide baseline forbids hand-rolled JSON-RPC and the flock daemon lock already enforces single-instance.
records.confidence_label: Package comment and CERB-2 commit read; socket permissions and stale-socket takeover covered by existing tests rather than re-run

relationships.note: the socket API this shapes
the MCP adapter that does speak JSON-RPC, via go-mcp
the daemon lock this leans on

records.body:
Two constraints met here and both are recorded only in a commit message and a
package comment.

`6c416f4` states the ban outright: "Transport is vanilla net/http over
net.Listen(\"unix\", path) — no dependencies, no hand-rolled JSON-RPC
(portfolio baseline forbids the latter)." `internal/cerbapi/socket_server.go:30`
carries the positive form — "The server is intentionally dependency-free:
stdlib net/http". The prohibition is not a Cerberus rule; it is a Hollis Labs
baseline that Cerberus is obeying, which is why no ADR in this repo argues for
it. Worth recording because the reasoning is invisible from inside the repo and
the shape of the socket API looks arbitrary without it: an ordinary REST-ish
route map over a unix socket, sitting next to an MCP server that does speak
JSON-RPC, via the vendored `go-mcp`.

The second constraint is subtler and rides on a dependency between two
subsystems. The socket server is "lenient on stale socket files because the
flock-based daemon-lock already enforces the single-daemon invariant". That is
an explicit division of responsibility: the listener does not try to work out
whether an existing socket file belongs to a live daemon, because
`daemon.AcquireDaemonLock` has already refused to start if one does. Removing or
weakening the flock guard would therefore silently make socket takeover unsafe,
in a file that says nothing about locking. The `0600` permission on the socket
is the other half — user-only, because the socket fronts `ssh_exec`,
`droplet_destroy` and `resource_remove` with no authentication of its own, the
same exposure `mcp-http` has without the filesystem boundary.
 

Since P2-1 the `0600` mode is no longer the only guard. Every connection's peer credentials are read, and a uid other than the daemon's is refused as `principal_refused` (CERB-CAP-401).

data.decision: Serve the daemon API as stdlib net/http over a 0600 unix socket with no transport dependency and no hand-rolled JSON-RPC, and rely on the flock daemon lock rather than the listener for single-instance safety.
alternatives_considered: Hand-rolled JSON-RPC over the socket — forbidden by the portfolio baseline, not re-argued here
A third-party RPC framework such as gRPC — not chosen; the recorded preference is zero transport dependencies, and the DTOs already match the JSON shapes the MCP tools emit

Have the listener detect a live peer before taking over a stale socket file — deliberately not done, because the flock lock is the authoritative single-instance guard and duplicating it would create two answers
data.rationale: A unix socket plus stdlib HTTP gives filesystem-permission access control and wire-compatible JSON with the MCP tools for no dependency cost. Single-instance safety is deliberately not re-implemented at the listener because the daemon flock already owns it — which makes the flock guard load-bearing for a file that never mentions it.

records.name: dev, uat and release map onto three runtime shapes, with a port and a data root per audience
records.summary: The runtime pattern formalised in ed1b096 assigns dev_session to repo-local dev, os_service plus run_from: artifact to uat, and os_service over a promoted artifact to release — and requires each audience to get its own port and data directory rather than sharing one process.
records.confidence_label: Pattern read in the handoff and the project-setup guide; its absence from the live estate confirmed by the briefing's ground truth (no os_service, no run_from: artifact on this machine)

relationships.note: the dev row
the uat and release rows
the artifact join the pattern justifies
the estate that implements none of it
the v2 model this policy sits on

records.body:
`ed1b096` (2026-05-01) is titled "Formalize dev-uat-release runtime pattern" and
has an empty body. The pattern it formalised is written down in two places
pass 1 never cited — the 2026-04-28 handoff and
`docs/guides/setting-up-a-project-for-cerberus-v2.md` — and it is the missing
answer to "when do I use `dev_session` and when do I use `os_service`?", a
question the two mode capabilities describe mechanically without answering.

The mapping:

    dev      dev_session, repo-local ports and data roots
    uat      os_service + run_from: artifact
    release  os_service over a promoted user- or system-owned artifact

And the constraints that come with it, each stated as a prohibition: "ports
should be unique per audience; do not reuse the dev port for UAT"; "do not point
`dev`, `uat`, and release-style resources at the same mutable data directory
unless that sharing is the explicit test scenario"; "do not force a project's
frontend dev workflow into the durable service lane"; and "do not let one port
or one process pretend to serve every audience". The release row is the one with
the subtle rule: a promoted release binary may come from a user-owned bin
directory rather than a workspace build, but "Cerberus should still treat it as
an explicit artifact, not a guessed PATH lookup".

Two things make this worth recording rather than restating. First, it is the
only place `run_from: artifact` is given a *reason* — artifact mode is not a
hardening option to apply everywhere, it is what makes uat and release
distinguishable from dev, and the guide concedes `run_from: repo` is acceptable
"when the service is intentionally launched from the repo and there is no clean
artifact-install story yet". Second, nothing on this machine follows it. There
are no `os_service` resources and no `run_from: artifact` resources at all, so
every resource here is a `dev` resource by this taxonomy, and the entire uat and
release half of the pattern — including the artifact staleness machinery it
exists to justify — is unexercised locally.

data.decision: Assign each audience its own runtime shape — dev_session for dev, os_service with run_from: artifact for uat, os_service over a promoted artifact for release — with a distinct port and data root per audience, and never a PATH lookup in place of a declared artifact.
alternatives_considered: One resource per service, promoted between audiences by changing its config — rejected implicitly by the per-audience port and data-root rules: the pattern wants the audiences to coexist so a uat resource can be compared against a running dev one
dev_session everywhere, with launchd only for the daemon — not chosen, but it is the de facto state on this machine, where zero resources use os_service
Let a release resource resolve its binary from PATH — rejected explicitly: 'Cerberus should still treat it as an explicit artifact, not a guessed PATH lookup'
data.rationale: dev_session and os_service are not two implementations of one idea; they carry different guarantees, and the handoff makes the split by audience rather than by preference. Sharing a port or a data root between audiences would make the comparison the pattern exists to enable impossible, and resolving a release binary from PATH would reintroduce exactly the 'which binary is actually running' ambiguity artifact mode was built to remove.

records.name: dev_session staleness stays silent when there is no build_strategy
records.summary: A dev_session whose built binary is newer than its running process is reported stale; one launched by `npm run dev` or `go run` is deliberately never reported stale, because a hot-reloading process has no built binary to compare against and every such report would be wrong.
records.confidence_label: Comment and the Layer 3 commit read; covered by the connector's own tests rather than re-run live

relationships.note: the mode this governs
the sibling judgement about a warning nobody trusts
the artifact staleness path it sits beside

records.body:
Layer 3 of the staleness remediation (`7d862ee`) added
`RecommendedDevSessionAction`: for a dev_session with a `build_strategy`, compare
the run binary's mtime against the process start time recorded in the PID meta
file at launch, and recommend `deploy` when the binary is newer. That is the
"rebuilt but not restarted" case, which until then was invisible because
`RecommendedStatusAction` only fired for `os_service` plus `run_from: artifact`.

The interesting half is the refusal, and it is stated in the code rather than
any document. `internal/connector/local/status_advice.go:73`: the check
"deliberately stays silent for dev sessions WITHOUT a build_strategy". The
commit gives the reason — "(npm run dev, go run), which hot-reload and have no
built binary to compare, to avoid false positives".

This is the same judgement `CERB-DEC-164` made about artifact staleness from the
other direction. There, repo HEAD and worktree dirtiness were *removed* from the
staleness computation because any commit in a shared repo flipped every artifact
in it to stale and operators stopped trusting the signal. Here a signal is
withheld rather than removed, for the same reason: a staleness warning that
fires on a correctly-working resource costs more than the case it catches,
because the operator learns to ignore the chip. Both decisions are about the
credibility of a warning rather than its coverage, and neither is written
anywhere outside the code and the commit.

It also has a consequence the record should name. `ensure-fresh` consumes this
signal, so a `npm run dev` session serving code from before the last `git pull`
is something Cerberus will never notice and never offer to fix — silently, and
by design. `docs/guides/local-runtime-troubleshooting.md` and the CLI help
(`6c5b1f9`) both carry the matching warning that `ensure-fresh` does not detect
unbuilt source.

data.decision: Report dev_session staleness only when a build_strategy declares a built binary to compare against, and stay silent for hot-reloading sessions rather than warn on every one of them.
alternatives_considered: Compare source-file mtimes against process start time for every dev_session — rejected as a false-positive generator: a hot-reloading dev server is correct while its sources are newer than its process
Warn on every dev_session that has been running longer than its newest source file, with an opt-out — not chosen; the recorded preference is silence by default rather than an opt-out per resource

Extend the signal to sessions without a build_strategy by probing the running process's loaded binary — not considered in the record; it would need procscan-style inode work, which is itself orphaned (CERB-GAP-820)
data.rationale: A staleness warning is only useful while operators believe it. Firing on every hot-reloading dev server would train them to ignore the chip, which is the same failure mode that led to dropping repo state from artifact staleness. The cost is accepted and documented: a dev session serving pre-pull code is invisible to both status and ensure-fresh.

records.name: Vercel stays a bounded deployment runner, and the two models must not be blurred
records.summary: The Vercel path was built as a deployment runner rather than a connector, and the handoff that shipped it names the follow-up choice explicitly — continue with the bounded runner, or promote Vercel to a first-class connector, but do not accidentally blur the two.
records.confidence_label: Handoff read in full; the single-importer status of internal/infra re-confirmed against the current tree

relationships.note: the subsystem this decision governs
the plugin-not-built-in rule a promotion would have to satisfy
the tombstone pattern a retirement would follow
the only surface that can reach it

records.body:
`docs/handoffs/2026-05-24-infra-deployments-handoff.md` is where the
`internal/infra` subsystem `CERB-GAP-439` reports on came from, and it contains
the decision the gap record is missing.

The handoff is precise about what Vercel is not: "Cerberus did **not** already
have a Vercel connector"; "the current Vercel path is therefore a bounded
deployment runner, not a full connector contract". Then it states the fork and
adds an instruction:

> The next session should either: 1. continue with the current bounded Vercel
> deployment runner, or 2. promote Vercel into a first-class connector
> intentionally. **Do not accidentally blur those two models.**

That is a decision-shaped instruction and it has held, by inaction. Four months
later `internal/infra` is imported by exactly one file, `internal/webui/infra.go`,
with no CLI command, no socket route and no MCP tool — so the runner has neither
been promoted nor retired, and the thing preventing the blur is that nothing
else can reach it.

What the runner actually does is worth recording because it is the concrete
shape of "not a connector": a repo existence check, git branch/commit/dirty
inspection, an optional preflight command, an optional build command, an
optional `vercel link --yes --project ...`, a `vercel --prod --yes` deployment,
output capture, and a deployment URL extracted from the last non-empty output
line. Every one of those is a property a connector operation would not have —
no `Definition`, no DTO allow-list, no `--ack` gate, no dry-run, no per-call
credential resolution, and a result parsed out of a CLI's final printed line.
The handoff's own "What Has Not Been Proven Yet" list concedes "the exact
deployment URL parsing behavior with real Vercel output" was never verified
against a real deploy.

Set against `CERB-DEC-290` — a new provider integration is a plugin, not a
built-in — the runner is now in the awkward third position: it is neither, and
the decision that would move it either way is five months old and unowned. The
2026-08-22 direction document pushes the same way from a different angle,
listing "provider-specific CLI, API, MCP, and GUI handlers can drift unless
generated or adapted from one capability description" as a current-model
tension, which is exactly what a console-only provider path is.

data.decision: Keep Vercel as a bounded deployment runner in internal/infra rather than a connector, and make promoting it to a first-class connector an explicit decision rather than something that happens gradually.
alternatives_considered: Promote Vercel to a connector immediately — explicitly offered as option 2 in the handoff and not taken; it would require a Definition, DTOs, an ack gate and per-call credential resolution the runner has none of
Let the runner grow connector-like features incrementally — explicitly warned against: 'Do not accidentally blur those two models'
Retire the runner — not considered in the handoff, which was written while chrispian.dev was the active dogfood target; it is the option pass 1's gap record now proposes
data.rationale: A deployment runner and a connector make different promises. A connector carries a capability definition, a response DTO allow-list, dry-run, acknowledgment and per-call credential resolution; the runner has none of these and parses its result from a CLI's last printed line. Growing one into the other by accretion would produce something with a connector's reach and a runner's guarantees, which is why the handoff forbids the gradual path specifically rather than either endpoint.

records.name: One connector instance per id, and multi-account provider registration is a named deferral
records.summary: The Connector interface conflates driver, configured provider and lifecycle, so there can be exactly one cloudflare — the 2026-08-22 direction names the split that would fix it and defers the work, which is why `cloudflare-personal` and `cloudflare-hollis` cannot both exist today.
records.confidence_label: Direction document read in full; the one-instance-per-id consequence traced through the reserved-id guard and the WP-3 host parameter

relationships.note: the discovery contract this limitation lives in
the per-call host parameter that works around it for Docker
the reserved-id guard that exists because an id is a single key
the admin lane built on one instance per id
the sibling deferral from the same document

records.body:
`docs/control-plane-direction.md` is cited by no pass-1 record, and it contains
the most consequential deferred decision in the repo. Its *Current-model
tensions to revisit* section opens with two lines:

> - `Connector` combines driver, provider registration, and universal lifecycle.
> - One connector instance per ID prevents clean multiple-account registration.

And it names the replacement in detail. A `ResourceKindDefinition` would own
Cerberus vocabulary — desired and observed schemas, conditions, readiness,
destructive annotations. A `DriverDefinition` would own an implementation and
which kinds it can operate. A `ProviderRegistration` would be an
operator-configured *instance* of a driver, with its own endpoint, account,
region, credential references and policy — so "this distinction permits multiple
registrations of one driver, such as `cloudflare-personal`, `cloudflare-hollis`,
or multiple Coder deployments", and a resource would reference a registration
rather than an implementation package.

None of that is built, and the document is explicit that it does not intend to
be a plan: "It deliberately does not define phases, estimates, task breakdowns,
migration steps, or compatibility strategy" and "These are architectural inputs,
not a task list." So the decision on record is to defer the split while naming
it — which is a decision, not a silence.

The limitation bites today in ways the catalog records separately without
connecting them to it. A connector id is a single key: the plugin reserved-id
guard exists because the secret channel namespaces by connector id
(`CERB-DEC-353`), a plugin claiming `docker` would be handed docker's
credentials, and `docker`'s answer to "which host?" had to become a per-call
`--host`/`--context` parameter (`CERB-DEC-296`) rather than a second
registration, precisely because a second registration is not expressible. WP-3
solved multi-target Docker with a per-operation parameter and the commit says so
approvingly — "One implementation serves the Azure box and muctlvaig; no new
connector" — which is the right local call and also the workaround this deferral
forces.

The same document lists the related tensions that would be resolved by the same
split: "Universal `Create/Start/Stop/Destroy/Status` semantics do not fit all
kinds", "Universal process-shaped resource states erase provider meaning", and
"`Resource.Config map[string]any` is useful at a serialization boundary but is
too weak as the internal semantic model".

data.decision: Keep one connector instance per id for now, and record the kind/driver/registration split as the intended resolution without scheduling it — so a second account for the same provider is expressed as a per-call parameter rather than a second registration.
alternatives_considered: Split Connector into ResourceKindDefinition, DriverDefinition and ProviderRegistration — the named intended design, deliberately left unscheduled: the document declines to define phases or a migration strategy
Allow multiple instances of one connector id — cannot be done without the split, because the secret channel, the plugin reserved-id guard and the CLI command namespace all key on the id being unique
Express a second account as a separate connector id such as cloudflare-personal — not proposed anywhere, and it would multiply the per-connector CLI command groups and MCP tool names
data.rationale: The split is a large refactor across the connector interface, the secret channel, the CLI command tree and every MCP tool name, and nothing yet needs two accounts for one provider badly enough to pay for it. Deferring while writing the target down keeps the per-call workaround — Docker's --host and --context — from being mistaken for the intended model.

records.name: Reconciliation posture is meant to be a per-resource policy; auto_restart is the only posture built
records.summary: The direction document makes continuous control a three-valued policy — Observe, Explicit, Converge — so the daemon may watch everything without permission to change anything; today the only expression of it is a boolean auto_restart on local dev sessions.
records.confidence_label: Direction document read in full; the absence of any posture vocabulary in config or the monitor confirmed against the current tree

relationships.note: auto_restart, the one posture that exists
a resource choosing Observe by turning every switch off
read-and-probe-only as a scope decision in place of a posture
the inert auto_start field one boolean leaves behind
the sibling deferral from the same document

records.body:
From `docs/control-plane-direction.md`: "Continuous control is a policy
dimension, not an assumption attached to every resource." The three postures are
named and defined — `Observe` detects, caches and reports but never mutates;
`Explicit` computes and presents a change but mutates only after a command or
approval; `Converge` restores declared state automatically within granted
policy — and defaults are sketched by resource class: local durable services may
reasonably use `Converge`, DNS and domain changes may default to `Explicit`,
workspace lifecycle may be driven by a lease. The stated payoff is the sentence
that follows: "The daemon may continuously observe every configured resource
without having blanket permission to mutate it."

Cerberus has none of this vocabulary. What exists is `auto_restart: true|false`
on a local/process resource, read by `shouldMonitorResource`, which is `Converge`
for one resource kind and nothing at all for the rest. There is no `Observe`
posture, so a connector-managed resource is not polled; there is no `Explicit`
posture, so there is nowhere for a computed-but-unapplied change to sit — which
is the same absence that makes `--ack` a per-call gate rather than an approval
record, and `--dry-run` a preview that is thrown away.

Recording this as a decision rather than a gap matters because it reframes three
things the catalog already holds separately. `CERB-DEC-671` — the work tunnel
runs with `auto_start` and `auto_restart` both false because an auto-restarting
`ssh` against a corporate auth endpoint can lock an account out — is a resource
asking for `Observe` and getting it by setting every switch to off. `CERB-DEC-292`
and `CERB-DEC-673` — work infrastructure implements read and probe operations
only — describe `Observe` as a scope decision taken per connector because it
cannot be expressed as a posture. And `CERB-CAP-104`'s finding that
`auto_restart` doubles as the auto-start switch while `auto_start` is inert
(`CERB-GAP-142`) is what one boolean standing in for a policy dimension looks
like.

The document is explicit that it is not a plan — "architectural inputs, not a
task list" — so the deferral is deliberate. It is the reasoning that is missing
from the catalog, not the conclusion.

data.decision: Treat continuous control as a per-resource policy with three postures — Observe, Explicit, Converge — as the intended model, and defer implementing it; ship auto_restart as the only expression of Converge in the meantime.
alternatives_considered: Implement the three postures now — deliberately deferred: the document declines to define phases or migration steps for anything it describes

Keep auto_restart as the permanent model and extend it per connector — not argued for anywhere, but it is the de facto state, and it is why work-infrastructure read-only had to be decided connector by connector

Poll every resource for observation without a posture field — not proposed; without an Explicit posture there would be nowhere to put a computed change, so observation would produce drift nobody can act on
data.rationale: One boolean cannot express 'watch this but never touch it' separately from 'do not watch it at all', which is why the tunnel has to set every switch to off and why read-only work infrastructure is a per-connector scope decision rather than a policy. The posture model would make those declarations instead of conventions — but it is a cross-cutting change to config, the monitor and every connector, and the direction document explicitly declines to schedule it.

records.name: Cerberus brokers Coder workspaces and refuses Coder's agent and AI surfaces
records.summary: The direction places Coder beneath Cerberus as a workspace provider with a first-class Workspace and WorkspaceLease model, and rules out depending on Coder Agents, Coder's AI Gateway or general-purpose Coder MCP access — a whole declared resource class the catalog does not mention.
records.confidence_label: Direction document read in full; zero mentions of Coder, workspace or lease-as-resource across all 291 pass-1 records

relationships.note: the admin lane a workspace driver would live in
the plugin-not-built-in rule a Coder driver would fall under
the driver/registration split a Coder deployment would need for multiple instances

records.body:
`docs/control-plane-direction.md` devotes a section to a resource class that
appears nowhere in the catalog: a search for "coder" across all 291 pass-1
records returns nothing. The reasoning is worth carrying because it is a refusal
as much as a plan.

The refusal: "Coder is a workspace provider beneath Cerberus, not an AI control
plane. Cerberus should not depend on Coder Agents, Coder's AI Gateway, or direct
general-purpose Coder MCP access." The composition it protects is that Nanite,
Tether and Torque each keep their own agent, session, job and workflow
semantics, and Cerberus "receives an opaque caller and subject reference; it does
not adopt those domain models". Taking Coder's agent surface would have pulled
those semantics into Cerberus — the same boundary the portfolio axiom draws
against owning business definitions.

The model itself is unusually specific for a directional document, which is why
it reads as decided rather than sketched. A `Workspace` is first-class rather
than a generic resource, with desired state deliberately reduced to
`Running | Stopped | Absent` while observed phases stay rich (`Pending`,
`Provisioning`, `Provisioned`, `Initializing`, `Ready`, `Stopping`, `Stopped`,
`Deleting`, `Failed`, `Unknown`), and `Provisioned` and `Ready` explicitly not
synonyms — `Ready` is derived from conditions including reachability, source
initialization and health verification. A `WorkspaceLease` is a caller's claim,
with `Pending | Granted | Released | Expired | Revoked | Failed`, exclusive by
default for agents and jobs, and a release disposition that may destroy, stop or
retain. Human attachment is "an access grant under a lease, not a transfer of
ownership".

One more constraint generalises past Coder, and it explains a property of the
whole architecture: "Interactive or high-volume data paths should normally
connect directly to the underlying substrate after authorization; Cerberus does
not proxy them merely to remain in the middle." Two agent placements are named
— `remote_tools`, with the agent loop outside the workspace, as the baseline
"because they keep LLM credentials and agent state outside workspace compute";
and `workspace_local` for self-executing CLI agents.

Nothing of this is implemented and there is no plan document for it. That is the
finding: the catalog's resource classes stop at local processes, containers,
hosts and provider resources, and an entire declared class with a designed state
machine sits outside it.

data.decision: Model Coder as a workspace provider beneath Cerberus with first-class Workspace and WorkspaceLease resources, and refuse to depend on Coder Agents, Coder's AI Gateway or general-purpose Coder MCP access.
alternatives_considered: Use Coder Agents and Coder's AI Gateway directly — explicitly rejected: it would make Cerberus an AI control plane and would pull each caller's agent and session semantics into it

Treat a workspace as another generic resource — explicitly rejected: 'A Workspace is first-class rather than another untyped generic resource', because a process-shaped state enum erases provisioning phases

Proxy execution traffic through Cerberus so it stays in the request path — rejected: callers connect directly to the substrate after authorization, and Cerberus 'does not proxy them merely to remain in the middle'
data.rationale: Cerberus owns the workspace and the lease; the caller owns the agent, the session and the work. Depending on Coder's own agent and AI surfaces would invert that and give Cerberus a domain model it explicitly declines to adopt, while proxying execution traffic would put a control plane in a data path it has no reason to be in.

records.name: Credential delivery has a declared preference order, and Cerberus implements the last resort
records.summary: The direction ranks four delivery modes with delegated CLI authentication first and in-memory plaintext resolution last, and forbids Cerberus from storing, creating, rotating or deleting secret material — while the console's infra page does exactly that through KeychainProvider.Set and Delete.
records.confidence_label: Direction document read in full; KeychainProvider.Set/Delete and their console call sites in internal/webui/infra.go read directly

relationships.note: the credential chain this ranks
credentials are named, never carried
the console-only surface where the mutation lives
the Azure plugin, the one delegated-authentication case

records.body:
`docs/control-plane-direction.md` states the boundary in one line — "Cerberus
should not store, create, rotate, update, or delete secret material. The desired
configuration contains opaque credential references only" — and then ranks how a
credential should reach a process, best first:

1. **Delegated authentication.** Invoke an authenticated official CLI and let it
   and its credential authority handle the secret.
2. **Process-scoped injection.** Have a credential tool launch the build, deploy
   or service process with temporary environment or file material.
3. **Short-lived access grant.** Obtain an audience- and scope-limited token.
4. **Ephemeral SDK resolution.** Resolve plaintext into memory for the duration
   of one provider request, "when delegated mechanisms cannot work".

That ranking is not in the catalog, and it changes how the existing secret
records read. `CERB-CAP-504` describes what Cerberus does: `keychain://` and
`helper://` references resolved in the consuming process, per call for
connectors, at exec time via `run-secrets` for service environments. Measured
against the ranking, `run-secrets` is mode 2 and every built-in connector is
mode 4 — the last resort. The one true mode-1 case in the portfolio is the Azure
plugin, whose `azidentity` CLI credential shells out to `az` and therefore never
sees a secret, and the cost of being at the top of the ranking shows up as the
PATH repair `3a5136f` records: `AzureCLICredentialOptions` has no field for the
binary's location, so PATH is the only lever under launchd's minimal
environment. The document also names the matching current-model tension — "the
secret provider exposes storage mutation and connectors eagerly resolve
plaintext credentials during composition" — so it knew both halves.

The mutation half is still live and is the part worth flagging.
`internal/secrets/keychain.go` exposes `Set` and `Delete`; `cmd_web.go` hands
the console a `KeychainProvider` directly; and `internal/webui/infra.go` calls
`s.secrets.Set(...)` and `s.secrets.Delete(...)` on the provider-settings route.
So the console creates and deletes keychain entries, which is precisely what the
direction says Cerberus must not do — and it does it on the same console-only
infra surface `CERB-GAP-439` reports, which is why nobody has noticed. The
document's own escape hatch is narrow and Cerberus does not take it:
"Credential management UX, if present, must be framed as an adapter acting on an
external authority rather than a Cerberus secret store."

data.decision: Carry opaque credential references only, and prefer delegated CLI authentication over process-scoped injection over a short-lived grant over in-memory plaintext resolution — with Cerberus never storing, creating, rotating or deleting secret material.
alternatives_considered: A Cerberus-owned secret store — explicitly rejected; any credential UX must be 'an adapter acting on an external authority rather than a Cerberus secret store'

Resolve plaintext at plist-generation or composition time — rejected twice: once in the direction as a named tension, once concretely in b8acb74, where resolving at plist-generation time 'would only relocate the plaintext' and resolution was moved to exec instead
Standardise on ephemeral SDK resolution everywhere because it is uniform — not chosen; it is ranked last precisely because it is the only mode where Cerberus holds the plaintext at all
data.rationale: Every step up the ranking removes Cerberus from the custody chain: a delegated CLI means Cerberus never holds the secret, process-scoped injection means it holds it for one exec, a scoped grant limits the damage if it leaks, and in-memory SDK resolution is only better than writing it to a file. The store-nothing rule is the same boundary drawn against data ownership — and the console's infra page currently breaks it by calling Set and Delete on the keychain provider.

records.name: Cerberus's own Makefile has no install target, because its own deploy would run it
records.summary: The BSD/GNU-convention `install` target added for Homebrew was renamed `homebrew-install` after Cerberus's deploy pipeline probed `make -q install`, ran it, and failed writing to /usr/local/bin without sudo — a self-inflicted collision every project adopting install_after_build can hit.
records.confidence_label: Makefile target list read directly (homebrew-install present, install absent); the probe read at internal/connector/local/install.go:52

relationships.note: the build-to-install join this sits in
the install_after_build flag
the sibling decision about an ambiguous build-to-artifact join

records.body:
`8da01c7` added `install_after_build`: after a successful `make build`,
`cerberus resource deploy` probes `make -q install` and, if the target exists,
runs `make install`. Skip semantics are careful — a missing target is an INFO
skip rather than an error — and a later review pass (`69d9293`) extended that to
a project with no Makefile at all, mirroring make's own discovery of
`GNUmakefile`/`makefile`/`Makefile`.

Then `6f6681c` gave Cerberus a BSD/GNU-convention `install` target with
`PREFIX`/`BINDIR`/`DESTDIR`, to unblock a Homebrew formula. `e73a69b` records
what happened next: "PR #14's BSD/GNU `install` target collided with cerberus's
RunInstall (which probes `make -q install` post-build and ran it, then failed to
write /usr/local/bin without sudo)".

The fix was to rename the target rather than to change the probe: `install:`
became `homebrew-install:`, and the reason given is that the Homebrew formula
never needed it — "The Homebrew formula uses `bin.install` on the prebuilt
tarball — it doesn't depend on the Makefile target." So the Makefile today has
`homebrew-install`, `go-install` and `uninstall`, and deliberately no `install`.

This is worth a record because the collision is structural rather than a
Cerberus quirk. `install_after_build` defaults to **true**, and a
`build_strategy: make_standard` resource with a conventional `install` target
will have it run by every deploy, as root-less root-writing, with a failed
install failing the deploy — the commit is explicit that a present-but-failing
target must fail the deploy because "the resource is in a half-deployed state
and the operator must know". The convention that makes a Makefile a good citizen
on Unix is therefore the convention that breaks a Cerberus deploy, and the only
thing standing between the two is a per-resource `install_after_build: false` or
a renamed target. Cerberus chose the rename for itself and left the default at
true for everyone else.

data.decision: Rename Cerberus's own BSD/GNU `install` target to `homebrew-install` so its deploy pipeline's `make -q install` probe finds nothing, rather than narrowing the probe or changing the install_after_build default.
alternatives_considered: Set install_after_build: false on the cerberus resources — not chosen; it would fix this machine and leave the trap armed for every other project
Narrow the probe so it only runs an install target the resource explicitly opted into — not chosen, and it is the change that would actually remove the trap: the default is still true
Keep the install target and run make install under sudo — never considered; a deploy that needs a password has nowhere to type it, which is the same constraint recorded for ssh elevation
data.rationale: A conventional Unix `install` target writes to /usr/local/bin and a Cerberus deploy has no privilege to do that, so the two conventions cannot coexist in one Makefile while install_after_build defaults to true. Renaming Cerberus's target was the cheap local fix; the general fix — making the install step opt-in rather than opt-out — was not made, so the collision is still reachable by any project with a well-behaved Makefile.

records.name: A release is a pipeline, not a resource
records.summary: The self-release flow is modelled as a Cerberus pipeline driving a repo-owned shell script, because a release build is an encoded repeatable workflow rather than a long-running runtime object — and faking it as a resource would have put a non-process into the process lane.
records.confidence_label: Release document read in full; the pipeline itself not run (no rebuilds or releases in a read-only audit)

relationships.note: the sibling refusal, from the resource side
the literal dir: property this config leans on
the supervision lane a release is kept out of

records.body:
`docs/release/self-release-via-pipeline.md` has a section called *Why Not A
Resource First* and it is one of the few places in the repo where a rejected
option is argued rather than listed:

> A release build is not a long-running runtime object. It is an encoded,
> repeatable workflow. That makes `pipeline` the better first fit than a fake
> release `resource`.

The positive decision is deliberately small: model the release as a pipeline,
use `shell` actions, and keep the packaging logic in `scripts/release-beta.sh`
rather than inside Cerberus. The document calls this "intentionally modest" and
names why the script exists rather than being absorbed — pipeline actions "do
not yet model archive artifacts directly", the logic is needed by CLI, docs and
future pipeline runs alike, and a script is invokable by a human during
bring-up.

This is the same boundary `CERB-DEC-162` and the unsupervised-reporting work
drew from the other side. There, a resource that is not local/process was named
a handle for connector operations rather than a broken workload; here, a
workflow that is not a process is kept out of the resource model rather than
given a fake lifecycle. Both are refusals to let the supervision lane's
vocabulary spread to things that do not have a running state — and the
direction document generalises it: "Unsupported actions are absent from
capability discovery. A DNS driver should not implement meaningless `Start` and
`Stop` methods, and a repository should not be reported as `Running` merely to
fit a universal state enum."

Two honest limits are recorded with it. The release config carries an absolute
repo path, accepted because "Cerberus project configs are app-owned local files,
not portable package manifests" — the same literal-`dir:` property
`CERB-DEC-555` describes, here stated as a feature rather than a limitation. And
the flow deliberately stops short: it does not publish a GitHub prerelease,
upload assets, generate notes, validate a clean-machine install, or persist any
release metadata inside Cerberus. So the pipeline produces candidate archives
and nothing downstream of them, which is why there is no release record to query
anywhere.

data.decision: Model the self-release flow as a Cerberus pipeline over shell actions calling a repo-owned packaging script, rather than as a release resource or a new release subsystem.
alternatives_considered: Model the release as a resource — rejected with reasoning: a release build has no running state, so it would need a fabricated lifecycle to fit the resource model

Build a dedicated release subsystem with first-class artifact and distribution records — deferred as 'inventing a parallel release tool first'; the recorded consequence is that no release metadata is persisted anywhere
Absorb the packaging logic into pipeline actions — not chosen because pipeline actions do not model archive artifacts, and because a shell script stays invokable by a human during bring-up
data.rationale: The resource model's whole vocabulary — running, stopped, restart, health, drift — presumes a process, and a release build has none of it. Using a pipeline keeps the workflow encoded and repeatable without teaching the supervision lane about things that do not run. The cost is accepted and written down: no release artifact records, no prerelease publishing, and an absolute repo path in the config.

records.name: MCP list responses are capped at 25 by the vendored budget, with offset paging as the recovery
records.summary: List tools return a budgeted envelope whose limit is hard-capped at 25 by go-mcp, chosen against a ~25k-token MCP response ceiling; review found the cap made items in unfiltered lists unreachable, so offset paging was added rather than the cap raised — and the one-week tuning review it scheduled never happened.
records.confidence_label: Commit and PR #13 review thread read; budgeted envelope shape confirmed from the commit record rather than by calling a tool

relationships.note: the MCP adapter this shapes
a budgeted list tool
the unbudgeted connector-op list path

records.body:
`7d8d4a6` adopted `go-mcp/budget` on the slice-returning MCP list tools, so
`resource_list`, `project_list`, `connector_list` and `pipeline_list` return
`{items,count,total,truncated,hint}` instead of an unbounded array. The
reasoning is specific: "MCP tool responses have a ~25k-token ceiling
(`MCPContentTooLargeError`) and our lists are small, so 25 minimizes truncation
while bounding pathological responses; agents narrow via existing filters when
truncated." The 25 is not a Cerberus choice — `budget.MaxLimit` in the vendored
library hard-caps `Apply`'s limit — which is why the commit describes it as
"tunable, see review note" and cannot simply be raised here.

Review then found the flaw. The Copilot pass on PR #13 pointed out that for the
no-filter lists — project, pipeline, connector — a truncation at a hard 25 with
no paging leaves the remaining items *undiscoverable*, since "narrow via
existing filters" is not available. The fix (`277cb2f`) added an `offset`
argument and made the hint paging-aware, so the envelope now says "Showing X-Y
of N. Pass offset/limit to page through the rest." Three smaller findings landed
with it and each is the kind of thing only a real review catches: `budgetedList`
now nil-guards items centrally so `connector_list` encodes `[]` rather than
`null` when `ListConnectors` returns nil; the `project_list` hint stopped
pointing at a per-project get tool that does not exist; and the tests were
rewritten to pass `limit`/`offset` as `float64`, matching what JSON-decoded MCP
arguments actually are.

Two consequences are worth recording. The commit scheduled its own follow-up —
truncations log `mcp.budget.truncated` to stderr "for a 1-week tuning review
(~2026-06-01)" — and there is no artefact anywhere of that review happening; the
limit is still 25 nearly four months later. And the scope exclusion is still in
force: "provider list tools (`cerberus_*_dns_list`, `droplet_list`) return via
the opaque connector-op path and are not budgeted here", so a DNS zone with
hundreds of records reaches an agent unbudgeted, through exactly the path the
ceiling was a concern for.

data.decision: Budget the four slice-returning MCP list tools at the vendored library's 25-item hard cap, and answer the resulting undiscoverability with an offset argument and a paging-aware hint rather than by raising the cap or dropping the budget.
alternatives_considered: Return unbounded arrays and rely on lists being small — rejected against the ~25k-token MCP response ceiling, which turns a pathological list into a tool error rather than a long answer
Raise the limit above 25 — not available: budget.MaxLimit in the vendored go-mcp hard-caps it, so tuning would mean changing the library
Tell agents to narrow with filters when truncated — the original answer, and review rejected it for the no-filter lists (project, pipeline, connector), where there is no filter to narrow with
Budget the provider list tools too — explicitly out of scope; they return through the opaque connector-op path and are still unbudgeted
data.rationale: A tool response that exceeds the transport ceiling fails entirely, so a bound is better than a long answer. But a bound without paging silently hides rows, and the lists least able to be filtered are exactly the ones most likely to truncate — so offset paging is what makes the cap honest. The scheduled one-week tuning review was never carried out, so 25 is a default nobody has revisited with data.

records.name: Service commands are not wrapped in a login shell; the child's PATH is augmented instead
records.summary: Running every service command through `$SHELL -l -c` to pick up Homebrew and nvm was tried and reverted within hours in favour of prepending known bin directories to the child's PATH — which is why ensurePath exists and why the daemon's own tool lookups were never fixed by the same mechanism.
records.confidence_label: Both commits read; ensurePath and the ownedPID/stopContext identity checks read in the local connector. The reason for the revert is not recorded anywhere — the consequences named here are derived from the current design, not from the commit

relationships.note: ensurePath, the surviving mechanism
the daemon's own tool lookup, which this did not fix
Docker's per-call resolution, a later answer to the same question
the helper lookup's own fallback chain

records.body:
A one-day reversal, visible only in two adjacent commit messages, that decided
the shape of local process launching.

`34cdc65` (2026-03-09) — "run service commands through login shell for proper
PATH": wraps service commands with `$SHELL -l -c` "so that Homebrew, nvm, and
other profile-dependent tools are available to child processes. Fixes 'no such
file or directory' errors when launching npm/node services."

`952265d`, the very next commit — "ensure Homebrew/Go paths in child process
PATH": "Reverts shell wrapping approach. Instead, ensures /opt/homebrew/bin,
/usr/local/bin, ~/go/bin etc. are in PATH before spawning child processes so
shebang scripts can resolve node, go, etc."

The revert is recorded; its reason is not. What is verifiable is what the
current design depends on, and a login-shell wrapper is incompatible with most
of it. `dev_session` launches `command[0]` directly with `Setpgid: true` and
writes a PID file plus a meta file holding a `ps -o lstart` launch identity;
`ownedPID` then refuses to adopt a PID whose recorded start time disagrees, and
`stopContext` refuses to signal a PID that is not its own process-group leader.
Under `$SHELL -l -c` the recorded PID is the shell, not the service, so the
identity Cerberus checks and the process an operator cares about are different
objects — and `-l -c` additionally makes the command string shell-interpreted,
so a `dir:` or an argument containing a space changes meaning. `ensurePath`,
which appends `/opt/homebrew/bin`, `/opt/homebrew/sbin`, `/usr/local/bin`,
`/usr/local/go/bin` and `~/go/bin` when they exist, is the surviving descendant
