of that revert.

The reason this is worth recording is the asymmetry it left behind, which
`AGENTS.md` states as a boundary without explaining where it came from: a
dev-session *child* gets a usable PATH even though the daemon that launched it
does not. The same problem in the daemon's own process — resolving `go` for a
build, `docker` for the Docker connector — was solved three more times by three
different mechanisms, none of them this one: per-call resolution with fallback
install locations plus a `CERBERUS_DOCKER_PATH` override (`41c76a2`), a
GOBIN/GOPATH/`~/go/bin`/`~/.local/bin` fallback chain in the secret-reference
helper lookup (`b8acb74`), and a per-credential-build PATH repair in the Azure
plugin (`3a5136f`). Four answers to one question, because the first one was
reverted before it became a pattern.

data.decision: Launch a service's command directly and prepend the known Homebrew, /usr/local and Go bin directories to the child's environment, rather than wrapping the command in a login shell to inherit the operator's profile.
alternatives_considered: Wrap every service command in `$SHELL -l -c` — implemented in 34cdc65 and reverted in 952265d the same day; the commit records the reversal without its reason, but a shell wrapper would make the recorded PID the shell rather than the service, breaking the launch-identity and process-group ownership checks dev_session is built on, and would make the command string shell-interpreted
Require every resource to declare absolute paths for its command — not chosen; the project-setup guide recommends it for artifact resources but ensurePath exists so a shebang script does not have to

Fix the daemon's own PATH instead, so children inherit a good one — not done here, and the launchd plist template still renders no EnvironmentVariables, which is why the daemon cannot find `go` at all
data.rationale: A login shell buys profile-dependent PATH and costs process identity: the wrapper becomes the child, so the PID file, the ps -o lstart launch identity and the process-group ownership checks all describe the shell instead of the service. Explicitly appending known bin directories buys the same PATH with none of that, at the price of a hardcoded list — and it fixes only the child, which is why the daemon's own tool lookups needed three further, unrelated mechanisms.

records.name: The daemon resource carries no auto_restart, and `protected` no longer implies one
records.summary: auto_restart was removed from the daemon's own resource because a daemon restarting itself produced a recursive fork loop and launchd KeepAlive already owns persistence — and in the same change `protected` was narrowed to mean only 'shielded from an external MCP stop'.
records.confidence_label: Commit read; the surviving form confirmed in shouldMonitorResource's os_service exclusion and in the live tunnel resource's flags

relationships.note: monitor enrolment, which excludes os_service for the same reason
the later, structural form of 'the daemon must not act on itself'
the resource that needs protection without restart
the port: 0 ban, from the same family of port-detection bugs

records.body:
`e2908da` (v0.3.0, 2026-03-14) fixed three things at once and two of them are
decisions nothing else records.

The first: "Remove `auto_restart` from cerberus-daemon — a daemon must not
restart itself (launchd `KeepAlive` handles persistence); this was causing a
recursive fork loop". This is the earliest member of a family the catalog holds
the later members of. `CERB-DEC-163` refuses a resource mutation targeting the
serving daemon; `CERB-DEC-470` keeps the binary-swap watcher out of
`cerberus mcp`; `CERB-CAP-104` records that `os_service` resources are excluded
from monitor enrolment entirely because launchd's `KeepAlive` already does that
job and "a second restarter would fight it". The principle in all four is the
same and was established here first: whoever supervises a process is the only
thing allowed to restart it, and Cerberus is not that thing for anything launchd
owns — least of all itself.

The second is a vocabulary narrowing: "Decouple `protected` from auto-restart —
`protected` now only means 'shielded from external MCP stop,' not 'auto-restart
when down'". Before this, one flag meant both "do not let an agent stop this"
and "bring this back if it dies", which are unrelated properties that happen to
co-occur on important services. Splitting them is what makes it possible to
declare a resource that must not be stopped by an agent *and* must not be
restarted automatically — which is exactly the shape `tunnel-muctlvaig` needs
today, and `CERB-DEC-671` records it choosing `auto_start: false` and
`auto_restart: false` without having to give up any protection.

The same commit carries a third fix that belongs with `CERB-DEC-551` rather than
here: `lsof` port detection was filtered to `LISTEN` state only, because stale
Chrome `CLOSED` connections were triggering false "port in use" conflicts. That
is the second of the three port-detection bugs — the first was `findPIDByPort(0)`
matching arbitrary system processes, the third was adopting a foreign listener as
if it were ours — and together they are why the current code treats a listening
port as evidence of occupancy and never of ownership.

data.decision: Never let Cerberus restart a process its supervisor already owns — remove auto_restart from the daemon's own resource and exclude os_service resources from monitor enrolment — and keep `protected` meaning only 'not stoppable from outside', not 'restart when down'.
alternatives_considered: Keep auto_restart on the daemon and suppress it during a restart — the shape of the accompanying pause/resume fix for other services, and rejected for the daemon itself: the failure was a recursive fork loop, not a race
Let the monitor restart os_service resources when launchd appears to have given up — rejected in CAP-104's enrolment rule: two restarters fight, and launchd's is the authoritative one
Keep protected as one flag meaning both protection and restart — rejected: they are unrelated properties, and separating them is what allows a resource to be un-stoppable and un-restartable at once
data.rationale: Two supervisors for one process is not redundancy, it is a fork loop — and for the daemon specifically the loser of the race is the control plane an operator would use to stop it. Narrowing `protected` to protection alone removes a coupling nothing wanted: the resources most worth shielding from an agent's stop are not always the ones that should come back by themselves.

records.name: The embedded default config is an empty skeleton, because agents kept editing it as if it were live
records.summary: config.go once embedded a full service list as its first-run template; agents repeatedly edited that Go constant believing it was the live config, so it was stripped to `projects: []` / `resources: []` with a comment saying so in capitals.
records.confidence_label: The current defaultConfig constant read directly at internal/config/config.go:144

relationships.note: the descendant: repo descriptors that are not live either
the config model this seeds
the seed path itself

records.body:
`b40c91a` (2026-03-16) is a two-line change with an unusually blunt reason:
"The embedded `defaultConfig` in config.go was a full service list that agents
kept editing thinking it was the live config. It's only a seed template for
first-time setup."

What replaced it is still there, and the shape of it is the decision:

    # This is a SEED template. It is only written when ~/.cerberus/config.yaml
    # does not exist. The live config is ALWAYS ~/.cerberus/config.yaml.
    # Edit that file directly — changes here have NO effect on running systems.
    version: 2
    projects: []
    resources: []

Two things were done at once and both matter. The content was emptied, so there
is nothing in the template worth editing — an agent that opens it finds no
service definition to change. And the warning was put *inside the emitted
template* rather than in a Go comment, so it survives into
`~/.cerberus/config.yaml` on a fresh install and is read by whoever opens the
file next.

This is the earliest instance of a failure mode that has since recurred twice in
different clothes, and `AGENTS.md` now carries both descendants. The repo's own
`cerberus.cerberus.yaml` and `infrastructure.cerberus.yaml` descriptors carry
`dir: /Users/<other-user>/...`, are not registered on this machine, and "editing
those descriptors changes nothing that runs here" — `CERB-DEC-670`. And a config
that exists only on a branch vanishes from the runtime on checkout while the
registry still points at its path — recorded in `26ee464`, which explicitly
declined to re-register a relocated config until it was on main. All three are
the same shape: a file that looks authoritative, is not, and gives no feedback
when edited. The seed template is the one that was fixed by removing the
temptation rather than by documenting it.

data.decision: Reduce the embedded first-run config template to an empty v2 skeleton and put the 'this is not the live config' warning inside the emitted text, rather than keeping a realistic service list as a starting point.
alternatives_considered: Keep a populated template as a worked example — rejected because that is what caused the problem: a realistic service list reads as live configuration and was edited as such
Keep the content and add a Go comment warning readers — insufficient by the same logic, and the warning was deliberately moved into the emitted YAML so it survives into the operator's own file
Ship no template at all and require `cerberus init` to write nothing — not chosen; the skeleton still supplies `version: 2`, which the strict loader requires
data.rationale: A template that looks like live configuration will be edited as live configuration, and the edit produces no error and no effect — the worst available feedback. Emptying it removes the possibility rather than warning against it, and placing the warning in the emitted file rather than in source puts it where the next reader actually is.

records.name: A documented workaround for the redactor was refused, and the redactor was fixed instead
records.summary: PR #29 proposed an AGENTS.md house rule telling future authors never to write 'Bearer' followed by a word; it was closed on the grounds that fixing looksLikeToken had already removed the constraint, and that merging it would teach agents to route around a problem that no longer exists.
records.confidence_label: PR #29's closing comment read in full via gh; the surviving AGENTS.md rule and the WP-3/WP-6 tests confirmed

relationships.note: the redaction capability this governs
a live defect in a different rule
the other live defect, also a different rule

records.body:
The only substantive review argument in the repository's PR history, and it is a
decision about what belongs in a house-rules document.

PR #29, "docs: warn that `redact.Text` mangles auth guidance in errors", was
closed unmerged with a comment that states the principle plainly:

> The premise was that `redact.Text` cannot distinguish a credential from
> prose, so the house rule had to be "do not write the word bearer followed by
> a word." That was true when it was written. `055ce87` fixed the redactor
> instead — `looksLikeToken` now requires the text after `Bearer` to be twenty
> or more characters or to contain something other than letters, so guidance
> survives. […] Merging this would tell future agents to route around a problem
> that is gone.

Three things make this worth a record. First, it is a rejection of a *correct*
document: the behaviour it described had been real, and the PR was closed
because the premise expired rather than because it was wrong. Second, the
comment distinguishes the instruction from the lesson, and says which one
survived: the specific prohibition was dropped, while the generalisable rule
went into `AGENTS.md` instead — "do not run redaction over a value that is a
name by construction, and if an error carries a recovery instruction, add a test
that it survives `redact.Text`" — with WP-3 and WP-6 both carrying such a test.
Third, it is the fourth recorded instance of the redactor eating its own
guidance, and `364ca0d` counts them: "Bearer prose, an env-var instruction, a
names-only `missing_secrets` field, and a doc branch proposing to work around it
permanently." That last item is this PR. The pattern named is that the fourth
occurrence was a *document* rather than a defect, and it was treated as one more
occurrence rather than as the remedy.

The closing comment also records a mechanical reason the PR was hard to judge,
worth keeping because it generalises: the branch was based on `41c76a2` rather
than `main`, so its diff showed a 44-line deletion of an onboarding section that
a merge would not actually have made. A stale base makes a docs diff say things
the author did not intend.

Two of the three live redaction defects the briefing reproduced —
`CERB-GAP-273` and `CERB-GAP-447` — postdate this and are separate rules with
separate triggers, so the decision here is specifically that the fix belongs in
the redactor, not that the redactor is now correct.

data.decision: Fix the redactor rather than documenting a house rule that tells authors to write around it, and keep in AGENTS.md only the generalisable rule — never redact a value that is a name by construction, and test that any recovery instruction survives redact.Text.
alternatives_considered: Merge the warning as a house rule — rejected: the constraint it described had been removed by fixing looksLikeToken, so the rule would train agents around a problem that no longer exists
Merge it as historical context with a note that it is obsolete — not chosen; AGENTS.md is house rules, and an obsolete rule in a rules document is read as current
Widen redaction and accept mangled guidance as the safe default — rejected by the whole family of fixes: 'a safety net that eats the instruction is worse than no instruction'
data.rationale: A house-rules document is read as current instruction, so a rule whose premise has expired is worse than no rule. When a safety mechanism damages output, the choice is between teaching every future author to avoid it and making the mechanism correct — and the mechanism is one place while the authors are unbounded. What generalises is kept; the specific prohibition is not.

records.name: The module was renamed to match the remote rather than shipping a replace directive
records.summary: go.mod declared github.com/chrispian/cerberus while the remote is hollis-labs/cerberus and the declared path did not resolve, so every external plugin needed a replace directive pointing at a local checkout — 390 import references across 189 files were rewritten instead of documenting the workaround.
records.confidence_label: Commit record read; the current module path and the absence of any replace directive confirmed in go.mod

relationships.note: the authoring contract an external module has to import
the pkg/plugin promotion that exposed the problem
the plugin lane this unblocked

records.body:
Recorded inside the PR #28 squash (`41c76a2`) and nowhere else. The problem
first appeared as a blocker on the plugin work: `pkg/plugin` had just been
promoted so an external module could import the authoring contract, and the
external module still could not resolve it. "go.mod declared
`github.com/chrispian/cerberus` while the remote is `hollis-labs/cerberus`, and
the declared path does not resolve — `go list -m
github.com/chrispian/cerberus@latest` returns 'Repository not found'. Every
external consumer therefore needed a replace directive pointing at a local
checkout, which works for a plugin developed beside one and does not work in
CI."

The intermediate state is the interesting part, because the workaround was
written down first and then deleted. The commit that promoted `pkg/plugin` says
"The module path question is unresolved and out of scope here […] so the
external module needed a replace directive. The verified go.mod shape is
recorded in the work package for the plugin repo to copy" — and an earlier
commit had marked the rename as "an owner call that is out of scope for that
package". So the sequence is: hit the wall, document the workaround, verify it,
escalate the decision, then take it and delete the documentation. "Renaming to
match the remote removes the problem rather than documenting it."

What made it cheap enough to take was a fact about the environment rather than
the code: `GOPRIVATE=github.com/hollis-labs/*` was already configured, so the
private repository resolves directly for anyone with access and no replace is
needed at all. The change itself was mechanical — 390 import references across
189 files, plus the `go install` lines in `README.md` and `docs/install.md` —
and two remaining `chrispian/cerberus` strings were left alone on purpose:
they are fixtures for a git remote URL parser in `internal/infra/deploy_test.go`
and have nothing to do with the module path.

This is the second time the same shape of decision was taken in this repo, and
recording it as a pattern is the value. `9598e91` had already done it for a
dependency rather than the module: `go.mod` required `go-mcp v0.0.0`, a
placeholder that only resolved because a `replace` pointed at
`../../libs/go-mcp`, so "nothing recorded which version cerberus actually built
against, and the build silently depended on the hollis-labs/{apps,libs} sibling
layout being present on disk". That was fixed by pinning `v0.2.0` and deleting
the replace, verified by building in a clone under `/private/tmp` where the
sibling layout does not exist, against an empty `GOMODCACHE` to force a real
proxy fetch. Both decisions say the same thing: a `replace` directive is a
recorded dependency on a local filesystem layout, and the fix is to make the
declared path true.

data.decision: Rename the module to github.com/hollis-labs/cerberus so the declared path matches the remote and resolves under the already-configured GOPRIVATE, rather than documenting a replace directive for every external consumer.
alternatives_considered: Keep the declared path and document a replace directive in each plugin's go.mod — implemented and verified as an interim step, then deleted: it works for a plugin developed beside a checkout and fails in CI
Publish the module under the declared chrispian/cerberus path — not considered; the remote is the organisation's, and the fix was to make go.mod agree with reality rather than the reverse
Vendor the contract packages into each plugin — never proposed; it would fork the authoring contract per plugin, which is what pkg/plugin exists to prevent
data.rationale: A replace directive is a recorded dependency on a filesystem layout: it makes a build work on the author's machine and fail everywhere else, and it hides which version was actually built against. Renaming was mechanical and one-time, GOPRIVATE already made the private path resolve, and it removed the workaround from every future consumer's go.mod rather than from one.

records.name: Repo drift is never probed on a high-fanout path; a background cache answers those
records.summary: A git probe per resource per poll made list and health calls scale with the number of resources, so those paths were cut back to basic artifact inspection and a background drift scan now fills a cache — which means the drift a list shows is as old as the last scan, not as old as the request.
records.confidence_label: PR #4 review comment and the drift_cache package comment read; the daemon's AttachDriftCache wiring read in cmd_daemon.go

relationships.note: the artifact drift this reports
the staleness flag that deliberately excludes repo state
the daemon that runs the background scan
the console list that reads the cache

records.body:
Two changes, four months apart, that together decided how freshness information
reaches a high-fanout surface — and neither is recorded outside a PR comment and
a package comment.

The first is in the PR #4 review response (`1d12581`): "Avoided live repo-drift
git probes on high-fanout list/health paths by using basic artifact inspection
there; explicit status/inspect/doctor paths still perform full repo freshness
checks." That is a deliberate two-tier design rather than an optimisation. A
`resource list` over N resources would otherwise shell out to git N times; a
`resource status <id>` asks about one resource and can afford the truth.

The second completed it. `0b1f179` (#9) added a "background artifact-drift scan
(`drift_cache.go`) wired into the daemon and resource runtime so the list path
surfaces repo drift without a live git probe per poll", and
`internal/cerbapi/drift_cache.go:26` still describes the contract: the
high-fanout list path reads from the cache rather than probing. `cmd_daemon.go`
starts it as a goroutine beside the resource monitor and attaches it with
`a.Runtime.AttachDriftCache(driftCache)`.

The consequence is a two-speed truth that no surface labels. What `resource
list` shows for drift is whatever the last background scan found; what `resource
status` shows is computed now. They can disagree, and nothing in either output
says which one is fresh — an operator comparing a list against a status has no
way to tell that one is a cache read. This also interacts with `CERB-DEC-164`,
which removed repo HEAD and worktree state from the *staleness flag* while
keeping them in the install manifest: the drift cache is what still carries repo
state to the console and the list, so the thing the cache is warming is
explicitly not the thing that decides whether an artifact is stale.

There is a third member of this family and it was solved the same way.
`9d0050b` includes "Keep runtime observers responsive during builds", because a
build holds locks a list path would otherwise wait on. In all three cases the
rule is the same: a path that fans out over every resource must not do work
proportional to the number of resources, and the price paid is staleness rather
than latency.

data.decision: Serve repo-drift information on list and health paths from a background scan's cache and from basic artifact inspection, and keep live git probing for the single-resource status, inspect and doctor paths.
alternatives_considered: Probe git per resource on every list and health call — rejected in review: the cost scales with the resource count on the two most frequently polled paths, including the console's own refresh
Drop repo drift from the list surface entirely — not chosen; CERB-DEC-164 had already removed repo state from the staleness flag, and the cache exists precisely so the list can still show it

Cache on first read with a TTL instead of scanning in the background — not proposed; a background scan keeps the cost off the request path entirely, at the price of showing data as old as the last scan
data.rationale: A surface that fans out over every resource must do work bounded by the surface, not by the estate. Moving the git probe into a background scan keeps list and health latency flat, and the accepted cost is that drift on a list is as old as the last scan while drift on a status is computed now — a discrepancy no output currently labels.

records.name: The loopback Host check ignores the port; Origin is matched exactly
records.summary: The web console and mcp-http refuse any request whose Host is not a loopback name or the listen host, whatever port it carries, and match a sent Origin exactly (scheme, host and port) against the same set, never against r.Host.
records.confidence_label: internal/loopback re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54); Host and Origin 403s probed live against mcp-http on a scratch HOME

relationships.note: the console this guards
mcp-http sits behind the same guard
closed the rebinding path, not the local-process one
the network and browser half of mcp-http exposure
the token design this completes against browsers
the bind rule that goes with it

records.body:
PR #48 added `internal/loopback`, shared by `cerberus web` and `cerberus
mcp-http`. `Guard.Middleware` runs before any handler and returns 403 unless
`Host` is `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]` or the configured listen host.

**The port is deliberately not compared.** A rebinding page always carries its
own hostname in `Host` and never a loopback name, so a port check stops nothing
the name check does not already stop. It would break `ssh -L
9000:127.0.0.1:4785` and the Vite dev proxy. A code comment beside the check
records this.

**Origin is the opposite: exact.** When a request carries an Origin, the
middleware compares scheme, host and port against the guard's set, and
`allowStateChangingRequest` checks it again for mutations. The old check
compared Origin with `"http://"+r.Host`. Under rebinding the attacker controls
both, so that comparison proved nothing. The server binds with `net.Listen` and
takes the port from the bound address, so the allowed origins use the port it
actually listens on.

The consequence an operator meets: over an `ssh -L` onto a *different* local
port, the console loads and reads, but mutations are refused, because the
browser's Origin carries the forwarded port. Forward onto the same port
(`-L 4783:127.0.0.1:4783`) to use actions. The Vite dev proxy rewrites Origin to
the console's own origin for the same reason.

data.decision: Compare Host by name only against the loopback names and the listen host; compare a sent Origin exactly, scheme, host and port, against the same set.
alternatives_considered: Compare Host and port together
Keep comparing Origin against r.Host
Allow only 127.0.0.1 and drop the name check
data.rationale: A rebinding attack cannot present a loopback hostname, so the name is the whole defence and a port check only breaks SSH local forwards and the dev proxy. Origin must not be compared against anything the request itself supplies, because under rebinding the attacker supplies it.

records.name: No --insecure-listen until the posture work
records.summary: --listen on the web console and mcp-http accepts only localhost or a literal loopback IP, with no override flag and no hostnames, until the permissive posture exists to scope and record an override.
records.confidence_label: internal/loopback re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54); both refusals run live against a branch build

relationships.note: the console's --listen
mcp-http's --listen
the missing authentication this stands in for
the Host allow-list the listen host joins

records.body:
`loopback.CheckListen` runs before either server starts. It refuses
`0.0.0.0`, `::`, an empty host (`:4783`), a LAN or link-local address, and, since
PR #50, any hostname, even one that resolves to loopback. The error says the
surface has no authentication yet. Verified live on a branch build:

    cerberus mcp-http: refusing to listen on 0.0.0.0:4796: not a loopback address,
    and this surface has no authentication yet; use localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1]

There is no override. Section 13 of `docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md`
describes a `permissive` posture that relaxes the listen guard among other
things, and `--insecure-listen` belongs there, in P2. Until then one flag would
move an unauthenticated endpoint that carries every connector operation onto the
network.

Hostnames went in the #48 review. Accepting a name that resolves to loopback
meant resolving it twice (once to check, once to bind) and putting an
operator-supplied name into the Host allow-list. Literal addresses avoid both.

data.decision: Refuse any --listen that is not localhost or a literal loopback IP, and ship no override flag in P0.
alternatives_considered: Add --insecure-listen now
Accept hostnames that resolve to loopback
Accept any address with a warning
data.rationale: Neither surface authenticates a caller. An override belongs to the permissive posture (Decision 13), where it can be scoped per target and recorded in the audit log, not to a bare flag. Literal addresses keep name resolution and operator-chosen names out of the guard.

records.name: `docker down` maps to stop, and stop is compose stop
records.summary: cerberus docker down and cerberus_docker_down invoke the connector's stop operation, which since P0 runs docker compose stop for a stack; removal is destroy, which runs docker compose down and requires acknowledgment.
records.confidence_label: docker connector and cmd_docker.go re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54)

relationships.note: the Docker connector
docker stop
docker destroy
destroy still has no verb

records.body:
Before PR #49, `Stop` and `Destroy` both ran `docker compose down` for a
compose resource. `stop` is neither destructive nor ack-gated, so `cerberus
docker down` quietly removed a stack's containers and networks with no gate.

Now `Stop` runs `docker compose stop` through `Backend.ComposeStop`, and
`Destroy` keeps `compose down` (or `docker rm` for a container) and stays
destructive with `--ack`. A test pins the argv of both against a fake docker
binary. The verb mapping did not change: `up` is `start`, `down` is `stop`, and
`destroy` has no CLI verb or MCP tool (CERB-GAP-272).

The cost is a name. Compose's own `down` removes; Cerberus's `down` does not.
The CLI help, the MCP description and the README all say so and name `destroy`
as the removal. `cerberus_docker_down` keeps `DestructiveHint: false`, which is
now accurate. For a compose stack this was a behaviour change: `down` used to
remove the stack and now stops it. A plain container was unaffected
(`docker stop` before and after).

data.decision: Keep the down verb mapped to stop, and make stop a compose stop, so down never removes anything; leave removal to destroy with acknowledgment.
alternatives_considered: Map down to destroy, matching Compose's naming
Rename the down verb to stop
Leave stop as compose down and make it destructive
data.rationale: An un-acked, non-destructive verb must not tear a stack down. Keeping the verb and fixing what it does changed no CLI or MCP contract, and the name mismatch with Compose is cheaper to document than a removal behind a verb that looks safe.

records.name: Targets on the socket, web and MCP are configured resources; free-form targets run in-process only
records.summary: An SSH or Docker operation arriving over the socket, web or MCP names a configured resource by id and the serving side resolves it; host, key, context and compose-file settings are refused there and accepted only in the operator's own CLI process.
records.confidence_label: resolveSSHTarget, resolveDockerResource and RefuseAdHocDockerTarget re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54)

relationships.note: SSH targets
Docker targets
enforced at the socket
MCP schemas carry only an id
enforced at the web API
discovery schemas advertise only what is accepted
what the in-process exemption leaves open
the two enforcement shapes this produced

records.body:
Before P0, every SSH caller resolved the resource on its own side and sent the
whole connection config over the socket (`host`, `port`, `user`, `key_file`,
`known_hosts_file`, `allow_insecure_host_key`). The daemon could not tell a
configured target from a free-form one. MCP's "configured resources only" held
at its tool-argument layer and nowhere else. Docker was the same shape with
`host`, `context` and `compose_file`. A compose file chooses images, commands
and host bind mounts, so an arbitrary one amounts to code execution with host
filesystem access, reachable by an agent through `cerberus_docker_up`.

**SSH (PR #50).** `resolveSSHTarget` runs at the top of `Execute`, before dry-run
previews, so a preview shows the real target. The config may carry `id` plus the
operation fields in `sshconn.OperationFields`; any other key is refused by name.
The id is resolved against whoever runs the operation: the daemon's live
snapshot, or the CLI's own config in-process. This applies on every surface,
in-process included.

**Docker (PR #52).** `RefuseAdHocDockerTarget` runs on the raw socket and web
request with an allow-list built from `internal/connector/docker/config_keys.go`:
`resource`, the container keys and the operation keys. Every target key and every
compose-file alias is refused. A declared resource's own `host`, `context` and
`compose_file` are configuration, not input, and still apply. `--host`,
`--context` and `-f` force the CLI in-process, where they still work. MCP
dropped `docker_host` and `docker_context`, and `up`/`down` take `resource_id`
instead of `compose_file`.

An explicit `--config` also forces connector verbs in-process, so an id is never
resolved against a config other than the one the operator named. PR #54 made
the discovery schemas advertise exactly these keys, with a drift test in both
directions.

## Since P2-3

The audit record now names which kind of target a call used. A call that carries a local-scoped input, such as `docker --host`, `--context` or `-f` in the operator's shell, records `target.adhoc: true` and unknown labels. A call that names a configured resource inherits that resource's `env`, `owner`, `admin` and `tags`. Section 2's `adhoc_targets` grant is defined as `target.AdhocTargets`, with a default (`target.DefaultAdhocGrant`) under which only a human holds it; the policy engine evaluates it in P2-4, in shadow mode, so the in-process exemption this decision keeps is unchanged for now.

**Since P2-4.** The policy engine evaluates the ad hoc marking: `builtin.adhoc` denies an ad hoc target to a caller without the `adhoc_targets` grant, recorded in shadow mode (`internal/policy/evaluate.go`).

data.decision: Resolve SSH and Docker targets from a configured resource id on the serving side for every remote surface; keep free-form targets only in the operator's own CLI process.
alternatives_considered: Keep accepting free-form targets everywhere
Refuse free-form targets in-process too
Add a host allow-list instead of resource ids
data.rationale: The declaration is the only thing an operator reviewed, so it has to be the authority for any call that crosses a process boundary. The operator's own shell keeps free-form power because removing it would break documented CLI use (docker ps --host ssh://...) for no gain against a caller that already has that shell. That exemption is also why in-process is not a trust boundary (CERB-GAP-846).

records.name: A plugin dry run is plugin-claimed
records.summary: The host forwards a dry run to a plugin only for an operation that declares a preview, never verifies that the plugin honoured it, and records it plugin_claimed; since P1-5 an accepted preview stands in for --ack on the dry run only.
records.confidence_label: pluginhost.Manager.ExecuteOperation and OperationAllowed re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54)

relationships.note: the plugin lane
closed in P1-5: an accepted preview stands in for --ack
the fall-through this closed for plugins too
the plugin whose writes this governs today

records.body:
Both plugin paths used to forward `dry_run` and trust the plugin with it: the
managed path through `ExternalConnectorService`, and one-shot `plugin exec`
through `PluginConnectorService`. PR #49 fixed it at their shared choke point,
`pluginhost.Manager.ExecuteOperation`. A dry run reaches the plugin only when
the manifest operation declares `supports_dry`. Otherwise it returns
`ErrPreviewUnsupported`, which the admin lane maps to `preview_unsupported`.

What a declared dry run returns is the plugin's claim. The host cannot check
that the plugin did not act, and a code comment says so. It cites Decision 7 of
`docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md`: a plugin preview counts as
trustworthy only once the operator has accepted the declaration in the install
review, and until then it is recorded as `plugin_claimed`.

That is also why `OperationAllowed` still runs its ack check before the dry-run
check. A built-in's dry run needs no `--ack`, because the host builds the
preview itself; a plugin's does, for a destructive operation. The phase plan
orders the change: the install review lands before plugin dry runs lose
`--ack`.

## Since P1-5

The install review exists, and the ordering the phase plan set has run its course. A reviewed plugin's dry run of an operation whose declared preview the operator accepted no longer needs `--ack` (`pluginhost.PreviewAccepted`). The review text says the previews are the plugin's claim, which Cerberus cannot verify. Every plugin dry run is recorded as `preview: plugin_claimed`. A plugin still pending review has accepted no preview, and keeps the `--ack` (CERB-GAP-652, closed).

data.decision: Forward a plugin dry run only when the manifest declares supports_dry, treat the result as the plugin's unverified claim, and keep --ack on destructive plugin dry runs until the install review exists.
alternatives_considered: Refuse every plugin dry run
Let a declared dry run skip --ack now
Verify the claim with a signed manifest
data.rationale: The host has no way to verify a plugin honoured dry_run. Declared-and-accepted is the strongest status available (Decision 7); declared alone is not accepted, so the acknowledgment stays. Signing was ruled out portfolio-wide (Decision 12).

records.name: `origin: installed | dev` replaces the plugin trust tiers
records.summary: A managed plugin records how it was installed, installed or dev, instead of a trust tier; the origin makes no claim about who built the plugin, and entrypoint_sha256 is kept as change detection, not as a trust signal.
records.confidence_label: internal/pluginhost/policy.go and plugin state re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54)

relationships.note: the unsigned-sits-with-trusted-tiers argument no longer has tiers to sit among
the capability this reshaped
closed by this
closed in P1-5 by the bundle digest
the dev origin needs a devmode build

records.body:
"Signed" was self-asserted. `--catalog-signed` and `--archive-signed` were
caller flags that selected a policy which then checked those same
caller-supplied booleans, and `OperationAllowed` treated `signed`, `unsigned`
and `builtin` identically. A `signed` tier told an operator, and an agent
reading `managed list`, that a plugin had been vetted when nothing had checked
anything. PR #51 removed the vocabulary rather than implementing signing,
because Cerberus does not vet plugins (Decision 12).

Two origins replace six tiers. `installed` is a plugin installed from a
directory; its destructive operations need `--ack`, like a built-in's. `dev` is
a development install with `--dev`, and keeps all three old restrictions: a
devmode build, a source under the developer root, and every destructive
operation refused even with `--ack`. It is documented as a restriction, not a
lower trust level.

The JSON followed. `managed list` reports `origin` instead of `trust_tier`, plus
the new `entrypoint_sha256`. The install argument `trust: {…}` became
`options: {dev_mode}`. The legacy `trust` object is still read for `dev_mode`
alone, in the API and in `plugin-connectors.json`, so neither an older CLI's
`--dev` nor an old state file is silently reinterpreted. The next write drops
it. `TestLegacyPluginStateStillLoads` and `TestLegacyDevModeIsHonored` hold
that.

## Since P1-5

The fingerprint became change detection in fact. The accepted bundle digest is compared on every load (CERB-GAP-336, closed), and the review decided to keep the `dev` origin devmode-only (CERB-GAP-848). The `origin` still makes no claim about who built a plugin, and neither does the digest: it says only "this is the bundle you reviewed".

data.decision: Record an install origin, installed or dev, in place of the trust tiers; keep the host-computed entrypoint hash as change detection only.
alternatives_considered: Implement signature verification
Keep the tiers and rename the self-asserted ones
Drop any install classification
data.rationale: A tier that implies vetting which never happened is worse than none. The only real distinction the old model enforced was the dev restriction, and an origin carries exactly that without a trust claim. Signing is ruled out by Decision 12.

Decision 14 in the live-systems security target, taken at the P1 cut and landed in PR #60. It is stricter than the P2 baseline on purpose: until the policy engine exists, the gate is the only control.

The operations that newly needed `--ack` were DigitalOcean start, docker start and stop (`cerberus docker up` and `down`) and, in review, ssh get and get_dir. PR #63 added every resource mutation and pipeline run. None lost it.

**Since P2-4.** The policy baseline matches this gate rather than loosening it. Humans need `approve` for write, lifecycle, destructive and exec, which a TTY confirmation will meet in P3 (Decision 3). The one exception is Decision 11, human lifecycle on a local `env: dev` target, and it is built into the baseline (`builtin.local-dev-lifecycle`). Section 4's example was amended to say so.

records.body: Landed in PR #63. EnsureFresh never acknowledges on its own: it forwards the caller's options to the one mutation it chooses. A socket request with an empty body carries no acknowledgment and is refused with 409.

data.decision: Pass acknowledgment as WithAcknowledged(bool) on each Client mutation, rename DeployResourceOption to MutationOption, and serialize MutationOpts as every mutation's socket body.

Change every mutator to take an args struct

records.name: The audit log is monthly JSONL, hash-chained, fsynced per record, with a keyed args digest
records.summary: Audit records go to one append-only JSONL file per calendar month, each fsynced before the write returns, chained by hash across files with chain_start, file_start and chain_break records, and arguments are recorded as an HMAC under a per-install key rather than a plain hash.
records.confidence_label: internal/audit/sink.go, record.go and their tests read on the P1-4a branch

relationships.note: the audit log
the trail it provides

records.body:
Taken on the P1-4a branch, within Decision 15 (keep everything, rotate
monthly) and Decision 8 (an unwritable log fails every non-read).

- **fsync on every record.** The intent must be durable before the effect it
  announces. Audit volume is one pair per operation, so the cost is small.
- **One file per month, never rewritten.** Rotation happens at the month
  boundary of the record's UTC time. Nothing is deleted automatically, and
  `prune` is a later admin operation. Since P1-4b it exists: `cerberus audit prune
  --before <date>` removes only whole month files, never the newest, runs only
  from a terminal with a typed confirmation, and is recorded in the chain it
  shortens, so `audit.Verify` accepts the shorter chain only when a recorded
  prune removed the missing file.
- **One chain across files.** `chain_start` opens a directory, `file_start`
  opens each new month and names the previous file, and the first link of the
  new file chains to the last hash of the old one. A torn write is never
  repaired in place: the next write appends `chain_break` and resumes from the
  last complete record, so `audit.Verify` can tell a crash from an edit.
- **Keyed digest.** A plain SHA-256 of the arguments would let a short secret
  inside them, a password or a PIN, be brute-forced from the log. An
  HMAC-SHA256 under a random 32-byte key in `.digest_key` (0600) keeps equal
  arguments recognisable to someone holding the key and nothing more.
- **flock plus a mutex.** The daemon and an in-process CLI share the directory,
  so appends take an exclusive `flock` on `.lock` and re-read the tail when
  another writer has appended.

data.decision: Monthly append-only JSONL, fsync per record, a hash chain across files with chain_start, file_start and chain_break, a keyed HMAC args digest, and flock-serialised appends.
alternatives_considered: SQLite (main.db was never created, and a DB file is edited in place)
Batching fsync for throughput
A plain SHA-256 args digest
One file forever, or size-based rotation
data.rationale: The record has to survive a crash between intent and effect, be checkable for tampering and truncation, and never become a credential store. Append-only files with a hash chain and a keyed digest give all three with no new dependency.

records.name: go_standard builds cannot resolve `go` when issued through the daemon
records.summary: exec.Command resolves the program name against the parent process's PATH, not cmd.Env, so a go_standard build run inside the launchd-started daemon fails with "executable file not found in $PATH".
records.confidence_label: reproduced with a standalone Go program under the daemon's exact PATH; daemon PATH read from the live process

relationships.note: the artifact build path is unusable through the daemon for go_standard
deploy goes over the socket first

records.body:
`cerberus resource deploy` is socket-first: the CLI only falls back to in-process execution on a `DaemonUnreachableError`. With a daemon running, the build therefore executes inside the daemon process.

The daemon's environment on this machine is launchd's minimal PATH, read directly from the live process:

```
$ ps eww -o command= -p 8188 | tr ' ' '\n' | grep '^PATH='
PATH=/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin
```

`sessionEnv` → `ensurePath` does append `/opt/homebrew/bin`, `/usr/local/bin`, `/usr/local/go/bin` and `~/go/bin`, and `build_strategy.go` assigns that to `cmd.Env`. But `buildCommand` constructs the command with `exec.CommandContext(ctx, command[0], ...)`, and Go resolves a bare program name via `LookPath` against **the calling process's** PATH at construction time. Setting `cmd.Env` afterwards does not re-resolve it. Reproduced:

```
PATH=/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin  (parent)
cmd.Env carries a PATH including /usr/local/go/bin and ~/go/bin
exec.Command("go", "version") → cmd.Path="go"  cmd.Err=exec: "go": executable file not found in $PATH
exec.Command("make", "--version") → cmd.Path="/usr/bin/make"  ok
```

So `make_standard` survives (there is a `/usr/bin/make`) and `go_standard` does not. `legacy_command` depends on whether its `command[0]` happens to live in the minimal PATH. AGENTS.md already warns that the daemon's environment is not your shell's and that per-call resolution beats boot-time resolution; this is the same class of bug as the Docker connector caching a failed lookup, and it has not been fixed for the build path.

It is invisible today only because no resource on this machine declares a `build_strategy`, so no deploy has ever attempted a build here. The first `run_from: artifact` + `go_standard` resource anyone adds will hit it, and the failure will read as a broken build rather than a broken PATH. The fix is small: resolve the toolchain explicitly (the augmented PATH is already computed in `ensurePath` — use it for `LookPath` too, or set `cmd.Path` from an explicit search), and add a test that pins a minimal parent PATH.

## Practical failure mitigated by PR #34, root cause untouched

PR #34 (#34, commit f5bbf93) fixes CERB-GAP-637/542 by composing the daemon's own process PATH at install time from the installing user's environment. Once the daemon is reinstalled, its base `os.Getenv("PATH")` should include `go` directly, which sidesteps this gap's actual defect: `exec.CommandContext` in `internal/connector/local/build_strategy.go` still resolves `command[0]` against the calling process's PATH rather than the augmented PATH `ensurePath` puts in `cmd.Env`. That code path was not touched by #34, so the defect resurfaces on any daemon whose base PATH lacks `go` for a reason the installer fix doesn't cover. `unlocks_when` (resolving `command[0]` against the augmented PATH, with a regression test under a minimal parent PATH) is not met.

data.unlocks_when: buildCommand resolves command[0] against the same augmented PATH it puts in cmd.Env, with a regression test that runs under a minimal parent PATH
data.effort: small — one function plus a test; the augmented PATH already exists

records.name: Generated launchd plists carry no PATH
records.summary: launchdEnvironment emits only env_file and env entries, so an os_service resource inherits launchd's minimal PATH and any tool it shells out to must be an absolute path.
records.confidence_label: read from launchdEnvironment and the plist template; no os_service resource exists here to observe it failing

relationships.note: the same minimal-PATH root cause, one level out

records.body:
`launchdEnvironment(spec)` builds the plist's `EnvironmentVariables` from `env_file:` and `env:` only, and the template omits the key entirely when that map is empty. A supervised service therefore starts with launchd's `/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`.

The asymmetry is the problem, not the value. `dev_session` children get `ensurePath` — homebrew, `/usr/local/bin`, `/usr/local/go/bin`, `~/go/bin` — so a resource that works in `dev_session` can break when it is promoted to `os_service`, and the failure surfaces as a service that starts and immediately exits with the real cause buried in `stderr.log`. Since ADR 0002's stated migration direction is "durable background services → mode: os_service", that promotion is the expected path, which makes this a trap on the happy path rather than an edge case.

Not must-have, because a resource can set `env: {PATH: ...}` today and the launchd diagnosis machinery does surface the exit code. But it is a footgun with a two-line fix (a default PATH entry that `env:` can override) and it is worth pairing with a `resource doctor` check that warns when an os_service resource's command is a bare name rather than an absolute path.

data.unlocks_when: launchdEnvironment seeds a default PATH (overridable by env:) and doctor warns on a bare-name command under os_service

records.name: auto_start has no effect on a v2 resource
records.summary: auto_start is parsed, round-tripped and hashed but never acted on in the resource lane; the only code that honours it is the frozen v1 ServiceRegistry, which the daemon never constructs.
records.confidence_label: traced every reference to AutoStart in non-test code; no live resource sets auto_start: true, so the inertness cannot be observed here either way

relationships.note: auto_restart is the de facto enrolment switch
the honouring code is in the lane ADR 0002 froze

records.body:
Every non-test reference to `AutoStart` is plumbing. `spec.go` parses it, `ToResourceConfig` re-emits it, `mapper.go` maps it to and from the legacy `ServiceDef`, and `dev_session.go` folds it into the config hash. The only code that *starts* something because of it is `internal/service/registry.go`'s `applyDiffLocked`, which reads `newCfg.Services` — the frozen v1 `services:` lane — and whose `ServiceRegistry` the daemon never constructs. `cmd_daemon.go` starts exactly two background workers: `cerbapi.NewResourceMonitor` and the drift cache.

What actually happens instead: the resource monitor's boot-time `checkAllResources` pass restarts any *down* resource that set `auto_restart: true`. So `auto_restart` doubles as the start-at-boot switch, and the two flags are effectively one. A resource with `auto_start: true, auto_restart: false` is never started by anything; a resource with `auto_start: false, auto_restart: true` is started at boot in spite of its own declaration.

This is `must-have` because it is silently inert config. AGENTS.md itself reasons about the tunnel resources being "deliberately on/off with `auto_start` and `auto_restart` both false" — which reaches the right outcome for the wrong reason, since only the second flag was load-bearing. Anyone who sets `auto_start: false, auto_restart: true` expecting "restart if it dies, but do not start it for me" gets the opposite. The cheapest honest fix is to make the monitor distinguish first-pass start (gated on `auto_start`) from subsequent restart (gated on `auto_restart`); the cheapest safe fix is to reject or warn on `auto_start` in registry validation so the field stops lying.

data.unlocks_when: the monitor's first pass gates on auto_start and later passes on auto_restart, or validation surfaces auto_start as unsupported in the v2 lane
data.effort: small for the warning, medium for honest semantics plus tests

records.name: Declared health probes are never executed by the supervision lane
records.summary: health: and health_check: are parsed and stored but only the pipeline resolver ever reads them; supervision status, the health DTO and auto-restart all run on process liveness alone.
records.confidence_label: traced all non-test readers of spec.Health / spec.HealthCheck, and confirmed live that healthy:true came back without the declared URL being fetched

relationships.note: healthy means PID-alive, not serving
restart is triggered by PID absence only
the local connector never emits healthy or unhealthy

records.body:
Six of the nine local process resources on this machine declare a `health:` URL — `jaeger` points at the OTel collector's health_check extension, `tesseract-api` at `/v1/health/readiness`, `torque-api` at a real API read chosen specifically because unmatched paths render the SPA. The config file's comments show real care went into picking endpoints that cannot false-positive.

None of them is ever fetched by the supervision lane. The only non-test readers of `spec.Health` / `spec.HealthCheck` outside serialization are `internal/pipeline/resolve.go`, for pipeline wait steps. `domain.StateHealthy` and `StateUnhealthy` exist but are produced only by the pipeline executor and the forge connector — the local connector never returns either. `resourceStateHealthy` accepts `running` or `healthy`, and in practice only ever sees `running`.

Verified live: `cerberus_health(resource_id="tesseract-api")` returned `{"healthy": true, "status": "running"}` with no request against `127.0.0.1:8089/v1/health/readiness`.

The consequences compound. A process that is alive but wedged reports healthy and is never restarted, because `resourceStateDown` only covers `stopped`, `failed` and `unknown`. `resource doctor` has no health check to run. `restart_delay`, `max_restart_attempts` and `restart_cooldown` are tuned against a signal that only fires on process death. And `docs/plans/infra-admin-control-plane.md` describes the supervision lane as having "health probes" as one of its four defining features, which overstates what is implemented.

`must-have`, and nothing blocks it: the config surface, the parsing, the state vocabulary and a per-resource probe timeout all already exist. What is missing is a prober — HTTP GET on `health_check.url` (or `health`) and exec on `health_check.command`, honouring `interval` and `timeout` — wired into `Health`, into `GetResourceRuntime`, and into `resourceStateDown` so a persistently unhealthy resource is restartable.

data.unlocks_when: a probe runs health_check.url / health_check.command and its result feeds Health, status and the monitor's down decision
data.effort: medium — the probe itself is small; deciding how an unhealthy-but-alive resource should be treated by auto_restart is the real design work

records.name: resource doctor has no dev_session checks
records.summary: Every substantial doctor check is gated on mode == os_service, so on this machine doctor reports "all checks passed" from a single runtime_status line.
records.confidence_label: observed live on tesseract-api: one check, and the summary still said all checks passed

relationships.note: a health probe would be the most valuable dev_session check

records.body:
`GetResourceDoctor` adds dependency warnings, config-key warnings, a runtime-status line and an operator-stop note unconditionally; everything else — install root, plist, secret-reference shim, log paths, artifact install, artifact source, workspace runtime, launchd loaded/throttled/exit/reason/diagnosis, daemon lock origin — sits inside `if inspect.Mode == os_service`.

Since all nine process resources here are `dev_session`, `doctor` is a one-line report:

```
$ cerberus resource doctor tesseract-api
Summary:     all checks passed
Checks:
  [PASS] runtime_status: runtime state is running
```

The CLI positions this verb as "use when apply or deploy fails", which is exactly when a dev_session operator gets the least from it. The checks that would earn the name are all cheap and all already computable: does `command[0]` exist and is it executable; is `dir` a real directory; does `env_file` exist; is the declared `port` reachable and is the listener the owned PID; does the log file exist and was it written since the recorded start; is there PID/meta drift; and — once a prober exists — does the health endpoint answer.

`nice-to-have` rather than must-have because nothing is broken and the information is obtainable from `inspect` and `logs`. But it is the single highest-leverage small improvement in this area, because it is the verb operators are told to reach for and it currently reassures without checking.

data.unlocks_when: doctor grows a dev_session branch covering command/dir/env_file existence, port-vs-owned-PID agreement and log freshness

records.name: apply and sync install from command[0] without the build-output contract
records.summary: ValidateDeployOutput closes the ambiguous build-to-artifact join on deploy only; apply and sync reach resolveArtifactSource directly and will install command[0] when the build strategy declares no output.
records.confidence_label: traced all callers of resolveArtifactSource and ValidateDeployOutput; not reproducible here, since no resource uses artifact mode

relationships.note: the decision this gap is the unfinished half of
apply reaches the installer via writePlist
sync reaches the installer directly

records.body:
AGENTS.md states the risk plainly: `resolveArtifactSource` installs the build strategy's declared `output`, falling back to `command[0]` without one, so a strategy missing an `output` rule can install a binary the build never wrote. The question is whether that is still a gap. It is — but a narrower and more interesting one than the framing suggests.

On `deploy` it is closed twice over. `ValidateDeployOutput` refuses up front: an artifact resource with a build strategy and no `rules.output` gets `artifact deployment requires build_strategy.rules.output naming the binary the build produces; command[0] is not a build-output contract`. And after a successful build, deploy stats the resolved source and fails with a message naming the exact fix if nothing is there. `go_standard` cannot even build without an `output`.

On `apply` and `sync` it is open. `SyncResource` calls `SyncArtifactInstall` → `installer.Sync` → `resolveArtifactSource` with no validation. `ApplyResource` reaches the same installer through `launchdBackend.writePlist`, which syncs before it renders the plist. So a `make_standard` or `legacy_command` resource in artifact mode with no `output` rule is refused by `deploy` and silently served by `apply` and `sync` — which install `command[0]`, hash it, write it into the manifest as the source of truth, and thereafter report the artifact as *current*. The staleness machinery then has nothing to complain about, because it is comparing the installed copy against the wrong source.

That inversion is what makes it must-have. A guard that only fires on the verb an operator is told to prefer, while the two verbs the advice system itself recommends (`apply` and `sync` are what `RecommendedStatusAction` returns) bypass it, is worse than no guard: it teaches the operator that the contract is enforced. The fix is to move `ValidateDeployOutput` down into `artifactInstaller.Sync` — or call it from `SyncResource` and `ApplyResource` too — so the refusal is a property of artifact installation rather than of one verb. A resource with `run_from: artifact` and no build strategy at all must keep working, since installing a pre-built `command[0]` is the intended use there.

data.unlocks_when: the output contract is enforced wherever an artifact is installed, not only on deploy, while still allowing artifact mode with no build strategy
data.effort: small — move or duplicate one validation call, plus tests for apply and sync

records.name: The port: 0 registry guard does not cover the live config
records.summary: ValidateProjectConfig's port:0 rejection runs only on registered project configs; the global ~/.cerberus/config.yaml is loaded with no validation, and on this machine it defines every resource.
records.confidence_label: traced resolveIndex's two-step load; confirmed live that cerberus registry health reports no project configs registered

relationships.note: a false-positive running state is a supervision-lane failure
the validation itself belongs to the registry area

records.body:
AGENTS.md says two guards hold "never set `port: 0`" and neither should be removed. Both exist and both pass. `findPIDByPort` in `internal/connector/local/dev_session.go` returns 0 immediately for `port <= 0`, so `lsof -ti :0` is never run and cannot return an arbitrary system PID to be misread as "running". `TestValidateProjectConfigPortZeroIsError` passes, and `internal/registry/schema.go:210` adds a `SeverityError` issue for a resource whose `port` decodes to 0.

The finding is about the second guard's reach. `resolveIndex` assembles the effective config in two steps: step 1 loads the global `~/.cerberus/config.yaml` with `config.LoadUnified` and no validation at all, and step 2 loads each *registered project config*, runs `ValidateProjectConfig`, and skips the whole file on an error. So the port:0 rejection protects `<app>.cerberus.yaml` descriptors and not the registry root.

On this machine that means it protects nothing. `cerberus registry health` reports `No project configs registered.`, and `~/.cerberus/config.yaml` defines all ten resources directly. A `port: 0` typed into the live config today would be loaded without complaint, and only `findPIDByPort`'s guard would stand between it and the false-positive the rule exists to prevent. One of the two guards is load-bearing here; the other is watching a door nobody uses.

`must-have`, and nothing blocks it — the validator exists and the resource shape is the same either side of the split. Either run the resource-level invariants over the global config's resources during step 1, or surface them as resolve warnings the way `PortConflicts` already is at the end of `resolveIndex`.

data.unlocks_when: resource-level validation runs over the global config.yaml as well as over registered project configs
data.effort: small — reuse the existing resource validation over the step-1 resources and report as errors or resolve warnings

No real `launchctl bootstrap` has been driven by this code on this machine, and no real build has been joined to a real install.

The evidence is in the output of `cerberus resource list`: nine local process resources, all `dev_session` / `workspace`, ARTIFACT column empty on every row, and `grep build_strategy ~/.cerberus/config.yaml` matches only comments. So `mode: os_service`, `run_from: artifact`, `install-manifest.json`, `activated_hash`, `artifact_stale`, `RecommendedStatusAction`, `waitRunning`, the bootstrap-conflict recovery, `make install` probing, the build lock and the build log have all never run for real here.

`cerberus --help` states: "The Cerberus daemon itself now also fits this model as the v2 local process resource `cerberus-daemon-service` on macOS launchd." `cerberus resource list` does not contain `cerberus-daemon-service`, and the running daemon (pid 8188, `~/go/bin/cerberus daemon --foreground`) comes from a hand-written `~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.fragments-engine.cerberus.plist` with no `EnvironmentVariables` — a plist Cerberus did not generate and does not manage.

AGENTS.md already records the ground truth ("the daemon itself is likewise not Cerberus-managed on this machine"), so this is drift between the shipped help text and reality rather than a hidden surprise. `nice-to-have`: fix the help text to say the daemon *can* be managed this way, or register the daemon resource and take the self-upgrade procedure for a real walk. The second would also resolve CERB-GAP-148 for the os_service path.

records.name: `--dry-run` silently executes when no preview case exists
records.summary: A dry-run request for an operation with no preview case falls through and runs the real operation, and for a non-destructive operation nothing stops it.
records.confidence_label: Execute and dryRunPreview re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54); TestDryRunNeverExecutes sweeps every declared operation

relationships.note: The fallthrough is in this service's Execute
cerberus_droplet_start is the live instance
WP-1 would be the natural place to fix it

records.body:
`Execute` handles dry-run like this:

    if args.DryRun {
        if preview, ok, err := s.dryRunPreview(args); ok || err != nil { ... return }
    }

When `dryRunPreview` has no case, `ok` is false, `err` is nil, and execution
continues into the real operation. `docs/plans/connector-work-packages.md`
records half of this as a known trap — "skipping the `dryRunPreview` case makes
`--dry-run` demand `--ack`" — which is true for a *destructive* operation,
because it falls through onto the acknowledgment gate and refuses. Annoying, but
safe.

The other half is not recorded and is not safe. A non-destructive operation has
no gate to land on, so `dry_run: true` is accepted, ignored, and the operation
runs for real.

There is a live instance. `cerberus_droplet_start` advertises a `dry_run`
parameter described as "Preview only" — it shares an MCP lifecycle helper with
`stop` and `destroy`, both of which do have preview cases. DigitalOcean `start`
has `SupportsDry: false` and no case in the switch. So
`cerberus_droplet_start {droplet_id, dry_run: true}` boots the droplet while
the tool schema says it will preview. The CLI is not exposed to this: `cerberus
server start` has no `--dry-run` flag, and `cerberus ssh` explicitly passes
`DryRun: destructive && sshDryRun` so a non-destructive ssh verb can never
reach the fallthrough. Both of those are per-callsite guards against a hazard
the service does not guard against centrally.

No test asserts that a dry-run request for an unsupported operation does not
execute. That test is most of the fix; the rest is one refusal in `Execute`.

Blocked on nobody — this is a small, local change plus a test.

## Shipped in PR #49

A dry run now either returns a preview or is refused with a new error code,
`preview_unsupported` ("nothing was executed"). The refusal comes before
credential resolution and before the acknowledgment gate, so a dry run never
reaches a built-in connector's real dispatch. A loaded managed plugin is the one
exception, and only for an operation whose manifest declares `supports_dry`:
`pluginhost.Manager.ExecuteOperation` refuses the rest with the same code
without calling the plugin (CERB-DEC-814).

`TestDryRunNeverExecutes` runs every operation in `Definitions()` with `dry_run`
and `ack` both set, against factories that only count, and asserts zero
resolves. `TestDryRunNeverExecutesAgainstFakes` repeats the sweep over the real
docker, DigitalOcean and Forge connectors on recording fakes, reads included.
`cerberus_droplet_start {dry_run: true}` now returns `preview_unsupported`
instead of booting the droplet.

`unlocks_when` is met for the half that mattered: a dry run for an operation
with no preview is refused, not ignored. The MCP tool still advertises a
`dry_run` parameter on `start` with nothing behind it, which is now a refusal
rather than a hazard.

data.unlocks_when: A dry_run request for an operation whose SupportsDry is false is refused rather than ignored, and every advertised dry_run parameter has a preview behind it.

records.body:
Across all nine connectors there are 14 destructive operations and 13
dry-runnable ones. The one destructive operation with no dry-run is `docker
destroy`.

`AGENTS.md` says destructive connector operations "most support `--dry-run`. Use
the preview first." That is accurate as a generalisation and has exactly one
exception, and the exception is on the connector whose targets can be remote —
where `Target.Describe()` exists precisely because the Docker CLI will not tell
you which host you are talking to. A preview naming the resolved target before
removing a stack is worth more here than on any other connector, not less.

Since PR #49 a dry run of `destroy` no longer executes. It returns
`preview_unsupported`, so the missing preview is a missing feature rather than a
hazard. Before that fix, `docker destroy --dry-run --ack` destroyed.

It stays `must-have`. `destroy` is reachable through the generic connector route
on the socket and from the web console's Connectors page, with `--ack`, and P0
carries "docker `destroy` has no dedicated verb, preview or MCP tool" into P1.
The preview belongs in the same change as the verb (CERB-GAP-272).
