relationships.note: Docker is the connector
Same operation, missing preview
why down maps to stop

records.body:
`cerberus connectors describe docker` lists five operations, of which
`destroy` is the only destructive one. Nothing invokes it.

`cerberus docker down <id>` sends `Operation: "stop"`. `cerberus_docker_down`
sends `Operation: "stop"`. The CLI has `ps`, `logs`, `up` and `down` and no
fifth command. There is no `cerberus_docker_rm`. The only way to reach `destroy`
is a hand-built call on the daemon socket.

This is a discovery lie rather than a missing feature: an agent reading
`connectors describe docker` is told the capability exists and given no tool
that reaches it, and the naming actively misleads — "down" reads like removal
and means stop.

Two acceptable resolutions, and picking one matters more than which. Expose it,
with the preview from the companion gap. Or withdraw it from the `Definition`
so discovery stops advertising a capability with no caller. What should not
persist is the current state, where `describe` and the surfaces disagree.

Blocked on nobody.

## Since P0

The naming half is settled. PR #49 made `stop` run `docker compose stop` for a
stack, so `cerberus docker down` and `cerberus_docker_down` stop and remove
nothing. The CLI help, the MCP description and the README say so, and name
`destroy` as the removal (CERB-DEC-812). "Down reads like removal" is now a
documented mismatch with Compose's own verb rather than a hidden one.

The reachability half is not. `destroy` still has no CLI verb and no MCP tool.
Besides a socket call, it can be reached from the web console's Connectors page,
which since PR #54 offers a resource picker for docker. Either way, a call names
a declared resource or a local container, because PR #52 refuses ad-hoc targets
on those surfaces. PR #49 deferred option C, `cerberus docker destroy <id>
--ack` plus `cerberus_docker_destroy`, to P1.

## Scheduled

The P1 cut in `docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md` (2026-09-25) schedules this: P1-3 adds `cerberus docker destroy <id> --ack` and a `cerberus_docker_destroy` tool, with hints derived from the contract.

**Closed on the P1-3 branch.** `cerberus docker destroy <id> --ack` (with the same `-f`, `--host` and `--context` as `up`/`down`, which force the call in-process) and the MCP tool `cerberus_docker_destroy` (`container_name` or `resource_id`, plus `acknowledged`) invoke `destroy`. Its hints come from the contract: destructive, not read-only, open-world. It still has no preview (CERB-GAP-271).

data.unlocks_when: Either a surface exposes destroy with a preview, or the operation is withdrawn from the definition so discovery stops advertising it.

records.name: Redaction eats the first word of every `credential_missing` error
records.summary: The admin lane's own error code parses as a credential assignment, so `redact.Text` replaces the first token of the cause with [REDACTED].
records.confidence_label: Two independent audits found this from different surfaces; reproduced directly against redact.Text during reconciliation

relationships.note: a defect in the redaction capability this record now hangs off
The formatting is in ExternalConnectorError.Error
Found via the live github failure
Same rule, the enforcement side of it
missing from this capability

records.body:
`ExternalConnectorError.Error()` builds `"<connector> <op>: <code>: <cause>"`
and then runs `redact.Text` over the whole string. When the code is
`credential_missing`, the redactor's credential-assignment rule —
`[a-z0-9_.-]*(?:credentials?)[a-z0-9_.-]*\s*:\s*(value)` — matches
`credential_missing:` as the label and the next token as the value.

Verified live on this machine:

    $ cerberus github status hollis-labs/cerberus
    Error: daemon: github status: credential_missing: [REDACTED] connector:
    no API token and gh CLI not found — set CERBERUS_GITHUB_TOKEN or install gh

The word eaten is `github`. Isolating the redactor against the real message
strings confirms it for every credentialed connector: `forge:`,
`digitalocean:`, `namecheap:`, `cloudflare` and the plugin lane's
missing-secrets message all lose their first token the same way. The same
strings pass through untouched without the code prefix, and the other error
codes — `connector_unavailable`, `acknowledgment_required` — do not trigger it.

This is the fifth instance of a failure mode `AGENTS.md` documents four of, and
it breaks the rule written directly above them: do not run redaction over a
value that is a name by construction. An error *code* is a name by
construction, and so is a connector id. It is also the error an operator sees
most often, because it is what every connector returns on a machine where the
credential has not been set up yet — which is to say, on a new machine, during
onboarding, which is exactly when a confusing diagnostic costs most.

Severity is bounded: the recovery instruction survives, so the operator is
still told what to do. What they lose is which connector said it, in a message
whose whole job is to identify that. Ranked `must-have` because the fix is
small, the mechanism is fully understood, and leaving it in place after finding
it would be the fifth regression becoming the permanent state.

Blocked on nobody.

## Also confirmed on the socket and HTTP surfaces

Found independently by the plugin-lane audit, which reached the same defect from
the other end. `POST /connectors/contextforge/operations/list_gateways` over
`~/.cerberus/cerberus.sock` returns

    credential_missing: [REDACTED] gateways at http://127.0.0.1:14444: unauthorized (401)

— the eaten word is `list`. `POST /connectors/digitalocean/operations/list_droplets`
returns `credential_missing: [REDACTED] no API token`, eating `no`. So this is not
a GitHub or a plugin problem: it is every `credential_missing` error on every
surface that formats the code into the message. The CLI `connectors plugin managed
exec` path escapes only because it returns the unclassified error instead.

Reproduced directly against the redactor during reconciliation:

    IN : credential_missing: reload it with cerberus connectors plugin managed load contextforge
    OUT: credential_missing: [REDACTED] it with cerberus connectors plugin managed load contextforge

The eaten word there is `reload` — the verb of the recovery instruction. A control
string of ordinary prose containing the same words is left untouched, which
confirms the trigger is the `credential_missing:` prefix and not the sentence.

## Shipped in PR #34

`fix/open-findings` (#34, commit f5bbf93) adds an `errorCodes` allow-list and `redactPairs` to `internal/redact/redact.go`: the `assignment` rule now recognizes the whole `ExternalConnectorErrorCode` vocabulary as a name by construction and hands the text behind it back to the same rule, so a real assignment riding behind the code (`credential_missing: API_KEY=...`) still redacts. Covered by `TestTextKeepsRecoveryGuidanceReadable` and `TestRecoveryGuidanceExemptionsStillRedact` in `redact_test.go`. `unlocks_when` is met.

data.unlocks_when: The error code stops being fed to the redactor as a label, or `credential_missing` joins the names-only allow-list, with a test per connector asserting the cause survives.

records.name: The redaction-survival rule is remembered, not enforced
records.summary: Two of fifteen recovery instructions in the connector lane have a test asserting they survive `redact.Text`; the redactor has already regressed four times.
records.confidence_label: gate_test.go and the P0 refusal tests re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54)

relationships.note: a defect in the redaction capability this record now hangs off
The lane whose error paths all run through redact.Text
The live instance this gap failed to catch
the failure this rule exists to prevent

records.body:
`AGENTS.md` states the rule: "if an error message carries a recovery
instruction, add a test that it survives `redact.Text` intact." Across the whole
repository there are exactly three `redact.Text` assertions outside the
redactor's own package:
`TestSocketPermissionRecoverySurvivesRedaction` in
`internal/connector/docker/target_test.go`, one in
`internal/pluginhost/secrets_test.go`, and the target-describe assertion beside
the first. The redactor's own tests add the Bearer-guidance and
`missing_secrets` cases — the regressions that already happened.

Running the redactor over the connector lane's actual recovery strings, fifteen
of them, all fifteen survive intact today: the `CERBERUS_*_TOKEN` guidance for
five connectors, the `ErrDockerNotFound` fallback list and override, the
known_hosts three-way recovery, the Namecheap per-record refusal with its MCP
recovery, the plugin load/uninstall recovery, and the acknowledgment message.
Thirteen of those fifteen have no test.

So the current state is: correct, and unguarded. That is the state the redactor
was in before each of the four regressions — `Bearer JWT` becoming `Bearer
[REDACTED]`, `set CERBERUS_..._TOKEN` swallowed as an assignment, `missing_secrets`
returning `["[REDACTED]"]`. Each of those was found by an operator reading a
useless error, not by a test. The fifth was found by this audit the same way.

The fix is not thirteen tests in thirteen packages. It is one table-driven test
over the lane's recovery strings, in a place a new connector's author will find,
plus the discipline of adding a row. The value is that the next loosening or
tightening of the redactor fails loudly instead of quietly eating an
instruction, and "a safety net that eats the instruction is worse than no
instruction" stops being a comment and becomes a gate.

Blocked on nobody.

## The daemon self-upgrade message is the most consequential untested case

The operational-reality audit reached this gap independently and named the
message that matters most: `internal/cerbapi/daemon_self_guard.go:54` is the
*only written form* of the daemon self-upgrade procedure — build to a temp path,
`mv` it over the artifact, then `launchctl kickstart -k`. `daemon_self_guard_test.go`
asserts the message contains "refusing to mutate serving Cerberus" and
"kickstart", but never runs it through `redact.Text`.

That audit rated this `nice-to-have`. On reconciliation that priority does not
hold: the redactor has now regressed twice more (CERB-GAP-273, CERB-GAP-447)
while this rule was enforced only by memory, and one of those regressions eats
the verb of a recovery instruction. A convention that has failed six times is a
`must-have` test, which is the priority kept here.

## Coverage improved by PR #34, systemic gap remains

`fix/open-findings` (#34, commit f5bbf93) adds `TestTextKeepsRecoveryGuidanceReadable` and `TestRecoveryGuidanceExemptionsStillRedact` to `redact_test.go`, covering the two new regressions (CERB-GAP-273, CERB-GAP-447) this pass fixed. That raises coverage from 2 of 15 connector-lane recovery instructions to roughly 4, still against string literals in the redactor's own package rather than against `ExternalConnectorError.Error()`'s composed output or a live plugin manifest field. This record's own bar — 'a table test over string literals in the source is explicitly not sufficient' — is not yet met, and the daemon self-upgrade message this record calls out as the most consequential untested case is still untested.

## P0 moved coverage toward composed output

PR #49's `TestGateRefusalsSurviveRedaction` runs every
`ExternalConnectorErrorCode`, followed by a recovery sentence, through
`redact.Text`. That is the error as composed, which is closer to this record's
bar than a table of literals. `preview_unsupported` joined the redactor's
error-code vocabulary before it could lose the word after it. P0 added four
families of refusal (listen, plugin directory, SSH fields, docker targets), each
with a test that it survives `redact.Text`, and needed no redaction rule change.
The P0 wrap-up names that as the default for every new error.

It is still a convention rather than a gate. Nothing fails when a new error
arrives without a test, and the daemon self-upgrade message is still not run
through `redact.Text`.

data.unlocks_when: Every error carrying a recovery instruction has a redaction-survival assertion over the text as composed and emitted — ExternalConnectorError.Error() output, and connector and operation descriptions as they arrive from a plugin manifest. A table test over string literals in the source is explicitly not sufficient.

records.name: No privilege elevation for `ssh exec`
records.summary: Every remote command runs as the operator's own account, so the connector covers inspection but not the deploys it was built toward.
records.confidence_label: Briefed as WP-8; confirmed by reading the ssh connector's operation set and config schema

relationships.note: The connector that needs it
Together these two complete the tools/ port
no PTY is the transport-level root cause; WP-8 cannot be closed without it

records.body:
`ssh exec` runs as the operator's own account. Every real deploy in
`~/Projects/tools` needs root for at least one step — `docker load`,
`systemctl`, writing under `/opt/agents` — and `lib/common.sh` carries a
dedicated `rsudo` for it. Without elevation the connector covers inspection and
not deployment, which is the thing the admin lane exists to grow into.

The design is already decided, with two constraints paid for in advance by the
shell scripts this would replace:

- **sudo on muctlvaig requires a tty.** `rsudo` uses `ssh -t` for exactly this;
  without it sudo refuses with "sorry, you must have a tty to run sudo". The Go
  client must call `session.RequestPty` when elevating.
- **Arguments must be quoted individually.** `rsudo`'s own comment records the
  bug: `"sudo $*"` joined arguments with spaces and threw the quoting away, so a
  display name of `"GPT-5.6 Terra"` arrived as two arguments, shifted everything
  after it, and SQL failed with `no such column: Terra`. Quote per argument.

And three that are policy rather than mechanics. Elevation is opt-in per
operation as a separate `elevate` boolean, never a flag that silently upgrades
an existing call. An elevated `exec` is already destructive and ack-gated; the
dry-run preview must say the command runs as root, because the preview is what
an operator reads before acknowledging. And no password prompting, ever — a
Cerberus-started ssh has no interactive terminal, so a sudo password prompt
hangs until timeout with no indication why. Passwordless sudo or a fast, clear
failure; that is an environment fact to report, not to work around.

`must-have` because it is the difference between a read tool and an admin tool,
and because the design work is done. Blocked on nobody; the acceptance test is
an elevated command reporting its own `id` as root, and an argument containing a
space arriving as one argument.

data.unlocks_when: An opt-in `elevate` flag requests a PTY, quotes each argument individually, fails fast when sudo wants a password, and says in the dry-run preview that the command runs as root.

records.name: No recursive directory transfer
records.summary: `ssh put` and `get` move one file, so moving a config directory or an agent definition tree has no supported path.
records.confidence_label: ssh definitions, CLI and MCP tools read on main; commit 8589c58 read

relationships.note: The connector that needs it
WP-8 comes first in the sequencing
The transport decision behind it
put_dir
get_dir

records.body:
`put`/`get` move a single file. A deploy moves a tree — which is precisely why
the shell-script toolkit this replaces builds a tarball before shipping anything.

The hard part is not the recursion, it is that there is no library to lean on,
and the survey is the finding rather than a lookup failure. `pkg/sftp`'s `Walk`
is the ecosystem's standard answer and recursion is still yours to write.
`bramvdbogaerde/go-scp` is tagged but speaks SCP, which OpenSSH has deprecated
and now implements over SFTP anyway. `povsister/scp` supports recursion and has
no tagged release. `melbahja/goph` wraps what is already here. So the sync logic
is ours either way — which is also what makes it a candidate to extract as an
OSS library once it has earned its keep.

The properties that make it safe to point at a real host are the ones a
general-purpose "copy a directory" helper tends not to have: preserve mode, so
an uploaded script stays executable; refuse to follow symlinks out of the tree,
so a link to `/etc/shadow` inside a synced directory cannot exfiltrate it;
temp-and-rename per file, matching `put`, so an interrupted sync never leaves a
half-written file in place of a good one; and honour cancellation *between*
files as well as within one, so a transfer over a dead VPN stops promptly.

`put_dir` is destructive and dry-runnable, and the preview should report file
count and total bytes — that is what an operator needs in order to decide.

Stated honestly, the tradeoff: SFTP has no delta transfer and no compression. It
copies every byte every time. Fine for compose files, env files, config
directories and agent definitions; wrong for a 600MB image, which is why
`tools/` tars and ships a single blob for that case. If a large tree shows up,
add a tar-over-exec path as a second strategy rather than replacing this one.

`must-have`, `large`, blocked on nobody but sequenced after elevation.

## Shipped in commit 8589c58 (WP-9)

`ssh put_dir` and `ssh get_dir` landed on 2026-09-17, after this record was
written, as `cerberus ssh put-dir|get-dir` and the MCP tools
`cerberus_ssh_put_dir` and `cerberus_ssh_get_dir`. The walk is
`hollis-labs/go-sftpsync`, released standalone because, as recorded above, the
ecosystem had no library for it. Cerberus resolves the target, calls the library
and maps its result, so mode preservation, the symlink-escape refusal,
temp-and-rename per file and between-files cancellation live in one place.
`put_dir` is destructive and dry-runnable, and its preview reports file count
and total bytes. `get_dir` is not destructive, and since PR #49 its MCP tool is
hinted destructive because it overwrites a local directory. Recorded as tools
CERB-TOOL-268 and CERB-TOOL-269. `unlocks_when` is met. Found closed during the
P0 catalog pass; the local-path policy both verbs lack is CERB-GAP-850.

data.unlocks_when: put_dir and get_dir over pkg/sftp, preserving mode, refusing symlink escapes, temp-and-rename per file, honouring cancellation between files.

records.name: Every dry-run preview lives in one switch in the service
records.summary: 13 previews across five connectors sit in a single switch in external_connector_service.go, which is the largest merge-conflict surface in the repo.
records.confidence_label: WP-1, explicitly skipped rather than done; confirmed by reading the switch and counting its cases

relationships.note: The switch is in this service
The deferral decision
The structure was why the fallthrough was easy to miss; the fallthrough itself closed in PR #49

records.body:
A connector declaring `SupportsDry: true` does not implement a preview. It is
asserting that `dryRunPreview` in `external_connector_service.go` has a case for
it. All 13 previews in the product — three Cloudflare, two Namecheap, two Forge,
three DigitalOcean, three SSH — live in that one switch.

Two costs, one real and one latent. The real one is what WP-1 names: it is the
largest merge-conflict surface in the repo and the reason adding a connector
feels invasive. Adding a verb means editing inside a shared switch rather than
adding a file, and two sessions adding two connectors collide.

The latent one is that the declaration and the implementation are in different
files with nothing tying them together. Today they agree — checked
operation-by-operation against `cerberus connectors describe` for all nine
connectors, 13 declared and 13 implemented. That agreement is a fact about care,
not about structure, and the failure mode when it lapses is the
silently-ignored dry-run recorded as a separate gap.

WP-1 is a pure refactor with the constraint stated sharply: behaviour must not
change, every existing preview must produce byte-identical output, do not
improve a summary string or reorder a target map while moving it. Its acceptance
is a captured `--dry-run` JSON before and after.

`nice-to-have` and honestly so — it buys maintainability, not capability. It was
skipped because it was never blocking, and it is still open. Worth doing next
time someone is about to add a connector, not before.

## Since PR #49

The latent cost is smaller now. `TestDryRunNeverExecutes` requires every operation declaring `supports_dry` to have a preview and every other one to get `preview_unsupported`, so a declaration and a case that disagree fail a test instead of silently executing. There are 14 previews now, after `put_dir` joined them. The merge-conflict cost is unchanged, and so is the priority.

data.unlocks_when: dryRunPreview becomes a dispatch table on connector id, with each connector's previews in internal/cerbapi/dryrun_<x>.go beside its execute<X>.

records.name: No surface tells a caller which operations need `--ack`
records.summary: `requires_ack` exists in the connector manifest and is dropped converting to the public Definition, so discovery only exposes `destructive`.
records.confidence_label: requireAcknowledgment and OperationAllowed re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54)

relationships.note: The lossy round trip is here
Plugins can set the two flags independently
the one refusal describe does not show

records.body:
`ManifestOperation` has three policy fields: `Destructive`, `SupportsDry` and
`RequiresAck`. `Operation` — the type `connectors describe` serialises — has
only the first two. `ManifestFromDefinition` derives `RequiresAck:
op.Destructive`; `DefinitionFromManifest` drops it.

So `cerberus connectors describe <id>` never emits `requires_ack`, for any of
the nine connectors. A caller who wants to know whether an operation will be
refused without acknowledgment has to infer it from `destructive`.

For built-in connectors that inference is sound, because the manifest derives
one from the other and `requireAcknowledgment` reads `Destructive` directly. For
a plugin it is not guaranteed: the plugin's `plugin.yaml` sets `destructive` and
`requires_ack` independently and `pluginhost.OperationAllowed` requires both to
be true before demanding acknowledgment.

The caller most affected is an agent, which is the caller the admin lane is
aimed at. An agent planning a sequence of operations has no way to read which
ones need an acknowledgment argument, so it either passes one everywhere —
which empties the gate — or discovers the requirement by failing.

`nice-to-have` rather than `must-have` because the inference is currently
correct for everything shipped. It becomes `must-have` the first time a plugin
ships with the two flags disagreeing. Blocked on nobody; it is one field on one
struct and one line in the converter.

## Resolved in PR #49, by a different route

`unlocks_when` asked for `RequiresAck` on the Definition. PR #49 removed the
reason to want it instead. Acknowledgment is now required for exactly the
operations that declare `destructive`, on both lanes: the admin lane's
`requireAcknowledgment` for built-ins, and `pluginhost.OperationAllowed` for
plugins, which no longer reads `requires_ack` (CERB-GAP-286). So `destructive`
in `connectors describe` is the complete answer for every connector, plugins
included, and `requires_ack` is deprecated metadata. Adding it to the Definition
now would advertise a field the host ignores.

One case `describe` still does not show: a plugin installed with the `dev`
origin refuses destructive operations outright, acknowledged or not. That
belongs to CERB-GAP-848.

data.unlocks_when: Definition carries RequiresAck and connectors describe emits it, so an agent reads the requirement instead of inferring it.

records.name: Write operations that are not flagged destructive
records.summary: Creating a billable droplet, powering a host off, and replacing a site's deployment script all bypass the acknowledgment gate.
records.confidence_label: connector definitions and CLI flags re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54); counts taken from connectors describe on a branch build

relationships.note: create_droplet and stop
update_deployment_script
The flags are the only thing enforcement reads

records.body:
The acknowledgment gate reads exactly one thing: the `Destructive` flag on the
operation's declaration. Three operations write and are not flagged.

**`digitalocean create_droplet`** creates a billable machine. `destructive:
false`, `supports_dry: true`. It has a preview, so an operator can look before
leaping — but nothing forces them to, and there is no acknowledgment.

**`digitalocean stop`** powers a host off. `destructive: false`, `supports_dry:
true`. Same shape.

**`forge update_deployment_script`** replaces the script that runs on every
future deploy of a production site. `destructive: false`, `supports_dry: false`.
No gate and no preview, in the one connector package with no tests.

The house rule in `docs/plans/connector-work-packages.md` is unambiguous:
"anything that writes, replaces, deletes or reboots gets `Destructive: true`,
and `SupportsDry: true` if a preview is meaningful. Read-only operations get
neither — making reads prompt empties the gate of meaning." The reasoning behind
the DigitalOcean choices is guessable — destroy is irreversible, a power-off is
not — but it is not written down anywhere, which means it reads as an oversight
whether or not it was one. If it was deliberate, it needs a line saying so; the
gate's credibility depends on `destructive` meaning one thing.

Forge is the one that is hard to defend on any reading. `deploy_site` and
`exec_site_command` beside it are both flagged and both dry-runnable; rewriting
what they will run is not.

Fixing the flags is trivial. Flipping `Destructive` to true also requires a
`dryRunPreview` case, or `--dry-run` starts demanding `--ack` — the trap the
work packages already document. So this is three flags and up to three preview
cases. Blocked on nobody.

## Shipped in PR #49

All three are now `Destructive: true`. DigitalOcean `create_droplet` is
destructive because it is billable and runs the supplied `user_data` as root,
and `stop` because a hard power-off takes down whatever the droplet serves.
Forge `update_deployment_script` is destructive because the script is what
`deploy_site` runs next.

The surfaces followed. `cerberus server create` and `cerberus server stop`
gained `--ack`; `--dry-run` on either still needs none. `cerberus forge
set-script` already bound `--ack` and now demands it. The MCP tools
`cerberus_droplet_create` and `cerberus_droplet_stop` now carry
`DestructiveHint: true`, and create gained an `acknowledged` argument.

`update_deployment_script` still has no preview. Because a dry run can no longer
fall through (CERB-GAP-270), its dry run returns `preview_unsupported` instead
of landing on the acknowledgment gate, so the trap described above is gone.
`TestReclassifiedOperationsRequireAck` pins the flags. `unlocks_when` is met.

data.unlocks_when: The house rule is applied: anything that writes, replaces, deletes or reboots carries Destructive: true, with SupportsDry where a preview is meaningful.

records.name: Cloudflare and Forge have no test files at all
records.summary: The two connector packages with no tests own five destructive operations between them, including arbitrary command execution on a production site.
records.confidence_label: go test ./internal/connector/... reports [no test files] for both packages

relationships.note: Cloudflare
Forge

records.body:
`go test ./internal/connector/...` reports `[no test files]` for exactly two
packages: `internal/connector/cloudflare` and `internal/connector/forge`. Every
other connector package has tests.

Between them those two packages own five destructive operations:
`create_zone`, `create_dns_record`, `delete_dns_record`, `deploy_site` and
`exec_site_command`. The last of those runs an arbitrary command inside a
production Laravel site and is the broadest write verb anywhere in the lane.

Both packages already have the structure that makes testing cheap. Cloudflare
puts `cloudflare-go` behind a `Backend` interface; Forge has its own HTTP client
that could take an injected transport. The house rules say tests use a fake
`Backend`, with `fakeSSHBackend` as the worked example. Nobody wrote them.

What is covered instead is the service-level dispatch in `internal/cerbapi` —
`TestExternalConnectorServiceExecutesCloudflareOperation`,
`TestExternalConnectorServiceExecutesForgeOperation` and the Cloudflare dry-run
tests. Those prove the admin lane routes to the connector. They do not prove the
connector builds the right request, maps the response correctly, or classifies
its errors the way the lane expects.

Neither connector has a credential on this machine, which means the untested
code is also unrun code: for these two, `verified: unverified` is the honest
value across the board and there is nothing short of a credential that improves
it.

`must-have`, because "no tests and no credential" on a connector that can run
arbitrary remote commands is the combination with no safety net at all. Blocked
on nobody.

data.unlocks_when: Each package has fake-Backend tests covering its definition, its destructive operations' argument handling, and its error classification.

records.name: ADR 0003's DTO rule is unimplemented for the SDK connectors
records.summary: digitalocean, github and cloudflare return vendor SDK types, and none carries the serialization test the ADR asks for.
records.confidence_label: go.mod carries the three SDKs; grepped for leak-assertion tests and found one, for namecheap's API key in transport errors

relationships.note: The decision this gap is the unimplemented half of
github
digitalocean
cloudflare

records.body:
ADR 0003 decided that a connector operation returns a DTO defined in Cerberus,
never a vendor SDK type, because the DTO is an allow-list and a vendor adding a
credential field in a minor release therefore cannot silently widen our output.
It also says each connector returning credential-adjacent data carries a test
asserting that a populated secret field does not appear in the serialized
response.

The ADR is equally explicit that `digitalocean`, `github`, `cloudflare`, `forge`
and `namecheap` are **not** retroactively in violation — they should be audited
in the order they are touched and migrated as part of the plugin migration they
are already scheduled for. So this is not a broken rule; it is a rule with a
known outstanding scope.

What the audit adds is the answer to the ADR's own narrow question — "does any
type this connector returns carry a token, password, key, header value or OAuth
blob?" — which is still unanswered for all three SDK connectors.
`go.mod` carries `cloudflare-go/v4`, `godo` and `go-github/v72`, and the only
leak-assertion test anywhere in the connector tree is
`TestTransportErrorDoesNotExposeAPIKey` in the namecheap package, which covers
an error path rather than a response body. Nothing asserts that a marshalled
`godo.Droplet` or a `go-github` repository carries no credential material.

ContextForge is the counter-example and the reason to take this seriously: its
vendor `Gateway` type carries `AuthToken`, `AuthPassword` and `OAuthConfig`
among 32 secret-bearing field references, and the natural implementation of
`list_gateways` would have emitted them into MCP results and from there into a
model provider. The severity was a property of the vendor type and invisible at
the call site.

`nice-to-have` because the ADR's own sequencing says so and because the three
SDKs here are less likely offenders than an auth-gateway SDK. The cheap version
that closes most of the risk is not a rewrite — it is three serialization tests
that fail if a credential-shaped field ever appears.

data.unlocks_when: Each connector defines response DTOs as an allow-list, with a test asserting a populated secret field does not appear in the serialized response — done as each is touched, per the ADR.

records.name: `live` means different things for different connectors
records.summary: For credentialed connectors `live` is a real probe; for ssh it is unconditionally true, and for docker it means a binary exists, not that the daemon answers.
records.confidence_label: Read the registration site and Probe; confirmed ssh is an eager instance and DetectDocker only stats a file

relationships.note: LiveDefinitionsContext
ssh is always live
docker live means binary found

records.body:
`LiveDefinitionsContext` probes by resolving, with the comment "a registered
factory whose docker binary is missing, or whose API token is unset, is not
live". That is true, and it is a real improvement over checking registration.
But `Resolve` means different things depending on how the connector was
registered, and `live` collapses them.

**Credentialed connectors** — cloudflare, digitalocean, forge, github, namecheap
— are registered as factories that read a secret. `live=no` on this machine
means the secret is genuinely absent. That answer is informative.

**ssh** is registered with `registry.Register(sshconn.New(sec))`, an eager
instance. `Resolve` returns it, `Probe` returns nil, and `live` is `yes`
unconditionally — VPN up or down, host reachable or not. It means "the ssh
connector is compiled in".

**docker** is a factory, so it does probe — but `DetectDocker` stats an
executable file and stops. It never asks whether the daemon is reachable. With
Docker Desktop stopped, `live=yes` and every operation fails with "cannot
connect to the Docker daemon".

There is also a degraded path worth naming. `cerberus connectors list` gets
liveness from the daemon precisely because the CLI has the user's shell PATH and
the daemon has launchd's — the comment says so, and it is the fix for the
original outage. If the daemon cannot answer, it falls back to the CLI's own
view, which is the same misleading answer, now on the path where the operator is
least likely to notice.

`nice-to-have`: nothing is broken, and the three answers are all defensible on
their own terms. What is missing is that the column does not say which question
it answered, and `AGENTS.md` has to explain in prose that `live` means
"constructible right now". A discovery surface should not need a prose footnote.

Blocked on nobody.

data.unlocks_when: Liveness reports what was actually checked — registered, constructible, or reachable — instead of collapsing three different answers into one yes.

records.name: MCP tools for built-in connectors are hand-written, so verbs go missing
records.summary: Only plugin connectors get generated tool names; built-in operations reach MCP only if someone writes and double-registers a tool, and several never did.
records.confidence_label: Enumerated every MCP tool against every declared operation; found five operations with no MCP tool and two MCP tools for disabled operations

relationships.note: The lane
Area 4 owns the surface story this feeds
docker destroy is the sharpest instance
hints derived

records.body:
`AGENTS.md` says "every capability added to a connector becomes a CLI command,
an API operation and an MCP tool at the same time — which is what makes it
usable by agents as well as by people." For a plugin connector that is true: the
host derives tool names from the manifest. For a built-in it is aspirational.
`docs/plans/infra-admin-control-plane.md` states the reality plainly — "the MCP
tool is **not** free for a built-in connector" — and budgets five touch points
per verb, including registering the tool in both `cmd_mcp.go` and
`cmd_daemon.go`, with the warning that missing the second makes the tool work
under `cerberus mcp` but not under the daemon.

Enumerating the 48 declared operations against the MCP tool list, the
asymmetries are:

- `docker destroy` — no MCP tool, no CLI command. Unreachable.
- `docker status` — implemented in the service, not even declared. Since PR #49
  it is unreachable: the ack gate refuses an operation the definition does not
  declare.
- `ssh stop` — CLI only.
- `forge get_deployment_script`, `forge update_deployment_script` — CLI only,
  and the second is a production write.
- `digitalocean status` — declared, exposed nowhere.
- `namecheap get_dns_record_set` / `set_dns_record_set` — MCP only, no CLI. The
  only *safe* Namecheap write path in the product is reachable only by an agent.
- `cerberus_dns_create` / `cerberus_dns_delete` — MCP tools for the two
  operations that are hard-refused, so they exist only to fail.
- Plugin connector operations (azure's six, contextforge's four) have no MCP
  tools at all; they are reachable only through
  `connectors plugin managed exec`.

Individually each is defensible. Together they mean the surface set is whatever
someone remembered to write, and the discovery metadata that promises otherwise
is the same metadata an agent plans from.

The cheap fix is not generation, it is a test: for every declared operation,
assert a surface exists or an explicit exemption is recorded. That turns the
next omission into a failing test instead of a discovery lie. This overlaps the
surfaces area and should be reconciled with it.

`must-have`. Blocked on nobody.

**Partly closed on the P1-3 branch.** The tools are still hand-written, but no hint is. Every tool's annotations are derived from the contract of the operation it runs (`contract.HintsFor`, bound in `internal/mcp/hints.go`), `TestNoHandWrittenHints` fails on a hint set anywhere else in `internal/mcp`, and a single `AllTools` list replaced the two copies. Generating tools from plugin manifests is cerberus-a5's H3, built on the same `mcp.WithHints` (CERB-DEC-818).

data.unlocks_when: Built-in connector operations generate MCP tools from their Definition the way plugin operations already do, or a test asserts every declared operation has a surface.

records.name: Operations implemented but not declared
records.summary: `docker status` and namecheap's per-record writes run through the service dispatch without appearing in any connector Definition.
records.confidence_label: requireAcknowledgment and executeDocker re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54)

relationships.note: Discovery is supposed to be authoritative
docker status
namecheap per-record writes

records.body:
`cerberus connectors describe docker` lists five operations. `executeDocker`
has six cases: the fifth is `status`, which is implemented, reachable over the
daemon socket, and declared nowhere. `executeNamecheap` similarly handles
`create_dns_record` and `delete_dns_record`, which are absent from the Namecheap
`Definition` — though those are also refused at the top of `Execute`, so the
code behind the guard is unreachable by design rather than hidden.

`docker status` is the live case. It is harmless in itself — a read — but it
exposes a structural point worth fixing cheaply: `requireAcknowledgment` looks
the operation up **by name in the Definition** and returns `nil` when it finds
no match. An undeclared operation therefore passes the acknowledgment gate
unconditionally. Today no undeclared operation is destructive, so nothing is
exposed. The gate is fail-open by construction, and the only thing keeping it
safe is that the set of undeclared operations happens to contain nothing
dangerous.

Two small changes close it independently. Declare `docker status` so discovery
matches dispatch. And make `requireAcknowledgment` refuse an operation it cannot
find a declaration for, rather than allowing it — fail-closed on an unknown verb
is the right default for a gate whose whole job is to stop unintended writes.

`nice-to-have` on today's operation set; the second half of it is what stops
this from becoming a real bug the first time someone adds a destructive verb and
forgets the declaration. Blocked on nobody.

## Narrowed by PR #49

The fail-open half is closed. `requireAcknowledgment` now refuses with
`operation_unsupported` when a connector has no definition, or when its
definition does not declare the operation: "whether it is destructive cannot be
checked; refusing". `TestAckGateFailsClosedWithoutDefinition` and
`TestAckGateFailsClosedOnUndeclaredOperation` hold it. The gate no longer
depends on the undeclared set happening to be harmless.

Still open: `executeDocker` still carries the `status` case, which is now
unreachable through `Execute` rather than hidden, and nothing checks the
dispatch against the declaration at build time. The Namecheap per-record cases
stay unreachable by design.

data.unlocks_when: The declared operation set and the service dispatch are checked against each other, so an undeclared operation is a build failure rather than a hidden verb.

records.name: Plugin acknowledgment is enforced on a flag the plugin sets itself
records.summary: The managed-plugin branch returns before the lane's ack gate, so a manifest declaring destructive with requires_ack false executes unacknowledged.
records.confidence_label: pluginhost.OperationAllowed and Execute re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54)

relationships.note: The lane whose gate is bypassed
Area 3 owns the enforcement point on the other side
The same flag pair, seen from discovery

records.body:
Acknowledgment is enforced in two places, and only one of them is under
Cerberus's control end to end.

In `Execute`, the managed-plugin branch dispatches and returns at line 169.
`requireAcknowledgment` is called at line 209. So a plugin connector operation
never reaches the lane's gate. The plugin lane has its own:
`pluginhost.OperationAllowed`, which refuses when
`op.Destructive && op.RequiresAck && !acknowledged`.

For a built-in, `RequiresAck` is derived — `ManifestFromDefinition` sets it from
`Destructive` — so the two flags cannot disagree. For a plugin, both come from
the plugin's own `plugin.yaml`, independently. A manifest declaring
`destructive: true, requires_ack: false` satisfies the plugin lane's condition
by failing it: `op.RequiresAck` is false, so the acknowledgment is never
demanded, and the lane's own gate was bypassed three lines earlier.

Neither plugin shipped today is affected — azure and contextforge declare no
destructive operations at all, which is why this is a latent gap rather than a
present exposure. But the plugin lane exists specifically to carry provider
integrations that will have destructive operations, and the trust model around
it is careful in a way that makes this inconsistent: unsigned plugins are
deliberately grouped with the trusted tiers on the argument that a signature
attests to provenance while the acknowledgment attests to intent, and the
comment says plainly "destructive operations still require `--ack`". On a
manifest that sets the flags apart, they do not.

Two one-line fixes, either sufficient. Derive `RequiresAck` from `Destructive`
on the host side when loading a plugin manifest, so a plugin cannot opt out. Or
move `requireAcknowledgment` above the plugin dispatch so one gate covers both
lanes. The second is better: one enforcement point instead of two is the
difference between a capability and a coincidence.

`must-have`, because the cost is a line and the failure mode is an
unacknowledged destructive operation. Blocked on nobody.

## Shipped in PR #49

`pluginhost.OperationAllowed` now demands acknowledgment for any operation the
manifest marks `destructive`, whatever `requires_ack` says. `requires_ack` is
documented as deprecated in `pkg/connector/manifest.go` and `pkg/plugin`, and is
kept so existing manifests still parse. Manifest validation still requires
`requires_ack: true` on a destructive operation, deliberately: an older host
still ANDs the two flags, so a plugin that dropped it would run unacknowledged
there.

This is the first of the two fixes proposed above. The managed-plugin branch
still returns before the lane's own `requireAcknowledgment`, so there are still
two enforcement points, but both now read the same flag and neither can be
opted out of by the thing it gates. `TestDestructiveOperationNeedsAckWhateverRequiresAckSays`
and `TestOperationAllowedIgnoresRequiresAck` hold it. `unlocks_when` is met by
its second clause.

data.unlocks_when: Either the lane's ack gate runs before plugin dispatch, or the host derives requires_ack from destructive for plugins as it does for built-ins.

records.name: ContextForge's credentialed reads have never run against a real gateway
records.summary: list_gateways, list_virtual_servers and list_tools are unit-tested against a fake only; there is no JWT on this machine to prove the real path or the DTO allow-list.
records.confidence_label: Briefed and confirmed: the plugin reports missing_secrets: [token] and no credential exists here

relationships.note: The connector
The DTO allow-list this would confirm

records.body:
Nothing is blocked on code. The host secret channel shipped, the plugin loads,
and it correctly reports `missing_secrets: ["token"]` while `get_health`
continues to work. What is missing is the credential, which makes this an
operator action rather than an engineering task.

The reason it is `must-have` despite being small is what the verification is
actually for. The DTO allow-list that keeps `AuthToken`, `AuthPassword` and
`OAuthConfig` out of `list_gateways` output is asserted against a fake. A fake
carries the fields the test author remembered to populate. A real gateway
carries whatever the real vendor type holds, from a real deployment, and
ContextForge gateways are by the team's own notes the only place upstream auth
can be set — so a real `list_gateways` response is the densest credential
payload in the estate. Confirming the allow-list against a fake confirms the
mapping, not the coverage.

The path is recorded: the token lives in the gateway container's environment on
muctlvaig, and `cburks` is not in the `docker` group there, so it comes from
whoever administers that host or from the CF admin UI through the tunnel. Store
it in go-keyring service `cerberus`, key `contextforge/token`, or as a
`keychain://` reference under `contextforge` in
`~/.cerberus/connector-secrets.yaml`. Then reload — secrets resolve at load, not
per call — and run the three reads.

Acceptance is two things, not one: the operations return real upstream
registrations, and `missing_secrets` is empty. And if any response carries
credential material, that is a defect in the DTO allow-list which outranks
everything else in the connector plan.

Until then these three operations are `verified: test` and must not be recorded
as anything stronger. Blocked on a credential the operator must obtain; nobody
is blocked on code.

records.name: No plugin operation reaches MCP, and none gets a CLI verb of its own
records.summary: A loaded plugin's operations are reachable only through `connectors plugin [managed] exec` and the socket API; there is no MCP tool and no per-connector CLI command.
records.confidence_label: Verified live: no cerberus_contextforge_* or cerberus_azure_* MCP tool exists, and `cerberus --help` lists no contextforge or azure command
records.body:
`AGENTS.md` opens with the claim that "every capability added to a connector becomes a CLI command, an API operation and an MCP tool at the same time — which is what makes it usable by agents as well as by people." The `cerberus-plugins` README repeats it almost verbatim. For the plugin lane it is not true.

Verified live. `cmd/cerberus/cmd_mcp.go` registers 51 tools, every one hand-written for a compiled-in connector or a resource verb; there is no generation from a connector definition, and the running MCP server exposes no `cerberus_contextforge_*` or `cerberus_azure_*` tool. `cerberus --help` lists `cloudflare`, `dns`, `docker`, `domain`, `forge`, `github`, `server`, `ssh` — and no `contextforge` or `azure`. The only surface with genuine parity is the socket/HTTP API, where `POST /connectors/<id>/operations/<op>` reaches a loaded plugin through `ExternalConnectorService.Execute` with the same error codes a built-in gets.

The consequence is specific, not cosmetic: an agent cannot call a plugin operation. `ToolNameForOperation` already produces the right name, the manifest already carries an `input_schema` per operation, and the description and examples are already there — the plumbing to turn that into a registered MCP tool is the missing piece, and once built it would serve built-ins too. Nothing blocks it but the work.

**Closed 2026-09-25.** A plugin operation reaches MCP as a generated tool,
`cerberus_<plugin>_<op>`, once the operator lists it under `mcp: expose:` in
`~/.cerberus/connector-config.yaml`; nothing is exposed by default. The schema
comes from the manifest, hints from the effective contract, and calls go through
the admin lane. The served list follows the daemon's loaded plugins and the file
within 15 seconds, and clients are told through tools/list_changed. On the CLI, `cerberus connectors exec <id> <op>` (CERB-GAP-437) is the generic verb for any operation.

records.name: The credential_missing recovery instruction is a no-op
records.summary: The error tells the operator to run `managed load <id>`, and `Manager.Load` returns immediately when the plugin is already loaded, so the credential is never re-resolved.
records.confidence_label: Verified live: `managed load contextforge` against the loaded plugin returned loaded true with missing_secrets [token] and left the state file byte-identical
records.body:
`MissingSecretsError` ends with: "… then reload it with `cerberus connectors plugin managed load contextforge`". `Manager.Load` begins with `if _, ok := m.running[id]; ok { return nil }`. The command an operator is told to run does nothing, and reports success while doing it.

Verified live. `contextforge` is loaded with `missing_secrets: ["token"]`. Running `cerberus connectors plugin managed load contextforge` returned `{"id": "contextforge", "loaded": true, "missing_secrets": ["token"], "trust_tier": "unsigned", "version": "0.1.0"}` (since PR #51 `trust_tier` is `origin`) and `~/.cerberus/plugin-connectors.json` kept the same md5. An operator who stores the JWT, runs the printed command, sees `loaded: true` and then gets another 401 has been actively misled.

The knowledge already exists in the repo: `docs/plans/connector-work-packages.md` has a section headed "`managed load` does not restart a running plugin subprocess", ending "unload then load". `docs/secrets.md` and the error text both say the wrong thing. This is the same class of failure `AGENTS.md` records four times for `redact.Text` — a recovery instruction that does not survive the path it travels — except here the instruction survives intact and is simply wrong. The cheap fix is the wording; the better fix is making `Load` re-resolve secrets and re-init, so the instruction becomes true.

records.name: No supervision of a plugin subprocess
records.summary: Nothing detects a plugin child dying; the manager keeps the dead handle, so `managed list` reports loaded: true and every operation fails until someone unloads by hand.
records.confidence_label: Read from the code path: only Unload deletes from m.running. Not induced live, because killing a live plugin child is a mutation
records.body:
The daemon holds a plugin's subprocess for its own lifetime. On this machine both children are alive and parented to daemon pid 8188. Nothing watches them.

`RPCProcess` does notice its own exit — `waitProcess` records the exit error and fails pending calls — but `Manager` only removes an entry from `m.running` inside `Unload`. So a plugin that crashes, is OOM-killed, or is killed by an operator stays `loaded: true` in `managed list` forever, `managed health` errors out on a closed pipe, and every operation returns a transport error. There is no relaunch, no backoff, no alert, and no state that distinguishes "loaded" from "alive".

This is the plugin-lane echo of the Docker-connector outage `AGENTS.md` records: a component reporting itself healthy while being unable to do its job. `managed list`'s `loaded` field means "the manager still holds a Process", which is not what anyone reads it as.

Nothing blocks the fix but the work, and there is a real design choice inside it: a crashed plugin could be reaped and reported (cheap, honest) or relaunched with backoff (useful, and needs care not to crash-loop against a failing credential). Reaping first is the right order — an honest `loaded: false` beats an optimistic restart. Note that `auto_restart` belongs to the supervision lane and must not be widened to reach here; this supervision is the plugin host's own.

records.name: No test asserts pluginLaunchEnv() is credential-free
records.summary: The property AGENTS.md and docs/secrets.md both declare load-bearing — that no credential is in the plugin launch environment — has no regression test.
records.confidence_label: Grepped the test tree for pluginLaunchEnv and for CERBERUS_*_TOKEN in cerbapi tests; the only hit asserts error text, not the environment
records.body:
`pluginLaunchEnv()` is a fourteen-name allow-list, and `AGENTS.md` says plainly that "adding a credential to it would hand that value to every plugin, not the one that asked". `docs/secrets.md` says it "must stay that way". Nothing enforces either statement.

There is no test named for it, and no test in `internal/cerbapi` inspects the launch environment at all — the one test mentioning `CERBERUS_CONTEXTFORGE_TOKEN` asserts that the *error text* names the variable, which is a different property. The function is a plain literal slice, and adding `"CERBERUS_CONTEXTFORGE_TOKEN"` to it to fix a stubborn bug would pass every test in the repo while handing that token to the Azure plugin too.

Two assertions would close it, both cheap: that no entry in the allow-list satisfies `redact.SensitiveKey`, and that a launched plugin's `cmd.Env` does not contain a credential-shaped variable set in the host's environment. The second is the one that would actually catch a regression, because it tests the behaviour rather than the literal.

Marked must-have despite being small: this is the plugin lane's principal security boundary, and it is currently held by a comment.

records.name: Trust tiers constrain nothing reachable
records.summary: The only tiers that gate an operation require a devmode build nobody produces, and the `signed` tier is asserted by a CLI flag with no signature verification anywhere in the codebase.
records.confidence_label: internal/pluginhost/policy.go re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54); removed flags checked against the CLI
records.body:
Six tiers exist. `OperationAllowed` gates on exactly two of them — `local_dev` and `unsigned_dev`, which are refused every destructive operation — and both are unreachable.

`DevModeEnabled` is a build-tag constant, `false` unless built with `-tags devmode`, and no Makefile target does. Verified live: `cerberus connectors plugin health --dev <dir>` on the installed binary fails with "developer trust mode requires a devmode build". So the tiers that gate cannot be entered.

The tier that sounds strongest is not verified. There is no signature verification in this repo — no cosign, no sigstore, no minisign, no key material, no verification function. `CatalogSigned` and `ArchiveSigned` are booleans the caller asserts, exposed as `--catalog-signed` and `--archive-signed`. Verified live: passing both against the plainly unsigned `dist/azure` directory is accepted, which under `DefaultTrustPolicy` records `TrustTierSigned`. Two flags promote an unsigned binary to the highest non-builtin tier.

What remains is `unsigned`, which is what both real plugins are, and which gates nothing beyond the `--ack` requirement that the manifest already imposes independently of trust. Neither shipped plugin declares a destructive operation, so even that is unexercised.

The honest reading is that `TrustPolicy` is a well-shaped place to put trust decisions, with no trust input yet. That is defensible as a stage — but the tier *names* imply verification that does not exist, and an operator or agent reading `trust_tier: signed` would reasonably believe something was checked. Either wire verification (large: key distribution, a catalog, revocation) or rename the self-asserted tiers so the model stops over-claiming. The renaming is the small half and worth doing first.

## Shipped in PR #51

The tiers are gone rather than verified. `TrustPolicy`, `TrustMode`,
`TrustTier`, `TrustDecision`, `TrustCheck`, `DefaultTrustPolicy`,
`RequireSignature` and `RequireArchiveSig` were removed, along with all six tier
names. `--catalog-signed`, `--archive-signed` and `--archive-sha256` now fail
with cobra's `unknown flag`. In their place is an install origin that makes no
trust claim: `installed`, or `dev` for a development install whose destructive
operations are refused (CERB-DEC-815).

The large half of this record, signature verification, is not built and is not
planned. Cerberus does not sign or vet plugins (Decision 12 in
`docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md`). The `dev` origin still needs a
devmode build to enter, which is now its own record (CERB-GAP-848).
`unlocks_when` is met by its second clause.

relationships.note: missing from this capability

data.unlocks_when: Either signature verification exists, or the tier names stop implying it

records.name: The entrypoint hash is computed and then discarded
records.summary: Closed in P1-5: the digest of the whole plugin bundle, entrypoint included, is accepted in the install review, persisted with the registration, compared on every load and reported by managed list; a mismatch refuses the load as plugin_changed.
records.confidence_label: bundle.go, manager.go and the P1-5 review tests read and run on the P1-5 branch
records.body:
`InstalledPlugin.ArchiveSHA256` carries a comment stating its purpose: "Recorded so a plugin binary replaced underneath us is detectable even when the plugin is unsigned." It is recorded and nothing more.

The value is computed at install from the entrypoint file when the caller supplies none — a good decision in itself, since asking an operator to paste a digest of a binary they just built is friction that buys nothing. But the persisted entry in `~/.cerberus/plugin-connectors.json` is `{plugin_dir, trust, loaded}`; the hash is not in it. `ManagedPluginConnectorState`, which is what `managed list` returns and what the web console renders, has no hash field either. And restore re-installs from the directory, which recomputes the hash from whatever is on disk now — so the one moment a comparison would be possible is the moment the old value is thrown away.

The observable state of this machine shows it: `plugin-connectors.json` holds two entries with `"trust": {}` and no digest, while both plugins have been rebuilt into `dist/` repeatedly.

Small to fix and it makes two other things possible at once — a tamper signal, and the version identity that upgrade and rollback need. Marked nice-to-have only because nothing depends on it today; it becomes must-have the moment plugins are distributed rather than built locally.

## Narrowed by PR #51

The field is now `entrypoint_sha256`. The host always computes it, since no
caller override remains, and `managed list` reports it
(`ManagedPluginConnectorState.EntrypointSHA256`). The code and API docs call it
change detection, not a trust signal, and say that nothing compares it yet.

Two of the three things `unlocks_when` asks for are still missing. The value is
not persisted: a `plugin-connectors.json` entry is `{plugin_dir, options,
loaded}`, and restore recomputes the hash from whatever is on disk. It is not
compared on restore or reload. So a binary replaced underneath the daemon is now
visible to someone who reads `managed list` before and after, and is not
detected by anything. Comparing it on load is carried into P1 in
`docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md`, where Decision 12 pairs it with a
re-review.

## Scheduled

The P1 cut in `docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md` (2026-09-25) schedules this: P1-5 compares the entrypoint hash on every load, refuses a mismatch and re-reviews it as a diff, with `--accept-changes` to re-accept on a TTY. The plan names this record as what that closes.

## Closed in P1-5

What load compares is broader than the entrypoint hash. `pluginhost.BundleDigest` covers every file in the plugin directory (relative path, executable bit and content), so an edited `plugin.yaml` counts as a change just as a rebuilt binary does. The digest is accepted in the install review and persisted as `bundle_digest` in the version 2 `plugin-connectors.json`. `CheckBundle` compares it in `Manager.Load` before anything starts, on every surface and at daemon restore. `managed list` reports it. A mismatch is `plugin_changed` (409), with `managed load <id> --accept-changes` named as the recovery. That re-reviews the change as a diff against the accepted summary on a TTY. A reload of a changed bundle is refused before the running plugin is touched. The plugin runs from its reviewed copy in `~/.cerberus/plugins/<id>/<digest>/`, so rebuilding the checkout changes nothing until it is installed again. Entries from before P1-5 have no accepted digest; they load as `review_pending`, unchecked, until `managed review <id>`. `TestChangedBundleIsRefusedUntilReaccepted` and `TestCheckBundle` hold it.

records.name: No plugin upgrade, rollback or version pinning
records.summary: The managed inventory now records an accepted bundle digest and version, and an upgrade is a re-review shown as a diff, but there is still no pin and no rollback to an earlier version.
records.confidence_label: plugin_connector_state.go re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54)
records.body:
Ask the boring question and there is no answer. How do you upgrade a plugin? You rebuild `dist/<plugin>` and then `unload` and `load`. How do you know which version is loaded? `managed list` reports `version: 0.1.0` — read from `plugin.yaml` *on disk right now*, not from anything recorded at install. How do you pin a version? You cannot. How do you roll one back? You rebuild the old source.

`~/.cerberus/plugin-connectors.json` on this machine holds two entries, each `{plugin_dir, trust: {}, loaded: true}`. No version, no hash, no source reference, no install timestamp. Restore re-installs from the directory and takes whatever is there. So a `make dist` in the plugins repo followed by a daemon restart silently swaps the implementation under a registration that looks unchanged, and nothing anywhere records that it happened.

Today this is survivable because both plugins are built locally by their own author from a sibling checkout. It stops being survivable the moment a plugin is distributed — which is the stated plan, with `cloudflare`, `digitalocean`, `forge` and `namecheap` due to migrate out of the binary. At that point "which version of the cloudflare plugin is this daemon running, and can I go back" is an operational question with no mechanism behind it.

Nothing blocks it but the work, and it starts with GAP-336: record the version and hash with the registration, and upgrade becomes a diff rather than a surprise.

## Since PR #51

A persisted entry is now `{plugin_dir, options, loaded}`. `options` carries only
`dev_mode`, and the legacy `trust` object is still read for `dev_mode` alone.
`managed list` now reports a host-computed `entrypoint_sha256`, but the hash is
not written to the state file and nothing compares it (CERB-GAP-336), so none of
version, pin or rollback has moved.

## Since P1-5

Two of the three pieces moved. The registration now records the accepted bundle digest, version and source (`plugin-connectors.json` version 2). A plugin runs from a store copy named for its digest. Installing a new build of an installed plugin is an upgrade, shown as a diff against the accepted review, and nothing new runs until it is accepted. A changed bundle is refused at load (CERB-GAP-336, closed). What is still missing is pin and rollback: accepting a new review removes the superseded store copy, so there is no earlier version to go back to except by reinstalling the old build.

data.unlocks_when: The registration records a version and hash, install refuses or warns on a change, and a previous version can be restored — the first two since P1-5; restore is still missing

records.name: Uninstall is registration-only, and absent from the console and MCP
records.summary: Uninstalling drops the inventory entry but leaves the plugin's directory and its stored credentials, and the verb exists on the CLI and socket only.
records.confidence_label: Read from Uninstall and the console page; not run live because it removes a registration
records.body:
`managed uninstall` unloads if needed, refuses to remove a still-running plugin, drops the record and persists. That is clean as far as it goes, and two things it deliberately does not do are defensible: it does not delete the plugin directory, which the host never owned and which usually lives in someone's checkout, and it cannot delete the plugin's credentials from `connector-secrets.yaml` or the keychain, because `SecretResolver` is `Get`-only by design.

The gap is that neither is said out loud. An operator who uninstalls a plugin is left with a JWT still in their keychain under that connector id and a `dist/` directory still on disk, and nothing tells them. If the same id is later installed from a different source — which nothing prevents — it inherits those credentials. A one-line report of what was left behind would close most of this.

The surface half is simpler: the web console has install, load/unload and health but no uninstall, so a plugin installed from the console can only be removed from the CLI. MCP has neither, so an agent cannot undo its own install — except it cannot install either, so the asymmetry is at least consistent.

Small, and nice-to-have rather than must-have because the consequences are confusion rather than breakage.

records.name: Manifest secrets[].env is validated but never resolved through
records.summary: A plugin must declare an env fallback or required: true, and the host ignores the env name entirely — both shipped plugins name a variable Cerberus does not read.
records.confidence_label: Grepped every use of the field: only the validator reads it; resolution goes through CERBERUS_<ID>_<NAME>
records.body:
`SecretRequirement.Env` is enforced into existence and then ignored. `validateConfigSchema` refuses a secret that declares neither `env` nor `required: true`, so a manifest author is pushed to fill it in — and `resolvePluginSecrets` never looks at it, resolving `<plugin id>/<secret name>` through the provider's own `CERBERUS_<ID>_<NAME>` convention instead.

Both shipped plugins therefore advertise a variable that does not work through Cerberus. `contextforge` declares `env: CONTEXTFORGE_TOKEN`; the host reads `CERBERUS_CONTEXTFORGE_TOKEN`. `azure` declares `env: AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET`; the host reads `CERBERUS_AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET`. A built-in is consistent — the GitHub connector declares `CERBERUS_GITHUB_TOKEN`, which is what `EnvVarName` produces — so the inconsistency is specific to plugins, where the author picks the name and the host does not use it.

In fairness the intent is visible in ContextForge's own error text: "set `CONTEXTFORGE_TOKEN` when running the plugin directly", i.e. the field documents the variable the plugin binary itself honours outside the host. That is a reasonable meaning. It is just not what the field's name or the validator's insistence suggest, and an operator reading the manifest alone will set the wrong variable.

Two acceptable fixes: honour the declared name as a fallback after `CERBERUS_<ID>_<NAME>`, or rename/document the field as the plugin's direct-run variable. Either is small. Cheap and confusing is a bad combination, which is why this is worth a record rather than a shrug.

records.name: The plugin authoring contract has no stability guarantee
records.summary: `pkg/plugin` and `pkg/connector` are the public authoring surface on a v0.x module; both real plugins compile against v0.4.0-beta.2 while the host runs a newer tree.
records.confidence_label: Read from both plugin go.mod files and the protocol constant; not exercised, because no incompatible change has been made yet
records.body:
A third-party plugin is meant to be a standalone repo importing `github.com/hollis-labs/cerberus/pkg/{plugin,connector,resource}`. Both of ours pin `github.com/hollis-labs/cerberus v0.4.0-beta.2` — a pre-release — while the daemon on this machine runs a binary built from a newer tree. So the contract a plugin compiles against is already not the contract the host serves.

One real guard exists, and it is the right one: `Manager.Load` compares the plugin's reported protocol integer against `SDKProtocolVersion` (currently 1) and refuses a mismatch rather than failing mysteriously later. That covers a breaking wire change. It does not cover a breaking *type* change — a new required manifest field, a renamed struct field, a changed validation rule — which would simply make a plugin built against an older tag fail validation at install with a message about its manifest rather than about its version.

`PluginYAML.SchemaVersion` exists and is required to be non-empty, and nothing branches on its value; there is no statement of what bumping it would mean. There is also no statement anywhere of what `pkg/plugin` promises: whether a plugin built against v0.4 will load on v0.5, what the deprecation path is, or which packages are in the contract at all beyond the doc comment naming three.

Medium effort because the hard part is the commitment, not the code. Nice-to-have while both plugins share an author and a laptop; it is the first thing an external plugin author will ask.

records.name: MCP tools are hand-written, not generated from connector metadata
records.summary: Every MCP tool is a hand-authored constructor hand-registered in a flat list, so new connector capability reaches agents only when somebody writes a tool for it — while the socket API and console get it for free.
records.confidence_label: Verified by reading every RegisterTool call and searching internal/mcp for any metadata iteration
records.body:
`buildCerberusMCPServer` in `cmd_mcp.go` is 52 `srv.RegisterTool(...)` calls
against 52 hand-written `NewCerberusXxxTool` constructors in `internal/mcp/`.
Nothing iterates `Definitions()` or a connector manifest. Confirmed by search:
`internal/mcp/` contains zero references to `plugin`, `azure` or `contextforge`.

`AGENTS.md` attributes "MCP tool generation" to
`internal/cerbapi/external_connector_service.go`. It does not do that. Its only
`go-mcp` usage is `NotifyMessage` and `NotifyProgress` for progress streaming.
`pkg/plugin.ToolNameForOperation`, documented as "MCP tool naming", names the
tool a plugin subprocess serves to the *host* over `mcp/call_tool` — host-to-
plugin transport, not an agent-visible tool. Both docstrings currently point a
reader at machinery that does not exist.

The mechanism does exist, in one place, and it works. `NewCerberusDNSRecordSetTools`
loops over `namecheap.Definition().Operations`, filters to two names, and derives
the tool name (`"cerberus_" + operation`), description and input schema straight
from the metadata, injecting `dry_run` and `acknowledged` properties when
`op.Destructive`. That is the whole generator, in about twenty lines, applied to
2 of 48 operations.

Generalising it is not a research problem. The discovery shape already carries
`Name`, `Description`, `InputSchema`, `Destructive` and `SupportsDry` for every
operation on every connector including plugins; `ExecuteConnectorOperation`
already dispatches any `(connector, operation, config, dry_run, acknowledged)`
tuple. The open design questions are naming collisions with the existing
hand-written tools (`cerberus_docker_ps` vs a generated `cerberus_docker_list_containers`),
whether generated tools should be registered at boot from a snapshot or
refreshed when a plugin loads, and how to keep `tools/list` from exploding past
what an agent can hold — the 9 connectors' full metadata is already a large
payload.

Nobody is blocking this. It is the single change that would make the
"every surface at once" premise true.

**Partly closed on the P1-3 branch.** The tools are still hand-written, but no hint is. Every tool's annotations are derived from the contract of the operation it runs (`contract.HintsFor`, bound in `internal/mcp/hints.go`), `TestNoHandWrittenHints` fails on a hint set anywhere else in `internal/mcp`, and a single `AllTools` list replaced the two copies. Generating tools from plugin manifests is cerberus-a5's H3, built on the same `mcp.WithHints` (CERB-DEC-818).

records.name: The MCP tool list is duplicated in two hand-maintained places
records.summary: Closed on the P1-3 branch: `mcp.AllTools(client)` is the one tool list, served by cerberus mcp, mcp-http and the daemon's stdio server.
records.confidence_label: Both lists extracted and diffed; identical at HEAD
records.body:
`cmd_mcp.go` registers tools through `buildCerberusMCPServer`. `cmd_daemon.go`
registers the same set inline in a goroutine, against its `InProcessClient`, for
consumers that pipe stdio directly to `cerberus daemon`. `cmd_mcp_http.go`
correctly reuses `buildCerberusMCPServer`, so only the daemon's copy is a fork.

Extracting the constructor names from both files and diffing them gives an exact
match: 52 unique constructors each. So this is a latent divergence, not a live
bug — and worth recording precisely because it looks fine. Adding a tool
requires editing two files, and the daemon's copy takes a different client type,
so a compile error will not necessarily catch an omission.

The fix is mechanical: have the daemon call `buildCerberusMCPServer(inProc,
logger)`, which already accepts a `cerbapi.Client` interface that
`InProcessClient` satisfies. The only obstacle is that the daemon's version
passes `a.Config` to the SSH tool constructors while `cerberus mcp` resolves its
own config — a signature difference, not a design one.

records.name: No MCP tools for the plugin lifecycle
records.summary: connectors plugin managed install/load/unload/uninstall/health/exec has CLI commands, socket routes, console HTTP routes and a console UI — and zero MCP tools.
records.confidence_label: Socket routes and CLI verified live; absence confirmed by searching internal/mcp for 'plugin'
records.body:
The managed plugin lifecycle is exposed on four of five surfaces:

- CLI: `cerberus connectors plugin managed {install,load,unload,uninstall,list,health,exec}`
- socket: `GET /plugins/connectors`, `POST /plugins/connectors/health`,
  `POST /plugins/connectors/install`, `POST /plugins/connectors/{id}/{load,unload,uninstall,operations/{op}}`
- console HTTP: the same set under `/api/plugins/connectors/...`
- console UI: the Plugins page does install, load, unload and health

MCP has none. `internal/mcp/` contains no occurrence of the word `plugin`.

Verified live: `cerberus connectors plugin managed list` returns both plugins
with `loaded: true`, `trust_tier: unsigned` (since PR #51 that field is `origin: installed`), and ContextForge's
`missing_secrets: ["token"]`. An agent cannot obtain that. It cannot tell that a
plugin is installed but unloaded, cannot load it, and cannot read
`missing_secrets` — which is the field that distinguishes "this operation is
broken" from "this operation needs a credential nobody has provisioned".

For a control plane whose stated purpose is to be usable by agents, not being
able to manage its own extension mechanism from the agent surface is the
sharpest form of the parity gap. The read half — `plugin managed list` and
`plugin managed health` — is the highest value and the lowest risk: both are
non-mutating, both already have socket routes, and both would be a
thirty-line tool each following the shape of `NewCerberusConnectorListTool`.

## Since P1-5

Install is now deliberately out of reach of MCP, not merely missing from it. It is an interactive review confirmed on the operator's TTY (`cerbapi.PluginReviewer`, not on `Client`), and an agent cannot install a plugin, grant it a capability or accept its suggested policy (section 10). The read tools, list and health, are still what this record asks for. `managed list` now also reports `review_pending` and `bundle_digest`.

data.unlocks_when: At minimum cerberus_plugin_list and cerberus_plugin_health exist; load/unload may follow. Install stays off MCP by design since P1-5
data.effort: small for the read tools, medium for the mutating ones (they need an acknowledgment story consistent with the connector tools)

records.name: Plugin connector operations have no MCP tools, and their own documentation points at the CLI
records.summary: Azure's six operations and ContextForge's four are loaded and live, reachable from every surface except MCP, and their declared examples tell an agent to run a CLI command.
records.confidence_label: Plugin exec verified live; MCP absence confirmed against the session tool list and internal/mcp
records.body:
Both managed plugins are loaded on this machine and both report `live`. Verified
live: `cerberus connectors plugin managed exec contextforge get_health` returned
`{"address":"http://127.0.0.1:14444","ok":true,"status":"healthy"}`.

All ten operations are reachable from the CLI (`plugin managed exec`), the socket
(`/plugins/connectors/{id}/operations/{op}` and the generic
`/connectors/{id}/operations/{op}`), the console HTTP API and the console UI.
None has an MCP tool, because MCP has no generic operation tool and nobody
hand-wrote ten.

The self-documenting failure is the part worth fixing first. Verified live via
`cerberus_connector_describe`: every Azure operation's `examples` array contains
strings like `cerberus connectors plugin managed exec azure list_subscriptions`,
and every ContextForge operation's contains
`cerberus connectors plugin managed exec contextforge get_health`. Those strings
come from the plugin manifests and are rendered verbatim on the MCP surface. So
an agent that does the right thing — ask the discovery tool what a connector can
do — is handed, as the canonical invocation, a shell command it has no tool to
run. It will either give up or try to shell out, which is the failure mode a
first-class tool surface exists to prevent.

This is also where the operational argument bites. ContextForge's `get_health`
is open and must keep working while `list_gateways` 401s, because that is how
you tell a down tunnel from a down gateway. An agent diagnosing a ContextForge
problem today cannot make that distinction at all.

**Closed 2026-09-25.** A plugin operation reaches MCP as a generated tool,
`cerberus_<plugin>_<op>`, once the operator lists it under `mcp: expose:` in
`~/.cerberus/connector-config.yaml`; nothing is exposed by default. The schema
comes from the manifest, hints from the effective contract, and calls go through
the admin lane. The served list follows the daemon's loaded plugins and the file
within 15 seconds, and clients are told through tools/list_changed.
