records.name: No generic connector-operation MCP tool
records.summary: MCP has no escape hatch equivalent to the socket's POST /connectors/{id}/operations/{op}, leaving 15 of 48 declared connector operations unreachable from the agent surface.
records.confidence_label: Operation lists from connectors describe live; MCP tool names cross-checked one by one
records.body:
The socket, the console HTTP API and the console UI all reach 48 of 48 connector
operations through one generic route. MCP reaches 33, and the 15 it misses are:

- `azure`: all six (`list_subscriptions`, `get_subscription`,
  `list_resource_groups`, `list_resources`, `list_ai_accounts`,
  `list_model_deployments`)
- `contextforge`: all four (`get_health`, `list_gateways`,
  `list_virtual_servers`, `list_tools`)
- `ssh`: `stop`
- `docker`: `destroy`
- `digitalocean`: `status`
- `forge`: `get_deployment_script`, `update_deployment_script`

A single `cerberus_connector_exec` tool taking `{connector, operation, config,
dry_run, acknowledged}` would close all fifteen and every future one, at the cost
of an agent having to call `cerberus_connector_describe` first to learn the input
schema. That is a worse agent experience than a typed tool per operation — the
schema is the whole point of a tool definition — but it is strictly better than
no access, and it is perhaps twenty lines given `executeConnectorMCP` already
exists in `internal/mcp/`.

The right answer is the generator in CERB-GAP-430; the generic tool is the
stopgap that makes the surface honest in the meantime. It would also give the
discovery examples somewhere true to point.

records.name: No MCP tools for validate, register, deregister, registry or config
records.summary: Config and registry administration exists on the CLI and the console HTTP API but not on MCP, so an agent cannot validate a config, register a project, or find out that a registered config stopped resolving.
records.confidence_label: Absence confirmed against the session tool list and a search of internal/mcp; socket and console routes verified live
records.body:
Present on other surfaces, absent from MCP:

- `cerberus validate` and `cerberus config validate` — console: `GET /api/config/validate`
- `cerberus register` / `cerberus deregister` — console: `POST /api/registry/{register,deregister}`
- `cerberus registry list` / `registry health` — console: `/api/registry`,
  `/api/registry/health`; socket: `GET /registry/diagnostics`
- config resolve, backups and restore — console only

The read side matters most, and specifically `registry health`. `AGENTS.md`
records that a config which only exists on a branch is a config that
disappears: registered configs are referenced by absolute path, so checking out
a branch without them silently drops those projects from the runtime while the
registry still points at the path. The CLI prints a stderr notice on
`resource list` and `project list` telling the operator to run
`cerberus registry health`, and the console shows it as a banner. An agent
calling `cerberus_resource_list` gets the bare JSON array — by documented
contract the notice is absent from `--output json` — and has no tool to ask the
question the notice would have told a human to ask. The README points machine
readers at `/registry/diagnostics` on the daemon, which an MCP client has no
way to call.

So the agent surface can be looking at a short resource list with no way to
learn that it is short.

`validate` before `register` is the other natural agent workflow, and neither
half exists.

data.unlocks_when: cerberus_registry_health and cerberus_config_validate exist at minimum; register/deregister are a second step

records.name: No CLI command for the namecheap record-set operations
records.summary: Closed: the record-set operations are reachable from the CLI through cerberus connectors exec namecheap get_dns_record_set / set_dns_record_set.
records.confidence_label: Verified live: connectors describe namecheap lists both ops; the CLI command tree does not
records.body:
`cerberus dns create` and `cerberus dns delete` are deliberately tombstoned:
both return `ncconn.ErrUnsafePerRecordWrite` because Namecheap's `getHosts` can
omit records, so a per-record write can silently delete what it could not see.
The corresponding MCP tools are tombstoned identically, with a description that
redirects to `cerberus_set_dns_record_set`.

`cerberus dns list`'s long help says: "Per-record create/delete are disabled
because getHosts can omit records. Use explicit set_dns_record_set for
authoritative whole-zone replacement."

There is no `set_dns_record_set` on the CLI. `cerberus dns` has exactly
`create` (disabled), `delete` (disabled) and `list`. An operator following the
tool's own instructions finds nothing. The operations are reachable from MCP,
from the socket's generic route and from the console — so an agent can do this
and a person at a terminal cannot, which inverts the usual direction of this
gap and is the reason it went unnoticed.

The operations are live in the connector (`cerberus connectors describe
namecheap` lists both; `set_dns_record_set` is `destructive` and
`supports_dry`), so the work is purely a cobra command: a `get` reading the
current set, and a `set` taking an authoritative records file plus
`--email-type`, `--dry-run` and `--ack`. The whole-zone payload is awkward to
pass as flags, which is plausibly why it was skipped — `--from-file` with the
JSON the MCP tool takes is the obvious answer.

**Closed 2026-09-25, through the generic verb rather than a typed subcommand.**
`cerberus connectors exec namecheap get_dns_record_set --arg domain=example.com`
reads the set, and `set_dns_record_set` takes the authoritative records as
`--arg-json records='[…]'` or a whole argument object with `--input file.json`,
plus `--dry-run` and `--ack`. The `cerberus dns` group itself is being dropped
when namecheap moves to a plugin (docs/plans/provider-plugin-extraction.md).

data.unlocks_when: cerberus dns get-record-set / set-record-set exist, taking the records array from a file with --dry-run and --ack
data.effort: small — the connector operation, its schema and its acknowledgment gate all exist; this is flag plumbing

records.name: No generic connectors exec for built-in connectors
records.summary: Closed: cerberus connectors exec <id> <op> runs any built-in or plugin operation through the admin lane, with arguments typed from the operation input schema.
records.confidence_label: CLI tree enumerated from the installed binary; gap computed against connectors describe output
records.body:
`cerberus connectors` has three subcommands: `describe`,
`write-plugin-prototype`, and `plugin`. Under `plugin managed` there is `exec`,
which runs an arbitrary `(connector, operation)` pair against a daemon-managed
plugin. Nothing equivalent exists for `ssh`, `docker`, `github`, `forge`,
`cloudflare`, `namecheap` or `digitalocean`.

The consequence is four operations that the connectors declare and the CLI
cannot run: `namecheap get_dns_record_set`, `namecheap set_dns_record_set`,
`docker destroy` and `digitalocean status`. It is also why every future built-in
operation needs a cobra command before anyone can use it from a terminal, and
why the CLI shares MCP's structural problem in milder form.

`cerberus connectors exec <id> <op> --arg k=v --dry-run --ack` would close it,
posting to the same socket route the console already uses. The argument against
it is that a generic verb is a worse operator experience than a typed
subcommand with real flags and tab completion, and that it makes destructive
operations easier to reach with less ceremony. That argument is legitimate for
the everyday verbs and weak for the long tail — `plugin managed exec` already
accepted it for plugins.

**Closed 2026-09-25.** `cerberus connectors exec <id> <op>` exists and posts to
the same admin-lane route the console uses, so a built-in and a loaded plugin
are reached the same way. It goes beyond the `--arg k=v` sketched above:
arguments are typed from the operation's input schema, a repeated key builds an
array, `--arg-json` and `--input` carry structured values, and an argument a
closed schema does not declare is refused before anything is sent. `connectors
plugin managed exec` became the same command limited to installed plugins,
which also moved it off the direct plugin call and onto the admin lane.

data.unlocks_when: cerberus connectors exec <id> <op> exists, mirroring plugin managed exec for built-ins
data.effort: small — the socket route and the plugin managed exec command shape both exist to copy

records.name: Verb-level asymmetries between the CLI and MCP
records.summary: Beyond the structural gaps, seven specific verbs exist on one of CLI or MCP and not the other, and two exist on neither despite being declared.
records.confidence_label: Every cell cross-checked between the installed binary's command tree, the live MCP tool list and connectors describe
records.body:
Each of these is individually small and collectively the thing a per-area audit
misses, because from inside any one surface everything present looks shipped.

**CLI yes, MCP no:**

- `ssh stop` — shut down a remote host. Destructive, `supports_dry`.
- `forge get_deployment_script`, `forge update_deployment_script` — read and
  write a site's deploy script.
- `resource show` — the config view of a resource, as distinct from
  `resource status`, the runtime view.
- `project show`, `pipeline show` — detail views whose list counterparts both
  have MCP tools.

**MCP yes, CLI no:**

- `namecheap get_dns_record_set`, `set_dns_record_set` (see CERB-GAP-436).
- `cloudflare create_zone` is on both — `cerberus cloudflare zones create` —
  noted because the flat help text hides the subcommand and it reads as missing.

**Declared by a connector and on neither:**

- `docker destroy` — remove a container, or take a compose stack down
  (`docker compose down`).
- `digitalocean status` — normalised runtime state for a droplet.

The `*_show` cases deserve a note of their own. `resource show` does not use the
daemon at all: it calls `registry.ResolveConfig(cfgPath)` in the calling process.
So it is not simply missing from MCP — there is no socket route to expose. An
agent can read a resource's runtime state and not its declared configuration,
which is a real hole when the question is "why is this resource configured the
way it is".

records.name: The infra provider and deployment subsystem is console-only
records.summary: internal/infra is imported by exactly one file in the tree — internal/webui/infra.go — so provider configuration and deployment profiles exist only behind a browser, and carry another user's hardcoded paths.
records.confidence_label: Import graph checked across the whole tree; endpoints probed live and returned empty
records.body:
`GET /api/infra` returns a provider list (Vercel, with scope and token fields)
and a deployment list; `GET /api/deployments` returns deployments plus
suggestions, backed by `~/.cerberus/infra.yaml`. `POST
/api/infra/providers/{id}` and `/api/deployments/{id}` mutate them. There is a
Deployments page in the console.

`grep -rl 'cerberus/internal/infra"'` over the whole tree returns one file:
`internal/webui/infra.go`. No CLI command, no socket route, no MCP tool.

On this machine both endpoints return empty, and the reason is instructive.
`infra.SuggestedProfiles()` hardcodes `/Users/<other-user>/dev/sites/<site>`
and only emits a suggestion if that directory exists — the same other-user path
problem `AGENTS.md` records for the repo's `*.cerberus.yaml` descriptors. So the
subsystem is not merely console-only, it is console-only and inert here.

Two defensible resolutions, and the catalog should force the choice rather than
leave it: either the subsystem is real, in which case it needs a socket route
and at least read access from the CLI and MCP like everything else; or it is a
console experiment that predates the connector lane, in which case it should be
retired the way config migration was — a tombstone with a test — instead of
sitting in the binary as a surface nothing else can see.

records.name: The 24-hour overview trend is console-only
records.summary: The daemon records an operational snapshot every minute, and the only way to read it is the console's /api/overview — no CLI command, no socket route, no MCP tool.
records.confidence_label: Endpoint probed live; absence from CLI and MCP confirmed by search
records.body:
`cerberus daemon` runs a `SnapshotRecorder` on a one-minute tick, persisting
resource, project, running/attention/stopped and registry-health counters to
`~/.cerberus/state/overview_snapshots.json`. `GET /api/overview` buckets them
into a 24-hour trend for the console's signal bars and mini-trend widgets.
Verified live: it returns `{"inventory":{"connectors":9,"pipelines":0,
"plugins":2,"projects":8,"resources":10}, ...}` plus the trend.

Searching `cmd/` and `internal/mcp/` for `Overview` returns nothing. The daemon
is accumulating the only historical operational data Cerberus has, and an agent
asked "has this resource been flapping?" cannot read it.

This is a smaller hole than the plugin lifecycle but a cheaper one to close: the
data is already computed and already shaped for JSON, and a `cerberus_overview`
tool would be a socket route plus a tool constructor. The one design question is
whether the budget envelope applies — 24 hours of one-minute samples is 1440
points, far past the 25-item list cap, so it wants either server-side bucketing
(which `/api/overview` already does) or explicit paging.

data.effort: small — the recorder, the state file and the bucketing all exist; this is a route and a tool over them

records.name: A fresh checkout does not compile, because internal/webui/dist is untracked
records.summary: internal/webui/dist has no tracked placeholder, so //go:embed all:dist fails and go build, go vet, go test and make test all break in a clean clone or worktree.
records.confidence_label: Reproduced live in a clean worktree with both go vet and go test
records.body:
Verified live in the audit worktree, which is a clean `git worktree` of `main`:

```
$ go vet ./internal/webui/
internal/webui/server.go:27:12: pattern all:dist: no matching files found

$ go test ./cmd/cerberus ./internal/mcp ./internal/cerbapi ./internal/daemon
# github.com/hollis-labs/cerberus/cmd/cerberus
internal/webui/server.go:27:12: pattern all:dist: no matching files found
FAIL    github.com/hollis-labs/cerberus/cmd/cerberus [setup failed]
ok      github.com/hollis-labs/cerberus/internal/mcp
ok      github.com/hollis-labs/cerberus/internal/cerbapi
ok      github.com/hollis-labs/cerberus/internal/daemon
```

`AGENTS.md` warns that a plain `make build` "embeds whatever bundle is sitting
there". That understates it. `internal/webui/dist` is gitignored
(`.gitignore:8`), the ignore file still carries the negation
`!/internal/webui/dist/.gitkeep` (`.gitignore:9`), and `make clean` still
protects that file (`find internal/webui/dist -mindepth 1 ! -name .gitkeep
-delete`) — but the file itself was deleted in commit `a54daa8`, "chore: remove
obsolete internal/webui/dist/.gitkeep". So the directory does not exist in a
fresh checkout and the embed has nothing to match. The console does not embed a
stale bundle; `internal/webui` does not build, and neither does anything that
imports it, which includes `cmd/cerberus`.

The blast radius is the whole quality gate. `make test` is `go test ./cmd/cerberus
./internal/... ./pkg/...` with no dependency on `ui-build`. `make lint` runs
`go vet` over the same set. Lefthook's pre-push hook is the full `go test`, and
`AGENTS.md` says "Lefthook is the gate; there is no CI." So the gate passes only
for a working copy where somebody has already run `make all` or `npm run build`
at least once, and fails for every fresh clone, every fresh worktree, and any
copy after `make clean` — with an error that names an embed pattern rather than
the missing build step.

Restoring the placeholder is a one-file fix and restores what `.gitignore` and
`make clean` already assume. The alternative, making `test` and `lint` depend on
`ui-build`, is worse: it puts an `npm install` on the path of every test run.

## Shipped in PR #34

`fix/open-findings` (#34, commit f5bbf93) restores `internal/webui/dist/.gitkeep`, with a vite plugin in `web/vite.config.ts` writing it back after `emptyOutDir` clears it on every build. Verified by an actual clone in the PR. `unlocks_when` is met.

data.unlocks_when: internal/webui/dist/.gitkeep is tracked again, or the embed tolerates an empty directory
data.effort: trivial — one committed empty file; the .gitignore negation and the make clean guard are already in place for it

records.name: The console's action token is CSRF defence, not authentication
records.summary: The console's action token used to be served to anyone; since P2-2 it is per session and served only to a signed-in session, which starts from a one-time link minted from a 0600 key file.
records.confidence_label: internal/loopback and webui re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54); listen refusal run live
records.body:
`allowStateChangingRequest` requires three things: a JSON content type, a
matching `X-Cerberus-Web-Token`, and a same-origin `Origin` — but only
`if origin != ""`. A request with no `Origin` header passes the third check
unconditionally.

`GET /api/session` returns the token with no authentication of any kind.
Verified live against the console running on this machine:

```
$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4783/api/session
{"action_token":"Q2BIeGCVhoMR3e7At2Hl72RsqTuu6DRrezFnmETmV40"}

$ curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}' \
    http://127.0.0.1:4783/api/resources/__audit_nonexistent_resource__/stop
{"error":"state-changing request rejected","success":false}   # HTTP 403
```

The guard works. The problem is that a non-browser client sends no `Origin`,
fetches the token from an open endpoint, and is then indistinguishable from the
console. Against a browser this is sound: same-origin policy stops a hostile
page reading `/api/session`, and the `Origin` check catches the cross-origin
POST. Against any other local process it is no barrier at all.

What is behind it: `POST /api/resources/{id}/{apply,deploy,reload,stop,sync,remove}`,
`POST /api/pipelines/{id}/run`, `POST /api/registry/{register,deregister}`,
`POST /api/config/backups/restore`, the whole plugin lifecycle, and
`POST /api/connectors/{id}/operations/{op}` — which accepts `acknowledged: true`
and therefore reaches every destructive connector operation, including
`namecheap set_custom_nameservers`, `digitalocean destroy` and `ssh exec`.

For comparison the socket API's model is coherent: mode `0600`, same uid, no
token theatre. The console is a TCP listener and inherits none of that. I did
not exercise the mutating path — every operation behind it acts on real
infrastructure — so the reachability claim is from source plus the two live
probes above.

Two honest resolutions: bind the token to something the caller must already
have (a file readable only by the owning uid, printed at startup like a Jupyter
token), or drop the token and document that the console offers no isolation from
local processes, which is at least true. The present arrangement reads as
authentication in code review and is not.

## Narrowed by PR #48 and PR #50

The browser half this record called sound was not. Under DNS rebinding, a page
on a hostile domain re-pointed its name at `127.0.0.1`, read `/api/session`
same-origin, and then passed the Origin check, because that check compared
Origin against `r.Host`, which the attacker also controlled. Any site the
operator visited could drive every route behind the token.

That path is closed. `loopback.Guard` returns 403 for any request whose `Host`
is not `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]` or the configured listen host, before
any handler runs, so it covers `/api/session` and the static assets too. Origin,
when sent, is matched exactly (scheme, host and port) against the same set,
never against `r.Host` (CERB-DEC-810). `--listen` refuses anything but
`localhost` or a literal loopback IP, with no override (CERB-DEC-811). PR #50
also retired web install-by-path and the `plugin_dir` routes with 410, which
shortens the list of what sits behind the token.

What this record is about is unchanged. Any local process can still
`GET /api/session` from loopback, send no Origin, and be indistinguishable from
the console. That is the "web login: one-time token exchanged for a cookie" item
in section 11 of `docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md`, deferred past
P0.

## Since P2-1

Console requests are labelled `kind: human, via: web`, marked self-reported, and nothing the browser sends is read as a claim. Since any local process can still drive the console, the label is only as good as this gap allows. P2-2's login is what makes it mean someone at this machine.

## Closed by P2-2

The action token is no longer obtainable by an unauthenticated request.
`GET /api/session`, like every `/api/` route, answers 401 without a session
cookie, and a session starts only from a one-time link minted from a 0600 key
file under `~/.cerberus/web/`. That is the "file readable only by the owning
uid" resolution this record proposed. The token itself is now per session, and a
state-changing request needs both the session's cookie and its token. A local
process with no sign-in link sees 401 everywhere. One that can read the key file
already is the operator's own account.

records.name: cerberus mcp-http exposes the whole tool surface over TCP with no authentication
records.summary: The HTTP MCP endpoint serves the whole tool surface with no credential; since P0 it binds loopback only and refuses a foreign Host or Origin, but any local process can still call every tool, destructive ones included.
records.confidence_label: cmd_mcp_http.go and internal/loopback re-read on main after P0 (#48 to #54); listen refusal and Host/Origin 403s probed live on a scratch HOME
records.body:
`cerberus mcp-http` mounts `buildCerberusMCPServer`'s full tool set at
`127.0.0.1:4785/mcp`, plus an always-open `/health`. The only access control is
`--allow-origin`, which sets `httptransport.HandlerOptions.AllowedOrigins`, and
`Origin` is a browser header — an MCP client over a tunnel sends whatever it
likes or nothing.

That set includes `cerberus_droplet_destroy`, `cerberus_ssh_exec`,
`cerberus_ssh_put`, `cerberus_resource_remove`, `cerberus_set_dns_record_set`
and `cerberus_forge_exec`. Destructive connector operations require
`acknowledged: true`, which is an operator-intent gate, not an authorisation
one: the caller supplies it.

The command's own long help states the intent — "so remote MCP clients and
tunnels can connect to it" — so the deployment the feature exists for is
precisely the one where the missing authentication matters. The default bind is
loopback, which makes the default safe and the intended use unsafe.

Marked `unverified`: nothing was listening on 4785 on this machine and starting
a fresh listener that fronts destructive tools was outside a read-only audit. It
is also absent from the README's port map, so an operator has no documented
reason to expect it.

Simplest credible fix is a shared bearer token resolved from the secret provider
and required unless `--insecure` is passed, with the flag named so it appears in
shell history.

## Narrowed by PR #48 and PR #50

`mcp-http` now sits behind the same `loopback.Guard` as the web console. A
request whose Host is not a loopback name or the listen host gets 403 on both
`/mcp` and `/health`. go-mcp's `AllowedOrigins` is set to the guard's origin
set, which is never empty, so the old "empty means allow every origin" default
cannot recur, and `--allow-origin` adds exact origins to it. `--listen` refuses
`0.0.0.0`, `::`, an empty host, a LAN address, and any hostname, with no override
flag. The long help no longer promises remote or tunnel use. It says the
endpoint is loopback-only and names WP-S8.

Probed live for this pass, from a branch build on a scratch `HOME`:
`--listen 0.0.0.0:…` and `--listen myhost.local:…` both exit 1 with the refusal.
On `127.0.0.1`, `/health` returns 200 for a loopback Host on any port and 403
for `Host: evil.example`. `/mcp` returns 403 for a foreign Origin and for a
loopback Origin on the wrong port.

An `ssh -L` forward still works; a tunnel or reverse proxy that forwards a public
hostname is refused, which is intended while there is no credential.
`unlocks_when` is not met. Authentication is WP-S8, placed in P5 of the phase
plan.

data.unlocks_when: The HTTP MCP endpoint requires a credential by default, with an explicit opt-out flag
data.effort: small — one middleware and a secret lookup; the decision about where the token lives is the real work

records.name: The socket API version header is enforced only when present
records.summary: The socket rejects a mismatched X-Cerberus-Api but serves a request that omits it, so version negotiation is opt-in and an unversioned or wrong-version client is served silently.
records.confidence_label: Behaviour confirmed live with a header-less curl against the running daemon
records.body:
```go
if got := r.Header.Get(APIHeaderName); got != "" && got != APIVersion {
    writeJSONError(w, http.StatusBadRequest, ...)
    return
}
w.Header().Set(APIHeaderName, APIVersion)
```

Verified live: `curl` with no header gets `HTTP 200` and a response carrying
`X-Cerberus-Api: v1`.

This is the permissive choice and it is defensible today — every client in the
tree sets the header, and being lenient means an old `cerberus mcp` subprocess
left running across a daemon upgrade keeps working rather than hard-failing.
`decodeDeployOptions` makes the same bet explicitly: "Empty body is valid and
yields no overrides — that matches the historical contract older clients depend
on."

It becomes a problem the first time `v2` changes a response shape. A `v1`-era
client that omits the header will be served `v2` bodies and misparse them, and
the failure will surface as a decode error in the client rather than a version
error from the server. The cost of fixing it now is one line and a
compatibility note; the cost later is a debugging session in whichever surface
happens to break.

data.unlocks_when: A missing version header is either rejected or explicitly documented as meaning v1
data.effort: trivial to change, small to decide — the question is whether to break unversioned clients now or carry the ambiguity

records.name: A long-lived console process is an unsupervised, separately versioned surface
records.summary: cerberus web runs detached with no supervision and is not a Cerberus-managed resource, so the instance on this machine has been serving a two-day-old binary's behaviour — visibly different output for the same field.
records.confidence_label: Process identified live with ps, and the behavioural divergence reproduced by querying both surfaces for the same field
records.body:
Found running during this audit:

```
  PID  PPID STARTED                      COMMAND
25756     1 Tue Sep 15 17:31:58 2026     cerberus web --open=false
```

Parent pid 1, listening on `127.0.0.1:4783`, started two days before the
installed binary was rebuilt (17 Sep 08:59), and not among the 10 registered
resources. Nothing restarts it, nothing notices it is stale, and `cerberus
resource list` does not know it exists.

The drift is observable, not theoretical. Asked for the ContextForge token's
description, the three surfaces served by the current binary all return:

```
Bearer only — X-API-Key [REDACTED] a raw token both 401.
```

The running console returns:

```
Bearer [REDACTED] — X-API-Key [REDACTED] a raw token both 401.
```

The extra corruption after `Bearer` is the regression `AGENTS.md` records as
fixed — "the redactor has since learned to leave a non-token-shaped word after
Bearer alone". The fix is in the binary and not in the process, so a
long-running console is a time capsule of every redaction, DTO and error-message
bug that has since been fixed, with no version indicator anywhere in its UI.

Cerberus supervises local workloads for a living. Its own console being a
detached orphan is a self-hosting gap rather than a deep design problem: a
`cerberus-web` resource in the registry with `auto_restart` would make the
console subject to the same staleness detection as everything else, and
`AGENTS.md` already notes that the daemon has the same problem for the same
reason.

records.name: Redaction corrupts connector manifest descriptions on every surface
records.summary: redact.Text rewrites the word after X-API-Key in a plugin manifest's documentation field, so CLI, socket and MCP all return 'X-API-Key [REDACTED] a raw token both 401' — a fifth instance of the redactor eating its own guidance, in a field that is prose by construction.
records.confidence_label: Two independent audits found this from different surfaces; reproduced directly against redact.Text during reconciliation
records.body:
Source, `~/Projects-apps/cerberus-plugins/dist/contextforge/plugin.yaml:30`:

```yaml
description: ContextForge admin JWT. Bearer only — X-API-Key and a raw token both 401.
```

What three surfaces return, verified live:

```
$ cerberus connectors describe contextforge | grep -o 'Bearer only.*401'
Bearer only — X-API-Key [REDACTED] a raw token both 401

$ curl -s --unix-socket ~/.cerberus/cerberus.sock http://localhost/connectors | grep -o 'Bearer only[^"]*401'
Bearer only — X-API-Key [REDACTED] a raw token both 401
```

and the same through `cerberus_connector_describe` over MCP. The word `and` is
gone: the redactor reads `X-API-Key and` as a header followed by its value.

`AGENTS.md` records four prior instances of this — `Bearer JWT` becoming
`Bearer [REDACTED]`, `set CERBERUS_..._TOKEN` swallowed as an assignment, and a
names-only `missing_secrets` field returning `["[REDACTED]"]`. The rule it draws
is "do not run redaction over a value that is a name by construction". A
connector manifest's `description` is documentation by construction. It is
authored text, it is the operator's and the agent's only explanation of how the
credential works, and it is being run through a credential scrubber.

The practical damage is specific. This description exists to say that
ContextForge accepts *only* `Authorization: Bearer`, and that both `X-API-Key`
and a bare token get a 401. Mangled, it reads as though `X-API-Key` might work.
That is the difference between diagnosing a 401 in one step and several.

It also provides the clearest available evidence of surface drift: the console
process still running from the 15 Sep binary returns
`Bearer [REDACTED] — X-API-Key [REDACTED] a raw token both 401`, mangling
`only` as well — the regression `AGENTS.md` says was fixed, still live in a
process nobody restarted.

The fix follows the existing rule: connector and operation `description`,
`examples` and secret-`description` fields are prose and should be excluded from
the redaction path the way `missing_secrets` now is, with a test that this exact
string survives `redact.Text` intact.

## Root cause, and why it is a second distinct defect

Found independently by the operational-reality audit, which named the mechanism:
this is the `flag` rule, not the `assignment` rule that corrupts
`credential_missing` errors (CERB-GAP-273). `flag` is
`(?i)(--?[a-z0-9_-]*(?:api[_-]?key|token|secret|…)[a-z0-9_-]*(?:=|[ \t]+))(value)`,
and the single hyphen inside `X-API-Key` satisfies `--?`. So the redactor parses
`X-API-Key ` as a command-line flag that takes a space-separated value and eats
the following word.

The two defects are separate regex rules with separate triggers, and each needs
its own fix. Confirmed side by side against `redact.Text` during reconciliation:

    IN : Bearer only — X-API-Key and a raw token both 401.
    OUT: Bearer only — X-API-Key [REDACTED] a raw token both 401.
    IN : Use Bearer only and nothing else will work.      (control)
    OUT: Use Bearer only and nothing else will work.      (unchanged)

Note what survives in the control: the `Bearer`-guidance fix that `AGENTS.md`
records is genuinely in place. This defect was layered on top of it.

## Shipped in PR #34, via the same regex fix as CERB-GAP-273's sibling defect

`fix/open-findings` (#34, commit f5bbf93) anchors the `flag` regex in `internal/redact/redact.go` on a word boundary before the dash (`(?:^|[\s"'`([{])--?...`), which is exactly the root cause this record names. Because `redact.Text` is one shared function across every surface, the fix applies to a manifest `description` field the same as an error message — it is not scoped to error text.

**Verification gap:** the regression test added in `redact_test.go` (`TestTextKeepsRecoveryGuidanceReadable`) covers `"set X-API-Key header on the tunnel"`, not this record's exact repro string (`"Bearer only — X-API-Key and a raw token both 401"` from the ContextForge plugin manifest). Same rule, same anchor fix, but that specific string has not been re-run to confirm — worth a quick `cerberus connectors describe contextforge` check after upgrading.

data.unlocks_when: Connector and operation description/examples fields are excluded from redaction, with a regression test on this string
data.effort: small — the exclusion mechanism already exists for the fields that carry names by construction

records.name: resource show bypasses the daemon
records.summary: cerberus resource show resolves the config in the calling process, so it reports the caller's registry view rather than the running daemon's, and has no route to expose on any other surface.
records.confidence_label: Read from source and compared against the socket route list; divergence not reproduced because it needs a branch switch
records.body:
`resourceShowCmd` calls `registry.ResolveConfig(cfgPath)` directly.
`resourceListCmd` asks the daemon. So `show` reflects the shell's `--config`,
its environment and whatever branch the working copy is on, while `list`
reflects what the daemon resolved when it started.

`AGENTS.md` describes exactly the situation where these diverge: registered
configs are referenced by absolute path, so checking out a branch without them
drops those projects from the runtime. A resource can therefore be absent from
`resource list` and fully described by `resource show`, or the reverse, with no
indication that the two commands consulted different sources.

It is also the reason `resource show` appears on no other surface: there is no
`/resources/{id}/config` route to wrap, so `project show` and the agent-facing
equivalent do not exist either (CERB-GAP-438). Giving the daemon a route for the
declared configuration of a resource fixes the divergence and the missing
surface in one move.

The counter-argument for keeping it local is that `resource show` is useful when
the daemon is down, which is when you most want to read a config. That argues
for a daemon-first read with a local fallback that says which it used, not for
silently preferring the local one.

data.unlocks_when: A socket route serves a resource's declared configuration, and resource show prefers it while saying when it fell back
data.effort: small — the config is already resolved server-side; this is a read route and a DTO

records.name: ensure-fresh is a client-side composite with no socket route
records.summary: cerbapi.EnsureFresh composes status plus deploy/apply/sync in the client, so the verb exists on the CLI and MCP but not on the API they both call, and not in the console.
records.confidence_label: Traced across CLI, MCP, socket and console; not exercised because it is a lifecycle verb and no artifact-backed resource exists here
records.body:
`EnsureFresh` takes an `EnsureFresher` — the narrow interface both the
in-process runtime service and the socket client satisfy — reads status, and
chooses `deploy`, `apply`, `sync` or `noop` from the runtime's own
`RecommendedAction`. `--force` short-circuits to `deploy`.

That is a good decomposition: the decision logic lives once and runs against
either transport, which is why `cerberus resource ensure-fresh` and
`cerberus_resource_ensure_fresh` behave identically. The cost is that the socket
API has no `ensure-fresh`, so anything that is not a Go client of `cerbapi`
cannot use it. The console is the concrete casualty: `performAction` handles
`apply`, `deploy`, `reload`, `stop`, `sync` and `remove`, and the drift-
reconciling verb that `AGENTS.md` names as one of only two ways to fix a stale
artifact is simply absent from the operator UI.

Worth noting the composite makes more round trips than a route would — status,
then the chosen verb — and the two are not atomic, so a resource can change
state between them. On a local socket that is an acceptable race; it is the kind
of thing that stops being acceptable if the API is ever served over anything
slower.

Since no resource on this machine uses `run_from: artifact` and none reports an
artifact state, ensure-fresh itself is `unverified` here regardless of surface.

data.unlocks_when: A POST /resources/{id}/ensure-fresh route exists, and the console offers the verb
data.effort: small — wrap the existing composite in a handler; keeping the composite as the CLI path is fine

relationships.note: the budget this is about
the discovery tools whose payload it governs

records.name: The MCP budget caps item count, not payload size
records.summary: cerberus_connector_list's description tells the caller to use describe for full schemas, but list already returns every operation's full input schema — nine items that are a very large response inside a 25-item budget.
records.confidence_label: Response observed live and compared against the tool's own description
records.body:
`cerberus_connector_list` is described as a "budgeted envelope" with "Use
cerberus_connector_describe for full schema and operations". Called live with
`limit: 25`, it returned `"count":9,"total":9` and, for each connector, the
complete `config.fields`, `config.secrets` and every operation with its full
`input_schema`, `examples`, `destructive` and `supports_dry`. That is the entire
content `describe` returns, for all nine connectors, in one response — tens of
thousands of characters.

The budget is doing what it was built to do: `budgetedList` bounds the number of
items. Nine is under twenty-five, so nothing truncates. But an agent surface's
real constraint is tokens, and a nine-item list where each item embeds several
JSON schemas is a large fraction of a context window spent on a call whose own
description promises it is the cheap one.

Two separable problems. The description is wrong and should be fixed regardless:
list does not defer schemas to describe. And the budget has no byte dimension,
so it cannot catch this or the analogous case of a droplet list with large
user-data. A byte ceiling that drops the heaviest fields — `input_schema`,
`examples` — and sets `truncated` with a hint naming `describe` would make the
description true and the response affordable.

This is squarely an MCP-surface concern: no other surface has or needs a
response budget, and no other surface pays per byte.

data.unlocks_when: Either connector_list omits operation schemas and the description becomes true, or the budget gains a byte ceiling that sheds them
data.effort: small for the list-shape fix; medium for a byte dimension, which lives in the shared go-mcp budget package

relationships.note: a hole in this capability

records.name: validate never checks that any path in a config exists
records.summary: A config whose dir, command[0], env_file or log_file does not exist on this machine validates clean and exits 0.
records.confidence_label: proved by running the installed binary: ./cerberus.cerberus.yaml returns OK with every dir: pointing at a nonexistent path
records.body:
`ValidateProjectConfig` touches the filesystem exactly once — to read the config file. Nothing a config *names* is checked.

Verified 2026-09-17 against the installed binary:

    cerberus validate ./cerberus.cerberus.yaml   →  OK   (exit 0)

Every `dir:` in that file is `/Users/<other-user>/dev/hollis-labs/apps/cerberus`, which does not exist on this machine. A purpose-built config with `dir: /nope/does/not/exist`, `env_file: /nope/also/missing.env`, `log_file: /nope/cannot/write/here.log` and `command: ["/usr/local/definitely-not-installed", "serve"]` also returned OK.

This is the single most valuable thing validate could add, because it is exactly the class of breakage the current estate has: a config that is structurally perfect and refers to a machine that is not this one. The operator learns about it at `resource deploy` time, from a build failure, rather than at author time.

The honest counter-argument is that a path check is machine-specific and would make a config authored on one machine fail validation on another. That argues for severity — warning by default, error under a flag — not for the check's absence. `registry health` already reports a *config file* that has moved; extending the same idea to what the config points at is a small change.

Nobody is blocking this. Only effort is missing.

data.unlocks_when: someone adds a filesystem pass to ValidateProjectConfig, as warnings for portability or errors behind a --strict-paths flag

records.name: validate does not check type: or connector: against what the binary has
records.summary: A resource declaring an unknown type or a connector that does not exist validates clean; the failure surfaces at operate time instead.
records.confidence_label: proved live: connector: totally-not-a-connector with type: quantum-widget returned OK, exit 0
records.body:
`ValidateProjectConfig` checks `resource.Type` and `resource.Connector` for *presence only*:

    if resource.Type == "" { add(SeverityError, field+".type", "missing") }
    if resource.Connector == "" { add(SeverityError, field+".connector", "missing") }

Verified 2026-09-17: a config with `type: quantum-widget` and `connector: totally-not-a-connector` validates OK.

The authoritative set exists and is cheap to reach — `cerberus connectors list` prints nine connectors today, and the connector registry is constructed by `app.newConnectorRegistry`. A typo'd connector name therefore produces a resource that resolves into the runtime, appears in `resource list`, and fails only when someone tries to operate it — and because a non-local resource legitimately reports `unsupervised` rather than an error, a typo'd connector looks very much like a correctly-declared remote handle.

The one real design tension: a config may legitimately name a connector supplied by a plugin that is not installed on this particular machine. That is the same portability argument as CERB-GAP-530 and has the same answer — warn, don't error, and let a flag escalate.

Nobody is blocking this. Only effort is missing.

data.unlocks_when: validate resolves connector: against the connector registry (and the loaded plugin set) and type: against the known kinds

records.name: secret references are never parsed at author time
records.summary: secretref.Parse would reject a malformed keychain:// or helper:// reference, and no validation path calls it; the error surfaces inside launchd at service start.
records.confidence_label: proved live: keychain:// , keychain://svc and helper://../../evil/x all validated OK; grep confirms Parse has no author-time caller
records.body:
`secretref.Parse` is a real validator. It requires a non-empty service and key, rejects empty path segments, and rejects a helper name containing a path separator or `.`/`..`. It is called from exactly one place: `Resolver.Resolve`, at resolution time.

Verified 2026-09-17 — a config with

    env:
      TOKEN: "keychain://"
      OTHER: "keychain://svc"
      THIRD: "helper://../../evil/x"

returned `OK`, exit 0. All three would be rejected by `Parse`.

Where that error eventually lands is the point. `writePlist` sees reference-shaped values, fronts the program with `cerberus run-secrets`, and writes the plist. The malformed reference is discovered by the shim in the service's own process under launchd, at start time, as a resolution failure — on an artifact that has already been installed and a launchd job that has already been loaded. The validator that would have caught it at author time is sitting in the same binary, one function call away.

This is the cheapest of the validation gaps: the parser exists, the values are in hand, and a reference is non-sensitive by construction so there is no redaction hazard in reporting it. Add a test that the resulting message survives `redact.Text` — the house rule for any error carrying a recovery instruction.

Nobody is blocking this. Only effort is missing.

data.unlocks_when: ValidateProjectConfig runs secretref.Parse over every reference-shaped value in env: and env_file:

relationships.note: a hole in this capability

records.name: a literal credential in a resource's env: validates clean and is copied into the plist
records.summary: connector-secrets.yaml refuses literal credentials by name; a resource's env: accepts them silently and writePlist copies them verbatim into ~/Library/LaunchAgents.
records.confidence_label: literal acceptance proved live; the plist copy is read from launchd.go's EnvHasRefs branch and docs/secrets.md, not reproduced (no resource here uses os_service)
records.body:
The whole point of `internal/secretref` is stated in its own package doc: a literal credential in a project config is copied verbatim into the generated launchd plist, giving two plaintext copies in files operators and agents read routinely.

Cerberus guards one half of that and not the other. `ReferenceProvider.Get` refuses a literal in `connector-secrets.yaml` explicitly:

    connector secret %s/%s must be a keychain:// or helper:// reference;
    literal credentials are not allowed in %s

A resource's `env:` has no such guard. Verified 2026-09-17: a config with
`LITERAL: "sk-live-…"` alongside three malformed references validated `OK`.
`launchd.go` only fronts the program with `run-secrets` when
`secretref.EnvHasRefs` is true, so a wholly-literal environment is rendered
straight into the plist with no shim and no warning.

A detector cannot be exact — "is this string a credential" has no clean answer — but it does not need to be. A warning on a value whose *key* matches `TOKEN|KEY|SECRET|PASSWORD|API` and whose value is not a reference would have caught every real instance, and the recovery text is a single line naming `keychain://<service>/<key>`. `redact.Text` already has the machinery to decide whether a string looks like a credential; this is the same question asked at author time instead of on an error path.

Priority is `must-have` because the consequence is a credential on disk in a world-readable location, which is precisely what the capability was built to prevent.

Nobody is blocking this. Only effort is missing.

data.unlocks_when: validate warns on a high-entropy or credential-named env value that is not a reference, naming the reference form as the fix

relationships.note: a hole in this capability

records.name: no depends_on cycle detection
records.summary: Two resources that depend on each other validate clean; nothing in the config lane detects a dependency cycle.
records.confidence_label: proved live: a↔b mutual depends_on returned OK, exit 0; whether the supervision lane then hangs or detects it was not tested
records.body:
`ValidateProjectConfig` checks `depends_on` only for whether the target exists in the same config, and warns (not errors) when it does not, because a cross-config dependency is legitimate. Cycles are not considered.

Verified 2026-09-17: two resources with `depends_on` pointing at each other validated `OK`.

Priority is `nice-to-have` rather than must-have for two reasons. First, cross-config dependencies mean a complete cycle check belongs at *resolve* time over the merged set, not in the per-config validator, which is a slightly larger change. Second, what actually happens downstream is unverified — the ordering code in the supervision lane may already refuse to make progress rather than spin. Establishing that is the first step, and it may downgrade this to a message-quality issue rather than a missing check.

records.name: nothing backs up ~/.cerberus/, and nothing creates a config backup
records.summary: The directory that defines every running resource has no backup mechanism; Cerberus can restore a config snapshot but has no code path that ever creates one.
records.confidence_label: confirmed by grep (no code writes a .bak except the pre-restore snapshot) and by inspecting the live dotdir; the restore path itself was not exercised
records.body:
Confirmed, and sharper than the premise. It is not that Cerberus has no backup story — it is that it has the *second half only*.

`internal/configops` provides `ListConfigBackups` (a glob of `config.yaml.bak*`) and `RestoreConfigBackup` (copy back over the live file, after taking a `pre-restore-<timestamp>.bak` snapshot). Both are reachable from the web console at `/api/config/backups` and `/api/config/backups/restore`. A grep for `.bak` across all non-test Go confirms three hits, all inside that one file: the glob, the default `.bak` suffix, and the pre-restore snapshot name. **No code path in Cerberus ever creates a backup.** The package has no test files.

The seven snapshots on this machine were made by hand, and their names prove it: `config.yaml.bak-hadron-20260915-140347`, `.bak-tether-20260916-163206`, `.bak-pathfix-20260916-163754`. They are all siblings of the file they protect, so `rm -rf ~/.cerberus` — which `docs/install.md` documents as the uninstall step — destroys the config, the registry, every snapshot and the plugin state in one command. `~/.cerberus` is not a git repository and is not tracked by any repository.

**What recovery would actually take, if `~/.cerberus/config.yaml` were lost right now.** This is the real content of the record, and the answer is: re-author it by hand, because no second copy of those definitions exists.

- The 10 resources and 8 projects are defined *only* in that file. The registry index is empty (verified: 1791 monitor samples, `registry_entries: 0` throughout), so not one definition is recoverable from a repo-owned config.
- All 10 resources are `mode: dev_session`, so there are **no launchd plists** to reverse-engineer a command, port or environment from. The only Cerberus plist on this machine is the daemon's own.
- `~/.cerberus/pids/<id>.meta` carries `pid`, `started_at`, `config_hash` and `cerberus_version` — a hash of the config, not the config.
- `~/.cerberus/state/overview_snapshots.json` carries per-minute counts only.
- The SQLite store would not help even if it were populated: the workspace directory is empty and `main.db` has never been created here.
- The `.bak-*` siblings *would* work, via the web console's restore — provided the loss was an edit rather than a directory deletion, and provided the operator knows which of seven partially-named snapshots is current. The newest is `bak-pathfix-20260916-163754`, one day stale.

So: reconstruct 10 resource definitions — dirs, commands, ports, env, health checks, modes — from each project's own repo knowledge and whatever is still running in `ps`. Recoverable, but a day's careful work, and the running processes are the only ground truth for half of it.

The cheap mitigation is not a backup system. It is (a) a snapshot on every write path, which the restore code already assumes exists, and (b) getting the definitions into the repos that own them via `cerberus register`, which is the documented model and would make each project's git history the backup. See CERB-GAP-544.

Nobody is blocking this. Only effort is missing.

data.unlocks_when: a `cerberus config backup` verb that writes a timestamped snapshot outside ~/.cerberus, plus a pre-mutation snapshot on any write path

records.name: no per-machine path portability: ~ expands only for local/process resources
records.summary: NormalizeV2 expands ~ in a resource's paths, but only when connector is local and type is process, so any other resource kind must hard-code an absolute path.
records.confidence_label: read from internal/config/paths.go; the restriction is an explicit early-continue, not an oversight, and no non-local resource on this machine carries a path to demonstrate it
records.body:
The broad question — *is config portability a gap?* — is answered as CERB-DEC-555: literal `dir:` with no `$VAR` interpolation is a deliberate limitation. This record is the narrower residue, which is a genuine gap.

`~` and `~/` **are** expanded. `normalizeV2Config` runs `ExpandHomePath` over `dir`, `env_file`, `log_file`, `artifact_path`, `install_root`, `install_work_dir`, `command`, `env` values, `health_check.command` and the `build_strategy` `source`/`rules` maps. So a portable config is already writable today — `dir: ~/Projects-apps/cerberus` would resolve correctly for both this machine and the author's.

But it is gated:

    if res.Connector != "local" || res.Type != "process" || res.Config == nil {
        continue
    }

Pipeline `action.Dir` is expanded unconditionally; everything else is not. A `container`/`docker` resource with a `compose_file`, or a `server`/`ssh` resource with a key path, gets no expansion — so those kinds must hard-code an absolute path even though the mechanism that would make them portable is right there. That asymmetry is invisible from the config file: `~/...` works in one resource and silently does not in the one below it.

Priority is `nice-to-have` because nothing on this machine hits it — the one non-local resource, `muctlvaig`, carries no paths — and because the fix has a real risk: the connector config map is open, so blanket expansion could rewrite a value some connector meant literally. The safe version is per-connector declaration of which keys are paths, which is more than a one-liner.

The sharper observation for the catalog is that this repo's own descriptors do not use `~` at all. They hard-code `/Users/<other-user>/dev/hollis-labs/apps/<app>`, on resources that *are* local/process and would therefore have expanded correctly. The mechanism existed; the descriptors did not use it.

Nobody is blocking this. Only effort is missing.

data.unlocks_when: normalizeV2Config applies home expansion to every resource kind, not only local/process, and to project-level and connector-level paths

records.name: a registered path that disappears is detected but not prevented
records.summary: Checking out a branch without a registered config silently drops those resources from the runtime; detection is after the fact and prevention is a convention.
records.confidence_label: the detection mechanism was read end to end and is real; with an empty registry on this machine it could not be demonstrated live
records.body:
The premise — "a convention holding a footgun shut is a gap" — needs narrowing, because **detection does exist and is good**, and the record should say which half is missing.

What exists. The index holds an absolute path, so a branch checkout that removes the file makes it dangle. `Resolve` catches that: `LoadProjectConfig` fails, the entry goes into `ResolvedConfig.Skipped` with status `missing` and detail "config file no longer exists at registered path", and every other project still resolves. `resource list` goes through `ResolveConfigDetailed` and prints a trailing stderr notice — "1 config(s) skipped / skipped: <owner> / run 'cerberus registry health' for detail" — and the web console surfaces `Skipped` and `Warned` as structured DTOs with counts. `cerberus registry health` exits non-zero. That notice was built for exactly this failure: on 2026-05-25 the registry was healthy, configs were being dropped, and the operator saw a bare "No resources found".

What does not exist:

- Nothing prevents it. `register` does not look at the file's git state, so registering from a feature branch is accepted with no warning, and the convention "register a new config only once it is on `main`" is the only guard.
- Nothing stops the resources from vanishing. Detection tells you *why* the list is short; it does not keep the resources. That is the direct consequence of CERB-DEC-552 (the index stores a handle, never content) and is the price that decision knowingly pays.
- Nothing prunes. A dangling entry stays dangling until someone runs `deregister`, so a permanently-deleted config leaves a permanent unhealthy row.

Priority is `nice-to-have`, not must-have, because the loud-failure half is already built and because the cheapest real fix is the one in CERB-GAP-544 — get the configs registered at all, at which point the convention has something to apply to. Recording a branch name in the index entry and having `health` report "registered from branch X, HEAD is on Y" is a small, well-scoped improvement on top.

Nobody is blocking this. Only effort is missing.

data.unlocks_when: register refuses (or warns on) a path whose git HEAD is not the default branch, or the index records the expected branch and health reports a mismatch

records.name: no CLI or MCP surface for writing a credential
records.summary: KeychainProvider can Set and Delete, but the only write surface is the web console — and it bypasses connector-secrets.yaml.
records.confidence_label: read from source and confirmed by docs/secrets.md stating outright that no such command exists; the web console's write path was not exercised
records.body:
`docs/secrets.md` states it plainly: "The Cerberus web UI can still manage unmapped keychain entries; there is no `cerberus secrets set` command." Confirmed — `KeychainProvider.Set` and `.Delete` exist and the only non-test caller of any write is the web console.

Two consequences worth recording.

First, this is an agent-accessibility gap, not just a convenience one. Every other capability in Cerberus reaches the CLI, the socket, the HTTP API and MCP together; credentials reach only the console, which an agent cannot drive. An agent that diagnoses `credential_missing` can name the fix and cannot apply it.

Second, the console's provider is the wrong one. `cmd_web.go` constructs a bare `secrets.NewKeychainProvider()`, not the `ReferenceProvider` that `app.ConnectorSecrets` builds. So the console sees the keychain and the `CERBERUS_*` environment, and does **not** see `connector-secrets.yaml`. A credential configured as a reference in that file is invisible to the one surface that manages credentials — it will report the entry as absent while the connector resolves it fine. That asymmetry is the more interesting half of this gap and is cheap to fix independently.

Priority `nice-to-have`: `security`, the environment and the console all work today, and the estate's real credentials live in external helpers rather than the Cerberus keychain anyway. It moves to `must-have` the moment an agent is expected to remediate a missing credential.

Nobody is blocking this. Only effort is missing.

records.name: the v1 config machinery is unwired and still shipping
records.summary: config.Source, FileSource, Watcher, DiffConfigs and the v1 Config/ServiceDef types have no production caller; the whole v1 lane's config plumbing is dead weight in the binary.
records.confidence_label: confirmed by grep: NewServiceRegistry has no caller outside internal/service, and NewWatcher/NewFileSource have no caller outside their own package and tests
records.body:
An inverse-sweep finding. Four well-documented pieces of `internal/config` have no production caller:

- `config.Source` / `FileSource` — used only by `service.ServiceRegistry`.
- `config.DiffConfigs` — used only by `service.ServiceRegistry.Reload`.
- `config.Watcher` — the fsnotify config watcher, with parent-directory watching and 250ms debounce, called only from its own tests.
- The v1 `Config` / `ServiceDef` / `config.Load` path — reachable only through `FileSource.Snapshot`.

And `service.NewServiceRegistry` has no caller outside `internal/service`. So the chain is orphaned at the top: nothing in the shipped binary constructs any of it.

This matters for the catalog rather than for correctness. Three of those files carry the most emphatic comments in the config package — "removes an entire class of 'daemon had stale config' bugs", "the caller is expected to route it through the same code path as SIGHUP / `cerberus daemon reload`" — and an auditor reading the package concludes Cerberus hot-reloads config on file change. It does not: `LoadUnified`/`Resolve` are re-read per operation instead, which achieves the same freshness by a different route. A catalog built by reading this code would have recorded a config watcher that does not exist.

It also means the v1 `services:` lane is frozen more thoroughly than "frozen" suggests: `LoadUnified` refuses any version but 2, so no live config can even produce a `ServiceDef`.

Priority `nice-to-have` — it costs nothing at runtime. The cost is comprehension, and it is paid by every future reader of the package.

Nobody is blocking this. Only effort is missing.

records.name: cerberus install renders a plist with no EnvironmentVariables
records.summary: The documented daemon bootstrap produces a launchd job with launchd's minimal PATH and no supported way to change it, so a go_standard build from the daemon cannot find go.
records.confidence_label: the template was rendered independently and is byte-identical to the live plist; the build failure itself is inferred from the repo's own descriptor comment rather than reproduced
records.body:
This **refutes** the briefing's premise and replaces it with a worse finding.

The premise was that the daemon on this machine runs from a hand-written plist with no `EnvironmentVariables`, and is therefore not Cerberus-managed. Verified 2026-09-17: rendering `cmd_install.go`'s `launchdPlistTemplate` with this machine's values — `BinaryPath=~/go/bin/cerberus`, `WorkingDir=$HOME`, `HomeDir=$HOME` — produces 785 bytes that `diff` reports as **identical** to `~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.fragments-engine.cerberus.plist`. Whether or not a human typed it, it is indistinguishable from `cerberus install`'s output.

So the missing `EnvironmentVariables` is not an artifact of hand-writing. **The template has no `EnvironmentVariables` key at all.** Every daemon `cerberus install` has ever produced inherits launchd's minimal `PATH` (`/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`), and the command offers no flag to change it.

That is the exact boundary `AGENTS.md` warns about, and the repo's own descriptor documents the consequence in a comment on the resource that supersedes this command:

    # launchd hands the daemon a minimal PATH (/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin),
    # so `cerberus resource deploy` can't find `go` to build.

So the documented bootstrap path in `docs/install.md` step 2 and the macOS quickstart step 3 produces a daemon that cannot build a `go_standard` resource. The step does not error — it succeeds, and the failure appears later as a build that cannot find `go`.

The asymmetry is the tell: `internal/connector/local/launchd.go` **does** render `EnvironmentVariables` for a managed resource. The resource lane can give a plist an environment; the bootstrap command cannot. The intended resolution is presumably that the daemon becomes the `cerberus-daemon-service` resource — which is what `cerberus.cerberus.yaml` declares, complete with a `PATH:` env — but that migration has not happened on this machine, and `cerberus install` remains the documented path.

`must-have`, because it is the one step in the documented bootstrap that silently produces a broken result.

Nobody is blocking this. Only effort is missing.

## Shipped in PR #34

Same defect and same fix as CERB-GAP-637 (`daemonLaunchPath` in `cmd/cerberus/cmd_install.go`, PR #34 / commit f5bbf93) — this record and 637 are the duplicate pair the audit itself flagged. Same live-daemon caveat: this machine's installed plist predates the fix until reinstalled.

data.unlocks_when: the install template grows an EnvironmentVariables block with a sane PATH, or an --env/--path flag, or the bootstrap explicitly hands off to the cerberus-daemon-service resource which already supports env

records.name: docs/install.md describes the on-disk layout incorrectly
records.summary: install.md says there is no separate database and that the registry resolves via go-apppaths; both are contradicted by cerberus path and by layout.go's own doc comment.
records.confidence_label: install.md read in full and every claim checked against the running binary's cerberus path output
records.body:
Three claims in `docs/install.md` are wrong, and they are wrong about where state lives — the thing the document exists to tell you.

1. Prerequisites: "No separate database; Cerberus uses local SQLite under `~/.cerberus/`." The main database is `~/.local/share/cerberus/workspaces/default/main.db`, per `cerberus path` run on this machine. Nothing SQLite-shaped is under `~/.cerberus/`.

2. First-Time Setup: "registry + main DB: resolved via `go-apppaths` (XDG-compliant)". The registry is **not** go-apppaths-resolved, and `internal/config/layout.go` says so in an explicit scope note: "this resolves ONLY the main database path. Everything else under the legacy `~/.cerberus/` dotdir — config.yaml, registry.yaml, projects/*.cerberus.yaml, the apps/<project>/ install roots, sockets, pids, locks — STAYS where it is by design". `registry.DefaultIndexPath` returns `~/.cerberus/registry.yaml` unconditionally. An operator following this document looks for the registry in the wrong place.

3. Daemon modes: "They share `~/.cerberus/` and the same SQLite store." They share the dotdir; the store is elsewhere. And on this machine there is no store at all — `~/.local/share/cerberus/workspaces/default/` is empty, because the store is lazily opened and nothing has opened it.

A fourth, smaller one: the macOS quickstart tells you to install the binary to `~/.cerberus/bin/cerberus`, while `cmd_install.go`'s own comment names "the 'I `brew install`ed but my plist still points at a stale `~/.cerberus/bin/`' footgun" as the thing `resolveDaemonBinaryPath` exists to avoid. The quickstart recommends the location the code calls a footgun. (Incidentally `~/.cerberus/bin` on this machine holds `jaeger`, not `cerberus`.)

`must-have` because this is the document a new machine is bootstrapped from, `cerberus path` already prints the correct answer, and the fix is to copy it.

Nobody is blocking this. Only effort is missing.

records.name: the registry lane is documented as the model and is not in use
records.summary: Every resource on this machine lives in the monolithic config.yaml that the migration command was retired in favour of leaving; the registry has never held an entry.
records.confidence_label: verified live: registry list is empty, validate reports 0 registered, and 1791 monitor samples report registry_entries: 0 continuously
records.body:
A drift finding, and the largest one in this area.

The documented model is unambiguous. `internal/registry`'s package doc: "Apps own a project-config file in their own repo and register it with Cerberus, which keeps only a pointer index." `configops.ErrCentralizedMigrationRetired`: "No migration writer remains: configs must be authored in the owning repos." `docs/guides/setting-up-a-project-for-cerberus-v2.md` leads with "Keep The Config In Its Owning Repo". `ValidateConfigLocation` actively refuses a config placed under the retired central directory.

The reality on this machine, verified 2026-09-17:

- `cerberus registry list` → "No project configs registered."
- `~/.cerberus/registry.yaml` does not exist.
- `cerberus validate` → `Config OK: 0 registered, resolved to 8 projects, 10 resources`.
- `~/.cerberus/state/overview_snapshots.json`: all 1791 samples from 2026-09-15T17:31 to 2026-09-17T10:52 report `registry_entries: 0`. It has never been non-zero for as long as monitoring has been recording.

All 8 projects and 10 resources are declared directly in the 12,897-byte monolith. Which is a supported source — `Resolve` reads it first by design, and a broken global file is fatal precisely because it is expected to carry many resources — but it is the source the incremental-migration rule exists to shrink, and it has not shrunk.

Three consequences that matter beyond tidiness:

1. **No backup by side effect.** A registered config lives in a git repo, so its history is a backup. The monolith is in no repo (verified: `~/.cerberus` is not a git worktree), which is what makes CERB-GAP-537 as bad as it is.
2. **The register/resolve path is untested in production.** Precedence, override warnings, skip-one-config isolation, bundle expansion, cross-config port conflicts — all unit-tested, none exercised here. Any record claiming maturity for that lane is claiming it from tests.
3. **The `dir:` portability question is moot in the wrong direction.** The repo's own descriptors carry another user's paths precisely because nobody registers them; they are maintained as templates, so nothing forces them to be correct. CERB-DEC-555 argues literal `dir:` is defensible — but only where the config is actually registered and therefore actually loaded.

`must-have` priority, and the effort is `medium` rather than small because it is ten migrations plus verification per project, not a code change. No code is missing: `register` works.

Nobody is blocking this. Only effort is missing.

records.name: No audit trail of who ran what
records.summary: Closed across P1-4a and P1-4b: every connector operation, plugin call, resource mutation, pipeline run, deploy-profile run and monitor restart writes an intent and an outcome to an append-only hash-chained log that `cerberus audit` reads and verifies; since P2-1 each record names the principal, with the socket uid verified from peer credentials, while kind and client stay self-reported (CERB-GAP-859).

relationships.note: the log is the only place this could go today
the remaining coverage

records.body:
This is the must-have gap, and it should be said in those words: **there is no
audit trail.**

Destructive operations require `--ack`. Nothing records that an `--ack` was
given, by whom, or to what. The only trace of any operation is a
`daemon.socket.request` line carrying `time`, `level`, `msg`, `method` and
`path` — verified by parsing all 2621 of them in `~/.cerberus/cerberus.log`,
which have no other fields. The path is informative, so you can tell that
`POST /connectors/digitalocean/operations/destroy_droplet` was called at a given
second. You cannot tell which droplet, whether `--ack` was passed, whether it
succeeded, or who called it.

That last point is the one that makes this must-have rather than nice-to-have.
Agents are first-class callers of this control plane — every connector capability
becomes an MCP tool by design — and an `--ack` arriving from an MCP tool call is
indistinguishable in the record from one typed by a human at a terminal. The
acknowledgment gate is therefore a speed bump with no accountability behind it.

`LogAudit` in `internal/service/lifecycle_log.go` is the vestige of an intent to
fix this. Its doc comment says it captures "who requested the operation and why,
so operators can trace service disruptions back to the responsible agent/task",
its signature takes `operation`, `serviceID`, `reason`, `taskID` and
`sessionID`, and it has zero callers in the repo. The one `lifecycle.audit` line
in the log is dated 2026-03-23 against a service that no longer exists.

The SQLite store is not a fallback: `cerberus path` resolves `main-db` to
`~/.local/share/cerberus/workspaces/default/main.db`, and that file
exists — created 2026-09-17 10:50 — but is zero bytes with no tables at all
(`sqlite3 … .tables` returns nothing). So the store is opened and never
migrated: there is no audit schema to write to, which is the same conclusion by
a different route.

Nothing blocks this but effort. The socket server already sees every request;
the connector service already knows the operation, the resolved target and
whether acknowledgment was supplied. What is missing is a caller identity to
thread through (surface, uid, and for MCP a session id) and somewhere durable to
write it.

## Confirmed independently from the connector lane

The admin-lane audit reached this from the other side and added the detail that
makes it concrete: the lane that *enforces* `--ack` holds no store handle at all.
`external_connector_service.go` emits only transient MCP progress notifications,
so the acknowledgment is checked and then forgotten in the same call. There is no
surface on which an `--ack` is durable.

Reconciliation also confirmed the two halves of the emptiness directly:
`grep -rn LogAudit` returns only the function's own definition and doc comment in
`internal/service/lifecycle_log.go` — no callers anywhere — and
`~/.cerberus/main.db` does not exist, so the store that would hold such a record
has never been created.

## Since P1-4a

The admin lane and the plugin paths now have the trail this gap asked for
(CERB-CAP-604). Every call writes an intent before it runs and an outcome after,
to `~/.cerberus/audit/YYYY-MM.jsonl`. The records are hash-chained, append-only
and fsynced, and name the caller surface, the target, the credential names and
whether `--ack` was given. A non-read whose record cannot be written does not
run. The caller surface is self-reported, not authenticated, and the
acknowledgment is still the caller's own (CERB-GAP-838).

It stays partial because the resource mutators, pipeline runs and deploy-profile
runs do not write records yet, and there is no audit CLI to read them
(CERB-GAP-856, P1-4b).

## Since P1-4b

The remaining coverage landed (CERB-GAP-856). The resource mutators, pipeline runs and deploy-profile runs write the same intent and outcome pair, the resource monitor's restarts are recorded as an `automation` principal with the reason, and no `cerbapi.Client` method is left pending. `cerberus audit tail`, `query`, `verify` and `prune` read the log without the daemon. `LogAudit` is deleted (CERB-GAP-648).

**Closed.** What remains is attribution, not recording: the surface is self-reported and the acknowledgment is still the caller's own (CERB-GAP-838).

## Since P2-1

Each record now names who ran it, as far as Cerberus can tell. The principal carries a kind (human, agent or automation), a via (cli, mcp_stdio, mcp_http, web, monitor or pipeline), the uid with `uid_verified`, the MCP client, and `on_behalf_of` for a pipeline's stages. The uid comes from the socket's peer credentials, and the rest is the caller's claim (CERB-GAP-859).

data.unlocks_when: the resource mutators, pipelines and deploy-profile runs write records, and the audit CLI (tail, query, verify, prune) exists — P1-4b (CERB-GAP-856) — done in P1-4b

records.name: The supervision lane never probes configured health: URLs, and the richer prober has no caller
records.summary: Six of nine local resources declare a health endpoint; the code that would fetch one has no caller outside its own tests, so liveness is a PID file and a TCP dial.
records.confidence_label: zero production callers proven by grep; the false-positive case could not be induced read-only
records.body:
`internal/service/healthcheck.go` implements exactly what is wanted: a URL
check with a timeout, a command check, an interval, and a status. It has eight
tests. `NewHealthChecker` is called from those tests and nowhere else — the only
repo-wide matches are `healthcheck_test.go`.

What actually decides health is `devSession.Poll()`: `ownedPID()` for the PID
file, then `findPIDByPort()` for the port, and `ResourceHealth.Healthy` is
`resourceStateHealthy(state)` on the result. The `health:` string is parsed out
of the resource config, survives into `sessionConfigHash` so editing it counts
as a config change, and is read by `internal/pipeline/resolve.go` — but the
supervision lane never issues the request.

The practical consequence: a process that has wedged but still holds its
listening socket reports `healthy: true`, and the monitor will not restart it.
`tether-daemon` is the clearest illustration — it listens on a unix socket and
declares neither `port` nor `health`, so its `healthy: true` rests on nothing
but the existence of a PID file.

On 2026-09-17 all six declared URLs returned 200 when curled directly, so this
is latent, not currently wrong. That is the reason to fix it now rather than
after an incident: the configuration looks like it is doing something, the
operator has every reason to believe a wedged service will be caught, and it
will not be. Nothing blocks this; the implementation already exists one package
away.

data.unlocks_when: NewHealthChecker is wired into the v2 lane, or its logic is reimplemented there

records.name: Alerting exists only on the frozen lane — nothing notifies a human
records.summary: The three-layer alert path lives in the v1 monitor, which has no callers at all; the live monitor logs a WARN and gives up, and its only ever remote destination was a hardcoded localhost port for an app that is not installed.
records.confidence_label: zero callers proven by grep; the two surviving alert files and their log lines date the death precisely
records.body:
A monitor that detects and tells nobody is a gap, not a capability, and that is
the situation here twice over.

`internal/daemon/monitor.go` contains the alerting the comments describe:
`alert()` fires a structured WARN, POSTs to the Volon API, and writes a fallback
JSON file to `~/.cerberus/alerts/` if the POST failed. It is bound to the frozen
v1 `service.ServiceRegistry`, and `daemon.NewMonitor` has **zero** callers —
not in `cmd/`, not in `internal/`, not even in a test. The whole file is
unreachable in the shipped binary.

The live monitor, `ResourceMonitor` in `internal/cerbapi/resource_monitor.go`
and the only one `cmd_daemon.go` constructs, has no alerting whatsoever. When a
resource exhausts its restart budget it emits
`daemon.resource_monitor.max_restarts_exceeded` at WARN and returns. That log is
`~/.cerberus/cerberus.log`, which nothing watches.

The date of death is on disk. `~/.cerberus/alerts/` holds exactly two files,
`hadron-daemon-2026-09-15T13:25:39-05:00.json` and the matching `jaeger` one,
and the log carries the corresponding `daemon.monitor.alert.volon_failed` and
`alert.file_written` pairs. Nothing has been written there since the v2 migration
on 2026-09-15.

Even restoring the old path would not notify anybody. Its remote destination is
a hardcoded `http://127.0.0.1:8085/v1/notifications` belonging to Volon, a
Hollis Labs app that is not installed on this machine and is not a registered
resource. There is no configuration for an alert destination anywhere: no key in
`schema/cerberus.yaml.schema.json`, no `alerts:` or `notifications:` section in
the config, and the only `CERBERUS_*` environment variables in the whole source
are `CERBERUS_DAEMON_CHILD` and `CERBERUS_SSH_KEY_FILE`.

Nothing blocks this. It needs a hook on the live monitor and a destination that
is configurable rather than compiled in.

data.unlocks_when: the live ResourceMonitor gains an alert hook and the config schema gains a destination

records.name: No rotation or retention on the daemon log
records.summary: ~/.cerberus/cerberus.log is opened O_APPEND with no size cap, no rotation and no retention; it currently holds six months of history in one file.
records.confidence_label: file inspected; no rotation library or logic anywhere in the repo
records.body:
