`InitLifecycleLog` does `os.OpenFile(..., O_CREATE|O_WRONLY|O_APPEND, 0644)`
and wraps it in `slog.NewJSONHandler(f, nil)`. There is no rotation anywhere in
the repo — no `lumberjack`, no size or age check, no logrotate fragment, and the
nil handler options mean the level is fixed at the default with no way to raise
or lower it.

On this machine that is 3050 lines and 385 KB whose first entry is dated
2026-03-22. Low volume so far, so this is nice-to-have rather than urgent, but
the trajectory is one-way and the log is currently the only record of what the
control plane did. The two launchd files,
`~/.cerberus/logs/launchd-std{out,err}.log`, are in the same position: appended
across all 31 daemon runs with no rotation, and the plist has no
`StandardOutPath` rotation mechanism because launchd offers none.

The upgrade in CERB-GAP-630 makes this more pressing, since a real audit record
would raise the write volume considerably.

data.unlocks_when: a rotating writer replaces the raw os.OpenFile, or an age/size policy is added

records.name: No health verb on the CLI
records.summary: cerberus health is an unknown command; health is reachable only over MCP, the daemon socket and the web console.
records.confidence_label: run live: `cerberus health` returns unknown command and health is absent from the help
records.body:
`cerberus health` exits 1 with `unknown command "health" for "cerberus"`, and
no health verb appears in the top-level help. The `cerberus_health` MCP tool
exists, `GET /health` over the daemon socket exists, and the console renders it.
The CLI does not.

That is a break in the property the project leads with — that every capability
becomes a CLI command, an API operation and an MCP tool at the same time — and
it lands on the verb an operator is most likely to reach for first. The endpoint
already exists and `SocketClient.Health` already calls it, so this is a thin
command away. Small effort, nothing blocking.

data.unlocks_when: a `cerberus health` command is added over the existing socket endpoint

records.name: Health silently omits unsupervised resources
records.summary: ResourceRuntimeService.Health filters to local process resources before doing any work, so the server/ssh resource is absent from every health surface with no note that it was dropped.
records.confidence_label: verified on three surfaces: the MCP tool, the socket, and the console's /api/system and /api/overview

relationships.note: doctor gets this right

records.body:
AGENTS.md states the rule plainly: a resource that is not local/process is a
named handle for connector operations, and supervision-lane verbs should report
it as `unsupervised` and name the connector commands that do operate it, "rather
than erroring or leaving a blank status."

Two of the three verbs honour that. `cerberus resource status muctlvaig` reports
`Status: unsupervised` with the context line and `Next Step: cerberus ssh status
muctlvaig | cerberus ssh exec muctlvaig -- <command>`. `cerberus resource doctor
muctlvaig` refuses with the same guidance. `cerberus resource list` shows it
with `unsupervised` in the status column.

`Health` does not. It filters on `r.Type != string(domain.ResourceProcess) ||
r.Connector != "local"` before any work, so `muctlvaig` never appears — verified
in the `cerberus_health` MCP response, in the console's `/api/system` health
block, and by arithmetic in `/api/overview`, which reports `resources: 10`
alongside `running: 8`, `stopped: 1`, `attention: 0`. One in ten resources is
invisible to the health surface and the counters do not sum.

This is must-have because it is a blank status by another name, and because a
health surface that omits a resource without saying so is worse than one that
says it cannot judge it — an operator reading "all healthy" has no way to know
one resource was never considered. Small effort; the DTO already has the fields
`status` and a recommendation reason to carry it.

data.unlocks_when: Health emits an unsupervised entry naming the connector commands, as status and doctor already do

records.name: The daemon self-upgrade is documented only as an error string
records.summary: The build-to-temp / mv / launchctl kickstart dance appears in AGENTS.md and in a guard's error message, but there is no runbook, no verb, and no test that the instruction survives redaction.
records.confidence_label: the guard read end to end and its message run through redact.Text by hand; the upgrade deliberately not performed
records.body:
The mechanism is good. `ProtectServingDaemon` captures the serving executable
and launchd label at startup, and `refuseSelfMutation` blocks any deploy, apply,
sync, reload, stop or remove that resolves to the running daemon — matching on
canonical resource id, launchd label, artifact path for an `os_service`
resource, or `command[0]` for a dev_session one. The refusal names the recovery
rather than just saying no: build to a temporary path, atomically move the
binary over the daemon artifact, then `launchctl kickstart -k
gui/<uid>/com.fragments-engine.cerberus` from an external terminal.

What is missing is that this is the only place it is written, besides a paragraph
in AGENTS.md. There is no runbook under `docs/`, no `cerberus upgrade` verb, and
no test asserting the instruction survives `redact.Text` — which AGENTS.md
explicitly requires of any error carrying a recovery, having been burned four
times. Running the redactor over that exact message by hand shows it passes
intact, so the guidance is currently safe by luck of wording rather than by
assertion.

The wording also assumes an install this machine does not have. "The daemon
artifact" is meaningful for an `os_service` resource with `run_from: artifact`;
here the daemon runs directly from `~/go/bin/cerberus`, so the
`mv` target is that path. The dance still works — moving over an in-use binary
is fine on macOS — but a first-time reader has to work that out.

Small effort, nothing blocking, and it is folklore until it is written down.
This audit did not perform it.

data.unlocks_when: the sequence is written down as a runbook under docs/ and asserted by a redaction test

records.name: cerberus install gives the daemon no PATH
records.summary: The installer's plist template has no EnvironmentVariables key, so every Cerberus-installed daemon inherits launchd's minimal PATH — the root cause of the Docker connector outage, and not a consequence of a hand-written plist.
records.confidence_label: installer template compared against the live plist; the os_service builder confirmed to emit the key

relationships.note: the outage this caused

records.body:
AGENTS.md attributes the daemon's minimal `PATH` to the plist on this machine
being hand-written with no `EnvironmentVariables`. The plist is byte-for-byte
what `cerberus install` produces — same label, same `ProgramArguments` of
`[~/go/bin/cerberus, daemon, --foreground]`, same
`WorkingDirectory`, `RunAtLoad`, `KeepAlive` and log paths. The template in
`cmd/cerberus/cmd_install.go` simply has no `EnvironmentVariables` key.

So this is not a local accident to be documented around. Every `cerberus
install` on every machine produces a daemon with launchd's
`/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`, and every consequence AGENTS.md warns about
follows from the installer rather than from this operator. The contrast makes it
sharper: `internal/connector/local/launchd.go:44` — the plist builder for
`os_service` resources — does emit `EnvironmentVariables`. The one process that
most needs a working `PATH`, because it shells out to `go` for builds and
`docker` for the Docker connector, is installed by the only code path that omits
it.

This is must-have because the failure it produces is the silent kind: the Docker
connector resolving `docker` once at boot, failing, and caching that failure for
the daemon's lifetime while `cerberus connectors list` reported it healthy. The
per-call-resolution fix treats the symptom; the template is the cause. Small
effort, nothing blocking.

Two smaller notes on the same pair of commands: both `install` and `uninstall`
use the deprecated `launchctl load`/`unload` rather than
`bootstrap`/`bootout`, and both discard the unload error. And the help text for
both points at a `cerberus-daemon-service` v2 resource as the canonical
management path, which is not registered on this machine.

## Shipped in PR #34

`fix/open-findings` (#34) adds `daemonLaunchPath` to `cmd/cerberus/cmd_install.go`, composing `EnvironmentVariables.PATH` for the installed daemon's plist from the installing user's own environment (absolute entries only, launchd's four directories as the tail). Covered by `cmd/cerberus/cmd_install_test.go`. `unlocks_when` is met in source.

**Not yet in effect on this machine.** The running daemon's plist (`~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.fragments-engine.cerberus.plist`) predates this fix and still carries launchd's minimal PATH until `cerberus install` is re-run to regenerate it.

data.unlocks_when: launchdPlistTemplate emits EnvironmentVariables with a resolved PATH. Note that the os_service builder is not a model for this: launchdEnvironment returns nil when env and env_file are both empty, so it seeds no PATH either — the default is missing in both places, which is CERB-GAP-141.

records.name: Validation does not check that a declared directory resolves
records.summary: Every descriptor in the estate validates OK, including eight that point at a home directory which does not exist on this machine.
records.confidence_label: all nine descriptors validated live; /Users/<other-user> confirmed absent
records.body:
`cerberus validate <path>` reports `OK` for all nine `*.cerberus.yaml`
descriptors across `~/Projects-apps/*`. Eight of them place every `dir:` under
`/Users/<other-user>`, which `ls -d` confirms is not a directory here. The ninth,
this repo's `infrastructure.cerberus.yaml`, uses the portable
`dir: /opt/homebrew/var` for PostgreSQL and Jaeger and only fails on its third
resource, at `/Users/<other-user>/.cerberus/bin`.

Validation is schema-only. It carries a guard for the one value that has bitten
this project before — `port: 0`, held both by `findPIDByPort` and by
`TestValidateProjectConfigPortZeroIsError` — and no check that a declared
working directory, command path or env file exists.

This is must-have because it is the gate that could have caught the entire
"these descriptors are templates, not configuration" problem at the moment
someone tried to use one, and instead it reports success. `dir:` is documented
as a literal path with no interpolation or override, which makes the check
trivially decidable: either the directory is there or it is not. A warn-level
result would be enough; it does not have to fail the validation to be useful.
Small effort, nothing blocking.

data.unlocks_when: a path-resolution check is added to validation, or a registerability probe is added to register

records.name: No read-only lane for remote exec
records.summary: ssh exec is unconditionally destructive, so a read-only probe like `id -nG` needs --ack exactly as a destructive write would — which makes promoting the ~70 proven probe scripts into connectors impractical.
records.confidence_label: the refusal run live against muctlvaig; the probe conventions read out of ~/Projects/tools
records.body:
`cerberus ssh exec muctlvaig -- id -nG` exits 1 with `acknowledgment_required:
destructive operation "exec" requires operator acknowledgment`. Verified live.
`exec` is classified destructive as an operation, not as a call, so the
classification cannot distinguish `id -nG` from `rm -rf`.

That is defensible as a default — Cerberus cannot parse an arbitrary remote
command for intent — but it has a concrete cost that shows up the moment you
look at the prior art. `~/Projects/tools` is 79 shell scripts, of which 36 are
`_remote-*` payloads shipped to the host and 8 are `probe-*` drivers. Its README
states the convention: "`probe-*` never changes anything and never prints a
secret — environment variable names only, never values, so output is safe to
paste into a doc." AGENTS.md calls that directory the capability spec connectors
should grow toward, and says to promote proven behaviour rather than redesign it.

Promoting it as things stand would mean every read-only probe carries `--ack`,
which trains an operator — and worse, an agent — to pass `--ack` reflexively.
The gate then protects nothing, because the habit is established on the harmless
calls. An acknowledgment that is required for everything is an acknowledgment
that means nothing.

The fix has a natural shape: let an operation declare read intent, the way
`can_health` and `can_destroy` already do on the connector's capability block,
and reserve `--ack` for the ones that declare a write. `cerberus ssh status`
already lives on that side of the line and needs no `--ack`. Nothing blocks
this; it is a classification change plus whatever read-only verbs the probes
need.

data.unlocks_when: operations declare read-only intent, or a probe/read verb is added beside exec

records.name: No PTY, so no privilege elevation — and the proven remote workflow needs it
records.summary: The ssh connector never requests a PTY, and the work host's sudo refuses without one, so `sudo -n docker inspect` and every other elevated step in the proven tooling is unreachable through Cerberus.
records.confidence_label: zero RequestPty matches in the repo; the host's sudo behaviour documented in-line in the prior-art scripts
records.body:
WP-8 is already briefed as a known gap: `ssh exec` has no privilege elevation.
This record sharpens it, because the obstacle is not just missing code.

`RequestPty` does not appear anywhere in the repo. `APIBackend.Exec` opens a
session, sets stdout and stderr buffers, and calls `session.Run` — no PTY
request, no terminal modes. And the target host requires one:
`~/Projects/tools/lib/common.sh` documents it in-line against its `rsudo`
helper — "Needs a tty — sudo on this host refuses without one ('sorry, you must
have a tty to run sudo'), which is why every ssh here is -t rather than a bare
ssh."

So adding a `sudo` prefix to `exec` would not work. Elevation needs the
connector to be able to allocate a PTY first, which is a transport change rather
than a verb change.

The knock-on is specific and already verified. Docker introspection on the work
host is done in the prior art as `rsh "sudo -n docker inspect ..."`, precisely
because `cburks` is not in the `docker` group, and that same group membership is
what makes `cerberus docker ps -H ssh://...` fail with `permission denied` on
`/var/run/docker.sock` (CERB-TOOL-225). The connector's own error message
suggests "run docker under sudo" as a recovery it cannot itself take.

The same helper file records the failure modes a PTY brings with it, which any
implementation should read before starting: never capture a tty'd ssh in `$( )`,
because a tty'd ssh whose stdout is a pipe has hung in practice with no output;
and quote each argument for the remote shell individually, because joining
arguments with spaces silently shifted every later argument by one and produced
a SQL error about a column named after half a display name. Prefer `sudo -n`
when a value is genuinely needed in a variable, so it fails immediately rather
than waiting on a prompt nobody can see.

Nothing blocks this beyond effort and care. It is must-have because every
elevated step in the workflow Cerberus is meant to absorb depends on it.

data.unlocks_when: the connector can request a PTY, or elevation is modelled explicitly (WP-8)

records.name: No composite stage-and-run verb for remote scripts
records.summary: The proven remote workflow is put-a-script-then-run-it; Cerberus has ssh put and ssh exec but no composition, and 36 of the 79 prior-art scripts are built on that single pattern.
records.confidence_label: pattern counted across ~/Projects/tools; the Cerberus operation lists taken from connectors describe ssh

relationships.note: the pattern runs the staged script as root

records.body:
`run_remote` in `~/Projects/tools/lib/common.sh` is four lines — check the
script exists, `scp` it to the host's home directory, then run it there as root
— and 36 of the 79 scripts in that repo are built on it, paired with a
`_remote-*.sh` payload each. Its comment explains why it exists rather than
inline commands: "anything with nested quotes, templates or Python belongs in a
file, not in a string that three shells take a turn at parsing."

Cerberus has the two halves. `cerberus ssh put` and `cerberus ssh get` work and
are in the connector's operation list. What it does not have is the composition,
and the composition is where the value is: staging a script sidesteps the
three-shell quoting problem that the prior art learned the hard way, including
the Go template with `$k` and `$v` in it that has to survive a local shell, ssh
and a remote shell untouched.

Ranked nice-to-have rather than must-have only because it is a convenience over
two verbs that already exist, and because it is blocked behind CERB-GAP-640 in
practice — the pattern runs the staged script as root, which Cerberus cannot do
yet. Recursive transfer (WP-9, already briefed) is the other prerequisite for
staging anything larger than a single file.

data.unlocks_when: a run_script verb stages a local file and executes it remotely, with elevation once that exists

records.name: No remote log retrieval
records.summary: The ssh connector reports can_logs: false, so reading a log on the work host is still a shell-script job.
records.confidence_label: can_logs: false taken from connectors describe ssh; the prior art's log scripts counted

relationships.note: the local equivalent works

records.body:
`cerberus connectors describe ssh` reports `can_logs: false`, and the live
config's own comment on the `muctlvaig` resource says the same: "can_health:
true, but can_build: false and can_logs: false ... It does NOT manage the remote
services or build them."

The prior art disagrees about how central this is. `~/Projects/tools` has
`nanite/logs.sh` with its `_remote-logs.sh` payload, `workday-ess/71-log-window.sh`
with `_remote-log-window.sh`, and 167 captured run logs under `out/` — and the
whole reason `70-audit-gate.sh` exists is to read a remote log to decide whether
an approval gate actually fired, because "the smoke test's own verdict is a
report *about* the gate, not the gate itself." Reading a remote log is not a
convenience in this workflow; it is how questions get settled.

Must-have, and small: the local equivalent already works well
(CERB-TOOL-115), the transport exists, and the operation is a bounded read.
The only design question is where the log paths come from, since the ssh
connector models a host rather than the processes on it. Nothing blocks it.

data.unlocks_when: an ssh logs or tail operation lands, or exec gains a read-only lane that makes it unnecessary

records.name: Cerberus emits no traces
records.summary: There is no OpenTelemetry dependency and no otel/otlp reference in the source; the jaeger resource is a collector Cerberus supervises for other applications, not an integration.
records.confidence_label: go.mod and a case-insensitive source grep both empty
records.body:
`go.mod` has no `go.opentelemetry.io` entry, and a case-insensitive grep for
`otel`, `opentelemetry` or `otlp` across the Go source returns nothing. Cerberus
emits no spans and no metrics.

`jaeger` is a registered resource because the applications Cerberus supervises —
`tesseract-api`, `hadron-daemon`, `torque-api` — send spans to it. Cerberus
supervises the collector and health-checks its `health_check` extension on
:13133; the live config even carries a comment distinguishing that endpoint from
the UI on :16686. That is the whole of the relationship. Do not read the presence
of the resource as integration.

Nice-to-have rather than must-have because the request volume is low and the
existing log plus the snapshot recorder cover most operational questions. It
becomes more interesting alongside CERB-GAP-630, since a span carrying caller
identity across the socket into a connector operation would answer the audit
question and the latency question at once.

data.unlocks_when: an OTel SDK is wired into the socket server and connector lanes

records.name: Monitor cadence and restart budget are not configurable
records.summary: The 30-second check interval, three-attempt default and ten-second cooldown are compiled in; only the per-resource attempt count and cooldown can be overridden.
records.confidence_label: defaults read from the code; schema and config confirmed to carry no monitor keys
records.body:
`cmd_daemon.go` constructs the monitor with `DefaultResourceMonitorConfig()`
and nothing else: a 30-second `CheckInterval`, three `DefaultMaxRestartAttempts`
and a ten-second `DefaultRestartCooldown`. A resource can override the last two
through `max_restart_attempts` and `restart_cooldown` in its spec. The check
interval cannot be changed at all, and `schema/cerberus.yaml.schema.json`
contains no monitor or alert keys of any kind.

Thirty seconds is a reasonable default and nothing here argues with it. The gap
is that there is no way to shorten it for a resource that matters or lengthen it
for one that is expensive to poll, and no way to discover the value short of
reading the source — it is not in the health response either (see
CERB-GAP-645), even though `DaemonHealth` has a `monitor_interval` field for it.
Small, nothing blocking.

data.unlocks_when: MonitorConfig is populated from the config file rather than DefaultResourceMonitorConfig

records.name: Monitor state is invisible
records.summary: ResourceMonitor keeps failure counts, last-restart times and last errors in memory and exposes none of them; the v1 monitor's GetStatus has no v2 equivalent.
records.confidence_label: no accessor on ResourceMonitor; DaemonHealth fields confirmed empty in the live response

relationships.note: the same blind spot alerting would have filled

records.body:
The frozen v1 monitor has `GetStatus()` returning a `MonitorStatus` with
`Running`, `CheckInterval` and per-service `FailureCount` and `LastRestart`.
`ResourceMonitor`, the one that actually runs, has no equivalent: its
`failureCount`, `lastRestart` and `lastError` maps are private and there is no
accessor. `DaemonHealth` has a `monitor_interval` field, and the live
`cerberus_health` response omits it, so it is empty.

The practical effect is that a resource which has burned two of its three
restart attempts looks identical to one that has never failed, and a resource
that has exhausted its budget looks identical to one that is simply stopped. The
information exists in the daemon's memory; nothing reads it out.

This compounds CERB-GAP-632. With no alerting and no status surface, a resource
that has given up restarting is discoverable only by grepping
`~/.cerberus/cerberus.log` for `max_restarts_exceeded`. Small effort, nothing
blocking.

data.unlocks_when: ResourceMonitor gains a status accessor and DaemonHealth carries it

records.name: LogAudit drops its operation argument
records.summary: Closed in P1-4b by deletion: LogAudit had no callers and was superseded by internal/audit, so it was removed rather than fixed.
records.confidence_label: read directly; the single historical log line shows the missing field

relationships.note: the audit log that superseded it

records.body:
`LogAudit(operation, serviceID, reason, taskID, sessionID string)` builds its
attribute list from `serviceID` and `reason`, appends `task_id` and `session_id`
when non-empty, and logs `lifecycle.audit`. `operation` is accepted and never
used. Go permits an unused parameter, so this compiles and no linter in the
`make lint` set flags it.

The single `lifecycle.audit` entry in `~/.cerberus/cerberus.log`, dated
2026-03-23, shows exactly the resulting shape: `service`, `reason`, and no
indication of what happened to the service.

It is a one-line fix and it is must-have, because the whole point of the
function is to answer "what was done, to what, by whom" and it silently drops
the first third. It is filed separately from CERB-GAP-630 because fixing the
trail without fixing this would produce a trail that still cannot answer the
question. Marked blocked on nothing but CERB-GAP-630 giving the function a
caller — there is no value in fixing the field of a function nobody calls.

## Since P1-4a

The audit log was built in `internal/audit` rather than on `LogAudit`, which
still has no callers and still drops `operation`. It is now dead code
superseded by the audit sink. The fix is to delete it, not to add the field.

**Closed in P1-4b.** `LogAudit` is deleted from `internal/service/lifecycle_log.go`; `InitLifecycleLog` and `GetLogger` stay. The audit log in `internal/audit` records the operation on every record.

data.unlocks_when: LogAudit is deleted: internal/audit (P1-4a) replaced it, and it still has no callers — done in P1-4b

records.name: Nothing on this machine exercises os_service or run_from: artifact
records.summary: All ten resources are dev_session and workspace-backed, so the launchd installer, artifact staleness detection, deploy/apply/sync and most of resource doctor have no live coverage here.
records.confidence_label: confirmed in the resource list, the live config, and doctor's single-check output
records.body:
This is a coverage gap rather than a missing feature, and it is recorded here so
that no other area's maturity claim rests on this machine.

Every one of the ten registered resources reports `mode: dev_session` and
`run_from: workspace`, and the artifact column in `cerberus resource list` is
blank for all of them. Nothing here is `os_service`. The live config's own header
says as much and says why: "mode: os_service + run_from: artifact is the fuller
model — build an artifact, install it, supervise via launchd — and is worth
moving to per-app once each build strategy is verified."

So on this machine there is no live evidence for: the launchd plist builder
(including the `EnvironmentVariables` it emits, which is the contrast that makes
CERB-GAP-637 legible), `launchctl kickstart -k` on a managed resource, artifact
staleness detection and the `artifact_stale` state, the `resolveArtifactSource`
build-output resolution that AGENTS.md warns can install a binary the build
never wrote, or the `deploy` / `apply` / `sync` / `ensure-fresh` verbs that
operate on an installed copy. `cerberus resource doctor` demonstrates the
shortfall directly: on a dev_session resource it runs one check,
`runtime_status`, because every other check it advertises applies only to
`os_service`.

Those paths are tested — Area 1 owns judging how well. But `shipped` means
runnable today by someone who is not the author, and this machine cannot
corroborate any of it. Anything in the catalog claiming live maturity for the
artifact or launchd lanes should be `test`, not `live`, unless another machine
supplies the evidence. Small effort to close — one migrated resource would do
it — and nothing blocks it but the caution in the config header.

data.unlocks_when: at least one resource is migrated to os_service with run_from: artifact, or the maturity claim is qualified

records.name: The overview counters do not sum
records.summary: The console reports ten resources beside eight running, one stopped and zero needing attention; the unsupervised resource is counted in the inventory and in none of the runtime buckets.
records.confidence_label: read live from /api/overview and corroborated in the snapshot history

relationships.note: same root cause in Health's filter

records.body:
`GET /api/overview` on the running console reports `inventory.resources: 10`
alongside `runtime: {running: 8, stopped: 1, attention: 0}`. The tenth,
`muctlvaig`, is bucketed nowhere, and the same arithmetic is baked into every
one of the 1792 samples in `~/.cerberus/state/overview_snapshots.json`, so the
trend history carries it too.

Same root cause as CERB-GAP-635 — the runtime counts derive from `Health`, which
filters unsupervised resources out before counting. Ranked nice-to-have because
it misleads mildly rather than dangerously; a reader notices the numbers do not
add up and goes looking. Worth fixing in the same change, since an
`unsupervised` bucket is the honest answer on both surfaces.

data.unlocks_when: the runtime buckets gain an unsupervised count, or the inventory total excludes what it cannot bucket

records.name: The main database is never created
records.summary: cerberus path resolves a main.db under the default workspace and that directory is empty; nothing on this machine persists state to SQLite.
records.confidence_label: path resolved live; directory confirmed empty

relationships.note: the audit trail would be the first real tenant

records.body:
`cerberus path` resolves `main-db` to
`~/.local/share/cerberus/workspaces/default/main.db`, and there is a
`--db` global flag and a `CERBERUS_DB_PATH` environment variable to override it.
The directory was created on 2026-09-15 at 17:31 and is empty. No database file
exists.

Recorded as speculative because nothing is currently broken by its absence — all
durable state on this machine lives in `~/.cerberus/config.yaml`, the JSON
snapshot store and the append-only log, and that is working. It is worth having
in the catalog for two reasons: a reader who sees `--db` in every help output
will otherwise assume a database is in play, and the audit trail in
CERB-GAP-630 is the obvious first tenant for one. If that gap is closed by
writing to the log instead, this row stays empty and that is a fine answer —
but it should be a decision rather than an accident.

data.unlocks_when: a feature needs durable state — an audit trail being the obvious candidate

records.name: A plugin's dry run still demands --ack
records.summary: Closed in P1-5: a dry run of a plugin operation whose preview the operator accepted in the install review runs without --ack and is recorded plugin_claimed; a plugin still pending review keeps the --ack requirement.
records.confidence_label: policy.go, manager.go and TestAcceptedPreviewStandsInForAck read and run on the P1-5 branch

relationships.note: the acknowledgment gate this weakens
the first plugin with dry-runnable writes
a plugin dry run is plugin-claimed

records.body:
OperationAllowed checks acknowledgment before the call reaches the plugin, and it does not look at dry_run. For a built-in that is fine: dryRunPreview answers the dry run in the host and never reaches the gate. A plugin has no host-side preview, so its dry run goes through the gate like a real write.

The obvious fix is not safe. Letting a dry run past the gate trusts the plugin to honour dry_run, and a plugin that ignored it would run an unacknowledged write. So the gate costs friction and buys a real guarantee. The honest fixes are to have an operator accept the plugin's dry-run claim at install, or to fold this into per-target write policy, where a dry run can be allowed without a human while the write still needs one. Verifying the claim is off the table: Cerberus does not sign or vet plugins (Decision 12 in `docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md`).

The friction is not only cosmetic. An operator trained to type --dry-run --ack will type --ack. Against a real cluster the plugin makes the dry run safe regardless, because the API server enforces dryRun=All, but that is a property of this plugin, not of the host.

## Since PR #49

The host no longer passes every dry run through. `Manager.ExecuteOperation`
forwards a dry run only for an operation whose manifest declares `supports_dry`;
anything else is refused as `preview_unsupported` and the plugin is never
called. The ack check in `OperationAllowed` still runs first, so a destructive
plugin operation's dry run still needs `--ack`. PR #49 kept that on purpose,
because the forwarded preview is the plugin's own unverified claim
(CERB-DEC-814). The phase plan orders the fix: the install review comes before
plugin dry runs lose `--ack`.

## Scheduled

The P1 cut in `docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md` (2026-09-25) schedules this: P1-5 builds the install review, which the phase plan puts before plugin dry runs lose `--ack`.

Deliberate through P1: `pluginhost.OperationAllowed` runs before the dry-run check and asks for acknowledgment on any operation whose contract needs it. Decision 7 keeps it that way until the P1-5 install review makes a plugin's preview claim something the operator accepted.

## Closed in P1-5

`pluginhost.PreviewAccepted` is true for a reviewed plugin (accepted digest, not `review_pending`) and an operation whose effective preview is not `none`. `Manager.ExecuteOperation` then treats the dry run as acknowledged for the gate, and still sends the plugin the caller's own `acknowledged` flag. The real run still needs `--ack`. Every plugin dry run is recorded with `preview: plugin_claimed` on both the admin lane and the managed direct route. A plugin installed before reviews existed has accepted nothing, so its dry runs keep needing `--ack` until `managed review <id>`. `TestAcceptedPreviewStandsInForAck` covers both.

data.unlocks_when: The P1 install review lets an operator accept a plugin's declared preview, after which a declared-and-accepted dry run may pass without --ack — done in P1-5

records.name: DaemonUnreachableError covers any transport error, so a sent mutation is retried in-process with the self-guard inert
records.summary: Six resource lifecycle verbs send an operation to the daemon and, on any transport-layer error including a mid-request EOF, re-run the same operation in-process where the serving-daemon guard and opMu do not apply — which the CLI's own comment says must never happen.
records.confidence_label: Both wrapping sites and all twelve fallback sites read directly; the contradiction with cmd_transport.go's stated invariant is explicit in the source. Not staged live, because reproducing it means killing the daemon mid-mutation.

relationships.note: the degraded-mode story is not safe until the classification is narrowed
the guard is inert on the path this reaches
the EOF this misclassifies is the exact failure mode that decision exists to prevent
an in-process retry is serialized by neither lock
resource deploy is the worst case
resource remove is the least idempotent

records.body:
`SocketClient.doJSON` and `doJSONStream` both end with:

    resp, err := c.http.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        // Distinguish "daemon not running" (dial failure) from other
        // errors so the caller can surface the operator-facing hint.
        return &DaemonUnreachableError{Path: c.dialPath, Err: err}
    }

The comment claims a distinction the code does not make. `http.Client.Do` returns an error for a dial failure, for a context or client timeout, and for a connection reset or EOF part-way through a request. All three become `DaemonUnreachableError`.

`cmd/cerberus/cmd_resource.go` then matches on that type in twelve places. Six are reads and the fallback is right. Six are mutations — `deploy`, `apply`, `reload`, `stop`, `sync`, `remove` — and all six follow the same shape: send to the daemon, and if the error is `DaemonUnreachableError`, run the identical operation against a freshly constructed `ResourceRuntimeService`.

`cmd/cerberus/cmd_transport.go`, eight files away, states the rule the connector lane follows: *"Choose a transport before executing anything. Once an operation is sent, an error must never trigger an in-process retry of a possible mutation."* `commandSocket` implements it by pinging first with a 2-second budget and only routing in-process when that probe comes back unreachable. The resource lane does not use it.

Three concrete consequences, in increasing order of cost.

**Double execution.** A daemon that accepts `POST /resources/<id>/remove`, unloads the launchd job, and then dies or times out before replying hands the CLI a `DaemonUnreachableError`. The CLI runs `RemoveResource` again in-process. `remove` is the least idempotent verb in the lane.

**The self-guard goes inert at the worst moment.** `refuseSelfMutation` returns `nil` unless `servingDaemon` is true, and `ProtectServingDaemon` has exactly one non-test caller. So `cerberus resource deploy cerberus-daemon-service` is refused by the daemon — and if that refusal cannot be delivered because the daemon restarted, the CLI performs the deploy the guard just refused. CERB-DEC-163's own account of the hazard is "the call dies on EOF": that is precisely the error being reclassified as *the daemon is not running*.

**Silence.** Nothing tells the operator the transport changed. Output on the fallback path is identical to output on the socket path.

The fix is small and already written once: route the resource lane through `commandSocket`, so the transport is chosen by a ping and a post-send error stays an error. Narrowing the wrap to genuine dial failures (`errors.Is(err, syscall.ECONNREFUSED)` or `ENOENT` on the socket path) is the complementary half, and would also stop a slow daemon being reported as a stopped one.

`must-have`: it converts a daemon restart into an unguarded self-mutation, and the invariant it violates is already stated in the codebase. Nobody is blocking it; only the work is missing.

## Shipped in PR #34

`fix/open-findings` (merged as #34, commit f5bbf93) narrows `DaemonUnreachableError` to genuine dial failures via `requestNeverSent` in `internal/cerbapi/socket_client.go`, and routes all seven resource mutation sites (the task named six; `resource remove` was a seventh) through `resourceMutationSocket` in `cmd/cerberus/cmd_resource.go`, choosing the transport before sending. Covered by `internal/cerbapi/transport_classification_test.go` and `cmd/cerberus/cmd_resource_mutation_transport_test.go`. `unlocks_when` is met.

data.unlocks_when: the resource lane selects its transport with commandSocket before sending, and DaemonUnreachableError is limited to dial failures
data.effort: small — one helper already exists and is used by the connector lane; the change is twelve call sites and one error classification

records.name: Nothing serializes a resource mutation across processes except the build lock
records.summary: opMu serializes mutations inside one daemon and the source-tree flock covers the build phase, so apply, sync, reload, stop and remove — and every verb on a resource with no build strategy — have no cross-process guard at all.
records.confidence_label: Every lock and every caller enumerated from source; no race staged, because staging one needs two concurrent live mutations

relationships.note: the concurrency story is incomplete outside the build phase
the in-process fallback is the likeliest second process
a misclassified transport error is how the second process appears without anyone asking for it
the monitor is the third concurrent actor
a pipeline run is a fourth
config.yaml has neither a backup nor a writer lock

records.body:
There are two locks and they do not meet.

`opMu` is process-wide and held for the whole of `ReloadResource`, `StopResource`, `DeployResource`, `ApplyResource`, `SyncResource` and `RemoveResource`, and `resource_monitor.go` takes it before acting. Inside one daemon, everything queues.

`buildlock.Acquire` is cross-process — an flock on the git toplevel — but `WithBuildLock` has exactly three callers: `DeployResource`, the pipeline `build` and `deploy` actions, and `BuildProcessResultContext`. It also returns a no-op when `HasBuildStrategy(spec)` is false.

So the uncovered set is: `apply`, `sync`, `reload`, `stop` and `remove` from any second process, plus *every* verb on a resource that declares no `build_strategy`. On this machine that is the whole estate — all ten resources are `mode: dev_session`.

The second process is not hypothetical. Three ways to get one without asking:

- the CLI's in-process fallback, which fires whenever a socket call returns any transport error (CERB-GAP-730), while the daemon is still loaded and its monitor still running;
- `cerberus web`, which is a separately started long-lived process (CERB-GAP-445) — its API proxies the socket, so it is safe, but it is another process holding the same config;
- an agent using `--config` on the pipeline lane, which deliberately bypasses the daemon's registry and constructs its own runtime service.

What a race costs depends on the verb. `reload` twice is harmless. `apply` racing `remove` writes and deletes the same install layout and launchd plist; `stop` racing the monitor's auto-restart flips the per-service pause file under a decision already taken; two `apply`s write the same plist path, and CERB-DEC-165's fresh-inode-and-rename covers the artifact but not the plist or the pid metadata.

The fix mirrors what already exists: take a cross-process lock keyed on the install root — not the source tree, since these verbs may have no source tree — for the same six verbs `opMu` covers, and reuse `buildlock`'s shape, which is already fail-fast, crash-safe and names its holder.

`must-have` rather than `nice-to-have` for one reason: agents are first-class callers here, two of them can be issued the same deploy by different sessions, and the failure is silent — there is no error to see, only a resource in a state neither caller asked for.

data.unlocks_when: the five unlocked lifecycle verbs take a cross-process lock keyed on the install root, in the same fail-fast shape as buildlock
data.effort: medium — the lock primitive exists; choosing the key and threading release through six call sites is the work

records.name: Two subsystems ship in the binary with no callers, and one of them was a fix
records.summary: internal/procscan and internal/selfexec have zero references anywhere outside their own packages; procscan's cascade-kill lost both call sites in the v2 cut-over, which silently re-opened the stale-subprocess bug it was written for.
records.confidence_label: grep for both import paths across the whole tree returns nothing; the losing commit identified by git log -S

relationships.note: the artifact join no longer kills processes running the replaced inode
selfexec.WatchAndExit was removed from cerberus mcp and has no other caller
cascade-kill was part of the rebuild path the supervision lane replaced
nothing here exercises run_from: artifact, which is why nobody has noticed

records.body:
`grep -rn 'hollis-labs/cerberus/internal/procscan'` over the whole repository returns **nothing** — not a caller, not a test outside the package. The same grep for `internal/selfexec` returns nothing. Together that is nineteen source files compiled into every Cerberus binary with no reachable entry point.

The two have different histories and only one is a loss.

**procscan is a fix that was undone.** `713dffb` — "feat(rebuild): cascade-kill stale subprocesses on rebuild (CERB-3)" — wired it into both rebuild surfaces, the `cerberus rebuild` CLI command and the `RebuildService` RPC handler. Its commit message names the exact bug: `cerberus rebuild clockwork-api` replaced `$GOBIN/clockwork` on disk but left Nanite-spawned `clockwork mcp` subprocesses executing the pre-merge inode indefinitely. The package resolves a service's command binary, captures its `(device, inode)` before the build, and SIGTERM/SIGKILLs anything still running that inode afterwards, filtered by UID, skipping interpreter commands whose binary the build does not replace. It has darwin and linux enumerators and its own test suite.

`0c37758`, "Finish Cerberus v2 runtime cut-over", deleted `cmd_rebuild.go` along with `cmd_up.go`, `cmd_down.go`, `cmd_pause.go` and the rest of the v1 verbs. `resource deploy` took over, and it does not cascade-kill. So the behaviour that stopped a stale child process outliving a rebuild is gone, the code that implements it is still shipping, and no record anywhere says the trade was made.

**selfexec is a decision that left its subject unreferenced.** CERB-DEC-470 records that `selfexec.WatchAndExit` must stay out of `cerberus mcp`, and it is out. What the decision does not say — because from inside `cerberus mcp` you cannot see it — is that there is no other caller. `9e5a7dd` removed the only one.

Two defensible resolutions and the catalog should force the choice rather than leave it, exactly as CERB-GAP-439 argues for `internal/infra`. Either cascade-kill is still wanted, in which case `DeployResource` and `SyncResource` are where it belongs, after the install and before activation, guarded by the same UID filter; or it is not, in which case both packages go and CERB-DEC-470 gains a sentence saying the watcher was retired rather than merely unwired.

`nice-to-have`, and the priority is honest rather than comfortable: nothing on this machine uses `run_from: artifact` (CERB-GAP-649), so the bug cascade-kill fixed cannot currently bite here. It becomes `must-have` the first time an artifact-backed resource spawns children — which is what the daemon and every MCP-serving resource do.

data.unlocks_when: either cascade-kill is re-wired into DeployResource/SyncResource, or both packages are deleted and CERB-DEC-470 records the retirement
data.effort: small to delete; small to re-wire, since the call-site shape is recorded in 713dffb's commit message

records.name: The pipeline lane has no acknowledgment gate and no dry-run
records.summary: Half closed in PR #63: a pipeline run is exec and needs acknowledgment on every surface; it still has no dry-run.
records.confidence_label: Flag sets read from the installed binary's help and from source; every action type read. Not executed — no pipeline is declared here, and running one was out of scope.

relationships.note: the lane is not safe to declare a pipeline in until this exists
the acknowledgment capability this lane sits outside
no surface tells a caller which operations need --ack, and this one needs it and does not say so
write operations not flagged destructive
nothing validates the action types at author time either
mcp-http fronts cerberus_pipeline_run with no authentication
the verb this is about
run is exec

records.body:
`cerberus pipeline run --help` against the installed binary registers no flags at all beyond `--help`. There is no `--ack`, no `--dry-run`, no confirmation prompt, and `cerberus_pipeline_run`'s input schema has one required property, `pipeline_id`.

What a run can do: `deploy` a resource, `stop` a resource, and `shell`, which is `exec.CommandContext(ctx, "sh", "-c", a.command)` with `CombinedOutput` in an optional working directory. In the daemon that runs as the daemon's user with launchd's environment; through the CLI's own fallback it runs as the operator with the operator's environment.

The asymmetry is the finding. `cerberus ssh exec` requires `--ack`. `cerberus forge exec` requires `--ack`. `cerberus server destroy` requires `--ack` and supports `--dry-run`. `cerberus cloudflare dns delete` requires `--ack`. All of those run one command against one system. `cerberus pipeline run` can run several of them, plus arbitrary local shell, and requires nothing — so the acknowledgment lane that CERB-CAP-604 owns has a hole the width of the pipeline lane.

For an agent caller the gap is sharper still. `cerberus_pipeline_run` is reachable from `cerberus mcp`, from the daemon's own stdio MCP server, and from `cerberus mcp-http`, which has no authentication at all (CERB-GAP-443). An agent that can list pipelines can run any of them, and cannot read one first, because there is no `cerberus_pipeline_show` (CERB-TOOL-721).

A `--dry-run` here would be cheap and unusually useful, because a pipeline is a declaration: resolving it already produces the full action list with names, so a preview is a walk over `Pipeline.Stages` printing `action.Name()` per level, with no per-action preview logic of the kind CERB-GAP-277 describes for the connector lane.

`must-have`, with the caveat that makes it tractable: nothing is declared under `pipelines:` on this machine, so today the gap is latent. It stops being latent the moment somebody writes the first pipeline, and the first pipeline anyone writes will be a deploy.

**Acknowledgment landed in PR #63.** `pipeline.Definition()` classes `run` as exec (CERB-DEC-820). `RunPipeline` passes the runtime gate before its lock, so `cerberus pipeline run <id>` needs `--ack`, `cerberus_pipeline_run` needs `acknowledged`, and the console's Run asks in a confirm step. The stages call the local connector directly and are covered by the run's one acknowledgment. There is still no dry-run: the contract declares `preview: none`.

data.unlocks_when: pipeline run gains --dry-run that prints the resolved action list, and --ack required for any pipeline containing a stop, deploy or shell action
data.effort: small for the dry-run, since Resolve already yields the action list; small for the ack, which is a flag and a predicate over the resolved actions

records.name: Pipeline rollback is a no-op for the two actions that change anything
records.summary: The executor rolls completed stages back in reverse on failure, but Build and Deploy both return nil from Rollback, so a pipeline that fails after deploying reports failed and leaves the new artifact installed and running.
records.confidence_label: Every Rollback implementation read directly; not exercised, because no pipeline is declared here

relationships.note: the lane advertises rollback and does not deliver it where it matters
undoing a deploy means keeping the previous artifact, which the install layout would have to retain
installing to a fresh inode and renaming is what would make a real rollback possible
the plugin lane has the same shape of gap — no rollback or version pinning

records.body:
`Executor.Run` ends with:

    // Rollback completed stages in reverse on failure
    if firstErr != nil {
        e.rollback(ctx, completed, env)

and `rollback` calls `action.Rollback` on each completed stage in reverse order, logging rollback errors rather than propagating them. The mechanism is correct and the implementations are mostly empty.

- `Start.Rollback` calls `Stop`. `Stop.Rollback` calls `Start`. Genuine inverses.
- `HealthWait.Rollback` returns nil. Correct — waiting has nothing to undo.
- `Shell.Rollback` returns nil, with a comment: "shell actions have no automatic rollback". Honest.
- `Build.Rollback` returns nil, with a comment: "builds are not rollbackable". Defensible, since a build writes an output the install step then consumes.
- `Deploy.Rollback` returns nil, with **no comment at all**. This is the one that matters: deploy builds, installs over the live artifact, and activates.

So a three-stage pipeline that deploys in stage one, health-waits in stage two and fails in stage three reports `failed`, runs its rollback, and leaves the newly deployed artifact installed and the service running it. The operator reads "failed" and has a half-applied change with no record of what was applied.

A real rollback is possible but not free: it needs the previous artifact retained, which is exactly what CERB-DEC-165's install-to-a-fresh-inode-and-rename makes feasible — the old inode survives until nothing references it. Keeping a `previous` slot per resource and pointing `Deploy.Rollback` at it is the shape.

The cheaper and possibly better answer is to stop advertising it: have `Deploy.Rollback` return an explicit "deploy is not rollbackable; resource <id> is running the newly deployed artifact" that the executor surfaces in `RunResult.Error`, so a failed pipeline names what it left behind. That is honest, and it is one string.

`nice-to-have` on effort and on today's exposure — no pipeline exists here. It is the second half of CERB-GAP-733: together they say the pipeline lane can make an unacknowledged change and then not tell you it stayed.

data.unlocks_when: either Deploy.Rollback restores the previous artifact slot, or it returns an explicit not-rollbackable error that RunResult surfaces
data.effort: small to make it honest; medium to make it real, since it needs a retained previous artifact per resource

records.name: Redaction passes `Authorization: Basic <credential>` through intact
records.summary: The assignment rule captures one whitespace-delimited word, so it redacts the scheme and leaves the credential; `bearer` is the only scheme-aware rule and there is no `Basic` equivalent.
records.confidence_label: Reproduced directly against redact.Text; the base64 in the output decodes to the input credential

relationships.note: a redactor that passes a credential through is not partial in the same sense as one that eats guidance
redaction sits on the error path of all five surfaces, so the leak is on all five

records.body:
Every previous finding in this family has been the safety net eating the
guidance it was meant to protect. This one is the inverse, and worse: a real
credential survives.

    IN : Authorization: Basic Y2J1cmtzOnN1cGVyc2VjcmV0cGFzc3dvcmQ=
    OUT: Authorization: [REDACTED] Y2J1cmtzOnN1cGVyc2VjcmV0cGFzc3dvcmQ=

The base64 decodes to `cburks:supersecretpassword`. The word `Basic` was
redacted; the credential was not.

The mechanism is an interaction between two rules in `internal/redact/redact.go`.
`bearer` covers `Bearer <token>` and nothing else. `assignment` matches the key
`Authorization` and then takes `[^\s,;&<>]+` as the value — one
whitespace-delimited word. For `Bearer <token>` that is harmless only because
`bearer` already fired and rewrote the token first; confirm the ordering
dependency by checking that `Authorization: Bearer eyJ…` yields
`Authorization: [REDACTED] [REDACTED]` and that it is `bearer`, not
`assignment`, doing the work. For `Basic <base64>` nothing fires first, so
`assignment` redacts `Basic` and stops at the space.

So the shape `Authorization: <scheme> <credential>` is safe only for the one
scheme that has a dedicated rule, and `Digest` and `Negotiate` are open too.

This reaches operators and agents. `redact.Text` runs on every connector error
path, and a connector that echoes a failing request's headers into an error —
a normal thing to do — publishes the credential to CLI stdout, the daemon
socket response, `~/.cerberus/` logs, and MCP tool results, which land in an
agent's context window and are then sent to a model provider.

The fix is to make the value side of an `Authorization`-like assignment consume
the rest of the value rather than its first word: an auth header's value is
scheme-plus-credential and is one unit. Adding a `Basic` twin of the `bearer`
rule closes this instance and leaves the next scheme open, so prefer the general
fix. Acceptance: a table test over `Basic`, `Bearer`, `Digest` and a bare token
asserting no credential material survives, with the existing `Bearer JWT` and
`use Bearer auth` guidance cases still passing unredacted.

data.unlocks_when: The value-boundary redaction AGENTS.md describes would remove the rule interaction entirely

records.name: The names-only exemption is wired into the JSON walk only, not prose
records.summary: `NamesOnlyKey` has one call site, inside redact.JSON's walk, so `missing_secrets` survives in a DTO and is still eaten when the same field is rendered into an error message.
records.confidence_label: Call sites enumerated; both the missing_secrets and the f-string case reproduced against redact.Text

relationships.note: the documented escape hatch does not cover the path the error text actually takes
the missing test discipline is what would have caught the gap between the two paths
MissingSecretsError is the prose that carries missing_secrets to the operator

records.body:
`AGENTS.md` says the redactor "has since learned to … skip fields that carry
names by construction", citing `missing_secrets` coming back as
`["[REDACTED]"]`. The fix is real but narrower than the sentence implies, and
the sentence is what a future contributor will trust.

    IN : missing_secrets: ["token"]
    OUT: missing_secrets: [REDACTED]

`NamesOnlyKey` has exactly one call site — inside the JSON `walk` in
`internal/redact/redact.go`. The prose path (`assignment` → `redactPairs`)
consults `isErrorCode` but never `NamesOnlyKey`, so the same field rendered into
a sentence is still eaten. That matters because `MissingSecretsError.Error()` in
`internal/pluginhost/secrets.go` is prose, and the entire purpose of that error
is to answer "which credential?"

A second instance of the same root cause, found while reading a Python file over
`cerberus ssh exec`:

    IN : "Authorization": f"Bearer {KEY}",
    OUT: "Authorization": [REDACTED] {KEY}",

`bearer` does not fire because `{KEY}` is not token-shaped, so `assignment`
takes the first word — `f"Bearer` — and the rendered file is now wrong in a way
that would mislead anyone reading code through Cerberus. Note the shared shape
with CERB-GAP-742: one-word value capture.

The fix is to have the prose path consult `NamesOnlyKey` the way it already
consults `isErrorCode`, with the same recursion so a real assignment sitting
behind a names-only key is still redacted. `AGENTS.md`'s redaction section then
needs amending to say which paths the exemption covers. Acceptance:
`missing_secrets: ["token"]` survives `redact.Text` intact, and a
`MissingSecretsError` carrying two secret names round-trips with both readable.

data.unlocks_when: Fixed alongside CERB-GAP-742 if the value-boundary rewrite lands

records.name: Reloading a managed plugin does not re-resolve its credentials
records.summary: `plugin managed load` reports a freshly stored credential as still missing; only a daemon restart picks it up, so the recovery instruction the error prints names a command that cannot work.
records.confidence_label: Isolated by experiment: same keychain entry, missing before a daemon kickstart and resolved after it

relationships.note: the documented recovery for a missing plugin credential does not work on this machine
the keychain entry is the last link of the credential chain the plugin host resolves through
ContextForge is the connector this was found on; its credentialed operations remain unrun

records.body:
The documented recovery for a missing plugin credential names a command that
does not do the thing it is named for.

Reproduce: write the entry the way `internal/secrets.KeychainProvider` reads it
— go-keyring, service `cerberus`, account `contextforge/token`, not
`security add-generic-password` (see `docs/secrets.md`). Run
`cerberus connectors plugin managed load contextforge` and observe
`missing_secrets: ["token"]` anyway. Then
`launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/com.fragments-engine.cerberus` and run
`plugin managed list` again: `missing_secrets` is empty and the credential is
handed over — `list_tools` stops failing as `credential_missing` and starts
failing on whatever is actually wrong with the request.

Same entry, same daemon binary, same session. The only variable is the restart,
which rules out the more alarming hypothesis this record was opened with: the
launchd-spawned daemon *can* read the login keychain. `keyring.Get` returns
`ErrNotFound` before the restart because the reload path never asks it again.

Two things follow.

**The error message is wrong, and confidently so.** It tells an operator to
store a token at `keychain://contextforge/token` "and reload the plugin —
Cerberus resolves it and hands it over", then names
`cerberus connectors plugin managed load <id>` as the command. An operator who
does exactly that sees no change and has every reason to conclude the credential
is stored wrong. Either make reload re-resolve, or say a restart is required;
the present text is the one thing it must not be, which is plausible and false.

**A credential that cannot be read is still indistinguishable from one that was
never stored.** `KeychainProvider.Get` maps `ErrNotFound` to `("", nil)` by
design, and `resolvedSecrets.Problems` — which would carry a store that refused
to unlock — is handed to `m.warn` and nowhere else, so the managed-plugin DTO
cannot report it. That was not the cause here, but nothing in the system would
have told us either way, and the comment on `Problems` already argues it should.

Acceptance: storing a credential and reloading the plugin makes the next
operation use it, without a daemon restart. Separately, a resolver that returns
an error surfaces the reason in `plugin managed list` rather than only in the
daemon's launchd stderr log.

records.name: The GitHub connector has no PATH fallback for `gh`, so it reports it missing when it is installed
records.summary: github's CLI backend resolves gh with exec.LookPath alone, so under the daemon's launchd PATH it fails and tells the operator to install gh — on a machine where gh is at /opt/homebrew/bin/gh; the Docker connector fixed exactly this with a fallback list.
records.confidence_label: Reproduced live: the error was re-run, gh's install path was checked, and the absence of a fallback was read at cli_backend.go:19 against docker's cli_backend.go:37

relationships.note: a defect in the connector this record hangs off
the same PATH defect on the build path; same root cause, different package
the connector that already carries the fix this one needs
the verb that surfaces it, and whose body repeated the false claim
the redaction defect that rides on the same error string

records.body:
`internal/connector/github/cli_backend.go:19` resolves the CLI with
`exec.LookPath("gh")` and nothing else. There is no fallback list and no
per-call override. On this machine that produces an error message that is
actively false:

```
$ cerberus github status hollis-labs/cerberus
Error: daemon: github status: credential_missing: [REDACTED] connector:
no API token and gh CLI not found — set CERBERUS_GITHUB_TOKEN or install gh

$ which gh
/opt/homebrew/bin/gh          # gh 2.101.0, installed 2026-09-16
```

`gh` is installed. The command routes through the daemon (`daemon: github
status:` in the error), and the daemon's live `PATH` is
`/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin` — read from `ps eww -p 8188`. Under exactly
that `PATH`, `command -v gh` finds nothing, so `LookPath` fails and the
connector reports the CLI as absent. The operator is told to install software
they already have.

The fix already exists one package over. `internal/connector/docker/cli_backend.go:37`
carries `fallbackDockerPaths` — `/usr/local/bin/docker`, `/opt/homebrew/bin/docker`,
`/usr/bin/docker`, `~/.docker/bin/docker` and Docker Desktop's bundled path —
with a comment naming this exact cause, plus a `CERBERUS_DOCKER_PATH` override
and a regression test (`internal/connector/docker/detect_test.go:52`) that runs
`DetectDocker` under an empty `PATH`. The Azure plugin got the same treatment
for `az`, which is why `connectors plugin managed health azure` works from the
daemon. GitHub is the connector that did not get it.

This is the third member of one family, and the only one still open:
`CERB-GAP-140` is the same defect on the build path (`go` unresolvable from the
daemon), `CERB-CAP-202` is the one that was repaired. `AGENTS.md` states the
rule — "Anything that shells out … must not assume a tool is on `PATH` just
because it resolves in your terminal. Prefer explicit paths, fallback search
locations, and per-call resolution" — and records the Docker outage that taught
it. The GitHub connector predates neither the rule nor the fix; it was simply
never revisited.

Ranked `must-have` because the cost is not a missing feature but a wrong
diagnosis. The message sends the operator to install a binary or mint a token
when the actual defect is a four-line slice literal, and it is the message every
`cerberus github` verb returns on a launchd-started daemon. Severity is bounded:
an operator with `CERBERUS_GITHUB_TOKEN` set never sees it, because the API
backend is tried first.

Blocked on nobody. The fix is `fallbackDockerPaths`' shape applied to `gh`, plus
a test asserting `DetectGH` succeeds under a minimal parent `PATH`.

data.unlocks_when: DetectGH searches fallback locations and honours an explicit override, with a test that it resolves under PATH=/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin
data.effort: small — a copy of fallbackDockerPaths plus one test

records.name: Every CLI command group exits 0 on an unknown subcommand
records.summary: cerberus <group> <typo> discards the unrecognised word, prints the group's own output or help, and exits 0 on all fourteen groups — so a mistyped verb is indistinguishable from success to any caller reading the exit code.
records.confidence_label: Exercised live against all fourteen command groups on the installed binary; exit status captured separately from output in each case

relationships.note: a hole in the CLI surface this record hangs off
the record whose body cites `cerberus connectors list`, a command this defect makes appear to exist
surface parity: the root command rejects unknown children, the groups do not

records.body:
Every command group in the CLI accepts an unknown subcommand, ignores it, runs
the group's own `RunE` or prints its help, and **exits 0**. Verified live across
all fourteen groups:

```
$ for g in resource registry docker project daemon connectors pipeline forge \
           cloudflare domain dns server ssh github; do cerberus $g bogus; done
# every one: exit status 0
```

Most groups print help text, which is merely unhelpful. Two are worse, because
they print output that reads as a successful answer:

```
$ cerberus connectors bogus
ID            TYPES       LIVE  OPERATIONS
azure         server      yes   6
...
$ echo $?
0
```

Compare a typo one level up, which behaves correctly:

```
$ cerberus healt
Error: unknown command "healt" for "cerberus"
```

So the root command rejects an unknown child and the groups do not. The cause is
that each group command carries a `RunE` (or inherits help) and no
`Args: cobra.NoArgs`, so cobra treats the unmatched word as a positional
argument and discards it.

Two concrete consequences, both already visible in this repository:

- **A script or agent cannot tell a typo from a result.** `cerberus resource
  statuss tesseract-api` exits 0 with help text. Anything that branches on the
  exit code proceeds as though the resource were healthy. This is the surface
  `AGENTS.md` says is used by agents as well as people, and an agent is exactly
  the caller that reads an exit code rather than the screen.
- **It has already misled this catalog.** `CERB-TOOL-322` cites
  `cerberus connectors list` as the command in which azure "reads like a
  built-in". There is no `connectors list` subcommand — the inventory taken from
  the installed binary lists only `describe`, `plugin` and
  `write-plugin-prototype`. The record's author ran a command that does not
  exist, got the right-looking table, and wrote it down.

`nice-to-have` rather than must-have: nothing is corrupted and the correct
output is one word away. But it is a one-line-per-group fix
(`Args: cobra.NoArgs` on the groups that take none, or
`cobra.OnlyValidArgs`), it removes a whole class of silent failure from the
surface agents drive, and the root command already demonstrates the behaviour
that is wanted.

Blocked on nobody.

data.unlocks_when: group commands declare Args: cobra.NoArgs (or OnlyValidArgs) so an unrecognised subcommand exits non-zero, with a table test over the groups

records.name: internal/procscan and internal/selfexec ship with no importer at all
records.summary: Two whole packages — a cgo-free process scanner with a raw darwin syscall, and a binary-replacement watcher — are compiled into the binary and imported by nothing, including their own non-test callers.
records.confidence_label: Import-graph grep over every .go file in the tree returns no importer for either path

relationships.note: the deferred cleanup pass that owns the verdict
the change that orphaned selfexec
the sibling inverse-sweep finding on the v1 config chain
the deploy path that has no cascade-kill equivalent

records.body:
An inverse-sweep finding that pass 1's equivalent sweep stopped short of.
`CERB-GAP-541` traced the orphaned v1 config chain; these two packages are
orphaned by a different route and were missed.

    grep -rl 'internal/procscan' over every .go file  ->  no files
    grep -rl 'internal/selfexec' over every .go file  ->  no files

Not "no production caller" — **no file in the tree names either import path**,
tests included. `internal/procscan` is fourteen files: `BinaryFingerprint`,
`PIDsByFingerprint`, `KillAndWait`, `CascadeKillStaleSubprocesses`, a
`syscall.Syscall6` call against `unix.SYS_PROC_INFO` written deliberately
without cgo because the libSystem `proc_pidpath` wrappers require it, a Linux
`/proc/<pid>/exe` implementation, uid filtering with its own regression test
against macOS `proc_bsdinfo` struct-offset drift, and a darwin-only integration
test that compiles a helper, fingerprints it, scans for it and kills it.
`internal/selfexec` is the binary-replacement watcher with its injectable
`ExitFn` and a `GO_TESTING` opt-out.

Both were wired in and then unwired, four months apart, and neither removal
mentioned the package it stranded. `selfexec` went first: `9e5a7dd` pulled
`WatchAndExit` out of `cerberus mcp` because a daemon deploy would make every
running MCP child exit at once, which is `CERB-DEC-470` — a decision worth
keeping, but it left the package with nothing to serve. `procscan` had two call
sites, the `cerberus rebuild` CLI command and the v1 `InProcessClient.RebuildService`
handler, and the v2 cut-over deleted both surfaces without comment.

The cost is not runtime — the linker drops unreferenced code — but it is not
zero either, and it differs between the two. `selfexec` is duplicated
documentation: an auditor reading it concludes Cerberus self-heals MCP
subprocesses on binary swap, and `AGENTS.md` says the opposite in so many words.
`procscan` is a lost capability wearing dead code's clothes. Its whole reason for
existing was that after `go install` replaces a binary, foreign long-lived
children keep mapping the old inode and serving pre-build behaviour
indefinitely — the symptom being a Nanite-spawned `clockwork mcp` child still
answering with pre-merge schemas. The v2 deploy path has no equivalent: nothing
in `resource deploy` notices or terminates a foreign process still executing the
replaced binary. Deleting `procscan` therefore closes that door, and keeping it
unreferenced does not hold it open.

Nobody is blocked. What is missing is the per-file verdict deferred in
`CERB-DEC-791`.

data.unlocks_when: Each package gets a verdict: delete it, or re-point it at a v2 surface — for procscan that means deciding whether resource deploy should terminate foreign processes still executing the replaced binary
data.effort: small to delete; medium to revive procscan, since it needs a v2 deploy hook and a policy about killing processes Cerberus does not own

records.name: protected has no effect on a v2 resource
records.summary: `protected: true` is parsed, round-tripped and carried onto the ManagedService a dev session builds, but IsProtected() has no caller — so nothing anywhere refuses a stop, restart or remove because a resource is protected.
records.confidence_label: IsProtected proven to have no caller by grep over every .go file; the field's parse, round-trip and mapper path read directly

relationships.note: the identical case for auto_start
the decision that narrowed protected to this one meaning
the tool that reports services_protected: 0 unconditionally
the lane that should enforce it

records.body:
The exact twin of `CERB-GAP-142`, and it was missed for the same reason: the
field works all the way up to the point where it should be read.

`protected` is declared on `ProcessSpec` (`internal/connector/local/spec.go:57`),
parsed by `SpecFromResourceConfig`, re-emitted by `ToResourceConfig` so it
survives a round trip, mapped onto the v1 `ServiceDef` in
`internal/connector/local/mapper.go`, and set on the `ManagedService` that
`dev_session.go:367` constructs. `service.IsProtected()` exists to answer the
question. Nothing calls it:

    grep -rn 'IsProtected' over every .go file -> only its own definition

So on the v2 lane `protected: true` is a comment. `cerberus resource stop`, the
MCP `cerberus_resource_stop` tool, the console's stop button and
`resource remove` all proceed exactly as they would without it. The field's
original purpose — `a89e85e` added it as a "Protected flag: blocks external stop
/restart on critical services", specifically to stop an agent over MCP from
halting something critical — is unserved, which matters more now than it did
then: the MCP surface is the one an agent drives, and `mcp-http` fronts
`resource_remove` with no authentication at all.

`CERB-TOOL-610` already records the visible symptom from the other end:
`cerberus_health` returns `services_protected: 0` and will always do so, since
it counts v1 `ManagedService` entries that the daemon never builds. That reads as
"no resources are protected" rather than "protection is not implemented", which
is the more misleading of the two.

Nothing blocks a fix. It is a check in the runtime service's stop, reload and
remove paths, and a decision about whether `--ack` or an explicit `--force`
overrides it — which is the same question `CERB-DEC-805` left open when it
narrowed `protected` to mean only "shielded from an external stop".

data.unlocks_when: The runtime service's stop, reload and remove paths consult the spec's protected flag, and an override verb is decided on
data.effort: small — the field is already parsed and carried; this is a guard in three service methods plus a decision about what overrides it

records.name: The console creates and deletes keychain secrets, which the architecture forbids
records.summary: internal/webui/infra.go calls Set and Delete on the keychain provider from its provider-settings route, so Cerberus writes secret material on one surface while every other surface and the direction document treat it as reference-only.
records.confidence_label: Provider methods and both console call sites read directly; no CLI or MCP secret-writing surface found by search

relationships.note: the delivery ranking and store-nothing rule this breaks
the reference-only chain every other surface honours
the console-only subsystem it lives in
the CSRF token that is the only thing in front of it

records.body:
`docs/control-plane-direction.md` states the rule without qualification:
"Cerberus should not store, create, rotate, update, or delete secret material.
The desired configuration contains opaque credential references only." The one
concession is narrow — "Credential management UX, if present, must be framed as
an adapter acting on an external authority rather than a Cerberus secret store."

One surface does it anyway. `cmd/cerberus/cmd_web.go:40` hands the console a
`secrets.NewKeychainProvider()` directly, and `internal/webui/infra.go` calls
`s.secrets.Set(r.Context(), id, key, value)` and
`s.secrets.Delete(r.Context(), id, key)` on the provider-settings route, plus
`s.secrets.Get(...)` when listing. `internal/secrets/keychain.go` exposes `Set`
and `Delete` for exactly this. The direction document knew: it lists "the secret
provider exposes storage mutation" among the current-model tensions.

Everywhere else the boundary holds, and the contrast is what makes this a defect
rather than a design. `CERB-CAP-504` describes reference-only resolution:
`connector-secrets.yaml` "accepts references only and refuses a literal by
name", `run-secrets` resolves at exec so the plist carries references and never
values, and a plugin is handed only the secrets its manifest declared. The CLI
has no secret-writing verb. The MCP surface has no secret-writing tool. Only the
browser does.

It has gone unnoticed because it sits on the console-only infra subsystem
`CERB-GAP-439` reports — one importer, no CLI, no socket route, no MCP tool, and
inert on this machine because `infra.SuggestedProfiles()` hardcodes another
user's path. So the write path exists, is reachable from a loopback listener
guarded by a per-process CSRF token rather than authentication
(`CERB-DEC-474`), and nothing exercises it.

Two resolutions, and the catalog should force the choice rather than leave it.
Either the infra subsystem is retired the way config migration was, taking the
mutation with it — which is what `CERB-GAP-439` already proposes — or the
console's credential UX is reframed as an adapter over an external authority and
`Set`/`Delete` come off the provider interface so no future surface can reach
them.

data.unlocks_when: Either the infra subsystem is retired with its secret mutation, or Set and Delete come off the provider interface and the console's credential UX becomes an adapter over an external authority
data.effort: small — the call sites are two lines on one route; removing Set/Delete from the provider interface is the larger half and has no other caller

records.name: The console serves inspect and doctor routes the console never calls
records.summary: internal/webui/server.go answers GET /api/resources/{id}/inspect and /doctor, and web/src/api/client.ts defines no method for either, so the operator UI has no diagnostic view although the API behind it is complete.
records.confidence_label: handleResourceByID read in full; web/src grepped for every inspect and doctor reference — the only hits are an unrelated recommended_action comparison and the plugin page's own inspect field

relationships.note: the row in the matrix this gap is
the console that does not call them
whose matrix records inspect and doctor as present on the console
what doctor would say if the console did call it: one check, and 'all checks passed'

records.body:
Two `GET` routes are wired, documented in `server.go`'s own route-map
comment, exercised by `server_test.go`, and dead: nothing in the React app
asks for them. `web/src/api/client.ts` exposes `listResources`,
`getResource`, `getLogs` and the generic `runResourceAction` — and no
`getResourceInspect` or `getResourceDoctor`.

The asymmetry is unusual enough to be worth stating plainly: this is not a
missing backend that a surface cannot reach, it is a present backend that
its own front end ignores. Every other console hole in the catalog costs a
route, a DTO or a decision. This one costs two lines in the API client and a
panel, and the token plumbing is not even involved because both routes are
reads.

It matters because of which lane it is. `doctor` and `inspect` are the two
verbs whose entire purpose is to answer "why does this look wrong", and the
console is the surface an operator opens when something looks wrong. The
console today can start, stop and remove a resource but cannot tell you
anything about why you might want to.

data.unlocks_when: web/src/api/client.ts gains getResourceInspect and getResourceDoctor, and the resource detail drawer renders both
data.effort: small — two client methods and a detail panel; no server work at all

records.name: Cerberus's only credential-write path is inside the subsystem two records propose deleting
records.summary: CERB-GAP-540 records that the web console is the only surface that can write a credential; CERB-GAP-439 proposes tombstoning internal/infra — which is that surface. Adopting either record's fix makes the other strictly worse, and no record says so.
records.confidence_label: Traced s.secrets across internal/webui: the only Set and Delete call sites in the whole console are internal/webui/infra.go:124 and :132, reached from POST /api/infra/providers/{id}; internal/infra's import graph re-checked and it is imported only by internal/webui/infra.go
