relationships.note: the record that names the console as the only credential-write surface
the record that proposes removing that surface
the credential chain that would be left with no writer
the same route, considered as a security exposure rather than a dependency

records.body:
This record exists because two pass-1 areas independently proposed
incompatible fixes and neither could see the other.

The surfaces area looked at `internal/infra`, found it imported by exactly
one file in the tree, found its endpoints returning empty, and proposed
either promoting it to the other surfaces or tombstoning it like the config
migration endpoints. The config and secrets area looked at the credential
chain, found that `KeychainProvider` can `Set` and `Delete` but that no CLI
or MCP verb calls either, and recorded the web console as the sole write
surface.

They are describing the same code. `s.secrets.Set` and `s.secrets.Delete`
appear in `internal/webui` exactly twice each, both in `infra.go`, both
inside `handleInfraProviderByID`. Tombstone `internal/infra` and Cerberus
has no way to write a credential at all — not a reduced way, none — while
`docs/secrets.md` continues to tell operators to store references and the
connector lane continues to fail `credential_missing` with a recovery
instruction that names a store nothing can write to.

The resolution is not obvious and that is the point of recording it: the
sequencing constraint has to be decided before either fix is scheduled. A
`cerberus secrets set` verb is a prerequisite for retiring the infra pages,
not an independent nicety, and it is the cheaper half of the pair.

data.unlocks_when: a cerberus secrets set/list/delete verb exists over the same ReferenceProvider the connector lane reads, at which point internal/infra can be tombstoned without removing a capability
data.effort: small for the CLI verb; the decision about ordering is the real work

records.name: The console writes and deletes keychain credentials past the connector-secrets guard
records.summary: POST /api/infra/providers/{id} stores arbitrary key/value pairs into the macOS keychain and deletes existing ones, without going through connector-secrets.yaml — the file whose whole job is refusing literal credentials — and its only gate is the action token GET /api/session hands out unauthenticated.
records.confidence_label: Route, handler and both keychain call sites read end to end; the unauthenticated token retrieval is pass 1's live-verified finding in CERB-GAP-442, and this route uses the same allowStateChangingRequest gate. Not exercised: writing a credential is a mutation and out of scope for a read-only audit

relationships.note: the unauthenticated action token that gates this route
the credential chain being written behind its own rules
the sibling finding: a literal credential in a resource's env: also evades the guard
the parity record that names this surface but not what it bypasses

records.body:
`~/.cerberus/connector-secrets.yaml` refuses a literal credential by name:
`internal/secrets/references.go` errors with "must be a keychain:// or
helper:// reference; literal credentials are not allowed". That guard is
the documented boundary in `docs/secrets.md` and in `AGENTS.md`'s "a
resource names a credential without carrying one".

`handleInfraProviderByID` does not use it. It takes a request body with a
`secrets` map and a `clear_secrets` list, and calls
`s.secrets.Set(ctx, id, key, value)` and `s.secrets.Delete(ctx, id, key)`
directly on the `KeychainProvider`, for any `id` in `providerCatalog()` and
any key the caller names. The value goes straight into the keychain. The
guard is not weakened here, it is simply not on the path.

The gate is `allowStateChangingRequest`, which pass 1 established is CSRF
defence rather than authentication: the token is served to any local caller
at `GET /api/session`, and the `Origin` check is skipped entirely when no
`Origin` header is sent. So any local process can both write a credential
Cerberus's own rules forbid and delete one an operator depends on, and
CERB-GAP-630 establishes that nothing anywhere records that it happened.

Recorded separately from CERB-GAP-442 because the reach is different in
kind. 442 is about driving destructive *operations*; this is about mutating
the *credential store* those operations resolve from, which outlives the
console process and is invisible from every Cerberus surface.

data.unlocks_when: the credential-write path goes through the same reference rules the read path uses, or the route requires a real credential rather than a token any local caller can fetch
data.effort: small for routing the write through the guard; the console's whole auth story is the larger question, and it is CERB-GAP-442's

records.name: Redaction runs on the connector lane's error-classification path, where it can only lose information
records.summary: unavailableCode decides between credential_missing and connector_unavailable by substring-matching a redacted copy of the error, so the redactor is given the chance to remove the very keywords the classifier is looking for — on a path where the redacted string is discarded and nothing is protected.
records.confidence_label: The code path is certain: external_connector_service.go:946 redacts before classifying and throws the redacted string away. The consequence is constructed, not observed — all nine of the connectors' real credential-missing causes still classify correctly, and I could not find a shipped error that misclassifies

relationships.note: the redactor being misapplied
the lane that classifies
the same function's other redaction defect, which is live rather than latent

records.body:
`unavailableCode` does this:

    msg := strings.ToLower(redact.Text(err.Error()))
    if strings.Contains(msg, "token") || strings.Contains(msg, "credential")
        || strings.Contains(msg, "secret") || strings.Contains(msg, "api key")

The redacted string is used for the comparison and then dropped; the error
that reaches the operator is redacted separately, later, in
`ExternalConnectorError.Error()`. So redaction here protects nothing and can
only subtract. The `assignment` rule replaces the token *after* a
credential-shaped key, and the classifier's keywords can sit in that
position: `authorization: token invalid` redacts to
`authorization: [REDACTED] invalid`, which contains none of the four
keywords and so classifies as `connector_unavailable` instead of
`credential_missing` — losing the recovery instruction the operator needs.

It is `speculative` and should stay that way until someone finds a real
error of that shape. I ran all nine of the built-in connectors' actual
credential-missing causes through the function and every one classified
correctly, because each of them repeats the keyword in the key position
where the redactor leaves it alone. The value of the record is not the bug,
it is the rule: `redact.Text` belongs on paths that emit text, and this one
does not emit anything. Deleting the call is a strictly safe change and
removes a whole class of future surprise.

data.unlocks_when: the redact.Text call is removed from unavailableCode, or a real error is found that misclassifies and the record is promoted

records.name: The supervision lane's verb table is hand-maintained in five places
records.summary: The connector lane has one generic route that every surface inherits; the supervision lane has thirteen verbs written out by hand in five independent lists, which have drifted to four different lengths.
records.confidence_label: All five lists extracted and compared: the cobra command tree from the installed binary, both switch statements, the two MCP registration blocks and the React ACTIONS array

relationships.note: the matrix this gap explains
the connector lane's equivalent — MCP tools hand-written rather than generated
the MCP half of the duplication, already recorded
the lane being exposed

records.body:
`CERB-GAP-430` argues that MCP tools should be generated from connector
metadata rather than hand-written. The same argument applies to the
supervision lane with more force, because there are five lists instead of
two and they have already diverged:

- `cmd_resource.go`: 13 verbs
- `cmd_mcp.go` plus `cmd_daemon.go`: 12 tools (no `show`)
- `socket_server.go handleResourcesID`: 11 actions (no `show`, no `ensure-fresh`)
- `webui/server.go handleResourceByID`: 11 actions, and a different 11 —
  it serves status at the bare `{id}` rather than at `status`
- `web/src/pages/resources.tsx ACTIONS`: 6 buttons, plus `list`, `status`
  and `logs` reached elsewhere, so 10 verbs

Unlike the connector lane, there is no metadata to generate from here. The
supervision verbs are not declared anywhere — no `Operations` slice, no
manifest — they exist only as the union of five switch statements, which is
why nothing can check them against each other. That is the actual finding:
the connector lane's parity problem is a missing generator over metadata
that exists, and the supervision lane's is missing metadata.

Priority is `nice-to-have` rather than `must-have` deliberately. Nothing is
broken by the duplication today; the two consequences worth having are the
console holes in `CERB-GAP-831` and `CERB-GAP-449`, which are cheaper to fix
individually than the structure is to replace. The structural record exists
so the fourth time someone adds a verb, the cost of adding it five times is
a known quantity rather than a discovery.

data.unlocks_when: the supervision verbs are declared once — as data the surfaces enumerate — or at minimum a test asserts the five lists agree
data.effort: medium — the declaration is small, but five call sites and a React component have to be rewritten onto it

records.name: MCP's four SSH tools are conditional on a client-side config load, and vanish with no signal the caller can see
records.summary: cerberus mcp registers cerberus_ssh_exec, _status, _put and _get inside an else branch: if loadUnifiedForTools fails, it logs a warning and serves 49 tools instead of 53, with nothing in the protocol telling the agent that the only verbs that reach the work host are gone.
records.confidence_label: Read from cmd_mcp.go:96-107 and cross-checked against the live session tool list, where all four are present; the failure branch was not induced, because doing so means making ~/.cerberus/config.yaml unreadable

relationships.note: the surface that loses the tools
the connector they reach
reaching the work host, which is what these four tools are for
the same fault in the CLI: a surface resolving config in its own process
found while re-deriving the MCP column

records.body:
Every other tool in `buildCerberusMCPServer` is constructed from
`socketClient` alone and is therefore a thin shell over the daemon. The four
SSH tools take `cfg` as well, because they resolve a resource id to an SSH
target in the MCP process rather than asking the daemon to. So they are
registered conditionally:

    cfg, cfgErr := loadUnifiedForTools(cfgPath)
    if cfgErr != nil {
        logger.Warn("client.mcp.config_load_failed", ...)
    } else {
        srv.RegisterTool(mcp.NewCerberusSSHExecTool(cfg, socketClient))
        ... three more ...
    }

The warning is honest and useless: it goes to the MCP process's logger,
which the agent on the other end of stdio never reads. What the agent sees
is a `tools/list` that is four entries shorter than the documentation, with
no error and no explanation — and the four missing entries are exactly the
ones `docs/plans/infra-admin-control-plane.md` builds on. An agent asked to
check the work host would conclude Cerberus cannot reach it.

Two things make this worse than an ordinary degraded mode. `cerberus mcp` is
a short-lived subprocess started per host, so the condition is sampled at
process start and never revisited — a config file that was briefly
unreadable costs the whole session. And the same tools are registered a
second time, identically, in `cmd_daemon.go`, so the daemon's own MCP server
has the same branch with a different config load.

The fix is the one the other 49 tools already demonstrate: resolve the SSH
target server-side and let the tool carry only a resource id, at which point
the branch disappears.

## Correction from reconciliation

An earlier draft of this record said the tools vanish *silently*. They do not quite: `cmd/cerberus/cmd_mcp.go:98-102` logs `client.mcp.config_load_failed` with the message "SSH tools will be unavailable; daemon-routed tools still work", and `cmd_daemon.go:597-600` mirrors the same structure.

The defect is narrower and still real: that warning goes to the MCP server's own log, which the calling agent does not read. In-band, an agent simply discovers four fewer tools than the contract advertises, with nothing in the tool list or any error to say why. These four are also the only MCP tools that parse the config file directly instead of routing through the daemon, which is precisely why they are the ones that can disappear.

data.unlocks_when: the SSH tools take a resource id and let the daemon resolve it, so registration is unconditional — or, short of that, a failed config load refuses to start the MCP server instead of serving a silently reduced tool set
data.effort: medium — a socket-side resolution for the ssh config, which the ssh CLI commands would share

records.name: pluginLaunchEnv hands every plugin the operator's SSH agent
records.summary: SSH_AUTH_SOCK, DOCKER_HOST and DOCKER_CONFIG are in the plugin launch allow-list, so any loaded plugin can authenticate as the operator to every host that trusts their key and reach any configured Docker daemon — regardless of what it declared.
records.confidence_label: Verified end to end: a throwaway plugin declaring nothing sees no SSH_AUTH_SOCK, DOCKER_HOST or DOCKER_CONFIG; declaring ssh_agent sees only SSH_AUTH_SOCK; an unknown capability is refused at install
records.body:
`pluginLaunchEnv()` carries a comment stating it "carries no credentials by design", and the allow-list includes `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, `DOCKER_HOST` and `DOCKER_CONFIG`. An agent socket is not a credential-shaped string but it is a live credential handle: a plugin holding it can authenticate as the operator to every host that trusts their key, without ever seeing the key. Docker socket access is root-equivalent on most hosts.

These are present for a real reason — the Docker connector reaches a remote daemon over SSH and needs both. The defect is not that they are granted, it is that they are granted **ambiently, to every plugin, undeclared**. That is precisely the pattern `CERB-CAP-302` exists to avoid for secrets: a plugin declares what it needs, the host resolves only that, and nothing travels in the environment because the environment reaches everything.

This refines `CERB-GAP-334` rather than duplicating it. That record treats the credential-free property as true but untested, and proposes asserting that no entry satisfies `redact.SensitiveKey`. `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` does not satisfy `SensitiveKey` — it is neither token- nor key- nor secret-shaped — so that test would pass with the exposure intact. The property does not hold, so there is a defect to fix before there is a test to write.

## What shipped

The three variables left the base launch allow-list in `pluginLaunchEnv()` and became capabilities a plugin must declare: `ssh_agent` unlocks `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, `docker_socket` unlocks the `DOCKER_*` set. `internal/pluginhost/capability.go` owns the vocabulary, the grant decision and the environment mapping; the grant is decided once at load and used for both the launch environment and the `granted` list the plugin is told about, because computing it twice is how those two drift. An unknown capability is refused at install rather than declined at load, so an authoring mistake is reported while an operator is watching. `plugin managed list` reports both what a plugin declared and what it holds.

The mechanism is `plugin-sdk` v0.5.0's `CapabilityRequest` and `InitParams.Granted`, which is why the type is the SDK's and the names are ours.

Verified with a throwaway plugin: declaring nothing, it sees none of the three variables; declaring `ssh_agent`, it sees `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` and still no `DOCKER_*`; declaring a misspelled name, installation fails naming the vocabulary this host understands.

## What did not ship

Granting is on the strength of the plugin's own manifest. A plugin that declares `ssh_agent` receives it, so this removes the ambient grant without yet requiring an operator to approve the specific one. What it buys is that the request is reviewable before the plugin runs and visible afterwards; what it does not buy is protection from a plugin that declares a capability it has no business having. Operator-held approval is the next step and wants its own record.

that record's proposed SensitiveKey test would not catch this
the lane that grants it

data.unlocks_when: A plugin declares the ambient access it needs, the host grants only that, and plugin managed list reports what each plugin holds

records.name: The acknowledgment gate is satisfied by the caller that is being gated
records.summary: acknowledged is an ordinary caller-supplied argument, so an MCP caller sets it exactly as it sets any other field — the destructive gate records deliberate intent but puts no human in the loop.
records.confidence_label: Field read at internal/cerbapi/external_connector_service.go:61; internal/mcp/namecheap_record_set_test.go passes acknowledged: true directly in the tool argument map
records.body:
`ExternalConnectorOperationArgs.Acknowledged` is a field the caller populates, and the MCP tool path passes it through like any other argument. An agent driving Cerberus therefore satisfies the destructive gate by setting a boolean.

This is worth stating precisely rather than alarmingly. The gate does real work: a caller has to assert acknowledgment deliberately, which stops an accidental destructive call and makes the intent explicit in the request. What it does not do is require a person, and `AGENTS.md` and the CLI's `--ack` flag together read as though it does.

Distinct from `CERB-GAP-286`, which is a bypass: there the managed-plugin branch returns before the gate is reached at all. This record is about a caller that does reach the gate. The two have different fixes and an audit trail wants both facts — whether acknowledgment was supplied, and whether the gate was reached.

The protocol already carries the missing half. MCP elicitation, present in the upstream SDK and unused here, asks the client's human a question mid-call — a gate the caller cannot satisfy for itself. Paired with operator-settable policy it becomes a real control; alone it only moves the decision.

Since PRs #60 and #63 the gate covers far more — every non-read connector operation, every resource mutation, pipeline and deploy-profile run — but it is still satisfied by the caller being gated. The console's confirm step is the first path where a human, not the caller's code, supplies the acknowledgment.

Since P2-1 the audit record says whether the caller claimed to be a human or an agent, and which MCP client it was. That does not change this gap: the label chooses default policy and is never approval, and an agent still supplies `acknowledged` itself.

relationships.note: the capability this qualifies
the bypass variant; this record is the reached-gate variant
an audit trail must record which of the two happened

data.unlocks_when: Operator-settable policy decides what needs approval and MCP elicitation delivers the ask to a human, so the gate is not satisfiable by the caller

records.name: No handling of personal data anywhere on the egress path
records.summary: Cerberus has no data classification, labelling or egress policy for personal data, while operations that return free-form text — resource logs, `ssh exec` output, `docker logs`, and a plugin's pod logs and cluster events — pass it verbatim into MCP tool results and therefore into a model provider's context.
records.confidence_label: Searched the repo for any classification, labelling or PII mechanism and found none; confirmed redact.SensitiveKey matches only token/key/secret-shaped names by calling it directly
records.pointer_locator: internal/redact/ (the only egress filter Cerberus has, and it is credential-shaped)

relationships.note: the only egress filter that exists, and it is the wrong shape for this
every surface carries the same operation output, so the exposure is on all of them
an audit trail of who read which logs is the other half of this

records.body:
Cerberus has exactly one egress filter, `internal/redact`, and it is built to
recognise credentials. Nothing in the repo classifies, labels or filters
personal data: there is no data category on an operation, no field marking a
result as sensitive, and no policy an operator could set about where such a
result may go.

That would be a theoretical concern if operations returned structured DTOs
only. They do not. Several return free-form text produced by someone else's
system:

- `ResourceLogs` (`internal/cerbapi/socket_client.go:121`) returns whatever a
  supervised process wrote to stdout and stderr.
- `cerberus ssh exec` returns a remote command's output verbatim.
- `cerberus docker logs` returns a container's log stream.
- The Kubernetes connector plugin returns pod logs and cluster events, which
  routinely carry usernames, email addresses, request payloads and customer
  identifiers — that is what application logs are.

The reason this matters more here than in an ordinary operations tool is the
agent surface. Every connector operation is reachable as an MCP tool, and an
MCP tool result lands in an agent's context window and is transmitted to a
model provider. So a pod log containing customer data leaves the estate as a
side effect of an agent being asked to debug a pod, with no operator decision
at the point of egress and no record that it happened.

**This is deliberately not filed as a redaction gap, and it is not one.**
`redact.Text` looks for things shaped like credentials; a person's name, an
email address in a log line or a customer id in a stack trace are not
token-shaped and never will be. Widening the redactor to chase them would make
`AGENTS.md`'s seven-patches finding worse, not better. It is filed against
`CERB-CAP-700` only because that is the sole capability standing on the egress
path — the absence of a data-handling capability to file it against is itself
the finding.

`docs/plans/agent-authority-and-secrets.md` owns the remedy as WP-S7. The
useful first step is smaller than a classification system: mark which
operations return third-party free text, since that set is short and known, and
decide per surface whether those results may reach an agent at all.

Acceptance: operations that return free-form third-party text are identified as
a set; an operator can express a rule about where their results may go; and the
decision is recorded per call rather than assumed.

data.unlocks_when: WP-S7 lands a data-handling capability and operations carrying third-party free text are labelled as such

records.name: No event bus, so no plugin-facing hook surface
records.summary: Cerberus has no internal event bus and no way for a plugin to observe or veto a host action; the SDK standardises an EventHandler interface and an ErrCancelled veto sentinel and Cerberus dispatches neither.
records.confidence_label: Searched internal/, cmd/ and pkg/ for EmitPreHook, EventHandler, MethodEvent, eventBus and Subscribe( — no production hits

relationships.note: the lane that would carry the hooks
an audit-sink plugin would subscribe to post-events rather than need its own mechanism
a policy engine needs the same fan-out point

records.body:
`plugin-sdk` standardises an `EventHandler` capability interface and
`ErrCancelled`, the sentinel a pre-hook returns to veto an action. Cerberus
dispatches neither, because it has nothing to dispatch from: there is no event
bus, no publish point and no subscription registry anywhere in the host.

The consequence is that every extension point Cerberus might want has to be
invented separately. An operator who wants a company approval service, a
change-window check or an internal allow-list consulted before a destructive
operation has no way to supply one short of patching the binary. An audit sink
has no way to observe operations without being wired into the service layer by
hand.

Nanite, the other host built on the same SDK, already has this: `Host.EmitPreHook`
emits to subscribed plugins and reports whether any cancelled, each hook bounded
by a five-second timeout, over roughly twenty-five event types. So the mechanism
is proven next door against the same contract.

The cost is real and should not be understated — an event bus is genuinely new
machinery, and this is the largest item in the plugin backlog. The argument for
it is that it is not new cost so much as shared cost: WP-S1's audit export and
WP-S5's policy gate each need a fan-out point, and building two is worse than
building one.

One design question to settle explicitly rather than inherit. A pre-hook that
can veto sits on the critical path of every operation it subscribes to, so a
hook that times out during a destructive operation has to resolve to something.
Fail-open and fail-closed are both defensible and the choice should be made
deliberately, not by whichever the first implementation happens to do.

Sequence this after WP-S1, so the audit record exists for hook decisions to be
recorded in.

data.unlocks_when: An event bus exists with at least one pre-hook point, so WP-S5 policy and WP-S1 export share one mechanism

records.name: No opt-in gate on the agent tool surface
records.summary: All 54 MCP tools are registered unconditionally with no per-tool or per-connector opt-in, so an operator cannot shrink what an agent can reach — and the fix for CERB-GAP-330 would put plugin operations on that surface automatically too.
records.confidence_label: Counted 54 unconditional srv.RegisterTool calls in cmd/cerberus/cmd_mcp.go; searched the repo for LoadType, toolFilter, enabledTools and allowTools and found no gating mechanism

relationships.note: the surface with no gate on it
its fix generates the tools this record says need a gate
the live evidence that plugin operations do not reach MCP today
both are about what an agent can do without an operator in the loop

records.body:
`cmd/cerberus/cmd_mcp.go` makes 54 unconditional `srv.RegisterTool` calls.
There is no allow-list, no configuration key and no environment variable that
narrows the set, so every agent that can reach `cerberus mcp` sees every tool,
including the destructive ones.

**A correction to the framing this record was opened with,** because the
catalog already had the contradicting evidence. The finding was reported as "a
plugin's operations reach the agent tool surface immediately". For plugins that
is not true today: `CERB-GAP-330` and `CERB-GAP-433` both verify live that no
plugin operation has an MCP tool at all, and the ten operations Azure and
ContextForge expose are reachable from every surface except MCP. Recording the
finding as reported would have contradicted two verified records.

The gap is real; it lands in two other places.

**Today it lands on the built-ins.** All 54 tools are always visible. An
operator who wants an agent to have `cerberus_resource_list` but not
`cerberus_droplet_destroy` has no way to express that short of not running the
MCP server.

**Tomorrow it lands on plugins.** `CERB-GAP-330`'s fix is to generate MCP tools
from connector definitions rather than hand-write them. The moment that lands,
installing a plugin puts its operations on the agent surface with no operator
step in between — which is when the reported framing becomes accurate. Adding
the gate before that lands is far cheaper than retrofitting it onto a
generator, and it is the sequencing argument for doing this first.

Nanite's manifest carries `LoadType: auto | opt-in` plus per-tool
`ToolOverrides`, so a plugin's tools stay hidden until an operator enables them.
Borrowing the field name keeps the two manifests agreeing where they overlap.

This is the cheapest agent-safety mechanism available in either codebase: it
needs no new machinery, only a default and a place to record the operator's
choice.

data.unlocks_when: A tool is exposed to the agent surface only after an operator opts it in, and the default for a newly installed connector is hidden

records.name: DataDir and CacheDir are declared on the Init wire and never populated
records.summary: SDKInitParams carries data_dir and cache_dir and nothing in the host ever assigns them, so a plugin gets empty strings, the SDK's ResolvedDataDir returns ErrNoDataDir, and plugin persistence is broken by omission rather than by decision.
records.confidence_label: SDKInitParams fields read at internal/pluginhost/sdk_protocol.go:22-28; searched the repo for any `DataDir:` assignment and found none, so the host sends empty strings. The SDK-side ErrNoDataDir behaviour is taken from docs/plans/plugin-capability-audit.md, not verified against plugin-sdk here.

relationships.note: the host side of the contract
the authoring contract a plugin author reads and reasonably believes

records.body:
`SDKInitParams` in `internal/pluginhost/sdk_protocol.go` declares `DataDir`
and `CacheDir` and sends them on every `Init`. Nothing in the repo ever assigns
either field, so every plugin receives empty strings.

On the SDK side that is not a benign default. `ResolvedDataDir()` treats an
empty data dir as `ErrNoDataDir`, and the SDK tells plugins to treat that as
fatal for persistence — so a plugin that wants to cache a token's expiry, a
resolved inventory or anything else across restarts finds the contract
unavailable and is expected to give up.

The distinguishing feature of this gap is that it is a declared contract the
host simply does not honour. A plugin author reading the manifest and the SDK
has every reason to believe the directory will be there. Nothing warns them,
nothing reports it, and the failure appears inside their plugin rather than in
Cerberus.

It is also the cheapest item in the plugin backlog. The install layout already
gives every plugin a directory, so populating the two fields is a matter of
deciding the path and creating it — plausibly a few lines.

Acceptance: a plugin's `Init` receives non-empty `data_dir` and `cache_dir`,
the directories exist and are writable, they are namespaced per plugin id, and
their lifecycle on uninstall is stated rather than left to chance.

data.unlocks_when: The host assigns and creates a per-plugin data and cache directory before Init

records.name: No policy engine, so every gate on an operation is compiled in
records.summary: A policy engine evaluates every gated operation and records its decision in shadow mode (P2-4), and since P3-1 the approval broker and the enforcement path exist behind a hook that nothing turns on yet: nothing is refused on the policy's account until P3-7 enforces by scope.
records.confidence_label: internal/approval and beginGated read on the P3-1 branch; shadow held by TestShadowAsksForNoApproval and TestShadowPolicyNeverChangesAnOutcome

relationships.note: the gate that exists, and the only one
install-time trust, which is a different question from per-call authorisation
that record is the defect; this is the mechanism whose absence causes it
a plugin-supplied policy hook needs the event bus
adhoc_targets is now evaluated in shadow

records.body:
Cerberus has three gates and an operator can change none of them.

The install policy decides at install time whether a plugin may run at all,
and records an origin (`installed` or `dev`) from rules defined in Go. A
connector definition or plugin manifest marks an operation `destructive`, and
since PR #49 that flag alone decides whether acknowledgment is needed. The
request then carries an `Acknowledged` boolean. That is the whole authorisation surface, and all of
it is either compiled in or declared by the thing being gated.

So there is no way for an operator to say any of the following, which are
ordinary things to want: `destroy_droplet` needs a second approver; nothing
writes to a production host outside a change window; this connector is read-only when
the caller is an agent; a plugin from outside the organisation may not reach
the SSH connector at all.

**Distinct from `CERB-CAP-306`,** which is sometimes read as covering this.
Install origin answers *is this plugin allowed to run, and with what
restriction*, once, at install, based on how it was installed. A policy engine answers *is this call allowed*, per invocation,
based on what is being done and to what. A plugin can be perfectly trusted and
the specific operation still be one an operator wants to stop.

**Distinct from `CERB-GAP-838`,** and the two should be fixed together. That
record says the acknowledgment gate is satisfied by the caller being gated. A
policy engine is precisely what turns that into a gate the caller cannot
satisfy for itself — 838 names the defect, this names the missing mechanism.

`docs/plans/agent-authority-and-secrets.md` owns this as WP-S5, and the
sequencing is already argued there: it consumes WP-S1's audit record, because a
policy decision is only meaningful if it is recorded, and it wants
`CERB-GAP-840`'s fan-out point if operator-supplied rules are ever to arrive as
plugins rather than as configuration.

## Direction since P0

`docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md` now carries the design: a small
YAML policy language with one combining rule (most restrictive wins, Decision
1), a strict baseline for humans and agents alike (Decision 2), and `Authorize`
wired into every path in shadow mode in P2, before enforcement is switched on
with the approval paths in P3. The signing tiers this record used to name as one
of the three gates were removed in PR #51 (CERB-DEC-815).

## Since P2-3

The target half of the policy input exists. Every audit record's target carries `env`, `owner`, `admin` (for the kind the operation touches), `tags`, the resource it was resolved through, and `adhoc`, from `internal/target`, with unknown for anything undeclared (Decision 17). The engine that decides on them is still P2-4.

## Since P2-4

The engine exists (`internal/policy`) and runs in **shadow mode**. `shadowDecision` in `internal/cerbapi/policy_point.go` is called from `beginAudit` for every operation that is not the monitor's automation, so every path the gates cover is authorized (I1). The result goes on the intent and the outcome as `policy: {decision, matched_rules, would_block, snapshot, shadow}`, and no outcome changes: `TestShadowPolicyNeverChangesAnOutcome` runs every gated lane under a decision point that denies everything and finds identical results, errors and outcome codes.

The evaluator has one combining rule, the most restrictive match wins (`deny > approve > dry_run_only > allow`), behind a narrow `PDP` interface (Decision 1). It combines these layers:
- a built-in baseline by effect and principal kind, aligned with Decision 14 and including Decision 11's local-dev exception;
- target defaults from Decisions 17 and 18: `admin: owner` or unknown denies changes, `admin: shared` approves destructive and exec, unknown env reads as prod, and an ad hoc target needs `adhoc_targets`;
- provider, target and principal rules from `~/.cerberus/policy/*.yaml`.

Only the applied snapshot decides (Decision 10). `cerberus policy apply` writes it on a TTY with a flip preview and a typed confirmation, and a snapshot failing its hash falls back to the baseline. The refusal codes are reserved and not returned.

What remains is enforcement. That is P3, with approvals.

## Since P3-1

The enforcement path exists. Every gated operation starts through
`beginGated` (`internal/cerbapi/approvals.go`), which, where an `Enforcement`
hook says enforcement is on, answers a deny with `policy_denied` and an
approve with `approval_pending`, asking the daemon's approval broker
(`internal/approval`) for a request the operator decides. The hook is off by
default and nothing installs it until P3-7, so shadow mode is unchanged and
held by `TestShadowAsksForNoApproval`. Approving a request comes with P3-3
(`tty_confirm`) and P3-4 (out of band), and using one by id with the plan
hash with P3-2.

data.unlocks_when: P3-2 to P3-6 give approvals a plan hash and channels, and P3-7 turns enforcement on scope by scope

the decision above this gap; refines rather than restates it

records.body:
`internal/secretref` parses exactly two schemes:

    keychain://<service>/<key>
    helper://<helper>/<authority>/<path>

The first is the macOS login keychain. The second shells out —
`<helper> resolve keychain://<authority>/<path>` — and is the only route to any
other store. There is no 1Password backend, no Keeper backend and no interface
a backend could be registered through, though both vendors ship Go SDKs.

The shell-out is not free, and its failure modes are the ones `AGENTS.md`
already warns about elsewhere. The helper has to be found on the daemon's
`PATH`, which launchd keeps minimal — the same trap that produced the Docker
connector outage. A vault that wants an interactive unlock cannot get one from
a TTY-less daemon. And the helper's exit status has to be mapped back into a
Cerberus error before an operator sees anything useful.

**This refines `CERB-DEC-800` rather than restating it.** That record captures
the decision: the direction ranks four credential delivery modes and Cerberus
implements the last one. This is the capability gap sitting underneath that
decision — the ranked-second mode, having a credential tool launch the process
with temporary material, has no native implementation either, so the ranking
describes a preference the code cannot currently act on at any level but the
bottom.

Priority is `nice-to-have` deliberately, and the reason belongs in the record.
`helper://` works. A native backend means a vendor SDK in `go.mod`, and
`AGENTS.md`'s "Core or plugin" rule says a vendor SDK is the signal you are in
the wrong lane. The honest shape of this gap is therefore not "add 1Password
support" but "the credential chain has no extension point, so the one thing
that should be a plugin cannot be one". That is the piece worth building
first.

data.unlocks_when: The credential chain takes a registered backend, so a vault integration can ship as a plugin instead of a shell-out

records.name: A plugin call has no deadline and a plugin process has no resource limit
records.summary: RPCProcess.CallTool passes the caller's context through with no timeout and no rlimit, cgroup or memory cap is applied to a plugin subprocess, so a plugin that never returns holds its caller indefinitely.
records.confidence_label: CallTool read at internal/pluginhost/subprocess_transport.go:145 — it forwards ctx with no WithTimeout; searched the repo for Setrlimit, rlimit and cgroup with no hits; the only bound is defaultProcessCloseTimeout = 3s at subprocess_transport.go:14, which governs shutdown

relationships.note: the crashed case; this is the hung case, and neither detects the other
the lane that spawns the subprocess
the install origin gates what a plugin may call, never how long it may take

records.body:
`RPCProcess.CallTool` forwards the caller's context to `p.call` and sets no
deadline of its own. Nothing else does either: there is no `rlimit`, no cgroup,
no memory cap and no CPU bound on a plugin subprocess. The single timeout in
the transport is `defaultProcessCloseTimeout`, three seconds, and it governs
shutdown rather than a call.

So a plugin that hangs holds whatever called it for as long as the caller's
context lives. Over the daemon socket that is an HTTP request that never
completes; from `cerberus mcp` it is an agent tool call that never returns, on
a surface where the agent's own retry behaviour then becomes part of the
failure. A plugin does not have to be malicious to do this — one blocking on a
TCP connect to a host behind a down tunnel is enough, which is a configuration
this estate has on purpose.

**Adjacent to but distinct from `CERB-GAP-333`, and the distinction is the
point of recording it separately.** That record covers a plugin child *dying*
undetected: the manager keeps a dead handle and `managed list` reports
`loaded: true` forever. This one is the opposite failure. The process is alive,
answers a liveness check, looks healthy in `managed list`, and simply never
replies to the call. A supervisor that notices exits does not notice this, and
a per-call deadline does not notice a crash. Both fixes are needed and neither
subsumes the other.

The deadline half is small and independent — a configurable per-call timeout
with a sensible default, surfaced as a distinct error so an operator can tell a
hung plugin from a failing operation. Resource limits are a larger and more
platform-specific question and should not hold up the timeout.

data.unlocks_when: A plugin call carries a deadline with a default, and a timed-out call is reported distinctly from an operation failure

records.name: In-process is not a trust boundary, and nothing decides what an in-process caller may target
records.summary: Every P0 target rule is enforced at the socket, web and MCP, while the in-process CLI keeps --config, docker --host/--context/-f and plugin exec <dir>; an agent with a shell has all of it. Since P2-1 and P2-3 the call is classified as human or agent and an ad hoc target is marked, but nothing yet decides what either may target.
records.confidence_label: carried into P1 by docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md; code read on main after P0 (#48 to #54)

relationships.note: the gate and the missing record
the decision that keeps free-form targets in-process
the audit record that would name the principal
the caller-satisfied acknowledgment
the policy engine that would act on the classification
the surface model

records.body:
P0 drew its line between surfaces, not between callers. SSH and Docker
targets must be configured resources on the socket, the web API and MCP, and
the one-shot `plugin_dir` routes are gone from the socket and web. The in-process
CLI deliberately keeps its free-form power (CERB-DEC-813):

- `--config <file>` forces connector verbs in-process and resolves ids against
  that file, which can declare any host, key or compose file.
- `cerberus docker --host`, `--context` and `-f` run against any daemon or
  compose file.
- `cerberus connectors plugin exec|health <dir>` installs, loads and runs any
  plugin directory, and the one-shot lane reserves no ids (CERB-DEC-357).

That is right for an operator at a terminal, and an agent with a shell tool gets
exactly the same thing. So a reader who takes "configured resources only" as a
statement about what an agent can reach is wrong whenever the agent can run
`cerberus` itself.

The P0 wrap-up in `docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md` states the
requirement. Principal identity must classify an in-process call as a local
principal, never as "the human" (Decision 9: agent unless an interactive TTY
with no agent marker, and never counted as approval), and the audit log must
record it. Neither exists yet. There is no caller identity on any path
(CERB-GAP-630).

Must-have. The P0 rules are otherwise easy to read as covering agents, and an
agent with a shell steps around them without meaning to. Blocked on nobody; it
waits on the P1 audit record and P2 principal identity.

## Scheduled

The P1 cut in `docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md` (2026-09-25) schedules this: P1-4a adds a caller surface header on the socket and records an in-process CLI call as a local principal, never as the human. That covers the recording half. Deciding what an in-process caller may target stays with P2's policy engine.

**Partly addressed in PR #60.** An in-process call is now classified: the CLI marks `in_process` in one place (`localConnectorExecutor`), and everything unmarked is `unknown` and treated as remote (CERB-DEC-817). Only in-process is allowed local-only inputs. It is still not a trust boundary — an agent with a shell has the in-process lane — and nothing records the classification until the audit log (P1-4). The resource lane's calls are marked too since P1-4b (CERB-GAP-855).

## Since P1-5

The one-shot `cerberus connectors plugin exec|health <dir>` still runs any plugin directory in-process, with no install and no review. P1-5 left it that way on purpose: it is as much power as running the binary yourself, and `docs/plugins.md` says so. The managed lane now reviews what it runs, but an agent with a shell can still reach this path, and can also write the plugin state file directly (CERB-GAP-857).

## Since P2-1

The recording half is done. The CLI classifies itself before any subcommand runs (Decisions 9 and 19): human only from an interactive terminal with no `CERBERUS_PRINCIPAL=agent`, an agent otherwise (`cerbapi.DetectCLI`). Every in-process record names that kind, via `cli`, and the process's own uid. `cerberus whoami` shows the classification. It is still a label and still not a trust boundary: an agent on a pseudo-terminal without the marker is classified human (CERB-GAP-859). What an in-process caller may target is the policy engine's to decide (P2-4, CERB-GAP-843).

## Since P2-3

The targeting half is now recorded as well. A call that names its target by connection settings, such as the in-process `docker --host`, `--context` or `-f`, records `target.adhoc: true`. Section 2's `adhoc_targets` grant is defined, and by default only a human holds it (`target.DefaultAdhocGrant`). What remains is the decision: P2-4 evaluates the grant in shadow mode, and P3 enforces it, at which point an in-process agent loses ad hoc targets.

## Since P2-4

The `adhoc_targets` grant is evaluated. A call carrying a local-scoped input matches `builtin.adhoc`, a deny for any caller without the grant, and humans hold it by default. A principal rule can grant it (`grants: [adhoc_targets]`). In shadow mode that decision is recorded with `would_block` and nothing is refused, so an in-process agent's ad hoc target is visible in `cerberus policy report` but still runs until P3.

data.unlocks_when: An in-process call is classified as a local principal, never as "the human", the audit record names that principal and its surface, and policy can decide what an in-process caller may target.
data.effort: medium — principal identity and the audit record are P1 and P2 work; the in-process lane itself needs no change until policy exists

records.name: SSH and Docker enforce caller keys in two different places
records.summary: Closed in PR #60: both ssh and docker enforce caller keys through one per-operation key table, checked in Execute with the caller's surface known.
records.confidence_label: carried into P1 by docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md; code read on main after P0 (#48 to #54)

relationships.note: where one check would live
the rule both shapes enforce
the discovery schemas generated from the same tables
plugin input is forwarded unchecked

records.body:
Both connectors enforce "configured resource, not connection settings", in
different places.

- **SSH.** `resolveSSHTarget` runs at the top of
  `ExternalConnectorService.Execute`, so it applies on every surface, in-process
  included. Allowed keys come from `sshconn.OperationFields`.
- **Docker.** `RefuseAdHocDockerTarget` runs in the socket and web handlers on
  the raw request. In-process is exempt so that `--host`, `--context` and `-f`
  keep working. Allowed keys come from `CallerKeys()` in
  `internal/connector/docker/config_keys.go`.

Each is correct today, and PR #54's `TestDiscoverySchemasMatchEnforcement` keeps
both in step with what discovery advertises. The issue is the shape. Whether a
check applies to a surface is decided by where the call sits, not by a rule that
names the surface, and a third connector with targets would have to pick one of
the two patterns.

Plugins have neither. `Execute` forwards `args.Config` to a loaded plugin as-is,
and `pluginhost` does not validate it against the manifest's input schema, so a
plugin decides for itself which keys it honours.

The P0 wrap-up names the fix: the operation contract replaces both with one
per-connector key table checked with the caller's surface in hand, and the same
table gives plugins a declared-input allow-list. Nice-to-have: nothing is exposed
today, since both built-ins enforce correctly on every remote surface. It becomes
must-have when a plugin declares a target-like input (a cluster context, a
subscription, a host) that should be configured-only.

## Scheduled

The P1 cut in `docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md` (2026-09-25) schedules this: P1-1 makes the per-connector input key table part of the operation contract, and moves both the SSH and the docker allow-list onto it, with the caller's surface known at the point of the check.

**Closed in PR #60.** The operation contract's `Inputs` is the one allow-list. `RefuseAdHocDockerTarget` and the separate SSH field check are gone. `ExternalConnectorService.Execute` runs `CheckInputs` on the raw request before resolution, on every surface, and docker's target keys are `local`-scope inputs accepted only in-process (CERB-DEC-817).

data.unlocks_when: One per-connector key table, on the model of internal/connector/docker/config_keys.go, checked in Execute with the caller's surface in hand, and the same mechanism gives plugins a host-enforced allow-list from their declared input schema.

records.name: The dev plugin origin exists only in devmode builds
records.summary: Decided in P1-5: the dev origin stays a devmode-build feature, documented in docs/plugins.md; a dev install is reviewed and digest-checked on every load, and only skips the store copy.
records.confidence_label: docs/plugins.md, policy.go and the dev-install test read on the P1-5 branch

relationships.note: the origin rules
the origin that replaced the tiers
the one refusal describe does not show

records.body:
`DevModeEnabled` is a build-tag constant, false unless built with
`-tags devmode`, and no Makefile target sets it. On a release build `--dev`
fails with "a development install (--dev) requires a devmode build". PR #51 kept
all three dev restrictions (devmode build, source under a developer root,
destructive operations refused) and renamed the result from two tiers to one
origin, so this is the old reachability problem under a new name.

What it costs: the restriction exists for a plugin in development, and the
people most likely to be developing a plugin (anyone building one against a
released Cerberus) cannot reach it. Their only option is `installed`, where a
half-finished write runs as soon as `--ack` is passed.

A second, smaller point: nothing on the discovery surface says a `dev` plugin
refuses its destructive operations. `connectors describe` reports `destructive`
and nothing else, and `managed list` reports `origin: dev` without saying what
that restricts.

Nice-to-have, because it narrows a development workflow and leaves no operator
exposed. Blocked on nobody; the P0 wrap-up hands the choice to the install
review.

## Scheduled

The P1 cut in `docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md` (2026-09-25) schedules this: P1-5's install review decides whether `--dev` is offered in release builds.

## Decided in P1-5

The install review kept `--dev` devmode-only and documents it in `docs/plugins.md`: a release build refuses it with "a development install (--dev) requires a devmode build". A dev install gets the same review and typed confirmation as any other, runs from its source directory instead of a store copy, and is digest-checked on every load. A rebuilt dev plugin is refused as `plugin_changed` until `managed load <id> --accept-changes`, which is the "re-reviews on every hash change" of section 10. Plugin authors on a release build use a normal install and re-review each build. The discovery-surface point is unchanged: `connectors describe` still does not say that a `dev` plugin refuses its destructive operations (CERB-GAP-278).

data.unlocks_when: The P1 install review either offers the dev origin in release builds or documents it as a build-time feature — documented in P1-5; describe still does not show the dev refusal (CERB-GAP-278)

relationships.note: the managed lifecycle
managed install
the same-uid caller this does not stop

records.body:
PR #50 removed every other way to make the daemon run a caller-chosen
directory: the one-shot `plugin_dir` health and operations routes answer 410 on
the socket and the web, web install-by-path answers 410, and managed exec
refuses a `plugin_dir` field. It kept `POST /plugins/connectors/install` on the
socket, because `cerberus connectors plugin managed install <dir>` uses it. The
socket is mode 0600 and same-uid.

Today that is a small exposure. Anything that can reach the socket can already
run the plugin binary itself. It becomes the wrong shape when the P1 install
review lands. Decision 12 of `docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md` makes
install a review with gaps called out and a confirmation, and Decision 3 puts a
human's confirmation on a TTY. A socket request cannot carry that confirmation.
The review has to happen in the operator's process and hand the daemon the
result.

Deferred to the P1 install review in PR #50 and listed in the P0 wrap-up.
Nice-to-have until that review exists, must-have with it.

## Scheduled

The P1 cut in `docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md` (2026-09-25) schedules this: P1-5 moves install fully in-process, with the review summary and a typed confirmation on a TTY, so the socket no longer records a path.

## Closed in P1-5

`POST /plugins/connectors/install` answers 410 with `PluginInstallRetired`, and `Client.InstallManagedPlugin` is gone. `managed install <dir>` runs `cerbapi.PluginReviewer` in the CLI process: it refuses a non-terminal, refuses any caller surface but `in_process`, and confirms on the typed plugin id. It writes the reviewed entry to `plugin-connectors.json`, and then the CLI calls `POST /plugins/connectors/{id}/reload`. That route takes an id, re-reads the reviewed entry and refuses a bundle whose digest does not match (`plugin_changed`). The socket now carries no path anywhere. What it cannot stop is a same-uid process writing the state file itself (CERB-GAP-857).

data.unlocks_when: Install and its review run in the CLI process with the confirmation on the TTY, and the daemon receives an already-reviewed registration; or the socket install route is retired — both done in P1-5

records.summary: ssh put and put_dir read any file the serving process can read and send it to a configured host; get and get_dir overwrite any local path it can write; an acknowledgment is the only gate and a caller supplies it.
records.confidence_label: ssh definitions, MCP hints and CLI path handling read on main after P0 (#48 to #54)

relationships.note: the SSH connector
ssh put
ssh get
the acknowledgment is caller-supplied
policy is where path rules would live

records.body:
PR #50 fixed where a relative path resolves: the CLI now makes `local_path`
absolute before sending, so a transfer through the daemon no longer resolves
`./app.env` against the daemon's working directory. It did not limit which paths
are allowed.

- `put` and `put_dir` read whatever the serving process can read, the daemon or
  the CLI, and write it to a configured host. They are destructive and
  ack-gated.
- `get` and `get_dir` overwrite whatever local path the serving process can
  write. As connector operations they are not destructive, so they take no
  `--ack`. PR #49 changed only their MCP hints to `ReadOnlyHint: false,
  DestructiveHint: true`.

The target is constrained, since it must be a configured resource
(CERB-DEC-813). The local side is not. An MCP caller supplies `acknowledged`
itself (CERB-GAP-838), so for an agent the acknowledgment does not bound what
`put` can read, and `get` needs no acknowledgment to overwrite a local file.

Must-have: this is the widest local-filesystem reach any agent tool has, and it
crosses to a remote host. PR #49 deferred it to P1/P2 path policy, and the P0
wrap-up lists it.

## Scheduled

The P1 cut in `docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md` (2026-09-25) schedules this: P1-1 adds a `local_fs` field to the operation contract, which declares an operation's local filesystem reach. Enforcing a path policy against it is later work.

records.name: Credential resolution runs before the acknowledgment gate
records.summary: Closed in PR #57 (P1-0): the acknowledgment gate runs before credential resolution; since PR #60 argument refusals do too.
records.confidence_label: Execute read on main after P0 (#48 to #54)

relationships.note: the order inside Execute
the gate

records.body:
In `ExternalConnectorService.Execute`, `s.registry.Resolve` runs the connector
factory, and a credentialed factory reads its token from the secret provider.
`requireAcknowledgment` comes after it. So an unacknowledged destructive call
resolves the credential and only then is refused. PR #49 checked that no API
call is made, and left the order as "a small follow-up if wanted".

Two costs. The credential is read, and touching the keychain can prompt, for a
call that could never run. And on a machine without the credential the call
fails as `credential_missing` before reaching the gate, which hides the more
useful answer (`acknowledgment_required`) and makes the gate impossible to test
without a real token.

Moving the gate up needs only the Definition, which does not need the
connector. Nice-to-have: nothing leaves the process. Blocked on nobody.

**Closed.** PR #57 moved `requireAcknowledgment` ahead of `registry.Resolve`, and `TestAckRefusalComesBeforeCredentialResolution` proves the connector factory is never called for an unacknowledged call. PR #60 moved every argument refusal ahead of resolution too, and P1-3 added JSON type checks, swept by `TestArgumentRefusalsNeverNeedACredential`.

data.unlocks_when: The definition lookup and the acknowledgment gate run before registry.Resolve, so a refused call touches no credential, and the gate is reachable on a machine with no credential configured.

records.summary: Closed in PR #60: a root PersistentPreRun sets SilenceUsage once flags and arguments are checked, so runtime errors print without the usage block.
records.confidence_label: reproduced live against a branch build

relationships.note: the CLI surface

records.body:
Seen live for this pass. `cerberus mcp-http --listen 0.0.0.0:4796` prints the
command's usage and every flag, then
`Error: cerberus mcp-http: refusing to listen on 0.0.0.0:4796: not a loopback
address, and this surface has no authentication yet; use localhost, 127.0.0.1 or
[::1]`. PR #48 found it and left it alone, because most RunE errors in the CLI
already behave this way. Only a few commands (`path`, `run-secrets`, part of
`resource`) set `SilenceUsage` themselves.

It matters more after P0 than before. P0 added refusals whose whole value is the
recovery they name (use a loopback address; pass `id=<resource-id>`; run it
in-process), and each one now appears under a screen of flags. Setting
`SilenceUsage` on the root command, and keeping usage for argument errors, is
the usual cobra pattern. Nice-to-have, because nothing is hidden, only buried.
Blocked on nobody.

**Closed in PR #60.** Cobra has parsed flags and validated arguments before a pre-run hook runs, so misuse still shows usage and every later failure — a refusal, a missing credential, a provider error — prints only its message. `TestRuntimeErrorsDoNotPrintUsage` pins both halves. The resource-only loop that did the same for one command group was removed.

records.body:
The connector verbs mark in-process through `localConnectorExecutor`. `newResourceRuntimeService()` in `cmd_resource.go` does not. Under CERB-DEC-817 an unmarked caller is remote, which only restricts local-only inputs, and the local contract declares none. It becomes a real refusal the day one is added.

records.name: Resource mutators, pipelines and deploy-profile runs write no audit record, and there is no audit CLI
records.summary: Closed in P1-4b: the resource mutators, pipeline runs, deploy-profile runs and the monitor's restarts write intent and outcome records, plugin telemetry enriches the outcome, and `cerberus audit tail|query|verify|prune` reads, checks and prunes the log.
records.confidence_label: TestClientMethodsAreClassifiedForAudit has no pending methods on the P1-4b branch; runtime, monitor, telemetry and audit CLI tests read and run

relationships.note: the audit log

records.body:
The P1-4a classification test lists the pending methods by name:
`DeployResource`, `ApplyResource`, `ReloadResource`, `StopResource`,
`SyncResource`, `RemoveResource` and `RunPipeline`. The deploy-profile run
(`cerbapi.RunDeploymentProfile`) is unrecorded too. All of them are gated
(CERB-CAP-212) but leave no record, so a resource removed through the console
is acknowledged and then forgotten.

`audit.Verify` exists, but only as a function. There is no `cerberus audit tail`,
`query`, `verify` or `prune`, so reading the log means reading JSONL by hand.
Plugin telemetry correlation (section 9 of the target-state plan) is also
P1-4b.

**Closed in P1-4b.** The seven methods are wrapped in `internal/cerbapi/runtime_audit.go`: the public `DeployResource`, `ApplyResource`, `ReloadResource`, `StopResource`, `SyncResource`, `RemoveResource` and `RunPipeline` write an intent before the runtime gate and an outcome after, so a refusal is recorded, and an `OpResult` or pipeline result that reports failure is recorded as `operation_failed`. An unwritable log refuses them as `audit_unavailable` before the operation lock (`TestUnwritableAuditRefusesRuntimeMutations`). A pipeline run is one record; its stages ride on its acknowledgment. `NewResourceRuntimeService` takes the sink as a required argument. `RunDeploymentProfile` records its run with the credential names `vercel/scope` and `vercel/token`, and `webui.New` requires a sink. The resource monitor's restarts are recorded as an `automation` principal on surface `monitor` with the reason, and are never gated: they still restart under an unwritable log.

Plugin telemetry correlation shipped too. A plugin returns events under `cerberus_telemetry` in its result (`pkg/plugin/telemetry.go`), which the host strips before the caller sees it, and the host tees the plugin's stderr to the calls in flight (`internal/pluginhost/telemetry.go`). Both are bounded (32 events, 32 lines, 512 bytes a field, 8 KiB a record), run through the per-plugin value redactor, and are attached only to the host-written outcome as `plugin_telemetry`. A plugin enriches a record; it never writes one.

`cerberus audit tail`, `query` (connector, op, surface, outcome, target, since/until), `verify` and `prune --before <date>` are in `cmd/cerberus/cmd_audit.go`. See CERB-CAP-604.

records.name: An accepted review is a file the operator's uid can write
records.summary: The review's result lives in ~/.cerberus/plugin-connectors.json and the plugin store, both writable by any process running as the operator, so an agent with a shell can write an accepted digest for a bundle nobody reviewed and have the daemon reload it by id.
records.confidence_label: read from plugin_connector_state.go and the reload route on the P1-5 branch; not exercised
records.body:
P1-5 made install a review confirmed on the operator's TTY and made the daemon apply only reviewed state (`POST /plugins/connectors/{id}/reload` takes an id and re-reads the state file). The review's outcome is still an ordinary file: `plugin-connectors.json` (0600) holds the accepted `bundle_digest` and `review`, and `~/.cerberus/plugins/<id>/<digest>/` holds the bundle. A process running as the operator, such as an agent with a shell tool, can write an entry whose digest matches a bundle it placed itself, then call reload over the socket. The load-time check passes, because it compares the bundle with the digest in that same file.

This is the same-uid boundary CERB-GAP-846 describes, and the digest was never meant to defend against it: it detects change, not authorship. It is recorded because a reader of the review could take "accepted on a TTY" to mean "only a human can make the daemon run a new plugin", and on the same uid that is not so. The audit log does show the difference. A real review has an `install`, `upgrade`, `review` or `accept_changes` record with a summary digest, and a forged entry has none, so `cerberus audit query --connector plugin` exposes it after the fact.

Nice-to-have. It closes only with an identity the agent's process does not hold: principal identity from peer credentials (P2), or keeping the accepted digests where the operator's uid cannot write them.

## Since P2-1

Peer credentials now verify the socket caller's uid. That is exactly the uid this gap is about, so it does not close: an agent with a shell still connects as the operator's uid, and still writes the same files.

## Since P3-1

The approval store has the same property: `~/.cerberus/approvals/events.jsonl`
is 0600 but the operator's uid, and every agent it runs, can write it, and its
hash chain only makes an edit evident. P3-1 does not rely on it for out of
band: an out-of-band decision must carry a presence proof that a
`PresenceVerifier` accepts at decide and again at consume, so a forged
"approved" line lets nothing through (`TestForgedApprovalDoesNotConsume`).
That verifier arrives with P3-4 (CERB-GAP-872).

closed; this is what it could not stop
a forged entry has no review record
the approval store is the same kind of file; presence at consume is the mitigation

records.name: Child processes inherit the daemon's whole environment
records.summary: Managed services, dev sessions, builds, docker, gh and deploy steps are started with os.Environ(), so any CERBERUS_* credential override in the daemon's environment reaches every child and whatever that child logs.
records.confidence_label: call sites traced read-only on main for the WP-S2 survey; the exposure depends on how the daemon was started and was not probed live
records.body:
`sessionEnv` (`internal/connector/local/dev_session.go`) starts every dev
session, build step and install probe from the daemon's full `os.Environ()`,
then adds the resource's `env_file` and `env`. The Docker connector
(`internal/connector/docker/cli_backend.go`) appends `DOCKER_HOST` to
`os.Environ()`, and the gh CLI fallback, the infra deploy steps and the
`secretref` helper leave `cmd.Env` unset, which inherits the same thing.

The secret provider reads `CERBERUS_<SERVICE>_<KEY>` from the environment
before it looks anywhere else, which makes a token exported in the operator's
shell a supported way to supply a credential. Whatever process holds it also
passes it to every child it starts. The output of those children goes to the
dev-session log, build logs and launchd `stderr.log`, which are not
value-redacted, and `FromEnv` covers only keys that match `SensitiveKey`.

The plugin host already solved this. `pluginLaunchEnv()` is an allow-list,
and a plugin receives only the secrets its manifest declares, over the Init
channel. Child processes of the local, docker, gh and deploy paths should get
the same treatment: a base allow-list (`PATH`, `HOME`, `USER`, `LANG`, `TMPDIR`
and the tool's own handles, such as `DOCKER_*` and `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`) plus what
the resource declares, and never a `CERBERUS_*` credential unless the resource
names it.

**Priority: must-have, placed in P5 (credentials and hardening), not fixed
now.** The launchd plist that `cerberus install` writes carries only `PATH`, so
the installed daemon is not exposed today. The exposure is the in-process
CLI, and a daemon started in the foreground from a shell that exports a
`CERBERUS_*` token. Changing a child's environment can break a managed service
that relies on something it inherits, so the allow-list needs a per-resource
`inherit_env` escape hatch and an audit of the live registry before it is
turned on. That is P5 work, not a WP-S2 side fix.

relationships.note: the credential chain that reads CERBERUS_* from the environment
found in the WP-S2 survey; value redaction does not reach a child's own logs
the plugin secret channel is the allow-list model to copy

data.unlocks_when: Children of the local, docker, gh and deploy paths start from an allow-listed environment plus what the resource declares, and a CERBERUS_* credential reaches a child only when the resource names it
data.effort: medium — the allow-list is small; auditing what live resources inherit, and the inherit_env escape hatch, is the real work

records.name: A principal's kind and client are the caller's claim
records.summary: Since P2-1 every request carries a principal, but only its uid is established by the kernel; human versus agent, the channel and the MCP client are what the caller says, so policy may key off them for defaults and never for approval.
records.confidence_label: read from internal/cerbapi/principal.go and cmd/cerberus/cmd_mcp.go on the P2-1 branch; the claim header and MCP capture are tested
records.body:
P2-1 gives every request a principal, and the audit record carries it. Only the uid is established: the socket's peer credentials, or the CLI's own process uid, marked `uid_verified`. Everything else is a claim:

- **Kind.** A socket caller sends `X-Cerberus-Principal: {"kind":"human"}` and is recorded human. The daemon reads a claimed `automation` as an agent, because only Cerberus is automation, but it cannot check `human`. In the CLI, an agent on a pseudo-terminal without `CERBERUS_PRINCIPAL=agent` is classified human (Decision 9 accepts this).
- **Client.** The MCP clientInfo is whatever the client names itself. `cerberus mcp-http` names each call from its `_meta`, so a client on the legacy handshake, which puts clientInfo only in initialize, is recorded as `mcp-client`.
- **The web console** is labelled human for every request until P2-2 adds a login (CERB-GAP-442).

This is the limit section 3 of `docs/plans/live-systems-security-target.md` states, and the design accepts it: the label picks default policy, and approval goes out of band (I5). It is recorded so that a policy rule keyed on `kind: human` is read as a default, not a control.

Nice-to-have. The label can stay weak once out-of-band approval exists (P3). The web label becomes real with P2-2.

the acknowledgment is still the caller's own
in-process is not a trust boundary
the console label, until P2-2

records.name: Plugin targets are not resolved to resources, so their labels read unknown
records.summary: A plugin operation names its target by its own fields, such as a kubernetes context or a cloudflare zone id, which no registered resource answers to, so its audit record's target is unknown unless the operator declares a resource and the call names it by id.
records.confidence_label: read from internal/cerbapi/audit_trail.go and internal/target on the P2-3 branch; the resolution is tested
records.body:
P2-3 labels a target from the registered resource a call names, by one of the operation's target fields or the `id` and `resource` keys (`resolveTarget` in `internal/cerbapi/audit_trail.go`). The built-in connectors that address a configured resource, SSH by `id` and Docker by `resource`, resolve. A plugin operation's target fields are the plugin's own: `context` and `namespace` for kubernetes, `zone_id` for cloudflare, `droplet_id` for digitalocean. None of them names a resource, so the target reads `env: unknown`, `owner: unknown` and `admin: unknown`.

That is the strict reading (Decision 17) and fails safe once policy runs, but it means a cluster or a zone cannot be labelled today. The operator could declare a resource for a cluster, but no plugin operation takes a resource id to resolve it by.

What would close it: a resource can declare the plugin target values it stands for (a cluster's context, a zone's id), so `resolveTarget` can match them, or a plugin operation accepts a `resource` input the host resolves. Either is a contract change best made with P1-6's plugin catch-up in view.

kubernetes contexts are the first case
policy keys off these labels

data.effort: medium — a resource-side match on plugin target values, or a host-resolved resource input on plugin operations

records.name: A pipeline run's target is not labeled
records.summary: A pipeline run is recorded against its pipeline id, which is not a resource, so its target carries no env, owner or admin, although its stages act on labeled resources.
records.confidence_label: read from internal/cerbapi/audit_trail.go and internal/target on the P2-3 branch; the resolution is tested
records.body:
P2-3 resolves labels for the admin lane, the runtime mutators and the monitor's restarts. A pipeline run is recorded once (P1-4b), against `pipeline.run` with the pipeline id, and its spec deliberately carries no resource lookup: a pipeline id that happened to match a resource id would otherwise inherit that resource's labels. So the record's target is `unknown` on every label, while the stages it runs touch resources that may be `prod`.

What would close it: label the run from the resources its stages name (the most restrictive of them, which is how policy would read it), or let a pipeline declare its own labels. Until then a policy rule on `env: prod` does not see a pipeline that deploys to prod; in shadow mode the audit log shows these runs as unknown.

the pipeline lane

records.name: Any process running as the operator can mint a console sign-in link
records.summary: The web login key is a 0600 file the operator's uid can read, so an agent with a shell can run `cerberus web open` (or read the key) and get a session the audit records as a human on the web console.
records.confidence_label: follows from the P2-2 design in internal/webui/session.go; not exercised as an attack
records.body:
P2-2 gave the console a login. `cerberus web` and `cerberus web open` mint a
one-time link from a per-process key the running console keeps at
`~/.cerberus/web/login-<listen>.key`, mode 0600 in a 0700 directory, and the link
becomes a session whose principal is `kind: human, via: web`. The file stops
other accounts, local processes that cannot read it, and web pages. It does not
stop the operator's own uid, because that is exactly who it is readable by.

A process running as the operator, such as an agent with a shell tool, can run
`cerberus web open --browser=false`, or read the key and compute a token itself,
and then drive the console's API with a session. The console cannot tell that
session from the operator's. The daemon's audit record then says `human, via
web` with a session id, and the only true part of that is the verified uid of the
console process. The label is how Decision 9's default policy tells a person from
an agent, so a same-uid agent could use it to reach what policy grants only to a
human.

This is inherent without a second identity, and it is the same boundary as
CERB-GAP-857 (an accepted plugin review is a file the operator's uid can write)
and CERB-GAP-846 (in-process is not a trust boundary). It is recorded so that
"signed in to the console" is not read as "a person at this machine did this".
It means "something running as the operator held the key".

What would close it is an identity the agent's process does not hold:

- a console running as a separate uid, with the key in that uid's home;
- a key held in the login keychain behind user presence (Touch ID or a
  password prompt), so minting a link needs a human at the machine;
- or workload identity, the WP-S9 direction in
  `docs/plans/agent-authority-and-secrets.md`: short-lived, attested identity
  for each caller, deferred until its trigger conditions hold.

Until then, the audit log keeps what can be kept. Every session's id is on
every record it produced, and `webui.session.started` is logged when a link is
spent. P3's human-in-the-loop approvals should not treat a web session alone as
proof of presence.
