records.name: The operation contract has no provisioning class, so owner-keyed rules are operator-written
records.summary: Decision 18 keys policy off admin for changes and off owner for provisioning-level operations, but the contract cannot say which operations provision, so the built-in baseline keys only on admin and owner rules must be written by hand.
records.confidence_label: internal/policy/evaluate.go and pkg/connector/contract.go read on the P2-4 branch

relationships.note: a layer the engine cannot default
the ownership rule this would complete

data.unlocks_when: An operation can declare itself provisioning-level in the contract, and the baseline denies it where owner is not self unless a rule allows it

records.body:
Decision 18 splits ownership: `admin` decides who may change a target's workloads and settings, and `owner` decides provisioning, meaning creating, destroying or resizing the target itself. The P2-4 baseline encodes the admin half (`builtin.admin-owner`, `builtin.admin-shared`). It cannot encode the owner half, because nothing in `pkg/connector` marks an operation as provisioning: `destroy` on a droplet and `destroy` on a container carry the same `destructive` effect.

So owner-keyed rules are operator-written today, for example `targets: [{match: {owner: "!self"}, rules: [{ops: [destroy, create_droplet], decision: deny}]}]`. A contract flag (for example `provisioning: true` on an operation) would let the baseline carry the default instead.

records.name: Shadow mode reports TTY-confirmed admin operations as would-block
records.summary: policy apply, audit prune and plugin reviews are confirmed by a typed TTY confirmation, but in shadow mode the policy has no approval to count, so their admin approve decision is recorded as would_block and appears in the policy report.
records.confidence_label: seen on the P2-4 branch: a policy apply's own record shows approve with would_block in cerberus policy report

relationships.note: shadow-mode noise until approvals exist

data.unlocks_when: P3's approval model counts a typed TTY confirmation as the approval a human's approve decision needs (Decision 3), so these record as met

records.body:
A human's `admin` operation is `approve` in the baseline. The operations that are admin today are `policy apply`, `audit prune`, plugin install, upgrade and review, and `plugin load --accept-changes`. Each already runs only on a TTY and needs a typed confirmation that shows what will change, and that is exactly the approval Decision 3 describes. But shadow mode has no approvals, so `combine` marks every `approve` as `would_block`, and these operations land in `cerberus policy report` as things that would be blocked.

This is noise, not a hole: nothing is enforced, and in P3 the confirmation is the approval. Until then, read `baseline.admin.human` rows in the report with that in mind.

records.name: The baseline is the only layer a policy file can loosen
records.summary: Because the most restrictive match wins, an allow rule never lowers a stricter match, so the only way to loosen a decision is a global baseline cell; there is no per-target allow exception except the built-in local-dev lifecycle one.
records.confidence_label: internal/policy/evaluate.go read on the P2-4 branch; TestCombiningAndDryRuns shows an allow rule leaving the baseline in place

relationships.note: a limit of the engine's one combining rule
the tightened baseline this makes hard to relax per target

data.unlocks_when: A policy file can scope a baseline exception to a target match (as builtin.local-dev-lifecycle is scoped to local env: dev), still under the one combining rule

records.body:
Section 4 chose one combining rule, most restrictive wins, so that no rule order can be got wrong. The price is that `allow` is only meaningful where nothing stricter matches, and the baseline always matches. With the Decision-14-aligned baseline, human `write` and `lifecycle` are `approve` everywhere. An operator who wants them unprompted on one lab host can override only the global cell (`baseline.by_effect.write.human: allow`), which loosens every target. The one scoped exception is built in: `builtin.local-dev-lifecycle`, for Decision 11.

A scoped baseline override (a target match with baseline cells) would keep the single combining rule and make per-target relaxation possible. It is not needed for shadow mode.

records.name: The approval store is a file the operator's uid can write
records.summary: ~/.cerberus/approvals/events.jsonl is 0600 but writable by any process running as the operator, and its hash chain only makes an edit evident, so nothing in it can be trusted to authorize on its own word; out-of-band decisions are held to a presence proof verified at consume, which arrives with P3-4.
records.confidence_label: read and tested on the P3-1 branch

relationships.note: the enforcement path these approvals serve
the same same-uid file, for reviews

data.unlocks_when: P3-4 verifies presence assertions against enrolled keys at decide and consume

records.body:
The broker's store is append-only, fsynced and hash-chained like the audit log, and the daemon folds it into state at start. None of that makes it trustworthy against the one uid everything runs as (the P3 cut's premise): an agent with a shell can append a line that says an approval was granted and rebuild the chain after it. P3-1 therefore never takes the store's word for an out-of-band approval. `Store.Decide` and `Store.Consume` both run the decision's presence proof through a `PresenceVerifier`, and the default, `NoPresence`, verifies nothing, so a forged `decided` line folds into state but never consumes (`TestForgedApprovalDoesNotConsume`). A `tty_confirm` decision is never stored at all; P3-3 makes and uses it on one call.

The real verifier, WebAuthn user verification against enrolled keys, is P3-4. Prevention rather than detection would need a second uid or hardware-bound storage, as for CERB-GAP-857.

records.name: Out-of-band approvals cannot be approved or consumed until P3-4
records.summary: Until P3-4 installs a presence verifier, an out-of-band approval request can be created but never approved or consumed, so wherever enforcement would require out of band the operation fails closed.
records.confidence_label: read and tested on the P3-1 branch

relationships.note: the enforcement path these approvals serve

records.body: `approvalTerms` requires out of band for prod or unknown env, shared admin and targets not owned by self (Decision 3). With `NoPresence` as the verifier, `Decide` refuses such an approval with `ErrNoPresence` and `Consume` would refuse it again, so a request made under enforcement stays pending until it expires. That is the intended fail-closed state, and it is harmless now because nothing turns enforcement on before P3-7, and P3-4 lands before P3-7.

records.summary: P3-1 builds consume in the store and broker, but no gated path accepts an approval id yet, so an approved request lets nothing through; retrying with the approval id, bound to the args digest and the plan hash, is P3-2.
records.confidence_label: read and tested on the P3-1 branch

records.body: `Broker.Consume` checks the args digest, the plan hash, a re-evaluated deny and, for out of band, presence, and writes the consumed event before anything runs. Nothing calls it from a gated path yet: `enforceDecision` asks for an approval and answers `approval_pending`, but a retry carrying the approval id is not read, and approvals have no plan hash until P3-2 computes one. `approvalExpiredError` and `planStaleError` exist as Guidance for that consume path.

records.name: resource list
records.summary: Lists every registered resource with mode, supervisor, run_from, live status, artifact state, recommended next step and its policy labels (env, owner, admin, tags), probing all resources concurrently.
records.confidence_label: run live against the running daemon; returned 10 rows
records.body:
`ListResources` filters by project, connector or tag, then fans out one goroutine per resource. Local process rows get a 750ms-bounded status probe plus artifact state — from the background drift cache when the daemon has one attached, falling back to a direct `InspectArtifactInstallBasic` before the first scan completes. Non-local/process rows are filled in with `unsupervised` and a next step instead — though only the API carries it: `cerberus resource list --output json` returns `recommended_next_step: "cerberus ssh status muctlvaig | cerberus ssh exec muctlvaig -- <command>"` for `muctlvaig`, while the table's NEXT column renders `-`, so the CLI operator never sees the next step the lane computed for them. Verified live: `cerberus resource list` returns 9 dev_session/workspace process resources and `muctlvaig` as unsupervised, all with an empty ARTIFACT column.

## Since P2-3

The table gains `ENV`, `OWNER` and `ADMIN` columns before `TAGS`, and `--output json` carries `env`, `owner` and `admin` on every row. An undeclared label shows as `unknown` rather than a dash, so a resource that still needs a label is visible (Decision 17). `ADMIN` prints a per-kind map as `default=owner,docker=self`.

records.confidence_label: run live against tesseract-api
records.body: Definition-only, not runtime: it echoes what the registry resolved for this id, including the raw `config:` map as JSON. Unlike `inspect` it works for any resource kind, because it never asks the supervision lane for state. It does not, however, name the file the resource came from: the output is id, name, type, project, connector, tags, the resolved mode/supervisor/run-from triple and the raw `config:` map, and there is no source-path field and no `--output` flag. Because it resolves the config in-process rather than through the daemon, it is the one resource verb that still answers with the daemon down.

records.name: resource apply
records.summary: Activates a resource from whatever build output already exists — no build, no source-freshness check — and says so in the result message.
records.confidence_label: test-covered only; running it would mutate a live service, which this audit forbids

relationships.note: refused when it targets the serving daemon
does not enforce the build output contract deploy enforces

records.body:
`ApplyResource` takes `opMu`, resolves the resource, refuses on a port conflict or a self-mutation, resumes the resource in `pausectl` if it is a dev_session, and calls the connector's `Apply`. For dev_session that starts the command; for os_service it syncs the artifact, writes the plist if changed, and bootstraps or kickstarts. On failure it appends the log, plist, install and artifact paths plus a pointer to `resource doctor`.

records.name: resource deploy
records.summary: Builds from the declared build strategy, optionally runs make install, verifies the build produced the artifact it will install, then activates — the only verb that makes a running service match current source.
records.confidence_label: test-covered; forbidden to run here, and no resource on this machine has a build_strategy for it to exercise

records.body:
`DeployResource` is the long one, and every step has a reason. Resolve; redact the whole result on the way out; refuse on port conflict and self-mutation; `ValidateDeployOutput` to refuse an artifact deploy whose build strategy declares no `output`; resolve three-layer `install_after_build` precedence (CLI override > resource > global default); take the build lock; build; write `logs/build.log` whether it succeeded or not; run `make install` if a Makefile with an install target exists; for artifact resources stat the resolved source and fail loudly if the build produced nothing there; resume pausectl for dev_session; then `ActivateBuilt`. It emits MCP progress notifications at each of four stages.

With no `build_strategy`, deploy degrades to "activate existing output" and says so in the message. That is all it can do on this machine, since none of the ten resources declares one.

**Needs acknowledgment since PR #63.** The runtime gate runs before the operation takes a lock or looks the resource up: `--ack` on the CLI, `acknowledged` on the MCP tool, the confirm step in the console. For os_service it is `launchctl kickstart -k`, and it refuses outright when the job is not loaded (`use resource apply`), then waits for a stable PID and records the artifact activation. It resumes a pausectl-paused dev_session first, so a reload also un-pauses. records.confidence_label: test-covered; not run, because it would stop a live service

relationships.note: the pausectl pause is what stops the monitor undoing this
refused when it targets the serving daemon

records.body:
For dev_session, `StopResource` pauses the resource in `pausectl` *before* stopping it and rolls the pause back if the stop fails — which is the right order, because the monitor's next tick is 30 seconds away at most. For os_service it is `launchctl bootout` with no pause, since launchd will not restart a booted-out job. The success message states that install state is preserved, distinguishing this from `remove`. `resource doctor` surfaces an active operator stop as a `pass` check naming the verbs that resume it.

records.body:
`SyncResource` hashes the source binary, compares it against `install-manifest.json` and the installed file, and copies only when they differ — reporting `artifact synced` or `artifact already current`. On a resource that is not `run_from: artifact` it returns success with "does not use artifact mode; nothing to sync", so it is safe to call blindly. Unlike `deploy` it does not run `ValidateDeployOutput`, so on a resource whose build strategy declares no `output` it will happily install `command[0]`.

records.name: resource remove
records.summary: Uninstalls a resource's runtime state — boots out the launchd job, deletes the plist and removes the whole install tree. Not a casual stop.
records.confidence_label: test-covered; deliberately not run — it deletes an install tree

relationships.note: refused when it targets the serving daemon

records.body:
`RemoveResource` pauses a dev_session in `pausectl` and then calls `Destroy`. For dev_session that is just a stop. For os_service it is `launchctl bootout`, `os.Remove` on the plist, and `os.RemoveAll` on `~/.cerberus/apps/<project>/<resource>` — logs, manifest, artifact and all. It removes runtime state, never the definition: the resource stays in the config and can be applied again.

Worth flagging for the reconciliation pass: unlike the connector admin lane, supervision-lane mutations carry no `--ack` or `--dry-run`, and `remove` is the one verb here where that asymmetry is uncomfortable. The CLI `Short` text ("not a casual stop") is the only guard rail.

The self-mutation guard is unchanged and still refuses the serving daemon, acknowledged or not.

records.name: resource ensure-fresh
records.summary: Reads the resource's own recommended action and performs it — deploy, apply or sync — or stops without changing anything when activation is unconfirmed.
records.confidence_label: test-covered; on this machine every resource yields the empty recommendation, so it can only ever reach the noop branch

relationships.note: dispatches on what status recommends

records.body:
`EnsureFresh` is the agent-facing convenience over the advice system, and it is written against an interface (`EnsureFresher`) that both the socket client and the in-process runtime satisfy, so it works identically over the daemon or standalone. `--force` goes straight to deploy. Otherwise it reads `recommended_action` and dispatches: `deploy`, `apply`, `sync`, or one of two noops. The empty-recommendation noop succeeds with "no built-binary drift detected; source freshness is not checked". The `inspect` recommendation noop deliberately *fails* — `Success: false` — because "activation unconfirmed" means a human should verify the running image before another automatic restart is attempted. The distinction is documented on the result type: a noop with `Success: false` is not a freshness confirmation.

Since `RecommendedStatusAction` returns nothing unless a resource is `os_service` + `artifact`, and nothing here is, `ensure-fresh` without `--force` is a guaranteed noop on this machine.

**Needs acknowledgment since PR #63.** `--ack` / `acknowledged` goes to the one mutation ensure-fresh chooses (deploy, apply or sync); ensure-fresh never acknowledges on its own (CERB-DEC-819).

records.name: connectors plugin managed install <dir>
records.summary: Shows the plugin's install review in the operator's terminal and, on the typed plugin id, copies the reviewed bundle into the plugin store, records the review and asks the daemon to reload it by id.
records.confidence_label: cmd and reviewer tests run on the P1-5 branch; not run live against the daemon
records.body:
Reads and validates `plugin.yaml`, refuses a reserved id, fingerprints the entrypoint, records an install origin (`installed`, or `dev` with `--dev` on a devmode build), adds the plugin to the inventory and persists it. The persisted entry is `{plugin_dir, options, loaded}`. It holds no version and no hash, which is why there is no upgrade or rollback story (CERB-GAP-337).

PR #51 removed `--catalog-signed`, `--archive-signed` and `--archive-sha256`, which now fail as unknown flags. The host always computes `entrypoint_sha256` and `managed list` reports it; nothing persists or compares it (CERB-GAP-336). The legacy `trust` object in an install request or an old state file is read for `dev_mode` alone.

PR #50 retired install-by-path on the web (410) and removed the console's install box. The socket route remains, for this CLI verb only (CERB-GAP-849).

Not exercised live for this audit. `TestManagedPluginInstallRefusesABuiltInID`, `TestManagedPluginInstallAllowsTheSameIDWhenNothingReservesIt`, `TestLegacyPluginStateStillLoads` and `TestDirectoryInstallerFingerprintsTheEntrypoint` pass.

## Since P1-5

The command runs in the CLI process, not the daemon, and only from an interactive terminal (stdin and stdout both a TTY). It stages the directory into `~/.cerberus/plugins/`, digests the copy and prints the section 10 review. On the typed plugin id it records an `admin` `install` event with the summary digest, commits the copy to `<id>/<digest>/` and writes a version 2 entry carrying `bundle_digest`, `source` and the accepted `review`. It then calls `POST /plugins/connectors/{id}/reload`. Reinstalling an installed plugin is an `upgrade`, shown as a diff, and a bundle identical to the installed one has nothing to review. A bundle with a symlink, an id that cannot name a store directory, a reserved id or a host range that excludes this Cerberus is refused. The socket install route answers 410 (CERB-GAP-849, closed). `TestPluginInstallIsAnInteractiveReview` and `TestInstallReviewStoresTheReviewedBundle` pass.

records.name: cerberus mcp
records.summary: Stdio MCP server that holds no config state and forwards all 53 tool calls to the daemon socket, re-dialing per call so it survives daemon restarts.

Boots, resolves the socket path, pings once with a warning-not-failure on unreachable, builds the server with `buildCerberusMCPServer` and runs stdio JSON-RPC. The boot ping is deliberately non-fatal because an MCP host may spawn the subprocess before the daemon exists; tool calls then return `DaemonUnreachableError` until it is up. Since PR #48 both paths sit behind `loopback.Guard`. A request whose `Host` is not `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]` or the listen host gets 403, whatever the port (CERB-DEC-810). go-mcp's `AllowedOrigins` is the guard's origin set, which is never empty, and `--allow-origin` adds exact origins to it. `--listen` accepts only `localhost` or a literal loopback IP, with no override (CERB-DEC-811). The long help says the endpoint is loopback-only, that an SSH local forward works and a public-hostname tunnel does not, and names WP-S8.

Verified live for this pass on a branch build with a scratch `HOME`: `--listen 0.0.0.0:…` and `--listen myhost.local:…` both exit 1 with the refusal; on `127.0.0.1`, `/health` returns 200 for a loopback Host on any port and 403 for `Host: evil.example`; `/mcp` returns 403 for a foreign Origin and for a loopback Origin on the wrong port.

records.name: Socket generic connector operation route
records.summary: POST /connectors/{id}/operations/{op} on the daemon socket runs any declared connector operation, built-in or plugin, with dry-run and acknowledgment; since P0 SSH and Docker configs are limited to a resource id and operation fields.
records.confidence_label: Route and dispatch read from source; read-only socket GETs verified live, POST not exercised because every operation behind it is a real infrastructure call
records.body:
Parses `/{id}/operations/{op}`, decodes an `ExternalConnectorOperationArgs` body, defaults `Config` to an empty map, then calls `ExecuteConnectorOperation`. That service resolves per call, prefers a loaded managed plugin over the built-in of the same id, enforces acknowledgment for destructive operations and fails closed on an undeclared one, answers `dry_run` with a preview or `preview_unsupported` and never executes it, and maps failures onto `ExternalConnectorError` codes that the route turns into 400 / 404 / 409 / 503. It also honours `X-Cerberus-Progress: 1` and streams NDJSON. This one route is why the socket, the console HTTP API and the console UI all reach 48 of 48 operations while the CLI reaches 44 and MCP reaches 33.

Since PR #50 and PR #52, `config` is not arbitrary for two connectors. An SSH operation takes `id` plus its operation fields, and a Docker operation takes `resource`, the container keys and `id`/`lines`. Anything else is refused by name before resolution (CERB-DEC-813). The plugin-scoped one-shot routes `/plugins/connectors/operations/` and `/plugins/connectors/health` answer 410.

`connectors.tsx` fetches `/api/connectors`, sorts by id, and for each `connector.operations` entry renders the name, description, a free-form JSON textarea, a dry-run checkbox disabled unless `supports_dry`, an ack checkbox disabled unless `destructive`, and a Run button gated on holding a session token. `runOperation` parses the textarea as JSON and POSTs `{config, dry_run, acknowledged}` to `/api/connectors/{id}/operations/{op}`. They get a resource picker populated from `/api/resources` and filtered by connector, sent as `id` (ssh) or `resource` (docker); an optional local container name for docker; and one input per remaining schema field. The config-fields panel is labelled as set on the resource, not per call. Every POST passes the loopback Host check and an exact Origin match before the token check (PR #48, CERB-DEC-810). records.body: `budgetedList` extracts `limit` (1..25) and `offset`, slices the page, and sets `Truncated` plus a caller-supplied hint template when the page is short of the total, logging `mcp.budget.truncated` for tuning. Verified live: `cerberus_connector_list` returned `"count":9,"total":9`. The tuning review CW-20260909-0009 deliberately kept the shared library's cap rather than raising it, on the grounds that offset paging recovers the rest. No other surface has any response bound — the socket's only limit is a 10MB read cap and the console's a 1MB request-body cap. Note also what "budget" means here: `budgetedList` bounds the *item count*, not the payload. `cerberus_connector_list` returns 9 of 9 items untruncated and roughly 25KB of JSON, because each item carries every operation's full input schema. A caller can be handed an arbitrarily large response as long as it is few enough rows.

records.name: Socket NDJSON progress stream
records.summary: X-Cerberus-Progress: 1 turns a socket call into an application/x-ndjson stream of notification/result/error envelopes, which reaches MCP hosts and is dropped for CLI and console callers.
records.confidence_label: Plumbing traced end to end in source; not observed on the wire because every streaming route is a mutating operation
records.body: `external_connector_service.go` and the resource runtime emit `gmcp.NotifyMessage` / `gmcp.NotifyProgress`. `handleStream` installs a `gmcp.WithNotifier` context that writes each notification as an NDJSON envelope, then the result. `SocketClient.doJSONStream` sets the header unconditionally and, on receiving a notification envelope, calls `gmcp.Notify(ctx, *env.Notification)` — re-emitting into whatever notifier the caller's context carries. For `cerberus mcp` that is the MCP host's notifier, so an agent sees progress. For a CLI command or a console handler the context has no notifier and the notification is discarded. Used by deploy, apply, sync, pipeline run, connector operations and the entire plugin lifecycle.

records.name: Connector discovery on every surface
records.summary: connectors list/describe is the one capability that is mechanical on all five surfaces, which is why it is authoritative for what a connector can do — and why the MCP gap is visible from inside MCP.
records.confidence_label: Run live on all of CLI, socket, console HTTP and MCP during this audit
records.body:
`pkg/connector.DefinitionFromManifest` converts plugin and runtime metadata into the one discovery shape CLI, API and MCP share, so all five surfaces report the same operations, input schemas, `destructive` and `supports_dry` flags. Verified live on four of them during this audit, with identical operation lists. Two problems show up only when you compare surfaces. First, every plugin operation's `examples` field names `cerberus connectors plugin managed exec <id> <op>` — so an agent calling `cerberus_connector_describe azure` is told to run a CLI command, because there is no MCP tool to name instead. Second, `redact.Text` corrupts the ContextForge token description in transit on all four surfaces, and differently on the older console binary than on the current one.

Since PR #54 the ssh and docker operation schemas advertise exactly what enforcement accepts: ssh operations require `id` and add `command`, `local_path` and `remote_path` where they apply, and docker operations take `resource`, the container keys, `id` and `lines`, with no target key anywhere. `TestDiscoverySchemasMatchEnforcement` fails in either direction of drift, and `ManifestFromDefinition` carries the same schemas into generated plugin manifests. The connector-level config fields (`host`, `key_file` and so on) still describe what a resource declares.

records.confidence_label: internal/infra/deploy.go, definition.go, internal/webui/infra.go and TestWebDeploymentRunConfirmsAgainstThePlan read after PR #63; confirm dialog driven in headless Chrome

records.body:
`POST /api/deployments/{id}/run` runs a profile through `cerbapi.RunDeploymentProfile`, which gates on the `infra` contract's `run_profile` (exec) and then calls `infra.RunDeployment`.

The console first fetches `GET /api/deployments/{id}/plan`. `infra.PlanDeployment` computes the exact steps with the Vercel token named as `VERCEL_TOKEN=<vercel token>`, never by value, and the confirm dialog lists every command and the directory it runs in (Decision 3). Only confirming sends `acknowledged: true`, and a request without it gets 409. The run executes that plan and records the displayed command, which since PR #63 keeps the Vercel token out of `steps[].command`, where only the regex net used to stand between it and the response. The token reaches the child only as `VERCEL_TOKEN` in its environment: it used to be passed as `--token` in argv and a `/bin/sh -lc` string, readable by every local user through `ps`, and the old `--token [vercel token]` display came back from the regex net as `[REDACTED] token]`.

The hardcoded suggestion of another user's site path, and the suggestions feature it was the only user of, were removed in the same PR.

`cerberus pipeline run <id>` runs the whole pipeline: levels in dependency order, stages within a level in parallel, first error wins, then reverse-order rollback of completed stages. `POST /pipelines/{id}/run` on the socket supports the NDJSON progress stream; `POST /api/pipelines/{id}/run` in the console is guarded by the per-process action token; `cerberus_pipeline_run` exposes it to MCP with `pipeline_id` as its only required argument.

The flag set is the finding. `cerberus pipeline run --help` registers no flags at all beyond `--help` — no `--ack`, no `--dry-run`, no `--yes` — while the actions it drives include `stop` on a production resource and `shell`, which is `sh -c` with the operator's environment. Every comparable verb in the admin lane requires `--ack`. `data.destructive` is set true here because the operation is destructive in fact; nothing in the code marks it so.

Deliberately not executed during a read-only audit, and there is nothing to execute: the live config declares no pipelines.

Since PR #49 the MCP tool `cerberus_pipeline_run` carries `DestructiveHint: true`, because a stage can be `sh -c`. That is a hint to the MCP client, not a gate. The CLI, socket and console still take no acknowledgment and offer no dry run (CERB-GAP-733).

records.body:
Verified live on 2026-09-17:

    {
      "launchd_managed": true,
      "origin": "launchd",
      "pid": 8188,
      "pid_source": "pidfile",
      "running": true,
      "socket_path": "~/.cerberus/cerberus.sock",
      "socket_present": true,
      "socket_ready": true
    }

Three of those fields answer questions no other command does. `origin` and `launchd_managed` separate a launchd-owned daemon from a manually started one, which is the distinction `resource doctor`'s rogue-daemon check is built on. `pid_source` says whether the PID came from the pidfile or from a process scan, so a stale pidfile is visible rather than trusted. And `socket_present` and `socket_ready` are separate, so a leftover socket inode is distinguishable from a daemon that is accepting connections — which is exactly the state in which every other command's in-process fallback fires.

JSON only; there is no table renderer. It is CLI-only: no socket route, no MCP tool, no console view, which is correct for a command whose job is to work when the socket does not.

records.name: cerberus daemon start / stop / restart
records.summary: Starts, stops and atomically restarts the daemon, forking to background by default, with a launchd-managed guard that has to be bypassed explicitly.
records.confidence_label: Source and help text read in full; deliberately not executed — stopping the daemon that serves this audit was out of scope

relationships.note: the lifecycle verbs of the daemon capability
these are the commands that end degraded mode
the daemon is launchd-managed but not Cerberus-managed on this machine
a started daemon inherits launchd's minimal PATH

records.body:
`cerberus daemon` with no subcommand is `daemon start`. It forks to background unless `--foreground` is passed, which is how the launch agent runs it (`ProgramArguments` is `[cerberus, daemon, --foreground]`). `daemon stop` stops the running daemon; `daemon restart` is described in the help as an "atomic stop-then-start with single-daemon invariant", and `--replace` on `start` routes through that same sequence.

Two flags carry policy rather than convenience. `--override-launchd` exists to "bypass the launchd-managed guard and route the manual path", and its own help marks it debugging-only — so the normal path refuses to hand-manage a daemon launchd owns, and the escape hatch is named loudly enough to show up in shell history. The single-daemon invariant is what makes `restart` safe to issue rather than a stop-then-start race.

CLI-only and correctly so: a socket route to stop the daemon would die on its own EOF, which is the same reasoning as CERB-DEC-163.

Unverified: these were not run. On this machine the daemon is launchd-managed with `KeepAlive`, and stopping it mid-audit would have taken every other surface with it.

records.body:
`cerberus dns create` and `cerberus dns delete` are registered cobra commands whose `RunE` is a one-liner returning `ncconn.ErrUnsafePerRecordWrite`, before any connector or HTTP client is built. Their `Short` is "Disabled: unsafe per-record Namecheap writes". `cerberus_dns_create` and `cerberus_dns_delete` are registered MCP tools whose descriptions say the same and point at `cerberus_set_dns_record_set`. The refusal text is the guidance:

    namecheap per-record create/delete is disabled: getHosts can omit existing
    records and setHosts replaces the entire zone, risking silent data loss;
    use the Namecheap dashboard or explicit set_dns_record_set
    (MCP: cerberus_set_dns_record_set) with a complete authoritative record set
    and email_type

They earn a record because they are reachable, not because they work. An agent enumerating MCP tools finds `cerberus_dns_create`, and a catalog that lists only the verbs that do something leaves it looking like an uncatalogued capability rather than a deliberate tombstone.

One loose end: `dnsCreateCmd` and `dnsDeleteCmd` still register `--ack`, `--type`, `--value` and friends in `init()`, on commands that can never use them. `cobra.ExactArgs` also fires before `RunE`, so `cerberus dns create` with no argument prints usage rather than the explanation — the refusal is only reached once you have supplied arguments for a write that will never happen.

Since the P1-3 branch the two stub tools have contracts of their own, `namecheap.DisabledOperations()` (create a write, delete destructive), so their MCP hints are derived like every other tool's. Nothing dispatches those operations: the admin lane still refuses them before the contract gate.

**Removed from the binary 2026-09-25.** The disabled `cerberus dns create`/`delete` commands and the `cerberus_dns_create`/`cerberus_dns_delete` tombstone tools went with the built-in, with no tombstones, by operator decision. The refusal itself remains: the namecheap plugin does not declare the operations, so the contract gate refuses them, and the plugin refuses the tool names directly, coded `invalid_args`, pointing at `set_dns_record_set`.

data.invocation: cerberus dns create <domain> | cerberus dns delete <domain> <record-id> | MCP cerberus_dns_create | MCP cerberus_dns_delete

records.name: cerberus status
records.summary: Shows, read-only and on one screen, the state an operator now needs at a glance: daemon, posture, the principal the daemon sees, plugins awaiting review, the audit chain, and running web consoles.
records.confidence_label: unit-tested per part and run against a scratch daemon and console on a scratch HOME
records.body:
`cerberus status` gathers what the commands that own each piece already
know and prints one line each. Nothing is changed, and a part that cannot be
read shows as unavailable while the rest still prints.

- **daemon** comes from `cerberus daemon status`.
- **posture** is the applied posture from the hash-checked policy snapshot: `secure`, `permissive`, or the global posture with its per-target rules (P2-5). A snapshot that fails its check reads as secure.
- **you** is the principal the daemon gives this caller (`GET /whoami`), with
  its verified uid.
- **plugins** counts the managed plugins the daemon has, and names the ones
  still `review_pending`.
- **audit** is the result of `audit.Verify` over every month file and the last
  record's time. A broken chain reads `NOT INTACT` and points at
  `cerberus audit verify`.
- **web** lists each console whose login key file is under `~/.cerberus/web`.
  Only the file's address is read, never its key, and the address is probed,
  because a console that crashed leaves its file behind.

The daemon is asked only when its socket answers, so a stopped daemon is one
line and not a page of dial warnings. `-o json` gives the same report as data.

relationships.note: a verb of the CLI
the you line is whoami's daemon view
reports the consoles P2-2's login key files name

records.name: cerberus policy explain
records.summary: Prints the policy decision for an operation against a target and a principal kind, and every rule that matched, from the applied snapshot or the working files.
records.confidence_label: run on the P2-4 branch against a labelled scratch config; TestPolicyExplain covers a local-dev human, an ad hoc agent and the refusals

relationships.note: a verb of the CLI
explains the engine that record now says exists in shadow

records.body: `cerberus policy explain local.deploy --target notes-api --as agent` resolves the operation from the declared definitions, which include the daemon's plugins when it is up. It labels the target from the registered resource (or `--adhoc`) and prints the decision, whether it would be blocked once enforced, which policy decided (the applied snapshot's hash, the baseline, or the baseline after a hash mismatch) and every matched rule with its decision and reason. `--working` evaluates the unapplied working files instead, so a change can be checked before `apply`. The principal kind defaults to how the terminal is classified. It also prints the posture the snapshot declares, which is reserved for P2-5 and not evaluated.

records.name: cerberus policy apply
records.summary: Makes the working policy files the applied snapshot, on a TTY only: shows every sampled decision that changes, and writes applied.yaml and its hash after a typed confirmation, recorded as an admin event.
records.confidence_label: run over a pty on the P2-4 branch (wrong confirmation, right one, no-change, tampered snapshot); TestPolicyApply covers the non-TTY refusal, the typed confirmation and invalid working files

relationships.note: a verb of the CLI
the apply is itself an admin audit event

records.body: `cerberus policy apply` loads `~/.cerberus/policy/*.yaml` and `providers/*.yaml` and refuses if any has problems. It samples every declared operation against every registered resource of its connector, plus an unregistered and an ad hoc target, for a human, an agent and automation, and prints the decisions that flip between the applied snapshot and the working files. It applies only when the operator types `apply <shorthash>`, which binds the confirmation to the snapshot shown. `cerbapi.ApplyPolicy` records an `admin` intent before writing, so an unwritable log applies nothing, then writes `applied.yaml` and `applied.sha256`. It is in-process only and refused from any other surface: policy never changes through the socket, the web console or MCP (Decision 10). The daemon's decision point notices the new snapshot on its next decision.

records.name: cerberus policy report
records.summary: Summarizes the operations shadow-mode policy would have blocked, from the decisions recorded in the audit log, grouped by operation, target, principal kind and deciding rule.
records.confidence_label: run on the P2-4 branch against a scratch audit log; TestPolicyReportGroupsWouldBlock covers the grouping

relationships.note: a verb of the CLI
the to-do list before P3 enforces

records.body: `cerberus policy report` reads the audit log directly and counts the intents whose recorded policy decision has `would_block`, out of all decided ones. It groups them by operation, target (resource or kind, marked ad hoc or unlabeled), principal kind, decision and the deciding rule, most frequent first, with the last time each was seen. It is the operator's list of what to label, write a rule for or call differently before P3 turns enforcement on.

records.name: cerberus approvals list
records.summary: Lists approval requests newest first, with status, operation, target labels, requester and channel, from the daemon's broker or, with the daemon down, the store read directly.
records.confidence_label: run on the P3-1 branch; TestApprovalsListAndShowFromTheStore covers the no-daemon path, TestApprovalsOverTheSocket the daemon's routes

relationships.note: a verb of the CLI
shows the requests the enforcement path asks for

records.body: `cerberus approvals list` asks the daemon (`GET /approvals`) and, when the daemon is not running, opens `~/.cerberus/approvals` itself and folds the store, saying which it read. Each row names the approval id, its status as it reads now (a pending or approved one past its expiry reads expired before the sweeper writes it down), the operation, the target with its env/owner/admin labels, who asked (kind, channel and client), the channel it must be met through and its expiry. Problems the fold found in the store are printed as warnings. It is a read: nothing here decides an approval.

records.name: cerberus approvals show
records.summary: Shows one approval request: what is to be approved, why (the rule and its reason), how it must be met, its decision, use or revocation, and the command that decides it while it is pending.
records.confidence_label: run on the P3-1 branch; TestApprovalsListAndShowFromTheStore covers the no-daemon path, TestApprovalsOverTheSocket the daemon's routes

relationships.note: a verb of the CLI
shows the requests the enforcement path asks for

records.body: `cerberus approvals show <id>` prints one approval as `approvals list` reads it: the operation and effect, the labelled target, the requester and when, the deciding rule and its reason, the channel, scope and expiry, the plan hash once P3-2 records one, the decision with the decider and the enrolled key it used, and when it was consumed (with the operation id) or revoked. A pending approval ends with the command that decides it, `cerberus approvals approve <id>`, which arrives with P3-4.

records.name: cerberus posture
records.summary: Shows the applied posture and what it relaxes, and changes it on a terminal through the policy apply path: the global posture for the host-wide switches, or a scoped posture rule for policy evaluation.
records.confidence_label: tested against a temp policy store: terminal-only, flips shown, typed confirmation, audit record, refusals; host-wide switches wired in P2-5d/e
records.body:
`cerberus posture show` prints the applied posture (from the hash-checked snapshot), the host-wide switches the global posture sets, the posture rules, and what never relaxes: the audit log, credential redaction, the `--ack` gate and the deny on a target labeled `admin: owner`.

`cerberus posture set <secure|permissive> [--scope key=value ...]` sets the global posture, or with `--scope` adds or replaces a posture rule; `cerberus posture reset [--scope ...]` returns to secure or removes one rule. Both run only on an interactive terminal. They write `~/.cerberus/policy/posture.yaml`, the working file the command owns, and apply through the `policy apply` path: the host-wide switches that change, the sampled decisions that flip, a typed confirmation, an `admin` audit record, and the snapshot hash checked on load. Nothing is written before the confirmation, and a failed apply puts the file back.

They refuse while another working file declares a posture, while the working files have unapplied changes (a posture change would otherwise carry them in unseen), and over a snapshot that fails its hash check. A scoped rule changes only policy evaluation, and a permissive one reaches only targets whose env and owner are declared.
